# Addenda Register — PSD Active Day App

Decisions **not** dictated by [`fds.md`](../../fds.md). Numbering is independent of the FDS's own
section numbers and of its `DC-001…DC-006` decision contexts, so the base spec stays stable and
this register appends forever.

Format and discipline: [`AGENTS-decisions.md`](../../AGENTS-decisions.md). Write the entry **in
the same change that makes the decision**.

---

## Supersession index

**Maintained by ADR-139. Append a row in the same change that renames or removes something an
earlier ADR named by hand** — the register is append-only, so an entry is never edited to keep
up with the code, and without this table a reader greps a name out of a decision and finds
nothing. A row here is not a correction of the old ADR: the old ADR was right on its date.

---

### ADR-001 — Adopt `GREENFIELD.md` as `AGENTS.md` with a sectioned documentation architecture

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** gap — the FDS specifies the product, not the engineering discipline
- **Decision:** The template is instantiated as a top-level `AGENTS.md` index plus five focused
  section files (`-decisions`, `-testing`, `-database`, `-function-design`, `-frontend`,
  `-workflow`). `GREENFIELD.md` is kept unmodified as the upstream template and is explicitly
  **not** operative.
- **Why:** The template itself (§0) prescribes an index + section files as a day-one decision,
  because retrofitting the split is churn. Agents `grep` one focused file instead of loading a
  16 KB corpus. Keeping the template unmodified preserves its reusability for other projects.
- **Impact:** `AGENTS.md` is the operative standard and wins over `GREENFIELD.md` on conflict.
  Every placeholder is replaced by a concrete stack choice (ADR-002). New standards go in the
  matching section file, not in the index.

### ADR-002 — Stack: TypeScript + Hono + Drizzle + PostgreSQL + React/Vite, npm workspaces

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** gap — the FDS is implementation-agnostic
- **Decision:** One language (TypeScript, ESM, strict) across `apps/api` (Hono 4 + Drizzle ORM +
  PostgreSQL), `apps/web` (React 19 + Vite 7 + React Router 7) and `packages/contracts` (Zod
  schemas shared by both), in an npm workspace.
- **Why:** Hono exposes `app.request()`, so integration tests exercise the real router with no
  listening socket — exactly the entrypoint discipline `AGENTS-testing.md` requires. Drizzle
  gives the single property→column mapping that `AGENTS-database.md` mandates. One package
  manager and one test runner (Vitest) across all three workspaces keeps the toolchain
  consistent rather than retrofitted.
- **Impact:** A field renamed in `@psd/contracts` is a compile error on both sides. Adding a
  second ORM, a hand-written mapper, or a second package manager is a standards violation.

### ADR-003 — PGlite for dev/test, `pg` for deployment, behind one driver switch

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** gap — the FDS names no database
- **Decision:** `DATABASE_DRIVER=pglite` (default) runs PostgreSQL compiled to WASM in-process,
  persisted at `PGLITE_DATA_DIR` for dev and `memory://` for tests.
  `DATABASE_DRIVER=postgres` uses node-postgres against a deployed server. Schema, migrations
  and repositories are byte-identical across both.
- **Why:** `AGENTS-testing.md` forbids mocking the data-access layer, so tests need a real
  Postgres engine — including partial unique indexes, `ON CONFLICT`, JSONB and
  `lower()` expression indexes, all of which this schema depends on. PGlite is the real Postgres
  source, so no engine-behaviour gap is introduced, and a contributor goes from clone to a
  passing suite with `npm install` alone (no Docker, no local server).
- **Impact:** Every test gets its own migrated in-memory database — parallel-safe by
  construction. Production readiness requires only `DATABASE_URL`. PGlite is single-connection,
  so the API must not assume a connection pool.

### ADR-004 — Session model: opaque token cookie, soft-invalidated, one row per sign-in

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §2 (actor notation), F3/F19 long-lived sessions
- **Decision:** A `session` table holds an opaque 256-bit token, exactly one non-null actor FK
  (`participant_id` | `facilitator_id` | `superadmin_id`), a `valid_until` TTL
  (`SESSION_TTL_DAYS`, default 30) and a nullable `expires_at` used for sign-out. The cookie is
  `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` when `COOKIE_SECURE=true`.
- **Why:** The FDS asks for long-lived cookie sessions but stores PINs in plaintext by directive
  (§9.6), so the cookie must never carry credentials — an opaque server-side token keeps the PIN
  out of the browser. A DB row lets a session be invalidated and lets `last_seen_at` be
  maintained (`fds.md` §2.1).
- **Impact:** Active = `expires_at IS NULL AND valid_until > now()`; sign-out sets `expires_at`
  (soft delete, per `AGENTS-database.md` §3). A CHECK constraint enforces exactly one actor FK,
  so an actor column is never a sentinel.

### ADR-005 — Match roster snapshot for point attribution

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §2.6 `#obj-tournamentmatch`, §4.2.12 (snapshot integrity), F23
- **Decision:** On completion a match snapshots both rosters into
  `team_a_roster_snapshot` / `team_b_roster_snapshot` (JSONB array of
  `{participantId, nickname, clusterCode}`), and cluster/individual tournament points are
  attributed from those snapshots.
- **Why:** The FDS says completing a match makes "team members' clusters gain points" but does
  not say *which* members — live membership or membership at completion. Live membership would
  let a participant switch teams after a match and silently move historical points between
  clusters, contradicting §4.2.12. Snapshotting is the pattern the spec already applies to
  activity names, round numbers and point values.
- **Impact:** Two JSONB columns on `tournament_match`, written only at completion. Voiding,
  unvoiding and superadmin winner edits re-use the stored rosters, so a leaderboard recompute is
  deterministic and independent of later roster churn.

### ADR-006 — Leaderboard is computed on read by one set-based SQL query

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md F16/F49 `#feat-clusterleaderboard`, "real-time"
- **Decision:** No materialised totals table. Cluster standings, top-10 individuals and
  participant totals come from a single analytical SQL statement over `fringe_scan` and
  `tournament_match`, wrapped in `db/entities/leaderboard.ts`.
- **Why:** Event scale is 150–300 participants for one day — thousands of rows, not millions.
  Void/unvoid and winner edits must make the leaderboard "recompute" (F44 acceptance criteria);
  with a cached total, every correction path becomes an invalidation bug. Computing on read
  makes correctness the default.
- **Impact:** The one deliberate exception to "no raw SQL" in `AGENTS-database.md` §1, confined
  to one commented repository function. If the event ever outgrows it, add a cache *behind* that
  function — the call sites do not change.

### ADR-007 — Cluster display names equal their codes

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §2.2 `#obj-cluster`
- **Decision:** The 16 seeded clusters use their code as `display_name` (`BP`, `PSC Sect`, …).
- **Why:** The FDS fixes the codes but supplies no expansions. Inventing full agency names risks
  shipping incorrect organisational copy to the people who work there; the codes are what staff
  recognise on the day.
- **Impact:** One `UPDATE` in a future migration is enough if the organisers supply official
  names. The wire contract already carries `displayName` separately from `code`, so no client
  change would be needed.

### ADR-008 — Avatar sprites are generated SVG files committed to the repo

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md DC-006, A5 (10 static sprites, 5 per gender)
- **Decision:** `apps/web/scripts/generate-avatar-sprites.mjs` emits ten deterministic pixel-art
  SVGs to `apps/web/public/avatars/{male,female}-{1..5}.svg`; both the generator and its output
  are committed. Components reference them by URL, never by runtime drawing.
- **Why:** A5 requires static shipped assets. SVG keeps them crisp on any DPI at ~2 KB each,
  and a committed generator makes the palette auditable and regenerable rather than a binary
  blob nobody can change.
- **Impact:** Changing the art is a script edit plus a regenerated commit. The avatar URL helper
  lives in one place so §5.5 (participant surfaces only) stays enforceable by grep.

### ADR-009 — Offline scan queue: client-minted UUID, server first-write-wins, round trusted

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md DC-004, F27, F51, §4.2.8/§4.2.11
- **Decision:** The scanner mints `clientScanUuid` (UUIDv7) **before** attempting the network
  call and stores the scan in `localStorage` through `lib/offline/scanQueue.ts`. The server
  treats `client_scan_uuid` as the idempotency key (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, then re-read and
  return the existing row with `200`), and honours the client's `roundId` even if that round has
  since closed. A `(participant, round)` collision is first-write-wins and returns the winning
  row, not an error.
- **Why:** Beach connectivity means the same scan may be POSTed several times from several tabs.
  Deduplicating on a client-minted id is the only way a retry is provably harmless. Re-deriving
  the round server-side at sync time would attribute a 10:05 scan to whatever round is open at
  11:40 — the opposite of the spec's historical-fidelity rule.
- **Impact:** A facilitator with a stale queue can write scans into a closed round; this is
  intended and audited via `scanned_at` ≫ `client_timestamp`. Superadmins correct mistakes by
  voiding, which is reversible and always leaves a `VoidAuditEntry`.

### ADR-010 — Standards are machine-enforced, not just documented

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** gap — `GREENFIELD.md` states the rules, nothing checks them
- **Decision:** `npm run lint` encodes the numeric function-design limits (ESLint 9 flat config:
  `max-lines` 800, `max-lines-per-function` 50, `max-depth` 3, `max-params` 3, `complexity` 12),
  and `npm run standards` (`scripts/check-standards.mjs`) checks the structural rules a linter
  cannot see: no `lib/api` import inside `components/`, no array-logic inside a JSX `return`,
  `data-testid` on interactive elements, no hand-written row mappers, UUIDs minted only in
  `db/ids.ts`, snapshot+migration twins in the same change, no avatars on admin surfaces.
  `npm run verify` chains typecheck + lint + standards + suites and is the merge gate.
- **Why:** A convention nothing checks decays within weeks, and "the reviewer will catch it" is
  not a mechanism. Each check corresponds to a rule that cost real rework in the template's
  source project.
- **Impact:** Violations fail the build with the file, line and the rule's rationale. Adding a
  standard to `AGENTS*.md` should come with its check; if a rule genuinely cannot be checked,
  say so where it is written.

### ADR-011 — Teams are disbanded softly, with partial unique indexes

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §3.1 (Team state machine), F13, AGENTS-database.md (no hard deletes)
- **Decision:** Disbanding sets `team.disbanded_at` instead of deleting the row. Uniqueness of
  `team_name` and `join_code` is enforced by partial indexes `WHERE disbanded_at IS NULL`, and
  every read path filters disbanded teams out.
- **Why:** Matches already played reference the team, and the FDS requires their results to stay
  on the feed and in the leaderboards. A deleted row would either break those references or
  force a second archive table.
- **Impact:** A disbanded team's name and join code become available again immediately, which is
  what organisers expect when a team is recreated after a mistake.

### ADR-012 — `max-lines-per-function` applies to `.ts`, not `.tsx`

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** AGENTS-function-design.md, eslint.config.js
- **Decision:** The 50-line function limit is enforced on `**/*.ts` only. Components in `.tsx`
  are bounded by `max-lines` (800) and by the JSX-purity and no-API-in-component checks instead.
- **Why:** A page component is one declarative tree; splitting it at 50 lines produces fragments
  that exist only to satisfy a counter, and hides the shape of the surface being rendered. The
  rule's real target — branching logic — is already banned from JSX by `npm run standards`.
- **Impact:** Logic must move into hooks to grow, which is the intended pressure. A `.tsx` file
  that needs a long function for anything other than markup is a code smell the reviewer sees.

### ADR-013 — 100% coverage with deletion, not ignore comments

- **Status:** Accepted — **thresholds superseded by ADR-080**, exclusion list by ADR-049; the
  deletion-over-suppression method stands. See the supersession index at the top of this file.
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** AGENTS-testing.md, both `vitest.config.ts` files
- **Decision:** Statements, branches, functions and lines are all gated at 100% for `apps/api`
  and `apps/web`. Only browser/CLI entrypoints are excluded (`apps/api/src/index.ts`,
  `apps/api/src/db/migrate-cli.ts`, `apps/web/src/main.tsx`). Unreachable defensive arms are
  **deleted** with the guaranteeing constraint cited in a comment — never suppressed with
  `/* v8 ignore */`. Narrowing lives in `apps/api/src/db/rows.ts`, `apps/web/src/lib/required.ts`
  and `useRouteId.ts` so it is tested once rather than re-implemented per call site.
- **Why:** A threshold below 100% is a budget for untested code and drifts downward. Forcing the
  question "what guarantees this arm is unreachable?" removed real dead code from both apps.
- **Impact:** `try/catch/finally` in hooks is avoided because v8 counts the continuation as an
  extra branch; `useAction.ts` uses an `attempt()` helper instead.

### ADR-014 — Sentosa motif sprites: generated, committed, decorative and participant-only

- **Status:** Accepted — sprite inventory superseded by ADR-068
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §5.5, DC-006, AGENTS-frontend.md §4, docs/screenshot/
- **Decision:** `apps/web/scripts/generate-motif-sprites.mjs` emits eighteen pixel-art SVGs to
  `apps/web/public/motifs/` (the PSD roundel, kueh lapis, Merlion, monorail, palm, wave tile,
  sun, beach ball, trophy, coin, tick stamp, crab, shell, starfish, sandcastle, flag, QR badge,
  trainer face). The roundel is traced from `images/ingest/PSD_logo-01-320x320.png` — navy
  disc, three white word-bars, crimson rule — and leads the participant title plate.
  Square sprites are rendered by `components/participant/PixelMotif.tsx`, which is always
  `aria-hidden` with an empty `alt`; the wide tiles are CSS background images in `gameboy.css`.
  Decoration never carries meaning: every heading, tab and row keeps its text.
- **Why:** The ideation screenshots set a scene — sea, sand, palms, a title plate — that plain
  CSS gradients cannot reach, and the FDS asks the participant app to read as a handheld game.
  Generating the art keeps it auditable and editable in a diff instead of being an opaque blob.
- **Impact:** `npm run motifs --workspace @psd/web` regenerates the set;
  `docs/screenshot/motif-sheet.png` is a render of the shipped sprites for reviewers. The scene (sun,
  monorail, palms) is gated to ≥760px because the panels cover it on a handset, and every
  animation is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`. `npm run standards` fails if a
  facilitator or superadmin surface imports `components/participant/` or uses a `gb-*` class,
  so the spartan console stays spartan.

### ADR-015 — The session cookie's attributes are configuration, and sign-in waits for it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-004, fds.md F1/F3/F30/F42, reported bug: "I can't log in after signing up"
- **Decision:** Two changes, one per side of the wire.
  1. `COOKIE_SAMESITE` (`Lax` default) and `COOKIE_PARTITIONED` join `COOKIE_SECURE` in
     `env.ts`, and the schema **refuses to boot** on `SameSite=None` or `Partitioned` without
     `Secure`. `endSession` repeats the same attributes so the browser actually drops the
     cookie.
  2. `SessionState.refresh()` resolves with the session it read, and every sign-in surface
     awaits it before navigating. A `null` result means the browser did not keep the cookie,
     and the surface says so (`messages.sessionNotStored`) instead of bouncing the participant
     back to an empty form.
- **Why:** Served inside another page — a preview iframe, an intranet portal — a `SameSite=Lax`
  cookie is cross-site: the browser stores nothing, every guarded route 401s, and sign-up looks
  like it silently failed. That is exactly what was reported, and three abandoned accounts in
  the dev database matched it. The old code also navigated before the session was confirmed, so
  the only feedback was a redirect with no message.
- **Impact:** A first-party deployment keeps the defaults. An embedded one sets
  `COOKIE_SAMESITE=None`, `COOKIE_SECURE=true`, `COOKIE_PARTITIONED=true` (documented in
  `.env.example`). `apps/api/src/tests/session-cookie.test.ts` pins the emitted attributes and
  `apps/web/src/acceptance/session-handoff.test.tsx` pins the hand-off, including the
  cookie-refused path, with latency in the stub so the race cannot hide.

### ADR-016 — The session token also travels as a bearer credential

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-004, ADR-015, fds.md §3 "long-lived cookie sessions", reported bug:
  "sign-in still fails inside the preview"
- **Decision:** The opaque session token stays the only credential, but it now has two carriers.
  The four sign-in/sign-up responses return `sessionToken` alongside the `Set-Cookie`;
  `apps/web/src/lib/session/tokenStore.ts` keeps it (`psd.sessionToken.v1`, in-memory when
  storage throws) and `lib/api/client.ts` attaches `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to every
  request. On the API, `readSessionToken(c)` reads the cookie **first** and falls back to the
  header, so nothing changes for a first-party browser. Sign-out clears both.
- **Why:** ADR-015 was necessary but not sufficient. With `SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned`
  on the wire — verified in the response headers — the embedded browser still kept no cookie,
  so the POST succeeded and the very next `GET /api/auth/session` came back signed out. A
  cookie the embedder refuses to store cannot be fixed with more cookie attributes; the
  credential needs a carrier the page itself controls. "Open it in a real tab" is not a fix.
- **Rejected:** putting the token in the URL (it leaks through history, logs and referrers);
  `postMessage` to a parent frame (the app must work without a co-operating embedder);
  dropping cookies entirely (a first-party install would lose HttpOnly protection for free).
- **Impact:** The token is readable by scripts on the page, which is the cost of working inside
  a frame; it stays opaque, server-side-revocable, and scoped to one actor by
  `ck_session_one_actor`. `scripts/check-standards.mjs` `storage-ownership` now sanctions two
  storage owners (the scan queue and the token store) and no others.
  `apps/api/src/tests/session-cookie.test.ts` covers bearer-only auth, a forged token, a
  non-bearer scheme, cookie-wins-over-header, and bearer sign-out;
  `apps/web/src/acceptance/session-handoff.test.tsx` drives the real router through a
  cookie-refusing browser and asserts the participant still lands on their badge.

### ADR-017 — The session credential escalates through carriers until one arrives

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-004, ADR-015, ADR-016 (extends it), reported bug: "sign-in still fails in
  the preview" (third report)
- **Decision:** One opaque token, four carriers, tried in a fixed order by the API —
  `psd_session` cookie, then the `x-psd-session` header, then `Authorization: Bearer`, then the
  `session_token` query parameter. The client sends the header pair by default; on a `401`
  while it is holding a token it retries the same request **once** through the query string,
  and if that succeeds it records the carrier (`psd.sessionCarrier.v1`) and uses it from then
  on. A `401` that survives the retry is a real signed-out answer and is reported as one.
- **Why:** ADR-016 assumed the only hostile link was the cookie jar. It is not: an intermediary
  can also rewrite or drop request headers, and `Authorization` in particular is the header
  proxies most often claim for themselves. Each fix so far has been one carrier deep, and the
  failure looks identical from the participant's side every time — signed in, then instantly
  signed out. A ladder ends the category instead of the instance.
- **Rejected:** putting the token in the URL unconditionally (it lands in every access log for
  every request, not just the rescue path); asking the operator to configure the carrier (the
  people running this are on a beach, and the app can find out by itself in one round trip).
- **Impact:** A first-party deployment never leaves the first rung: the cookie is found and
  nothing else is read. The query-string rung costs one extra request, once per browser, and
  only after a 401. `LOG_AUTH_CARRIER=true` prints which carriers reached the API and what the
  answer was — presence only, never the token — so the next "it still doesn't work" is one log
  line to diagnose rather than another guess. Covered in
  `apps/api/src/tests/session-cookie.test.ts` (all four carriers, precedence, empty values) and
  `apps/web/src/lib/api/client.test.ts` (header by default, escalation, the carrier is
  remembered, a genuine 401 stays a 401).

### ADR-018 — Sprite URLs carry a content stamp

- **Status:** Superseded by ADR-067
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-008, ADR-014, reported bug: "I don't see the psd motif being updated"
- **Decision:** `npm run motifs --workspace @psd/web` hashes the grids, writes the first eight
  hex digits to the generated `src/lib/motifVersion.ts`, appends `?v=<hash>` in `motifUrl()`,
  and rewrites the `url('/motifs/*.svg')` references in `gameboy.css` to match. Redrawing a
  sprite therefore changes its URL everywhere it is used.
- **Why:** Sprite filenames are stable by design — they are readable and referenced from CSS —
  so a redrawn motif reuses an URL a browser or an intermediate cache already has an answer
  for. The PSD mark was replaced twice and kept rendering as its previous version, which reads
  as "the change did not ship".
- **Impact:** One generated module joins the committed output; the generator is still the only
  thing that writes it, and the sprite workflow is unchanged (edit the ASCII grid, regenerate).
  `PixelMotif.test.tsx` asserts the stamp is on the URL and that it is a content hash.

### ADR-019 — Every surface is a URL, and the last one is remembered

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-009, fds.md §5.1–§5.4 (60 surfaces), reported bug: "the URL always stays
  at / — a reload loses the page I was on"
- **Decision:** Two parts.
  1. **Addressability stands as built and is now pinned by a test.** All 60 surfaces are
     routes under `BrowserRouter` — `/home`, `/board`, `/teams/:teamId`, `/staff/court/:courtId`,
     `/admin/participants/:participantId`, and so on — reached with `Link`/`NavLink`, including
     the console tabs. Nothing is a mode flag inside another page, so every page and every tab
     can be linked, bookmarked and reloaded.
  2. **The current path is remembered** (`psd.lastPath.v1`, written as it changes while signed
     in) and restored **once**, on boot, **only** when the app starts at `/` with a live
     session. Signing out forgets it. `useLocationMemory` does both.
- **Why:** The URL is only half the mechanism — something has to still be holding it. Two
  things on event day are not: a phone that drops the tab under memory pressure reopens the
  app at its start URL, and an embedded frame is re-mounted at its `src` by the page around
  it. Both land on `/`, which is how a facilitator loses the court they were scoring. Guards
  are unaffected: whatever is restored still has to pass `RequireActor`.
- **Rejected:** `HashRouter` (it makes every URL uglier to solve nothing — a container that
  re-mounts at `src` discards the fragment too); restoring from any path rather than only `/`
  (then an in-app visit to the front door would bounce back, and the actor could not leave).
- **Impact:** `localStorage` now has exactly **one** owner, `lib/storage/localStore.ts`, with
  three key-owning modules on top of it (`scanQueue`, `tokenStore`, `locationStore`); the
  standards rule was narrowed to match. Storage is the source of truth whenever it works —
  memory holds a key only while the store is refusing it, so clearing site data really clears.
  A queued scan now also survives a device whose storage throws, which it did not before.
  Deployment note: any static host must rewrite unknown paths to `index.html`; the dev server
  and `vite preview` already do. Covered by `src/acceptance/location-memory.test.tsx`
  (restore, record-as-you-go, signed-out visitor, nothing remembered, no hijack of a
  deliberate visit to `/`, sign-out forgets).

### ADR-020 — Avatars are 32×32 persona portraits, not recoloured silhouettes

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** ADR-008 (supersedes its art, keeps its pipeline), ADR-018, fds.md §5.5 /
  DC-006 / A5, [`../design/avatar-face-matrix.md`](../design/avatar-face-matrix.md)
- **Decision:** The ten sprites are now head-and-shoulders portraits on a 32×32 grid: five
  personas — **Skipper, Sprinter, Strategist, Hype, Sundowner** — across two presentations.
  `avatarVariant` 1–5 *is* the persona, in that order, and the same five are offered to both
  genders; presentation is carried by hair mass, brow weight, a lash pixel, one pixel of jaw
  and the lip tone. Backdrop colour is baked per persona. The generator asserts the anchors
  it is given (eyes on row 15, shoulders filling the bottom edge, ≤ 16 colour keys per
  sprite) and refuses to write art that breaks them.
- **Why:** The old set was two body silhouettes recoloured five times — identical pose, face
  and expression — so at 32 px in a leaderboard row every participant looked the same, and a
  third of each sprite was unreadable torso. A portrait spends those rows on a jaw and a
  collar instead. The rejected half of the proposal is recorded in the design doc: RPG
  archetypes (scars, piercings, "deceptive") are wrong for colleagues at a PSD family day,
  and three-point lighting, chiaroscuro and per-archetype camera angles cannot exist in a
  flat palette at this size — the last of those also contradicts the eye-line rule.
- **Impact:** No schema change: `avatarVariant` stays `1..5`, so no record breaks, but anyone
  who already picked a number gets a new face for it — which makes this a pre-event change.
  Display sizes are now 32 / 64 / 96 only, so every art pixel lands on a whole device pixel
  (the profile hero moved 72 → 96, the picker is a fixed 64). Runs of one colour merge into
  one `<rect>`, which took a portrait from ~60 kB to ~13 kB. URLs carry the grid hash
  (`avatarVersion.ts`), so a redrawn face cannot be served from cache. Alt text names the
  persona ("Sprinter portrait") and the sign-up picker labels each option, so the choice is
  describable without seeing it.

### ADR-021 — Avatars are composed from layers, and the participant chooses the colours

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-020 (keeps the personas, replaces the fixed art), ADR-008 (the generator
  now emits a typed art module instead of SVG files)
- **Relates to:** fds.md §2.1 #obj-participant, §5.5 / DC-006,
  [`../design/avatar-face-matrix.md`](../design/avatar-face-matrix.md) §7
- **Decision:** An avatar is composed at render time from 34 hand-drawn 32×32 layers and the
  participant's own palette. Six choices — skin tone (8), hair style (5 per build), hair
  colour (10), facial hair (3, masculine), shirt colour (10) and backdrop (10) — travel as
  one dash-joined code in a new `participant.avatar_look` column; `avatar_variant` keeps its
  FDS meaning and now selects a **persona preset** (prop, expression and starting kit). The
  two builds are redrawn so they differ in jaw, brow, eyes, mouth, neck, shoulders and
  neckline, not only in hair. `PUT /api/me/avatar` lets a participant redraw themselves after
  sign-up; the studio is the same component on S1 and S4.
- **Why:** Ten files gave everyone at a 300-person event one of ten faces, and the two builds
  were the same doll in different wigs. Ten *more* files would not fix either problem: the
  fix is to make colour a parameter and the build a drawing decision. Layers cost 34 grids
  and cover 1.2 million appearances; the equivalent as files would be 1.2 million SVGs.
- **Impact:** `public/avatars/*.svg` and `generate-avatar-sprites.mjs` are deleted —
  `npm run art` now emits `src/lib/avatarArt.ts`, and `avatarUrl()` returns a memoised
  `data:` URL, so a face costs no request at all (the ADR-018 cache stamp becomes moot for
  avatars and survives as `ART_VERSION` on the cache key). Migration `0002_avatar_look.sql`
  adds the column with the default look, so every existing row stays valid. Every participant
  wire view gained `avatarLook`, which is what lets a leaderboard row draw a stranger
  correctly. The art source of record is `scripts/avatar-art-source.mjs`, where a layer is 32
  readable rows; the generated module is the machine's copy, one line per layer.

### ADR-022 — The participant backdrop is a generated pixel panorama with CSS-animated layers

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-014 (same rules as the motifs: hand-drawn, deterministic, committed,
  referenced by URL), ADR-018 (URLs carry an art stamp)
- **Relates to:** fds.md §5.5 / DC-006, `images/ingest/sentosa_backdrop.jpeg`
- **Decision:** Participant surfaces sit in a 480×270 pixel-art panorama of Sentosa —
  CBD skyline, VivoCity, the Merlion on its terrace, a pier pavilion, the resort's
  terracotta roofs and clock tower, the Universal globe, coaster track, the cable-car
  span, the Sentosa Express viaduct, the bay and a beach volleyball court. Eleven PNG
  layers are generated by `npm run scene` from `scripts/scene-art.mjs`; `<BeachScene>`
  stacks them in a fixed 16:9 box pinned to the bottom of the viewport and
  `styles/gameboy.css` animates eight of them: drifting clouds, moving swell, two-frame
  surf, three cable cars on the span, the Express emerging from a tree clump, gulls,
  palm crowns in the breeze and a volleyball rallying over the net.
- **Why:** The old scene was two 16×16 palm sprites blown up to 148 px either side of the
  column plus a bobbing sun — sparse at any width, and nothing on screen said *Sentosa*.
  A raster panorama can carry twenty landmarks for 17 kB; the same drawing as SVG `<rect>`
  runs (ADR-014's format) is roughly a megabyte, which is why `pixel-canvas.mjs` has a PNG
  encoder. Art is authored at 480×270 rather than at device resolution so the pixels stay
  chunky: on a 1440 px window every art pixel is exactly 3 device pixels.
- **Impact:** Layer geometry is percentages of the scene box, generated next to the art in
  `src/lib/sceneArt.ts`, so a sprite stays glued to its pixel of the panorama at any
  width and `<BeachScene>` holds no numbers. Landmarks are placed away from the middle
  because the phone column covers it on desktop, and nothing that matters lives in the
  bottom 22 rows, which the fixed nav bar hides. The backdrop is hidden below 760 px, as
  the motif scene was. `prefers-reduced-motion` stops every animation and hides the cable
  cars and the train outright — parked mid-air they read as broken art. Scene PNGs total
  17 kB and are served from `public/scene/` with the art stamp on the URL. With no
  headless browser available (ADR-139), review is
  `npm run scene:review`, which composites the shipped layers exactly as the CSS stacks
  them into `docs/screenshot/sentosa-backdrop.png`.

### ADR-023 — The scene is drawn at two pixel densities, and every sprite sheet gets a one-frame box

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-022 (the generated Sentosa panorama), ADR-019 (one owner per storage key)
- **Relates to:** `images/ingest/sentosa_backdrop.jpeg`, fds.md §5.5 / DC-006
- **Decision:** `pixel-canvas.mjs` became scale-aware — a `Canvas(units, unitsHigh, scale)`
  keeps drawing in art units while writing `scale × scale` device pixels — so the same
  drawing code emits two complete variants: `public/scene/` at one pixel per art unit and
  `public/scene-2x/` at two. `SCENE_PARTS_FINE` mirrors `SCENE_PARTS` with the same
  geometry, and `?backdrop=fine` (or `classic`) on any participant URL switches between
  them and is remembered in `psd.backdrop.v1`, owned by `lib/scene/backdropChoice.ts`.
  Separately, a two-frame sheet no longer lives in a full-box layer: `frame()` gives it a
  box exactly one frame wide with `background-size: 200% auto`, and one keyframe,
  `gb-scene-frames`, steps `background-position-x` from 0% to 100%.
- **Why:** Which pixel density looks right is a judgement call that cannot be made from a
  crop — it needs the running app, both variants, the same window. Shipping the finer art
  as a replacement would have thrown away the chunkier look if it lost, so it ships
  alongside at 44 kB for the whole set. The one-frame box is a bug fix: a layer sized to
  the whole sheet painted *both* frames, which is why each palm trunk carried a second
  crown hovering beside it and the gulls doubled.
- **Impact:** The scene grew from eleven layers to fifteen. Four `player` sheets put two
  women and two men in PSD kit on the court, each with its own flip period so they never
  move as one, and the volleyball rallies over them — the people in the reference photo
  are now in the art. The cable span runs from x −24 to x 504 so it leaves the frame at
  both edges instead of ending in mid-air, and the cabins are animated across 107.292% of
  the box to match. The Merlion is drawn in side profile: head-on, a maned bust reads as a
  lighthouse. `render-scene-review.mjs` gained `--scale`, `--zoom`, `--crop` and `--out`,
  which is how the players and the Merlion were reviewed at 6× without a browser.

### ADR-024 — Live surfaces update in place, on a jittered schedule

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §5.4 (F9 leaderboard, F51 match feed), `lib/hooks/useAsyncData.ts`,
  `lib/hooks/useLiveList.ts`
- **Decision:** Three changes to how a polled surface behaves. (1) `isLoading` now means
  "nothing to show yet", not "a request is in flight": a surface that already has data
  keeps showing it while the next load runs. (2) `usePolling` no longer takes an interval
  — it waits a fresh random delay between 45 and 75 seconds before every tick, drawn per
  client. (3) `useLiveList` animates the DOM the render just produced: rows fade in when
  they appear, slide from their old offset to their new one when the order changes, and
  flash when their own value changed. A list opts in by putting `data-live-key` and
  `data-live-signature` on its rows and holding the returned ref.
- **Why:** Every client polled on the same 30-second interval, and they all started when
  the event did, so the whole field asked the one laptop for the leaderboard at the same
  instant twice a minute — a self-inflicted thundering herd that gets worse with every
  phone that joins. Randomising each wait spreads the load and costs nothing. Meanwhile
  each poll flipped `isLoading` back to true, so the board and the feed tore themselves
  down to "Loading…" and rebuilt: a flash, a jump in layout, and a silent reshuffle that
  the eye could not follow. Values that change need to be *seen* changing.
- **Impact:** Refreshes are quieter and slower, which is right for a leaderboard: nothing
  on these surfaces is second-sensitive, and a facilitator's own actions still reload
  immediately through `useAction`. FLIP runs on the real DOM, so the hook needs no state
  and triggers no re-render; it is skipped entirely under `prefers-reduced-motion` or
  where the Web Animations API is missing (jsdom, older browsers), and the content is
  correct either way. The offline scan queue keeps its own 15-second drain — that is a
  retry loop for work already accepted, not a refresh of a screen.

### ADR-025 — Event-day load is simulated by a virtual-user harness in the repo

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** fds.md §1 (150–300 participants, 10–20 facilitators, 2 superadmins),
  ADR-024 (jittered polling), `scripts/stress-test.mjs`
- **Decision:** `npm run stress` runs a virtual crowd against the real HTTP API: 300
  participants walking the surfaces with realistic weights and think times, court marshals
  starting and finishing matches, fringe marshals scanning at a configurable rate, and the
  superadmins' console on a poll. Personas run in `node:worker_threads` so the generator is
  not the bottleneck, every call is labelled with its route template, and the report gives
  per-endpoint p50/p90/p99/max, throughput, the peak-to-mean **herd factor** and the first
  real failures. `--poll=fixed` reproduces the pre-ADR-024 aligned interval so the two can
  be compared. It exits 1 above a 1 % failure rate.
- **Why:** The event has no staging day and no autoscaling — one API process, one beach,
  everybody at once. The load question is not "how many requests per second can this
  serve" but "what happens when 300 phones do the same thing at the same moment", and only
  a concurrent client can answer that. A dependency-free harness (Node's `fetch` plus
  worker threads, ~600 lines) beats a load-testing framework here: it runs offline, it
  needs no configuration language, and it can speak the app's own sign-in, snapshot and
  idempotency rules — a generic tool cannot post a `client_scan_uuid`.
- **Impact:** It confirmed the fleet is comfortable — 300 participants are about 25 req/s
  and every endpoint answers inside 30 ms on a 2-vCPU sandbox with PGlite — and it
  measured ADR-024 rather than assuming it: synchronised clients peak at 294 req/s with a
  1 269 ms median leaderboard, jittered clients peak at 42 req/s with a 12 ms median. It
  also surfaced a genuine race (two marshals completing one match), which the state
  machine rejected correctly. The harness lives in `scripts/`, so it is outside the
  coverage gates and outside `npm run verify`; the numbers and how to read them are in
  `docs/design/stress-test.md`.

### ADR-026 — Avatars are 64×64 anime mugshots, drawn as shapes and shipped run-length encoded

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Supersedes the art in:** ADR-021 (the layer/palette system itself stands)
- **Relates to:** fds.md §5.5 / DC-006, `scripts/avatar-art-source.mjs`
- **Decision:** The art is now 64×64 instead of 32×32 and framed as a portrait: crown at
  row 4, eyes across rows 31–39, chin at 50, shoulders filling the bottom edge. The style
  is anime — an ink contour, oversized two-tone eyes with a pupil and catchlights, a
  tapered lash line, blush, a hair highlight band, one expression per archetype, and the
  iris taking the archetype's accent colour. Each of the five archetypes now has its own
  garment as well as its own headwear (`body.{gender}.{persona}`): sailor collar, track
  jacket, hoodie, cheer chevron, open shirt with a lei. Layers are no longer typed as
  ASCII: they are drawn with `KeyCanvas` (`scripts/avatar-canvas.mjs`), a grid of role
  keys with `span/rows/ellipse/curve/triangle/mirrorLeft/outline`, and the generated
  module ships each row run-length encoded (`.22s20.22`).
- **Why:** At 32×32 a face had about nine cells for an eye, so every character was the
  same doll in a different hat, and at 32 px on a leaderboard it read as a blur. Four
  times the cells buys an iris, a lash, a jawline and a collar — the things that make two
  characters different people. Hand-typing 42 layers of 64 rows is not possible to keep
  symmetric or to edit, hence the canvas; `mirrorLeft()` alone halves the drawing and
  guarantees a symmetric face.
- **Impact:** The generated module is 34 kB (170 kB raw, hence the encoding) and the
  runtime expands each layer once. An avatar is composed into rectangles — greedy
  horizontal runs merged vertically, then one `<path>` per colour — which took the data
  URL from 81 kB to 8.7 kB, so thirty faces in a leaderboard cost about what one used to.
  Anchors are checked on all 100 combinations at generation time, and now include "the
  eyes are not covered" and "the cheeks are not covered", which is how a hairstyle that
  ate the face got caught. `npm run art:review` renders the contact sheet at
  `docs/screenshot/avatar-sheet.png`; with no headless browser (ADR-139) it is the only
  way to see a face before it ships.

### ADR-027 — Actions that move points ask first; the forms stop wasting taps

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** `docs/design/ux-friction.md`, fds.md §2.13 (corrections), F23, F28–F30
- **Decision:** One `ConfirmDialog` and one `useConfirm` hook guard every action that
  awards points, ends a phase or removes somebody: declare a winner, cancel a match, end
  or advance or reopen a fringe round, leave a team, remove a member, hand over the
  captaincy, lock a team, enable or disable a court, activate or deactivate an activity,
  and reset a participant's PIN. The dialog names the thing, says what will happen in one
  sentence, and holds focus on **Cancel**. Alongside it, six form frictions are gone:
  sign-up validates in reading order and moves the caret to the rejected field; a second
  line under the error says which nickname problem it is; the 51 trait controls fold away
  behind "Customise hair, skin and colours"; PIN fields carry proper `autocomplete`; a
  wrong PIN clears itself and keeps the caret; the badge tells you a facilitator can type
  your nickname; and the scan box returns focus to the nickname field after every outcome.
- **Why:** These came out of driving the app as a picky user
  (`docs/design/ux-friction.md`). The confirmations are about the one-way doors: a marshal
  declaring the wrong winner has to find a superadmin to void it, and the two winner
  buttons are the largest targets on the screen. The form fixes are about the other end of
  the scale — a tap or four saved, but paid every time, by three hundred people on one
  beach.
- **Impact:** The scan button is deliberately exempt: a queue of twenty cannot afford a
  modal per person, and a wrong scan is a 15-point correction rather than a match result —
  the right remedy there is an undo, which is still open. Void and unvoid already require a
  typed reason, a stronger guard, and are unchanged. `PinField` now *requires* an
  `autoComplete` value, so a new PIN field cannot be added with the browser locked out.
  Tests press through the dialog with one shared `confirmDialog(user)` helper, so a new
  destructive button that forgets the guard fails its test rather than surprising a
  marshal.

### ADR-028 — Shirt and backdrop are free colours; skin and hair stay a list

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Amends:** ADR-021 (the look code), ADR-026 (the art)
- **Decision:** `AvatarLook.outfitColour` and `AvatarLook.backdrop` become `#rrggbb`
  strings instead of indices, and the studio offers the platform's colour input — the
  phone's own colour wheel — next to the ten named swatches, which stay as quick picks.
  Skin tone, hair style, hair colour and facial hair remain indices, because each one is a
  hand-drawn layer and there are eight skins for the reason that eight were drawn. The
  look code keeps its shape and its position in the wire format:
  `3-1-2-1-ff7ac3-0b0f1a`. `avatarLookSchema` validates *and normalises*, so the database
  holds one canonical spelling however the client wrote it, and `parseAvatarLook` still
  reads a pre-ADR-028 index as the swatch it used to mean.
- **Why:** The two axes that are not anatomy were the two where ten choices chafed: a
  cluster wants its own colour, and a participant wants their own backdrop. Nothing in the
  art depends on those being from a list — the shade is derived with `darken()` and the
  ink contour (ADR-026) keeps the figure readable against any backdrop — so the limit was
  arbitrary. Using `<input type="color">` rather than a hand-built wheel is deliberate: it
  is the picker the device already has, it is keyboard- and screen-reader-reachable, it
  works on iOS and Android, and it cannot hand back anything but `#rrggbb`.
- **Impact:** Migration `0003_avatar_free_colours.sql` rewrites every existing row from
  the index it held to the colour that index meant — verified on a PGlite database seeded
  with pre-migration rows: `3-1-2-1-9-3` becomes `3-1-2-1-333b49-33477a`, the same face —
  then tightens the CHECK to the new shape. `AVATAR_LOOK_AXES` splits into
  `AVATAR_INDEX_AXES` (drawn lists) and `AVATAR_COLOUR_AXES` (free colours), which is what
  the studio loops over. The generated `OUTFIT_COLOURS` / `BACKDROP_COLOURS` in
  `avatarArt.ts` are no longer consulted at render time; the swatch hexes now live in
  `@psd/contracts`, where the labels already were.

### ADR-029 — Ties go to whoever got there first; consoles wait before they judge; the avatar gains a build

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Relates to:** `docs/design/ux-friction.md` (P1 findings), fds.md §4.4 leaderboard,
  ADR-026/028 (the avatar)
- **Decision:** Three things the friction audit and a close look at the art asked for.
  (1) **Tie-break:** every scoring row now carries `reachedAt`, the moment it reached the
  total it holds, and the boards order by `total_points DESC, reached_at ASC`. Level on
  points, the cluster or the player who got there first is ahead, and the board says
  `first to 83` on the row that earned it. (2) **Empty states wait:** the court console
  and the fringe station render a loading panel until their first answer arrives, instead
  of showing the empty state of data that has not loaded. (3) **Build:** a fifth index in
  the look code — Slight, Lean, Regular, Sturdy, Broad — drawn as five neck widths and
  five shoulder lines.
- **Why:** Ranking by array position meant BP and CHROO, both on 83, were shown as first
  and second with nothing to explain it; that board goes on the projector at the closing
  ceremony. "First to the score" is the rule the organisers would use in the room, and it
  is already in the data. The consoles were telling marshals that the event had no teams
  while five existed, and that a round needed opening while it was open with fourteen
  scans. And build is the personalisation people asked for after skin and hair: at
  mugshot framing it reads through the neck and the slope of the shoulders, which is
  exactly what a portrait shows.
- **Impact:** The look code becomes `skin-style-hair-facial-build-outfit-backdrop`;
  migration `0004_avatar_build.sql` inserts the middle build into every existing row
  (verified on a PGlite database: `3-1-2-1-9-3`, two formats old, ends up
  `3-1-2-1-3-333b49-33477a`). The body layer splits into `torso.{gender}.{build}` and
  `outfit.{gender}.{persona}`, so five builds and five archetypes cost ten layers rather
  than twenty-five, and the generator now checks 500 combinations. The stubble, which
  painted a checkerboard rectangle over the cheeks and the neck, is clipped to the jaw
  and thins around the mouth; both beards derive their shape from the head they sit on,
  so a change to the skull cannot leave facial hair hanging in the air again. The
  face-visibility anchor now looks for *hair* across the middle of the face rather than
  counting skin, because a beard on the jaw and spectacles on the nose are both fine.

### ADR-030 — The jaw belongs to the build, and facial hair is cut from the jaw it sits on

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-029 (build), ADR-026 (the art)
- **Decision:** `headRows()` takes the build: below row 42 the half-width is scaled
  (0.80 for Slight … 1.22 for Broad), so a Slight face runs to a narrow chin and a Broad
  one keeps its width down to the jawline. The head is therefore a layer per build
  (`head.{gender}.{build}`) and so is each beard (`beard.{build}.{2|3}`), derived from
  the same rows. Every beard ends with `clipToHead()`, which clears anything outside that
  skull, and the blush moved from the face layer into the head layer, where it can be
  clipped to the cheek it sits on.
- **Why:** ADR-029 gave the build a neck and shoulders but left one skull, so a Broad
  character had a Slight person's chin, and the stubble — which had just been taught to
  follow the jaw — was following a jaw nobody else had. Only rows **below 42** move,
  which is under every hairstyle's side band: hair keeps framing every build with no gap
  of backdrop opening between hair and cheek, and the hair layers stay build-independent
  (ten, not fifty).
- **Impact:** 68 layers, 52 kB encoded, and the generator checks all 500 combinations.
  Two invariants are now tested rather than eyeballed: every build has a head, a torso
  and both beards, and **no beard cell lands where its skull has nothing** — the test
  that caught a chin highlight hanging off the Slight jaw. A Broad beard is measurably
  wider than a Slight one on the same row, which is the thing the eye actually checks.

### ADR-031 — A participant may wear their own photograph, converted to a sprite in the browser

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-021/026 (the drawn avatars), ADR-028 (free colours)
- **Relates to:** fds.md §5.5 / DC-006, `docs/design/avatars.md` §7
- **Decision:** Alongside the five characters, the studio offers "use a photo". The
  browser decodes the chosen file, finds the face, crops it to the framing the drawn
  avatars use, averages it down to 64×64, cuts the colours to fourteen, replaces the
  studio background with the participant's own backdrop, inks the silhouette, and emits a
  **sprite code**: `64:<palette>:<runs>`, an indexed grid run-length encoded, two to four
  kilobytes. That string is what is stored (`participant.avatar_photo`) and what travels
  on the wire. **The photograph itself is never uploaded and never kept.**
- **Why:** People want to see themselves, and a passport photo is the one picture
  everybody has. Doing the conversion on the device keeps a face out of the database and
  off the network, which is the difference between a fun feature and a data-protection
  conversation — and it means no image storage, no resizing service and no new
  dependency. A sprite also composes with everything already built: it is the same 64×64
  grid, rendered by the same rectangle merger, cached by the same key.
- **Impact:** The pipeline is plain arithmetic over pixels, so all of it is testable
  without a canvas; only `readPhoto.ts` needs a browser, and its tests hand it a doubled
  canvas. Two things earn their keep in the algorithm: the resample pulls each cell 30 %
  toward its **darkest** sample, because a plain average erases eyes and lips at this
  size, and a **despeckle** pass drops single-cell specks, because quantisation freckles
  a face otherwise. `npm run photo:review --workspace @psd/web` renders
  `docs/screenshot/photo-sprites.png` — each photo beside the sprite it becomes — which
  is how the conversion is judged, there being no headless browser (ADR-139). A sprite
  that will not parse falls back to the drawn character rather than to a hole.

### ADR-032 — The backdrop is found by hue and by walking, not by matching one colour

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Amends:** ADR-031 (photo → sprite)
- **Relates to:** `images/ingest/booth-*.png`
- **Decision:** Background removal in the photo pipeline is three rules together, not a
  tolerance: **seed** from the frame, because that is wall by definition; **step** only to
  a neighbour close to the wall already found *there*, which follows a gradient but will
  not cross an edge; and only accept a cell that still **looks like the wall** — near its
  median colour, or the same hue as it. Skin is never crossed. The wall's colour is the
  **median of the border ring**, and the head is sized from the **widest band of skin in
  the upper half of the face**, not from the skin box's height.
- **Why:** The first version assumed a photo booth looks like a photo studio. Real
  induction-booth photos — teal fabric, a hotspot behind the head, a shadow down one
  side, a vignette, sensor noise and a soft lens — broke it four different ways, and each
  naive fix broke something else: a wider tolerance walked through the blurred edge and
  ate a white blouse; a bilinear model fitted from the four corners decided the wall
  turned navy because the subject's shoulders filled the bottom corners; and measuring
  the skin box top to bottom put the "cheekbones" on the collarbone of anyone in an open
  collar, so the crop slid down and cut the crown off. Hue is what actually separates a
  lit teal wall from a white blouse, a grey hijab and a navy polo at every brightness.
- **Impact:** Six photographs are committed as test material — two studio, four booth —
  and `npm run photo:review` renders all of them side by side. The unit tests build the
  same conditions synthetically: a lit teal wall with a hotspot and a vignette, a subject
  whose clothing runs off the frame, and a cool wall behind a warm shirt so the hue
  comparison has to wrap around the circle. One deliberate non-fix: a *beige* wall is
  skin-coloured by the same rule that protects faces, so it is left in place — keeping a
  wall beats erasing a face.

### ADR-033 — A segmentation model cuts out the background when it can; colour does when it cannot

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-031 (photo → sprite), ADR-032 (colour segmentation)
- **Relates to:** Transformers.js + ONNX Runtime Web, `Xenova/modnet`
- **Decision:** The studio now answers twice. The colour cut-out runs first — no download,
  a few milliseconds — so the participant sees themselves immediately. Then the same
  pixels go through **MODNET via Transformers.js**, running on WebGPU where the browser
  has it and WebAssembly where it does not, and if a mask comes back the sprite is
  replaced. If the library, the weights, the browser or the network are not there,
  `segmentSubject` returns **null** and the colour cut-out stands. Transformers.js is
  imported from a CDN at run time rather than bundled.
- **Why:** The colour rules are exact on a wall and helpless against a selfie — a café, a
  beach, a crowd — and a selfie is what people will actually have. A model handles those,
  and running it in the browser keeps the promise the feature was built on: the
  photograph never leaves the device, even now that something clever is looking at it.
  Two answers rather than one because the first run downloads tens of megabytes: nobody
  should watch a spinner to find out whether their face fits.
- **Impact:** Nothing is added to the bundle — the build is unchanged at 664 kB, and the
  import is a single lazy URL, so an app whose main job on the day is showing a QR code
  on a beach never pays for it. A deployment that forbids third-party script origins
  simply gets the colour cut-out, which is why that path stays a first-class feature
  rather than dead code. The model is never fetched in a test: the loader is injected,
  the double returns a mask, and the failure paths — no network, empty result, a mask
  whose size does not match — are all asserted to end in null. The real loader is
  exercised too, and asserted to reject outside a browser.

### ADR-034 — Finding the head, leaving a photo alone, shipping it, and standing the studio down

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-031/032/033 (photo avatars)
- **Decision:** Four things the photo feature was missing.
  1. **Finding the head** now has three sources, best first: the browser's own
     `FaceDetector` (Shape Detection API) where it exists — free, instant, a real face
     box; then the **segmentation mask**, whose top edge is the top of the head and whose
     pinch is the neck (`headBoxFromMask`); and only then the skin-colour estimate, which
     is all there was before and is a guess.
  2. **Leaving a photo alone** is now a deliberate outcome. If the colour rules would
     remove almost everything (a picture of a wall) *or* almost nothing (a café, a
     crowd), the mask is discarded and the whole frame is pixelated as it is.
  3. **Shipping it**: the API gzips. A sprite is 2.4–3.7 kB of run-length text and a
     leaderboard carries ten of them — measured on the demo event, 41.8 kB of board
     becomes **2.3 kB**.
  4. **The studio stands down** while a photo is worn: character, hair, build, beard,
     skin, shirt and backdrop are all hidden, because none of them can touch a
     photograph.
- **Why:** A selfie is the hard case, and all four gaps showed up there. Skin-colour
  bounding boxes wander on a busy background; a partial cut-out carves holes out of a
  face and is worse than no cut-out at all; three hundred phones pulling 42 kB of board
  every minute is 200 kB/s out of one laptop; and a colour picker that cannot change the
  colour of anything is a promise the app does not keep.
- **Impact:** `photoToSprite` takes an optional crop and an optional mask, so the same
  pipeline serves all three head-finders and both cut-out strategies. Compression is one
  middleware line and needed no other change. The studio's trait rows now live behind
  `avatarPhoto === null`, and the tests assert both that they disappear and that removing
  the photo brings them back.

### ADR-035 — A photo sprite is addressed by its hash and kept on the device

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-031 (photo avatars), ADR-019 (one owner per storage key)
- **Decision:** Rows carry `avatarPhotoId` — a 64-bit FNV-1a hash of the sprite — instead
  of the sprite. `GET /api/avatars?ids=…` returns the bodies for up to sixty ids, and the
  browser keeps what it gets in `localStorage` under `psd.sprites.v1`, owned by
  `lib/avatar/spriteCache.ts`: 400 faces, least-recently-seen evicted first. A
  `SpriteProvider` collects the ids an entire screen asks for and fetches the missing ones
  in **one** request; `useSprite` hands each `<Avatar>` its body, or null, in which case
  the drawn character stands in.
- **Why:** A sprite is 2.4–3.7 kB and a leaderboard carries ten, so the board was 41.8 kB
  of mostly-repeated picture every poll, per phone, for the whole day. A sprite is also
  immutable — change your photo and the hash changes — so it is perfectly cacheable, and
  the only reason it was being re-sent was that it had no name. Measured on the demo
  event: **41.8 kB → 2.3 kB gzipped → 902 B** once rows carry ids, and the sprite fetch
  behind it happens once per device rather than once a minute.
- **Impact:** `GET /api/avatars` is readable by any signed-in actor — these are faces
  already on the board and rosters that actor can see, and an id is a hash, so nothing can
  be enumerated by guessing. A browser that will not store anything (private mode, a
  sandboxed frame) keeps missing and re-fetching, which is slower and still correct. The
  standards checker now recognises `spriteCache.ts` as a key owner alongside the session,
  queue and location stores.

### ADR-036 — When nothing can find the face, the participant places the square

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-29
- **Extends:** ADR-034 (the three head-finders)
- **Decision:** If the browser has no `FaceDetector` **and** the segmentation model did
  not run, the crop was a guess from skin colour — so the photo is shown with a square the
  participant drags over their own head and pulls bigger or smaller. The square is always
  square, never leaves the picture, and never shrinks below a fifth of it. "Choose the
  square myself" is also always available, whatever found the face.
- **Why:** Skin-colour framing is the weakest of the three and it is exactly the one left
  on a locked-down browser with a busy selfie — the case where the crop is most likely to
  put someone's ear in the middle of their trainer card. Asking is better than guessing
  badly, and it takes one drag.
- **Impact:** The geometry lives in `lib/avatar/cropBox.ts` as arithmetic on a box inside
  a box — a pointer is hard to test, a rectangle is not — and the component only wires
  pointer events to it. One code path for finger, stylus and mouse. Re-cropping re-runs
  the same pipeline over the bitmap already in memory, so it costs nothing and needs no
  second decode.

### ADR-037 — Photo sprites are generated and stored at 128×128

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-031 (photo → sprite), ADR-035 (addressed by hash)
- **Decision:** `photoToSprite` now works on a 128×128 grid, the browser decodes the
  photo at a 640 px working size (five photo pixels per cell instead of two and a half),
  and the column CHECK, the parser and the schema accept both 128 and the legacy 64.
  `AVATAR_SPRITE_MAX_LENGTH` rises to 50 000; the device cache budget drops to 150 faces.
- **Why:** At 64×64 an eye is two cells and a face survives only with good lighting; on
  the social-media photos in `images/ingest/social-*.png` the likeness sharpens visibly
  at 128. The format itself was left alone — same RLE, same sixteen-colour cap, same
  three-base-36-digit run length (which holds to 46 655, comfortably over the 16 384
  cells) — so nothing that stores, ships or draws a sprite had to learn anything new.
  Rewriting stored 64×64 sprites was rejected outright: a sprite is immutable and named
  by its own hash (ADR-035), so "upgrading" one is by definition minting a different
  sprite, and the photo it came from was thrown away on the phone that made it.
- **Impact:** A sprite is now ~10–20 kB before gzip instead of 2.4–3.7 kB. The board is
  unaffected — rows carry ids (ADR-035) — and the body fetch happens once per device, so
  the cost lands exactly where it is paid for in likeness. `docs/screenshot/`
  `photo-sprites-social.png` reviews the pipeline over forty social-media-styled test
  photos (full/half body, overhead angles, profiles, open-mouth expressions); the
  review script lays batches that size out as a grid.

### ADR-038 — Hot reads are decorated with a bought cache; every scoring write voids it

- **Status:** Accepted · amends ADR-006 ("computed on read")
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** fds.md F16/F44/F49, ADR-028 (polling), ADR-035 (sprite ids)
- **Decision:** `apps/api/src/lib/cache.ts` provides `cachedRead` — a decorator that
  wraps an entity read `(db, ...args)` without changing its signature — built on
  `lru-cache` (the bounded store) and `@epic-web/cachified` (request coalescing, TTL,
  stale-while-revalidate). Decorated: cluster standings, top individuals, participant
  totals (5 s TTL, `SCOREBOARD_TAG`) and the cluster catalogue (60 s). Every write that
  can move a score — scan create/void, match complete/void/winner-edit, signup, avatar
  redraw — calls `invalidateTag(SCOREBOARD_TAG)`. `listAvatarSprites` keeps resolved
  bodies in a content-addressed LRU, so the full-column scan runs only for ids the
  process has never seen. Keys are scoped per database handle (a WeakMap), so the test
  harness's parallel databases never answer for each other.
- **Why:** Three hundred phones on a jittered minute poll (ADR-028) ran the two
  leaderboard aggregates — a CTE over every scan and match of the day — about five times
  a second, and the answer between writes was identical every time. ADR-006 refused a
  *materialised* leaderboard because void/unvoid had to be correct by construction; that
  guarantee is kept here by construction too, since every mutating path deletes the
  entry and the next read recomputes — the TTL is only the net under a write path someone
  adds later and forgets to tag. Hand-rolling the cache was rejected (stampede control
  and SWR are exactly the fiddly parts worth buying); `@type-cacheable`-style method
  decorators were rejected because the entities are functions, not classes, and a
  higher-order decorator keeps them that way.
- **Impact:** Between writes the aggregates cost the database at most one query per 5 s
  window (plus one per totals-holder), whatever the phone count; a scan or a correction
  triggers one recompute on the next poll. The sprite scan drops from once per
  `/api/avatars` request to once per unknown id. Cache entries live in process memory —
  `index.ts` is the only listener, so there is exactly one cache to be wrong in, and it
  never is for longer than a write leaves it.

### ADR-039 — The photo studio is proven in a real Chromium, over the whole corpus

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-031/033/034/036/037 (the photo pipeline), AGENTS-testing.md §5–§6
- **Decision:** `e2e/photo-sprites.spec.ts` drives the real studio — real app, real API,
  real database — over every photo in `images/ingest/social*` (this branch's twenty
  male/female pairs and the forty-photo adversarial corpus adopted from PR 2), under
  each availability the beach can produce: the segmentation model reachable, only a
  `FaceDetector`, or nothing at all — plus the awkward rest: a file that is not a photo,
  a model that loads and then returns garbage, a model that throws mid-run, a detector
  that throws, taking the photo off again, and the sprite surviving save-and-reload.
  The CDN is the one thing the suite owns (ADR-033 made the model a network guest, so
  the network is a legitimate test input): the jsdelivr route is answered with a tiny
  stand-in module shaped like Transformers.js, or refused outright.
- **Why:** Unit tests prove the arithmetic; what they cannot prove is the ladder — that
  the *browser* falls from model to detector to manual square without dropping the
  photo, in the engine the event actually runs on. Both Playwright projects are already
  Chromium, and the corpus runs once, on the desktop project, because sixty conversions
  are about the pipeline, not the viewport. Downloading the real MODNET weights in CI
  was rejected: a third-party CDN in the loop makes the suite fail on someone else's
  outage, and the seam being tested is availability, not model quality.
- **Impact:** `PSD_E2E_PHOTO_SAMPLE=n` converts every n-th photo while iterating
  locally; the full corpus is ~1.6 minutes. Sandboxes that cannot reach the Playwright
  browser CDN point `PSD_E2E_CHROMIUM` at any Chromium binary (the `@sparticuz/chromium`
  npm tarball carries one, plus `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` for its libs) — the suite stays pure
  Chromium either way. `apiSignUp` in `e2e/fixtures.ts` now sends `avatarLook`, which
  the signup schema had since grown to require.

### ADR-040 — The demo seed is recorded, not written

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-039 (the corpus e2e suite), `scripts/seed-demo.mjs`
- **Decision:** The demo crowd comes from a recording. `scripts/demo-personas.json`
  names eighty Singaporean personas — one per photo in the corpus, which now includes
  PR 2's final twenty adversarial shots (`images/ingest/social/41…60`). `npm run
  demo:record` wipes a dedicated data directory, boots the full stack against it, and
  runs `e2e/demo-onboarding.spec.ts` (gated by `PSD_E2E_ONBOARDING`, so ordinary
  `test:e2e` runs never touch it): the suite asserts the server holds zero
  participants, then walks every persona through the real sign-up screen and the real
  photo studio on the happy path — the FaceDetector finds the face, the cut-out model
  removes the background — and finally asks the server what it holds, via the
  superadmin directory and the `/api/avatars` batch route. That answer is written to
  `scripts/demo-participants.dump.json`, and `seed-demo.mjs` now replays it verbatim
  instead of inventing twenty-four participants.
- **Why:** Demo data that was typed in cannot drift-check the pipeline; demo data that
  was *recorded* is a standing proof that eighty real onboardings — form, PIN, cluster,
  gender, avatar, photo, 128×128 sprite — all still work end to end, and the leaderboard
  demo then wears exactly what the studio produced. Dumping through the HTTP API rather
  than the database keeps the recording honest (only reachable state is captured) and
  respects PGlite's single-process lock.
- **Impact:** the dump is ~1 MB of sprites and rides in git like the photos do; the
  recording takes ~3 minutes under the ADR-039 Chromium knobs. `seed:demo` is still
  idempotent (409 → sign-in). Re-record whenever the corpus, the studio, or the sprite
  format changes.

### ADR-041 — iOS Safari is a first-class engine, and the suite says so

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-033/034 (the photo ladder), ADR-039 (the corpus suite)
- **Decision:** Nothing the participant needs may depend on an API WebKit does not
  ship. The audit found the app already mostly true to that: QR capture decodes with
  jsQR on a canvas rather than `BarcodeDetector`, the camera `<video>` carries
  `muted playsInline`, and `FaceDetector` was always an optional rung — on an iPhone
  the ladder is model-or-manual, with the model's own mask doing the head-finding
  (`headBoxFromMask`). Two things were tightened. First, the model's device is now a
  ladder, not a pick: WebGPU is tried where `navigator.gpu` exists and WASM catches it
  when the attempt throws — Safari ships `navigator.gpu`, and ONNX Runtime's WebGPU
  backend is its least-proven one, so a throw there must cost one retry, never the
  whole model path. Second, the corpus suite gained the explicit iOS shape — model
  available, detector *forced* absent — so the ladder every iPhone walks is pinned on
  any host, whatever that host's Chromium ships.
- **Why:** Half the phones on the beach are iPhones. A suite that only proves Chromium
  proves half the event.
- **Impact:** `PSD_E2E_WEBKIT=1` (with `npx playwright install webkit`, on a host that
  can fetch it) adds mobile-safari and desktop-safari projects and runs the corpus in
  the true Safari engine. Known Safari footnotes, all benign: iOS transcodes HEIC to
  JPEG at the file picker (and Safari decodes HEIC natively anyway); `crypto.randomUUID`
  needs a secure context, which the event serves; ONNX-WASM runs single-threaded
  without COOP/COEP, slower but correct.

### ADR-042 — Take a selfie now: a live viewfinder in the studio

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-031/033/034 (the photo ladder), ADR-041 (iOS Safari first-class)
- **Decision:** Next to "use a photo" the studio offers "take a selfie": the front
  camera (`facingMode: 'user'`) streams into a mirrored viewfinder, and where the
  browser ships a FaceDetector the live face boundary is drawn over the preview as
  the participant lines up — polled off a work canvas every 300 ms, never letting a
  slow detector stack behind itself. Where there is none (every iPhone, ADR-041) a
  fixed oval guide stands in. Capture pulls one un-mirrored frame off the video and
  hands the Blob to the SAME conversion ladder an uploaded photo walks; the live
  boundary is a viewfinder aid, never a second pipeline. The camera lifecycle was
  extracted from the QR scanner (F26) into `useCameraSession`, now shared by both
  lenses; refusals keep their caller's copy — "choose a photo instead" here, "type
  the nickname instead" there — because the fallback is the page's, not the camera's.
- **Why:** Picking a file is a detour when the face is right there in front of the
  phone. The live boundary also answers "will it find me?" before the photo is taken,
  which the upload path can only answer after.
- **Impact:** Chromium in CI grows `--use-fake-device-for-media-stream` /
  `--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream` (inert outside camera tests; WebKit projects
  override launchOptions wholesale), and `webServer.url` now waits on `/api/health`
  rather than Vite's door, which a cold-started stack exposed. `e2e/selfie.spec.ts`
  proves both browser shapes and the back-out; the hook's decisions are unit-tested
  including the detector-less and throwing-detector cases.

### ADR-043 — One container, one origin: Docker image with a built-in tunnel

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-041 (real-world hosting), AGENTS-workflow.md §2 (env in one place)
- **Decision:** The deployment unit is a single `node:22-alpine` container that runs
  the API, serves the built SPA, and holds its own Cloudflare tunnel — supervisord
  (from apk) is PID 1 with two programs, both mirrored to the container log stream.
  Two repo truths shape the image: the API's build step is a typecheck, so production
  runs `tsx` over source (which is why `tsx` moved into `apps/api` dependencies —
  a runtime dependency was mislabelled a dev tool); and the API never served the web
  bundle, so a new `WEB_DIST` env (unset in dev, where Vite owns the origin) wraps
  the fetch handler with same-origin static serving — `/api` passes through, hashed
  `assets/` cache forever, everything else falls back to `index.html` for the SPA
  router, and resolved paths are prefix-checked against the dist root so encoded
  `..` cannot escape it. `cloudflared` has three modes decided by env: `TUNNEL_TOKEN`
  runs the named tunnel, no token opens a throwaway trycloudflare URL (printed in
  logs), `TUNNEL_DISABLE=1` leaves only the published port. PGlite persists in the
  `/data` volume via absolute `PGLITE_DATA_DIR`; `DATABASE_DRIVER=postgres` +
  `DATABASE_URL` swaps in external Postgres unchanged.
- **Why:** Behind a tunnel there is exactly one public origin; splitting web and API
  across origins would re-open every cookie and relative-fetch problem ADR-030/041
  closed. Packing the tunnel into the container means the host needs no inbound
  ports at all.
- **Impact:** New files: `Dockerfile`, `docker/` (supervisord.conf, app.sh,
  cloudflared.sh), `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore` (the 185 MB photo corpus
  must never enter a build context). `withStaticWeb` is unit-tested including the
  traversal case; the runtime stage was rehearsed outside Docker by `npm ci
  --omit=dev` into a bare copy of exactly the files the image carries and booting
  `docker/app.sh` against it. `SUPERADMIN_INITIAL_PASSCODE` stays a runtime secret;
  compose refuses to start without it.

### ADR-044 — Both engines by default, and the selfie's empty-handed cases

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-041 (iOS Safari is first-class), ADR-042 (the selfie viewfinder)
- **Decision:** WebKit stops being opt-in. `PSD_E2E_ENGINES` selects `chromium`, `webkit`
  or `all`, and **unset means both** — the config asks `webkit.executablePath()` whether
  the engine is on disk and, if it is not, runs Chromium with a warning rather than failing
  a fresh clone. Asking for WebKit explicitly on a host that has not fetched it is a loud
  error, never a silently halved run. `PSD_E2E_WEBKIT=1` remains as an alias for `all`, and
  `npm run e2e:install` fetches both browsers.
  The camera needs nothing new: Chromium keeps its two fake-media flags and Playwright's
  WebKit already boots with its own mock capture devices — a `getUserMedia` track there
  reports itself as `Mock video device 1` — so the whole selfie suite runs on all four
  projects with no physical camera anywhere. The suite then gained the cases the beach
  actually produces and nothing covered: a selfie with **no cut-out model** (detector
  present → colour cut-out and the "model was not available" copy; no detector → the
  participant places the square, ADR-036), a **refused** camera, and a device with **no**
  camera. Both refusals are injected at `getUserMedia`, because Chromium's
  `--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream` grants the prompt unconditionally and withholding the
  Playwright permission cannot reach those branches.
- **Why:** A suite that only proves Chromium proves half the event (ADR-041), and an opt-in
  second engine is a second engine nobody runs. The selfie path was proven only with the
  model *available*, which is the one condition a beach with no data does not meet — the
  likeliest failure was the least tested.
- **Impact:** `npm run test:e2e` now runs four projects; `test:e2e:chromium` /
  `test:e2e:webkit` / `test:e2e:all` narrow it. The photo corpus still runs desktop-only,
  now once **per engine** — `PSD_E2E_PHOTO_SAMPLE=n` is the knob for iterating.
  `openStudio`/`savedSprite` moved into `e2e/photo-stubs.ts` so the photo suites share one
  copy. Text now goes into controlled React inputs through `typeInto()` — `fill('')` then
  `pressSequentially`, checked and retried — and the sign-in fixtures wait for the form's own
  submit gate instead of clicking a disabled button. WebKit can land a `fill()`'s single input
  event before React has attached its listener: the DOM holds the text and the component's
  state does not, which showed up as a nickname whose submit never enabled and a PIN the form
  rejected as "PIN must be exactly 4 digits." while the screenshot showed four digits. Per
  keystroke, a dropped event leaves the field visibly short, so the check can see it.

### ADR-045 — Ask the browser for a WebGPU adapter before asking the runtime for the device

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Extends:** ADR-033 (the segmentation model), ADR-041 (the device ladder), ADR-044
- **Decision:** `segmentPhoto.ts` now calls `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()` first and only
  puts `webgpu` on the ladder when a real adapter comes back; `null` or a throw means the
  ladder is `['wasm']` alone. The catch-and-retry rung stays for the case where an adapter
  exists and the runtime still refuses it.
- **Why:** This was a bug, found by the first test that ran the *real* library end to end
  (`PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1`). ADR-041 promised that a throw from the fast device costs one
  attempt and never the photo. It did not: ONNX Runtime Web resolves its backend once and
  keeps the answer, so the WASM call meant to rescue a failed WebGPU init fails with the
  **first** call's error —

  ```
  device webgpu failed: no available backend found. ERR: [webgpu] Failed to get GPU adapter.
  device wasm   failed: no available backend found. ERR: [webgpu] Failed to get GPU adapter.
  ```

  — and the participant drops all the way to the manual square on a device where the model
  would have worked. Asked WASM-first, the same library builds MODNET happily. Every browser
  that advertises WebGPU without being able to produce an adapter hit this: headless
  Chromium in CI, and Safari builds where the backend is unproven — the very case ADR-041
  was written for.
- **Impact:** `e2e/model-available.spec.ts` covers the model **working**, which nothing did
  before: the task and model asked for (`background-removal`, `Xenova/modnet`), every rung
  of the device ladder including the no-adapter one, the weights fetched once per session,
