  and the mask genuinely changing the sprite (the same photo converted with and without the
  model must differ, and the model's corners must be the participant's backdrop). Its last
  test is the real library and the real weights, gated on `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1` because it
  needs the internet — that gate is the only reason this bug survived to now, so run it
  whenever the model path is touched.

### ADR-046 — The chat room: one process, one bus, no Redis

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** **fds.md §9.5 promotion** — "Participant-to-participant social features (chat,
  friends)" is listed as explicitly deferred scope, and that section says to *"document them
  separately if pursued later"*. This addendum is that document. Also ADR-003 (PGlite
  in-process), ADR-004 (sessions), ADR-016 (the token carriers), ADR-024 (jittered polling),
  ADR-034 (gzip), ADR-038 (cached reads with tag invalidation), ADR-043 (one container, tunnel).
- **Decision:** One global room, every signed-in actor may read and post, reached from the
  participant shell. The transport is **SSE**, not WebSockets and not short-polling:
  `GET /api/chat/stream` holds one idle socket per phone, sending is an ordinary
  `POST /api/chat/messages`, and the message reaches open streams through an **in-process Node
  `EventEmitter`** (`lib/chatBus.ts`). The steady-state database cost is therefore **one INSERT
  per message and zero reads**. Reads happen only when a phone reconnects, against
  `GET /api/chat/messages?after=`, which is wrapped in `cachedRead` under a new `CHAT_TAG` so a
  Wi-Fi blip that reconnects three hundred phones at once collapses to about one query per TTL
  window. That same endpoint is the documented fallback for a client without `EventSource`.
  `id` is a UUIDv7 and does four jobs at once: primary key, sort order, SSE event id, and
  resume cursor — so `Last-Event-ID` resume needs no extra column and no extra index.
  Four things bound the blast radius: a **500-character body cap** in `@psd/contracts`
  (mirrored as a SQL CHECK, so the cap is a property of the data and not just of the error
  message), a **per-session token bucket** (`lib/rateLimit.ts`, 3 deep refilling every 2 s,
  429 on excess), a **200-message catch-up window**, and **plain text only** — no rich text and
  no images, because images are the real table-growth vector and belong to the gallery where
  they are capped and kept out of the database entirely.
  The author label and cluster are **snapshot at write time** (non-negotiable #7), so a later
  rename cannot rewrite what the room saw. Moderation is a superadmin **soft hide**
  (`hidden_at`), never a delete; hidden rows stay for the audit trail and leave every read via
  the partial index's own predicate.
- **Why:** Redis is genuinely redundant here, and that is a property of this architecture
  rather than a shortcut: PGlite runs in-process and the deployment unit is a single container,
  so there is exactly one Node process. A broker exists to carry messages *between* processes;
  with one process there is nothing to carry. If this app ever runs several processes against
  external Postgres, the replacement is `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` — still no Redis, and only
  `chatBus.ts` changes, because nothing else knows how a message reaches another stream.
  SSE beat WebSockets on a repo-specific ground, not a general one: an SSE route stays
  exercisable through `app.request()` with no listening socket, which preserves the integration
  testing doctrine in AGENTS-testing.md §2, whereas `@hono/node-ws` would need an upgrade
  handler in `index.ts` and break "index.ts is the only file that opens a port". Sends are
  fine as POSTs, so bidirectionality buys nothing.
  Short-polling was rejected on measurement, not taste. Chat needs 3–8 s latency, which at 300
  phones is ~50 requests/s, and **every authenticated request already costs two writes before
  the handler runs**: `loadActor` calls `touchSession`, and for participants also
  `touchParticipantSeen`. That is ~100 writes/s of pure bookkeeping through PGlite's single
  serialized connection — the "blow up the database" scenario, caused by polling frequency
  rather than by chat data. Under SSE the same room costs one insert per message actually sent.
- **Impact:** New `chat_message` table (migration `0007_chat.sql` + its `snapshot.sql` twin),
  `db/schema/chat.ts`, `db/entities/chat.ts`, `views/chat.ts`, `routes-chat/`, `lib/chatBus.ts`,
  `lib/rateLimit.ts` — the first rate limiting of any kind in this API.
  **`compress()` is no longer applied to every path.** gzip buffers in order to compress, so on
  `text/event-stream` it converts a live stream into a stalled one; `app.ts` now consults
  `UNCOMPRESSED_PATHS`, and that list is exported so a test asserts membership rather than
  inferring it from response headers. ADR-034's measured board result is untouched, and the
  same list is where the gallery's binary renditions will go, since gzipping a WebP spends CPU
  to achieve nothing.
  A comment in `lib/cache.ts` now says, at the `store` declaration, that blobs must never go in
  it: `max: 5000` counts **entries** and there is no `sizeCalculation`, so 5,000 × 300 kB would
  be 1.5 GB of resident memory, silently.
  Tests: `tests/chat.test.ts` reads the SSE body as a stream through `app.request()` — proving
  the exact property the transport was chosen for — and covers backlog replay, live push,
  `Last-Event-ID` resume, the body cap and empty-body wording, the 429, cursor rejection, and
  hidden-message exclusion. `tests/rateLimit.test.ts` drives the bucket with an injected clock,
  because a test that sleeps two real seconds to prove a two-second rule is a test nobody runs
  twice. Three rules were added to `authorization-matrix.test.ts`, whose coverage gate would
  otherwise have failed the build — which is the gate working as intended.

### ADR-047 — The photo gallery: the client shrinks, the disk stores, the database only indexes

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** **fds.md §9.5 promotion** — this addendum covers two of its explicitly deferred
  entries, *"Photo/media features"* and *"Broadcast/display mode for leaderboard TVs"* (the photo
  wall), under the same *"document them separately if pursued later"* licence §9.5 grants. Also
  ADR-003 (PGlite in-process), ADR-031/041 (the canvas photo ladder), ADR-034 (gzip),
  ADR-038 (cached reads), ADR-040 (the recorded demo seed), ADR-043 (one container, one volume),
  ADR-046 (the compress carve-out this reuses).
- **Decision:** **No image byte enters the database.** Photos are files under a new
  `GALLERY_DATA_DIR` — `/data/gallery` in the container, beside PGlite, so the one volume stays
  the whole backup unit and a read-only root filesystem is satisfied. `gallery_photo` carries
  only metadata, and the row id *is* the directory name, so a row and its files share one
  UUIDv7. Serving copies `webStatic.ts` exactly: `createReadStream` → `Readable.toWeb`, with
  `content-length` and `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and **its traversal guard is
  re-made in `galleryStore.ts`** rather than assumed — resolve, then prefix-check against the
  root.
  **The client produces both renditions** (~1280 px full, ~256 px thumb, WebP) by reusing the
  canvas pipeline it already has for avatars. The server therefore needs no `sharp` and no
  native dependency. Three caps are enforced server-side and are what make "the volume cannot
  blow up" arithmetic rather than aspiration: 400 kB per rendition, 10 photos per participant,
  140 characters of caption. Uploads are multipart through Hono's own `c.req.formData()`, behind
  the **API's first `bodyLimit`**, and every upload is **magic-byte sniffed** — a declared
  content type is caller-controlled, and a non-image must never be handed back to three hundred
  phones under an image content type.
  Voting is a **like-toggle**: one row per (photo, participant) with a partial unique index
  `WHERE expires_at IS NULL`, so a double-tap is idempotent and un-voting *invalidates* rather
  than deletes. Participants may vote; staff may not. Moderation is **post-hoc**: photos appear
  immediately, any participant may **report** one (the PDPA-shaped case — being photographed
  without consent must not require finding a facilitator), and a superadmin **hides** it, which
  stops the bytes being served, not merely the listing.
- **Why:** The database-as-image-backend variant was assessed in
  `docs/design/photo-gallery-assessment.md` §7 and rejected on arithmetic. PGlite is one
  serialized in-process connection (ADR-003), so a hundred phones opening a 24-thumb grid cold
  is ~2,400 blob reads — seconds of solid queue during which **a facilitator cannot submit a
  match score**. The gallery would be able to stall the actual sports day. Against disk, the
  same burst costs zero database queries and the kernel page cache does the work the mitigated
  DB design would have needed two bespoke cache tiers to imitate.
  The client-side shrink is load-bearing rather than an optimisation: raw camera files are
  3–12 MB and would melt one laptop's uplink, while ~250 kB renditions will not. It pays a
  second dividend for free — **canvas re-encoding strips EXIF, including GPS**, so the step that
  saves bandwidth is also the privacy scrub for a public-service event.
- **Impact:** Migration `0008_gallery.sql` with its `snapshot.sql` twin (`gallery_photo`,
  `gallery_vote`, `gallery_report`), `db/schema/gallery.ts`, `db/entities/gallery.ts`,
  `views/gallery.ts`, `routes-gallery/`, `lib/galleryStore.ts`, and `GALLERY_DATA_DIR` in
  `env.ts` (ESLint bans `process.env` everywhere else).
  The compress carve-out from ADR-046 grew a second member and **changed shape to a predicate**:
  `/api/gallery/photos` is *also* the JSON listing and the upload route, both of which should
  still gzip, so only the `/{id}/{rendition}` blob beneath it is exempt. `skipsCompression()` is
  exported and asserted directly, including the negative cases, because a carve-out that
  silently widened would quietly undo ADR-034's measured board result.
  `lib/cache.ts` gained `GALLERY_TAG` for the listing's counts — and the "no blobs in this
  store" warning added in ADR-046 is precisely why the bytes are not cached there.
  **Two findings from writing the tests, both kept as tests.** A traversal attempt in the id
  position (`..%2F..%2Fsnapshot`) reached Postgres as a uuid and returned **500 with a driver
  error**; ids are now shape-checked before any query, so a malformed id is a clean 404. And the
  listing's vote tallies were written as correlated subqueries and silently returned **zero**;
  they are now two small indexed aggregates merged in the repository, which is both predictable
  and easier to read. A subquery per row is easy to write and easy to get quietly wrong.
  **Two console surfaces**, both promoting §9.5's "Broadcast/display mode": `/admin/photos` is the
  moderation queue — reported photos sorted first, hidden ones listed too (an unhide is impossible
  if they cannot be seen), and a hide that is **reversible**, because moderation nobody can undo is
  a decision nobody wants to make. `/admin/wall` is the projected wall: no shell, no navigation,
  one photo at a time on an 8 s timer, `object-fit: contain` because cropping somebody's photo on
  the big screen is the one thing a wall must not do. It asks for `top`, which is what makes it a
  reason to upload. Neither carries an avatar, a motif or a `gb-` class — `check-standards.mjs`
  rule 7 forbids participant styling on console surfaces, so the wall shows photos, captions and
  nicknames only.
  **The cost claim is measured rather than asserted.** `scripts/stress/personas.mjs` gained a
  `chat` and a `gallery` surface, weighted *into* the existing participant mix rather than added
  on top, since someone looking at photos is not also looking at the board. At 300 users over
  90 seconds: 4,252 requests, **zero failures**, gallery listing p90 10 ms, chat send p90 9 ms,
  and `POST /api/tournament/matches/:id/complete` — a facilitator's score write, the thing the
  whole disk-over-database decision exists to protect — at **p50 10 ms, p90 14 ms**. The gallery
  does not starve the event, and that is now a number rather than a paragraph.
  **Known follow-on, not yet done:** the demo seed (ADR-040) is a pure DB dump whose
  `demo-participants.dump.json` holds sprite strings, not image files, so a *seeded* gallery
  needs a seed-time upload step in `seed-demo.mjs` (which already replays HTTP). Recorded here
  rather than discovered later.

### ADR-048 — Photo bytes move into Postgres, with the mitigations that make it defensible

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** **Supersedes the storage half of ADR-047** (its routes, contracts, caps,
  moderation and surfaces are unchanged). Implements the alternative assessed in
  `docs/design/photo-gallery-assessment.md` §7, including its mitigations M1–M8. Also ADR-003
  (PGlite in-process), ADR-034 (gzip), ADR-038 (cached reads), ADR-043 (one container, one volume).
- **Decision:** Photo bytes are rows in Postgres, not files on disk. `GALLERY_DATA_DIR` is gone,
  and with it the second storage location — bytes now persist wherever the database does, which is
  the PGlite data directory in the container or an external server via `DATABASE_URL`.
  The assessment was explicit that this is defensible **only mitigated**, so the mitigations are
  part of the change rather than a follow-up:
  - **M1 — two tables.** `gallery_blob` is separate from `gallery_photo`, so a listing *physically
    cannot* read a byte. `payload` is `bytea` with `STORAGE EXTERNAL`: TOAST out-of-line, TOAST
    compression off, because WebP and JPEG are already compressed.
  - **M2 — raw-bytes route outside the JSON idiom.** Already true from ADR-047; the blob path stays
    in `skipsCompression()`, so bytes are never base64'd and never gzipped.
  - **M3 — the browser is tier one.** Responses carry `immutable` **and a strong `ETag`**, and a
    conditional request returns **304 with no body, having touched neither cache nor database**.
    The ETag is derived from the photo id and rendition, not from hashing the payload — hashing
    would mean reading the bytes in order to avoid reading the bytes.
  - **M4 — a byte-budgeted process cache as tier two.** `lib/blobCache.ts`, its own `LRUCache` with
    `maxSize` 64 MB and a `sizeCalculation`. Explicitly **not** `lib/cache.ts`, which counts
    *entries* (`max: 5000`) and would have become 1.5 GB of resident memory at 300 kB a photo —
    the assessment's R4. 64 MB is sized against the corpus: ~3,000 thumbs at ~20 kB is ~60 MB, so
    the whole thumbnail set, which is what a grid asks for, fits.
  - **M5 — the caps are unchanged and still the load-bearing wall**: 400 kB per rendition, 10 per
    participant, 140-character caption. The corpus is bounded by arithmetic.
  - **M6 — selection discipline made structural.** `entities/galleryBlobs.ts` exposes exactly ONE
    payload read, by `(photo_id, rendition)`, columns named. There is no "list blobs" and no bare
    `select()` in that file. Corpus size comes from `sum(byte_size)`, never `length(payload)`.
  - **M7 — lifecycle.** The demo seed replays HTTP and never dumps blobs, so ADR-040's artefact is
    unaffected. Post-event reclaim is `TRUNCATE gallery_blob` — instant, no `VACUUM FULL`.
- **Why:** Asked for directly. The gains are real and are what §7 listed: **transactional
  integrity** (a photo and its bytes commit or vanish together — there is no longer such a thing as
  an orphaned file, and the upload path no longer has to order two storage systems), **one backup
  unit** (dump the database and you have everything), **read-only-rootfs compliance for free**, and
  **no second storage abstraction** beside the Drizzle entities.
- **Impact — and the honest cost, measured.** `scripts/gallery-blob-spike.mjs` is mitigation M8,
  committed so the claim is reproducible. Against 200 distinct photos at concurrency 50:

  | | cold (empty cache) | warm (M4 populated) |
  |---|---|---|
  | thumb read p50 | 214 ms | 48 ms |
  | thumb read p95 | 476 ms | 53 ms |
  | write p95 during burst | 5.7 ms (8.2 ms quiet) | 5.3 ms (6.6 ms quiet) |
  | **write max during burst** | **1,128 ms** | **151 ms** |

  §7's decision rule was "score-write p95 unaffected during a cold-cache gallery burst". **It
  passes** — write p95 does not move, and across a 300-user 90-second run
  (`npm run stress`) the score write held p50 9 ms / p90 14 ms, matching the disk design's 10/14
  exactly, over 4,469 requests with zero failures.
  **But the tail tells the truth p95 hides, and it is a real regression against disk.** Head-of-line
  blocking does not shift a median; it puts *one* unlucky write behind the whole blob queue. Cold,
  that write waited **1.1 s** — against 17 ms quiet. On disk it would have waited for nothing,
  because a file read never enters the database's queue at all. So: **the two cache tiers are not
  polish, they are the feature.** M4 alone cuts the tail 7.5× (1,128 ms → 151 ms) and the cold read
  p50 4.5× (214 ms → 48 ms). Keep them, keep the grid lazy-loading, and keep the per-rendition cap
  low — those three together are what make a cold burst rare and survivable rather than routine.
  Re-run the spike whenever the caps, the cache budget, or the page size change.
- **Also fixed here, because the spike found it:** `app.onError` did not handle Hono's own
  `HTTPException`, so **every framework-level refusal became a 500**. It surfaced as an oversized
  upload answering "Something went wrong on our side." — blaming the server for the caller's
  mistake and telling a participant nothing actionable. `HTTPException` is now rendered into the
  standard error envelope with its own status, and the upload route's `bodyLimit` additionally
  reports **413** with owned copy from `@psd/contracts`. This was a latent bug across the whole
  API, not just the gallery, and it had no test; it has one now.

### ADR-049 — One schema file, no migrations, while the app is pre-production

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** **Replaces AGENTS-database.md §5's twin-file workflow** and AGENTS.md
  non-negotiable #5. Supersedes the migration halves of ADR-046, ADR-047 and ADR-048 (their schemas
  live on, in `snapshot.sql`).
- **Decision:** The nine numbered migrations are deleted. `apps/api/src/db/snapshot.sql` is the one
  schema definition, and schema changes edit it **in place**. `db/bootstrap.ts` applies it to any
  database that does not already have the schema — automatically on boot, and standalone via
  `npm run db:setup` (which replaces `npm run migrate`).
  Whether the schema is present is answered by asking Postgres (`to_regclass('public.cluster')`)
  rather than by a `schema_migrations` registry, which is also deleted. With one definition there is
  no version to track: either the tables are there or they are not. The check is idempotent, so the
  same call is safe on every boot.
  The demo seed needed nothing: it was always data rather than schema, and it drives the real HTTP
  API (ADR-040), so it is unaffected.
- **Why:** The app is pre-production. Nothing is deployed, so there was nothing to migrate *from* —
  which made the nine files a description of steps nobody would ever take again, and, worse, a
  second home for the schema and a second chance for it to drift. The twin-file rule existed to
  police exactly the drift that having two homes created.
  **The squash was verified, not assumed.** Two databases were built — one by applying all nine
  migrations in order, one from the snapshot alone — and `information_schema` was compared:
  **148 columns, 225 constraints and 50 indexes matched exactly.** The snapshot was already a
  faithful squash; the verification is what made deleting the originals a safe act rather than a
  hopeful one. The throwaway comparison script was removed with the migrations it compared, since a
  script that references a deleted directory is worse than a recorded result.
- **Impact:** Gone: `db/migrations/`, `db/migrate.ts`, `db/migrate-cli.ts`, the `schema_migrations`
  table, and `npm run migrate`. New: `db/bootstrap.ts`, `db/setup-cli.ts`, `npm run db:setup`.
  **`check-standards.mjs` rule 11 changed rather than disappeared.** It used to demand that every
  snapshot table appear in some migration. It now demands the opposite thing, which is the one worth
  policing: that every table Drizzle maps in `db/schema/` is actually created in the snapshot. That
  drift — code querying a table the database was never told to build — is a runtime failure the old
  twin rule never covered, and the new rule was checked by inducing the drift and watching it fail.
  It also refuses a reintroduced `migrations/` directory, so the decision cannot rot silently.
  `bootstrap.test.ts` now asserts what matters instead of a migration count: an empty database is
  provisioned and the schema is really usable afterwards, and a second call is a no-op.
- **When this must change back:** the first real deployment holding data anybody cares about. A live
  database cannot be handed a fresh snapshot, so a numbered chain earns its keep again at that
  moment — and AGENTS-database.md §5 says so, in those words, where the next person will read it.

### ADR-050 — Keep the original for Corporate, serve only the compressed copy

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** Extends ADR-047 (the gallery) and ADR-048 (bytes in Postgres). Builds on ADR-031's
  canvas pipeline.
- **Decision:** Every upload now carries three payloads and two new pieces of identity.
  - **`raw`** — the file exactly as the camera produced it, HEIC and all, stored as a third
    `gallery_blob` rendition and **never served to the gallery**. `GALLERY_RENDITIONS` (what a
    browser may request) stays `['full','thumb']` while `GALLERY_STORED_RENDITIONS` adds `raw`, so
    the public route cannot resolve `.../raw` at all — the separation is structural rather than a
    rule to remember. The only way a raw byte leaves the system is
    `GET /api/gallery/photos/:id/archive`, superadmin-only, which sets `content-disposition` with
    the original filename and deliberately **ignores `hidden_at`**: hidden means hidden from the
    event, not deleted, and an archive that silently dropped moderated photos would be the wrong
    archive. It also bypasses the blob cache, because a once-per-event bulk export has no business
    evicting the thumbs three hundred phones are reading.
  - **`original_filename`** on `gallery_photo`, kept unaltered so the archive is recognisable.
  - **`sha1_raw`** on `gallery_photo`, with a **globally unique index** — the duplicate guard.
  - **`raw_byte_size`**, so storage can be accounted without reading a payload.
  **Raw goes in its own blob row, not a new column beside the thumb.** A 12 MB archival payload
  sharing a row with a 20 KB thumb puts both in the same TOAST chain, and the served path — the hot
  one — would pay for the archive's presence. Separate rows keep ADR-048's single-key read cheap.
  **The compressed format is WebP, with JPEG fallback**, which is what `shrinkPhoto.ts` already
  did and what the assessment asked me to settle. iOS Safari has decoded WebP since 14 (2020) and
  every current Android Chrome does; it is ~30 % smaller than JPEG at equal quality. AVIF compresses
  ~20 % better again but needs iOS 16+/Android 12+ and encodes slowly in-browser — it would risk the
  oldest phone at the event for a margin nobody looking at a 256 px thumb can see. The check is on
  the encoder's *result* rather than a feature test, because a canvas asked for a type it cannot
  encode silently returns PNG, and a PNG of a photograph is larger than the JPEG we wanted.
  **Conversion stays on the phone.** Server-side HEIC decoding would need libheif or WASM on the
  same single-threaded event loop PGlite already runs on — the CPU three ADRs have been spent
  protecting. The device that shot the HEIC can already decode it (that is how it shows a preview),
  so it converts for free, and the server keeps needing no `sharp` and no native dependency on
  alpine. A browser that cannot decode the chosen file fails the upload with owned copy, which is
  the honest outcome: the alternative is archiving an original nobody can ever view.
- **Why:** Corporate wants publication-quality originals; the event wants bandwidth and IOPS. Those
  are not the same artefact, so the system now keeps both and is explicit about which is which.
- **Impact — and the number that should drive the next decision.** Archival changes the storage
  arithmetic by more than an order of magnitude: **300 uploaders × 10 photos × 12 MB ≈ 36 GB worst
  case**, against ~1 GB before. The cheapest lever is not the raw cap but
  `GALLERY_PHOTOS_PER_UPLOADER` — halving it halves the whole corpus. The request body ceiling grew
  to ~12.8 MB for the same reason, which is now dominated by the original rather than the thumbs.
  Dedup is **global**, not per-uploader: an identical file is the same photo however many people
  share it, and storing it twice buys nothing but 12 MB. The refusal message deliberately does not
  say who shared it first. SHA-1 rather than SHA-256 because this is a same-file check and not a
  security boundary — and it is computed **server-side**, since a hash the client supplies proves
  nothing about the bytes that arrived.
  **Two bugs found by the tests, both kept as tests.** `content-disposition` carries a
  participant-supplied filename, which is a header-injection vector — quotes, CRLF and control
  characters are now stripped, and the test asserts the real property (no second header, the quoted
  parameter not closed early) rather than cosmetics. And `/photos/:photoId/archive` was registered
  *after* `/photos/:photoId/:rendition`, so Hono matched the generic route first and `archive` was
  swallowed as a rendition name — it 404'd before its guard ever ran. Specific routes now precede
  the wildcard, with a comment saying why.
  **Consequence of ADR-049 worth knowing:** these are `NOT NULL` columns and there are no
  migrations, so an existing development database cannot be upgraded in place — recreate it
  (`npm run db:setup`, then `npm run seed:demo`). That is the trade ADR-049 made explicit.

### ADR-051 — A Postgres container, and `DATABASE_URL` as the only switch

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-003 (two drivers, one schema), ADR-043 (the single-container deployment),
  ADR-049 (boot provisioning is what makes a fresh server self-installing).
- **Decision:** **`DATABASE_URL` alone selects the driver.** Set it and the app connects to that
  server; leave it unset and the database is embedded PGlite. `DATABASE_DRIVER` still exists but is
  now optional and only overrides the inference.
  Two compose files, for two different jobs. `docker-compose.db.yml` runs a `postgres:17-alpine`
  server on `127.0.0.1:5432` for local development — one command, then `DATABASE_URL=… npm run dev`.
  `docker-compose.yml` gains that same server as a `db` service which the app waits on via
  `condition: service_healthy`, and **Postgres is now the deployed default** rather than PGlite.
  Connection strings are passed to `pg` unaltered: it parses `sslmode` itself, so a managed URL like
  Neon's `postgresql://…?sslmode=require&channel_binding=require` works with no bespoke TLS code and
  unknown provider parameters are simply ignored.
  There is no migration step anywhere in this. An empty database is provisioned from `snapshot.sql`
  on first boot (ADR-049), so `docker compose up` against a fresh volume is the entire install.
- **Why:** Requiring two variables to mean one thing is a trap, and the failure mode is bad in a
  specific way: forget `DATABASE_DRIVER` and the app starts happily on an embedded database nobody
  else can see, which looks like it worked. Inferring from the connection string makes the intent
  unambiguous. `env.ts` also now refuses `DATABASE_DRIVER=postgres` without a URL at startup, naming
  the missing variable, rather than failing at the first query.
  `depends_on: service_healthy` rather than plain `depends_on` because Postgres accepts connections a
  moment after its container exists, and provisioning a schema against a server that is still
  starting fails in a way that reads as a bug in the app.
- **Impact:** New `docker-compose.db.yml`; `docker-compose.yml` gains `db` and a `psd-pg` volume, and
  its db port is deliberately **not** published — the app reaches it over the compose network, and a
  database port on an event laptop is an invitation nobody needs.
  **A new opt-in test covers the driver we actually deploy on.** Everything else runs on PGlite,
  which left `node-postgres` with no automated coverage at all — and the drivers genuinely differ
  where it hurts: `pg` returns a `Buffer` for `bytea` and PGlite a `Uint8Array`, so a photo that
  round-trips perfectly in the suite could still come back corrupt in production.
  `apps/api/src/tests/postgres-driver.test.ts` runs when `PSD_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is set and asserts
  exactly that round trip, with the byte sequences a naive text path mangles.
  **Two ergonomics bugs found by running it rather than reasoning about it:** `.env.example`
  hard-coded `DATABASE_DRIVER=pglite`, and `scripts/dev.mjs` loads that file — so an explicit value
  won and setting `DATABASE_URL` silently did nothing. And `index.ts` logged
  `env.DATABASE_DRIVER`, which is now optional, so it would have printed `undefined`; it logs the
  resolved driver instead, which is what made the first bug visible at all.
- **Verified against a real server, not just typechecked:** the container reported healthy in 4 s,
  `npm run db:setup` created 19 tables and seeded 16 clusters from an empty database and was a no-op
  on the second run, and the app booted reporting `driver: postgres` from `DATABASE_URL` alone. Then
  end to end on that server: signup, sign-in, an upload carrying a HEIC original, both the served
  rendition and the archival original returned **byte-identical**, the duplicate refused 409, a chat
  message delivered over SSE, and the leaderboard served.

### ADR-052 — Fit an oversized original instead of handing the problem back

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** Extends ADR-050 (the archival original) and is a **deliberate, recorded exception**
  to its "keep the original unaltered" rule. Uses ADR-031's canvas pipeline.
- **Decision:** A file over `GALLERY_RAW_MAX_BYTES` is no longer refused. The phone walks a ladder
  until a copy fits, and only refuses if the whole ladder fails:
  1. **Quality first, at full resolution** — re-encode at 0.92, then 0.85, then 0.75.
  2. **Then resolution** — scale by 0.95 progressively, at the lowest quality.
  3. **Floor: the served rendition size.** The ladder stops once the longest edge would fall below
     `GALLERY_FULL_SIZE` (1280 px).
  `archiveAttempts(sourceLongestEdge)` is pure data with no canvas in it, so the ladder can be
  reasoned about and tested directly — above all that it **terminates**.
  The archive copy's **filename gains the new extension** (`IMG_4242.HEIC` → `IMG_4242.webp`),
  because a `.HEIC` that is no longer HEIC misleads every tool pointed at the archive. And
  `raw_is_original` is stored and shown in the moderation console, so the archive never claims to be
  pristine when it is not.
- **Why:** Refusing means trusting whoever is holding the phone to resize a photo on a beach, which
  in practice means the archive simply does not get that photo. A fitted copy at full resolution is
  worth far more than a refusal.
  **PNG gets exactly one rung, for a lossless source only — and the first draft of this ADR got that
  wrong.** It claimed PNG is never useful. Measured in Chromium with the same `toBlob` the app uses:

  | source | → PNG | → WebP q0.92 |
  |---|---|---|
  | 3.4 MB JPEG, 2752×1536 | 9.0 MB (**2.68×**) | 1.0 MB |
  | 104 kB JPEG, 746×560 | 800 kB (**7.71×**) | 108 kB |
  | 2.9 MB PNG, 1024×1024 | 2.24 MB (**0.77×**) | 198 kB |

  For a **lossy** original PNG is hopeless, and worse than the original claim suggested — the file is
  already over the cap and PNG multiplies it. But an **already-lossless** original re-encodes
  *smaller*, and if it fits then it is a strictly better archive than any lossy copy, because
  Corporate gets the pixels exactly. That is worth one attempt. So a PNG source now gets a PNG rung
  before the quality ladder, detected from the file's own magic bytes, and a lossy source skips it.
  What PNG genuinely lacks is a way to *ask* for compression from a browser. The format has plenty —
  DEFLATE level, per-scanline filters, colour type, interlacing — but `canvas.toBlob` applies its
  quality argument to lossy formats only, verified here as byte-identical output at 0.1 and at the
  default. A hand-rolled encoder over `CompressionStream('deflate')` could reach those settings;
  rejected, because it would buy perhaps 5–20 % on a format that measured **11× larger than WebP** on
  the same image, in exchange for an encoder in the bundle and heavy CPU on the phone.
  **Quality before resolution** matters because of how far quality goes: the e2e case is a 13 MB
  file that became a **345 kB WebP at full resolution**. A PNG-first or downres-first ladder would
  have thrown away pixels to reach a size that quality alone comfortably reached.
  **The floor is the served rendition, not an arbitrary fraction.** An earlier draft floored at 20 %
  of the original, and a test exposed what that means: an 800 px "archive" *smaller than the 1280 px
  copy the gallery already hands out on tap* — worthless to Corporate and to everyone else. Below
  that size, refusing is the useful answer.
- **Impact:** `shrinkPhoto.ts` gains `archiveAttempts`, `archiveFilenameFor` and `fitArchive`;
  `ShrunkPhoto` gains `rawIsOriginal`, which the client sends and the server records in a new
  `gallery_photo.raw_is_original` column (default true, so silence means "original" — what every
  client before this ADR did). The server treats the flag as **provenance, not a guarantee**: it
  cannot verify the claim, nothing is authorised by it, and the worst a wrong value does is mislabel
  one archive row.
  The archive cap itself is unchanged and still enforced server-side; this only changes what the
  client does *before* hitting it.
  **The participant is not told.** That is the point of the feature — the alternative is the
  interruption this ADR exists to remove — and the provenance is recorded where it matters, on the
  moderation console rather than in a dialog on a beach.
  Tests: nine unit tests over the ladder and the encode decisions, driven through a canvas double
  because jsdom has no canvas, plus an e2e that feeds a genuine 13 MB file through a real browser's
  real encoder — the only place the actual `toBlob` behaviour can be observed. Writing them caught
  two things: the floor problem above, and that a naive test double makes the *rendition* cap fire
  before the archive ladder ever runs.

### ADR-053 — The recorded crowd's avatars are misframed, and why the seed harness could not see it

- **Status:** Accepted (tooling and findings; the framing defect is **closed by ADR-054**)
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-031 (the canvas photo ladder), ADR-033/036 (model cut-out and the manual
  square), ADR-037 (128×128 sprites), ADR-040 (the recorded demo seed), ADR-045 (the device ladder),
  AGENTS-workflow.md §4b.
- **Decision (tooling):** `apps/web/scripts/avatar-align-check.ts` renders a few recorded avatars at
  512 px beside their source photographs, with the crop rectangle drawn on the photo.
  `seed-sprite-compare.ts` already rendered all eighty, but at ~64 px a row — enough to audit colour
  drift, far too small to see *where* a crop landed, which is why misframing survived it.
  `demo:record` gains `PSD_DEMO_LIMIT` (record the first N personas) and now uses **one browser
  context with a fresh page per persona** instead of a context each. A context per persona threw away
  the HTTP cache, so under `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL` the MODNET weights were re-fetched and the runtime
  re-initialised **eighty times** — the reason a real-model recording took an hour, and the reason its
  per-photo budget was 180 s. Both changes exist so the recording can be iterated on in seconds;
  a defect in an hour-long job does not get investigated.
- **Finding (open defect, product code not just the seed):** MODNET's cut-outs are good — background
  cleanly removed on this engine, confirmed by `e2e/model-available.spec.ts`. **The framing is wrong.**
  `headBoxFromMask` infers a head from the silhouette alone, and that inference holds for exactly one
  shape:
  - a **bust** — head above shoulders — is framed correctly;
  - framed **head-to-waist**, the neck search window (35–80 % of the subject's height) lies entirely
    inside the torso, no pinch is found, and the "head" becomes the whole person: one avatar is a
    plate of chicken rice;
  - with a **raised arm**, the topmost mask pixel is the hand holding the phone, everything is
    measured from there, and the avatar is a hand.
  This affects **real participants**, not only the seed: an arm's-length selfie is the commonest
  photo a phone takes, and it produces a picture of the user's hand.
- **Why it is recorded rather than fixed:** an attempt to fix it — skip thin appendages, find the neck
  as the first pinch-then-flare below the crown — passed synthetic-silhouette unit tests and then
  **regressed the one real photo that had been correct**, turning a good head-and-shoulders into a
  torso with a bowl of noodles. Idealised circles and rectangles do not represent real masks, where
  arms, bowls and held food create width variation everywhere. It was reverted rather than shipped.
  The honest conclusion is that **silhouette-only head-finding is a dead end**: a mask says where a
  *person* is, never where a *face* is.
- **The way forward:** a real locator instead of a heuristic. Keypoints are the strong fit — a pose
  model (`rtmlib-ts`, Apache 2.0, 17 keypoints including nose, eyes, ears and shoulders, on the ONNX
  Runtime Web this app already ships for MODNET) gives the head centre *and* the shoulder width that
  `HEAD_SHARE` and `EYE_LINE` already expect, and is immune to all three failures above: a wrist is
  labelled a wrist. A dedicated face detector (BlazeFace-class, ~1 MB) is the lighter alternative but
  gives no shoulders. Two things to measure before committing: the **model download size**, against
  ADR-047's beach-Wi-Fi budget, and the **Safari floor** — rtmlib-ts states Safari 16.4+, and ADR-041
  made iOS Safari first-class, so anything older needs a fallback to today's behaviour or ADR-036's
  manual square.

### ADR-054 — Find the face with a face detector, and make "not found" honest

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-031 (the canvas photo ladder), ADR-033 (the MODNET cut-out), ADR-034 (the
  crop-source ladder), ADR-036 (the manual square), ADR-041/044 (iOS Safari is first-class),
  ADR-045 (the device ladder), ADR-053 (which recorded this defect as open). **Supersedes ADR-034's
  crop ladder** and closes ADR-053's open item.
- **Decision:** Locate the face with `@mediapipe/tasks-vision`'s **Face Detector** (BlazeFace
  **full range**, Apache-2.0), loaded from a CDN at run time and warmed in the background. The crop is
  built from the detector's **eye keypoints**, not its box: eye midpoint gives the centre and
  **inter-ocular distance** gives the scale. MODNET keeps its job — the cut-out — and loses the one it
  was never able to do. `headBoxFromMask` is **deleted**, not demoted: it is the defect. When no face
  is found the participant is sent straight to ADR-036's manual square.
- **Why keypoints rather than the bounding box:** `HEAD_SHARE` (0.72) and `EYE_LINE` (0.52) are stated
  in terms of the eye line and head height, so eye keypoints answer the question the framing constants
  actually ask. Inter-ocular distance is also the **steadiest scale in a photograph** — adult
  interpupillary distance is ~63 mm against a ~230 mm chin-to-crown head, so crop size is
  `3.65 / 0.72 ≈ 5.07 ×` inter-ocular — and unlike shoulder width it does not move with clothing,
  posture or a raised arm. It shrinks under yaw, so the detector box height is kept as a **floor**: a
  profile face is framed a little wide rather than cropped into.
- **Why the failure now routes to the manual square:** the bug was never only a bad guess, it was a
  **silent** bad guess. `AvatarStudio.tsx` read
  `needsHelp = refined === null && quick.crop === null`, so a *successful MODNET mask suppressed the
  offer of help* — yet a mask says where a person is and never where a face is. A participant got a
  picture of their own hand, presented as finished, with no hint anything had failed and no route to
  fix it. It is now `quick.crop === null`: **nothing found a face, so ask.** A visible failure the user
  can correct beats a plausible-looking wrong answer, and both fallbacks already exist and are tested
  (`PhotoCropper`/`cropBox.ts`, and drawn archetypes as the signup default).
- **The download, measured rather than remembered** (brotli, as a CDN serves it):

  | | wire |
  |---|---|
  | `vision_bundle.mjs` | 38 kB |
  | `vision_wasm_internal.js` | 64 kB |
  | `vision_wasm_internal.wasm` | 2.40 MB |
  | `blaze_face_full_range.tflite` | 1.03 MB |
  | **added** | **~3.5 MB** |

  Against what the studio **already** fetches — `transformers.min.js` 166 kB, ORT
  `ort-wasm-simd-threaded.jsep.wasm` 4.54 MB, MODNET `model_quantized.onnx` 6.63 MB, **~11.3 MB** —
  this is **+31 %**, not a doubling. The package's advertised 36.8 MB unpacked is three WASM variants;
  exactly one is fetched. Acceptable because the weights download in the **background** and the studio
  is reached after sign-up, so nothing on the critical beach path waits for them.
- **Full range rather than short range, because the short one was measured and failed.** Short range
  is the intuitive pick — it is documented for faces "within 2 metres", which sounds exactly like a
  selfie — and on this corpus it found **no face at all in 7 of the 14** social photographs: every
  landscape one, where the person is in a scene rather than filling the frame. Full range found
  exactly one face in **13 of 14** at the default 0.5 confidence, for 1.03 MB instead of 224 kB.
  Lowering short range's confidence to 0.2 to rescue it is a worse trade, also measured: at 0.2 the
  detector reported **ten** faces in one photograph and found a face in the **PSD logo**. The single
  remaining miss gets the manual square, which is the honest outcome, not a failure. Recorded because
  the first choice here was made from the model's name and was wrong — the same mistake in miniature
  as ADR-053's, and caught only by running it over real photographs.
- **Why MediaPipe over the alternatives.** `rtmlib-ts` would ride the ONNX Runtime Web we already load
  and so cost only weights, which is a real advantage — but it is a single-author dev.to project
  against a Google-published package (1.0.1, Apache-2.0), and a pose model answers a much bigger
  question than "where is the face". ADR-053 reached for shoulders; that turned out to be unnecessary,
  because **MODNET's mask already supplies body extent**, and inter-ocular distance is a better scale
  than shoulder width anyway. `@tensorflow-models/blazeface` was ruled out on maintenance (last
  published 2023) and `face-detection` can use the MediaPipe runtime regardless, so it is baggage with
  no unique benefit.
- **The old Safari floor is deliberately not defended.** Per product direction, browsers too old for
  the detector's WASM get the two fallbacks that already ship: drawn archetype avatars, or their photo
  with a square they place themselves. No third path is built for them.
- **Found while measuring, and deliberately NOT acted on:** MediaPipe's own `selfie_segmenter.tflite`
  is **244 kB** against MODNET's 6.63 MB, so one MediaPipe stack could replace the whole
  transformers.js + ORT + MODNET chain — **~2.97 MB in place of ~11.3 MB**, 3.8× cheaper, one runtime
  instead of two. It is recorded and not taken: MODNET's matte quality is *verified good* on this
  corpus, the swap would rewrite ADR-045's device ladder and `e2e/model-available.spec.ts`, and
  trading a known-good cut-out for an unmeasured one is not part of fixing the framing. Worth a
  measured comparison of the two mattes before anyone spends the saving.
- **Impact:** `headBoxFromMask`, `neckRow` and `maskRows` are gone from `photoSprite.ts`, with their
  tests. `photoToSprite` no longer invents a crop from a silhouette. New `lib/avatar/locateFace.ts`
  mirrors `segmentPhoto.ts`'s shape — CDN import behind a loader seam, module-level `pending`, a
  `forget*` seam, and **never throws**: every failure is a reason to ask for the square, not to lose
  the photo. `e2e/photo-sprites.spec.ts` test **1b flips**: the iOS shape (model, no browser detector)
  used to assert `HINTS.refined` with the cropper hidden — it asserted the defect, over all eighty
  photos — and now asserts the detector frames the face. Test 1 gains an injected detector so
  "never demanded" is true by construction rather than by host luck. The seed is re-recorded with
  `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1` and checked with `avatar-align-check.ts`.

### ADR-055 — Give the backdrop back to photo avatars

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-028 (shirt and backdrop as free colours), ADR-031 (the photo sprite pipeline),
  ADR-032/033 (colour and model background removal), ADR-034 (which hid these controls),
  ADR-054 (the face locator, and the sprite-palette surgery this reuses).
- **Decision:** When a participant's avatar is a photograph, the studio offers the **backdrop**
  colour and nothing else. Picking one rewrites the sprite's backdrop palette entry in place, so the
  picture changes with the choice. Hair, skin, shirt, build and persona stay hidden.
- **Why the backdrop is different from the rest:** ADR-034 hid every colour control behind a photo on
  the grounds that "a photo is not a character" — hair and shirt are *photograph*, not layers the
  studio can repaint, so offering those controls would offer something that does nothing. That
  reasoning was right and still is. It simply stopped being true of the backdrop once background
  removal shipped: `photoToSprite` paints the cut-out cells from the sprite's own palette, so there
  is a real backdrop behind the person and it is the one colour in a photo sprite the participant
  genuinely owns. The control was disabled for a condition that no longer holds.
- **Why the palette is rewritten rather than the pipeline re-run:** the source photograph is
  deliberately discarded (ADR-031) — nothing is uploaded and nothing is kept but the sprite — so a
  sprite restored from a draft has no pixels left to re-derive from. `photoToSprite` always emits
  its palette as `[...colours taken from the photograph, backdrop, ink]`, making the backdrop the
  second-to-last entry *by construction*, so `recolourSpriteBackdrop` in `@psd/contracts` swaps it
  with pure string surgery: no canvas, no model, no decode, and it works for a photo taken in an
  earlier session. It re-parses before and after, so a malformed swatch can never corrupt a stored
  avatar.
- **One handler, one `onChange`:** the look and the sprite must move together, because a photo
  sprite carries its backdrop baked in — changing the look alone would leave the picture showing the
  old colour. `setBackdrop` therefore commits both in a single `onChange`; two calls would race and
  the second would overwrite the first. The drawn-avatar swatches route through the same handler, so
  there is one code path rather than two that must agree.
- **Impact:** new `recolourSpriteBackdrop` in `packages/contracts/src/sprites.ts` (5 unit tests,
  including that the pixels are untouched and that a bad swatch is refused); `AvatarStudio` renders a
  single `ColourRow` for a photo avatar and routes both cases through `setBackdrop`; one acceptance
  test asserts the row is offered, that hair and shirt are still absent, and that the rendered
  preview actually changes. The sprite wire format is unchanged, so avatars already stored stay
  readable — a recoloured sprite is simply a different sprite, and ADR-035 already addresses sprites
  by a hash of their contents.

### ADR-056 — Show the square on the face we found, and let the participant confirm it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-031 (the photo pipeline), ADR-033 (the MODNET cut-out), ADR-036 (the manual
  square), ADR-040 (the recorded demo seed), ADR-053 (the misframing), ADR-054 (the face locator).
  **Supersedes ADR-036's "shown only when nothing could find the face".**
- **Decision:** After every photo conversion the studio shows the photograph with the crop square
  **already sitting on the face the detector found**. Accepting it is one tap; correcting it is a
  drag. When nothing found a face the square opens in the middle of the frame, as before. The
  "Choose the square myself" button is gone, because the square is no longer something you have to
  ask for.
- **Why this is better than ADR-054's "ask only when nothing was found":** that was still a system
  deciding *for* the participant whenever it was confident, and confidence is exactly what was wrong
  before — ADR-053's avatars were produced confidently. Showing the square makes the detector's
  answer **reviewable**: the participant sees where it framed them before committing. The dishonest
  case disappears rather than being handled, and the good case costs one tap.
- **`photoToBox`, the inverse of `boxToPhoto`:** the detector answers in photo coordinates and the
  participant drags in screen coordinates, so the box has to be handed over in theirs. Seeding
  happens on mount *and* on the image's `load` event, because the surface has no real size until the
  photo has laid out — in `useState` the frame is still the 240 px placeholder.
- **A latent bug this exposed, and the fix.** `useCrop` rebuilt the sprite **without the model's
  mask**, so adjusting the square silently discarded the background removal and fell back to the
  colour rules, which cannot cut a hawker centre out from behind anybody. It was already reachable
  through "choose the square myself"; making the square the normal path made it happen to every
  photo. `PhotoRefinement` now carries the `SubjectMask` and `useCrop` reuses it — the same pixels,
  so re-running the model would be a second download and inference for a crop the participant merely
  nudged. **Found by rendering the recorded seed and looking at it, not by a test.** Every unit and
  acceptance test passed throughout, because none re-cropped after a successful model run and then
  examined the background.
- **The regression test for it had to be fixed twice, which is the lesson worth keeping.** The first
  version asserted backdrop corners on the default stub photo — *a face on a plain wall* — which the
  colour rules cut out perfectly, so it passed with the bug deliberately reintroduced. A test that
  does not fail on the bug it was written for is worth nothing. It now installs a **busy** photograph,
  where ADR-032's rules correctly refuse to guess, so backdrop corners can only come from the mask.
  Verified by putting the bug back and watching it fail.
- **The recorder accepts a good crop and drops a bad one.** It waits for the square, then taps "use"
  when a face was found; when none was, it clears the photo and the persona keeps its drawn archetype.
  Blindly tapping "use" is what put an arm holding a phone on the seeded crowd, and demanding
  `HINTS.refined` for all eighty made one unframeable photograph abort the whole recording — that is
  asserting a model's recall rather than the app's behaviour. The dump therefore allows a null
  `avatarPhoto` (the contract is already `.nullish()`), and asserts only that the crowd is at least
  80 % photographic.
- **Measured result of the whole ADR-053 → 056 arc:** all 80 personas re-recorded with the real
  Transformers.js/MODNET and the real BlazeFace in **4.0 minutes** (it was an hour before ADR-053's
  shared-context fix). **75 of 80** wear a correctly framed photo avatar; **5 keep archetypes**, and
  they are precisely the adversarial photographs — `social-02-male` (shot upside down; BlazeFace does
  not detect inverted faces), `26-leaning-overhead`, `29-distant-group-crop`, `55-reading-down` and
  `59-tiny-face-wide-scene`. Checked by eye with `avatar-align-check.ts`, which gained an **offset**
  argument for exactly this reason: the interesting photographs are never the first few.
- **The diagnostic stopped drawing its crop rectangle.** It drew `FAKE_FACE_DETECTOR`'s hardcoded box,
  honest only for a *stubbed* recording; against a real one that rectangle is fiction, and a box drawn
  in the wrong place invites precisely the confident wrong conclusion the script exists to prevent.
  The dump stores sprites, not crops, so the true box is not recoverable there — the sprite beside its
  source is the evidence.

### ADR-057 — The sprite grid is as big as the data says, never a constant

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-026 (the 64×64 drawn art), ADR-031 (photo sprites), **ADR-037** (which made
  photo sprites 128×128), ADR-054/056 (the framing work that made this visible).
- **Decision:** `rectsFor`, `blockAt` and `svgOf` in `lib/avatars.ts` take their grid size from
  `rows.length` — the sprite's own size — instead of `ART_SIZE`. The drawn-character path now goes
  through `svgOf` too, so there is one place that decides a viewBox rather than two.
- **The defect:** `ART_SIZE` is 64, the size of the hand-drawn art. `avatarSvg` rendered a *photo*
  sprite through the same helpers, whose comment read "a photo sprite is already a finished picture:
  **same size**, same renderer" — true when it was written, and false from ADR-037 onward. So for
  every real photo avatar the scanner read only `x 0–63, y 0–63` of 128-wide rows and emitted
  `viewBox="0 0 64 64"`: one quadrant of the sprite, stretched over the whole frame. Measured on a
  seeded sprite, the region it drew was **28 % subject** against **54 %** for the sprite as a whole,
  and the head's centre sits at x ≈ 64 — exactly the boundary it cut. Participants saw a corner of
  their own head.
- **Why the whole avatar test suite missed it, which is the part worth keeping:** the existing photo
  test builds its fixture with `formatAvatarSprite({ size: 64, … })`. A 64×64 sprite renders
  perfectly under a 64×64 assumption, so the test could not fail however wrong the renderer was.
  **A fixture that no longer resembles production data is a test that cannot fail.** The new test
  uses a 128×128 sprite with a colour that exists *only* in the bottom-right quadrant and asserts
  both that colour and its exact rect (`M96 96h32v32h-32z`), so the whole grid must have been read.
  Confirmed by restoring the old behaviour and watching it fail.
- **Also worth noting:** `avatar-align-check.ts` could never have caught this. It decodes sprites with
  `parseAvatarSprite` and rasterises them itself, so it proves the *stored* sprites are right and says
  nothing about how the app draws them. The framing was fixed and verified while the renderer was
  still broken — two different bugs with the same symptom, "the avatars look wrong".
- **Impact:** one renderer, both call sites; `claim()` gains a `size` parameter. Any sprite size in
  `AVATAR_SPRITE_SIZES` (64 and 128) now renders correctly, so old 64×64 sprites stored before
  ADR-037 keep working.

### ADR-058 — Supply Web Storage in tests when the environment does not

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-009 (the offline queue owns localStorage), ADR-019 (surface memory),
  `check-standards.mjs` rule 8 (`storage-ownership`).
- **Decision:** `apps/web/src/test-setup.ts` installs a standards-compliant in-memory `Storage` for
  `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` **only when the global is absent**. `storage-ownership` names
  that file as exempt, alongside the two modules that own storage keys.
- **Why:** measured on vitest 3.2.7 + jsdom 27.4.0, exactly as the lockfile pins them — inside a
  test `window === globalThis` and both storages read as `undefined`, while the same jsdom driven
  directly returns a working `Storage`:
  `new JSDOM('<p>x</p>', { url: 'http://localhost:3000' }).window.localStorage`. jsdom 27 exposes
  storage as a per-instance accessor and vitest's environment copies window properties onto the
  global before it resolves, so a getter returning `undefined` is what lands. It took out **86 tests
  across 14 files** — the offline scan queue, the sprite cache, the backdrop choice and surface
  memory — and it reproduces at a clean `HEAD`, with `--no-cache`, in and out of the sandbox.
- **Why this restores coverage rather than hiding a defect:** production already tolerates missing
  storage deliberately. `lib/storage/localStore.ts` reads `window.localStorage` inside `attempt(...)`
  and degrades to null, so a Safari private window costs a participant nothing. With no Storage in
  tests, every assertion that something *was* persisted fails outright, and every
  graceful-degradation test passes for the wrong reason. Supplying the standard object makes both
  honest again.
- **Why the standards exemption is not a weakening:** rule 8 exists so *product* code cannot scatter
  storage keys. This file owns no key — it supplies the object itself, the opposite concern — and it
  is test-only by construction: `vite.config.ts` loads it as `setupFiles` and no `src` module imports
  it. It is named explicitly only because it is not a `*.test.ts`, which the rule already skips.
- **Impact:** installed conditionally, so the day either dependency fixes this the real
  implementation wins and this becomes dead weight to delete. Worth re-checking on the next vitest or
  jsdom bump.

### ADR-059 — One avatar source at a time, and a character to come back to

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-027 (traits folded away at sign-up), ADR-031 (photo avatars), ADR-034 (which
  hid the trait controls behind a photo), ADR-055 (backdrop for photo avatars), ADR-057 (the renderer
  fix that made a worn photo visible at all).
- **Decision:** While a photo avatar is worn, the studio shows **no "Use a photo" and no "Take a
  selfie"** — only a **"Remove my photo"** button, *disabled* until the participant has chosen a
  character to fall back to. The character pictures stay on show for exactly that purpose. The
  preview keeps showing the **photo**, and the backdrop swatches stay available (ADR-055). Hair,
  skin, shirt and build remain hidden, as ADR-034 established.
- **Why:** two pickers beside a worn photo invite the question "which of these am I actually
  wearing?", and nothing on the screen answered it. Removing the alternatives makes the current
  source unambiguous: to change photo you take the old one off, which is one more tap and one less
  thing to misread. Gating removal on a chosen character encodes the rule that **an avatar is never
  nothing** — the disabled button says "pick a character first" without needing a sentence to say it.
- **Choosing a character no longer discards the photo.** `setPersona` used to call `onChange` with a
  fresh object omitting `avatarPhoto`, so it dropped the photograph by omission. Harmless while the
  character row was hidden behind a photo; actively wrong now that it is visible, because the
  character is a *destination* the participant is lining up, not a change they have asked for yet. It
  spreads the draft and the photo survives until "Remove my photo" is pressed.
- **Impact on the suites, which is the interesting part.** The corpus tests walk **eighty**
  photographs through a single studio, and the picker is gone after the first — so `convert()` in
  `photo-sprites.spec.ts` and `model-available.spec.ts` now takes the previous photo off (choose a
  character, remove) before setting the next file. That is the real swap flow a participant follows,
  so the corpus exercises it eighty times per availability rather than once. The demo recorder does
  the same on its five unframeable photographs. Two acceptance tests asserted the old contract —
  characters hidden while a photo is worn, removal immediate — and now assert the new one, including
  that the preview stays a photo after a character is chosen.
- **Not changed:** the seed still records 75 photo avatars and 5 archetypes out of 80, re-recorded
  through this flow with the real models in 3.9 minutes.
- **"Change my look" opened on the wrong avatar, which is a second bug with the same symptom.** The
  draft was built from `avatarVariant` and `avatarLook` only, so a participant wearing a photograph
  opened the studio and saw their **drawn character** — and saving from there dropped the photograph
  without a word. The draft now leaves `avatarPhoto` `undefined`, meaning *"whatever is worn"*, and
  `withWornPhoto` resolves it on **every render** rather than snapshotting it when the button is
  pressed: the sprite body arrives asynchronously (the profile row carries only `avatarPhotoId`,
  ADR-035), so a snapshot taken a moment too early would seed an empty studio and then save it.
  `null` still means "removed", which keeps all three states expressible.
- **The lookup has to happen inside the shell, and getting that wrong is invisible.** `SpriteProvider`
  is mounted inside `GameboyShell`, which `ProfilePage` *renders* — so a `useSprite` call in
  `ProfilePage`'s own body sits **above** the provider and reads no context. It does not throw: it
  returns null, which is indistinguishable from "this participant has no photo". The first attempt at
  this fix therefore passed a new unit test and still showed the drawn character in the running app.
  The studio and its lookup now live in a `LookEditor` component rendered *inside* the shell.
  **Only looking at the real app caught it** — worth remembering next to ADR-057, where a stale test
  fixture hid the same class of mistake.

### ADR-060 — Say something useful, and mark what is actually worn

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-027/034 (the studio's controls), ADR-031/033 (the photo pipeline),
  ADR-055 (backdrop for photo avatars), ADR-056 (confirming the square), ADR-059 (one avatar source
  at a time).
- **Decision (copy):** the studio's status line describes what the participant can do or what just
  happened, never how it works. Gone: *"Your photo never leaves this phone — it becomes a 128×128
  sprite here, and only the sprite is saved"*, *"by the cut-out model"*, *"Still all on your phone"*,
  *"the cut-out model was not available"*, *"first time takes a moment while it downloads"*. A
  participant cannot act on any of it.
- **The old copy was also in the wrong place.** `idle` means "nothing is happening", which covers two
  opposite situations: no photo yet, and a photo restored from the saved avatar when the studio opens.
  Both got the no-photo sentence, so somebody already wearing a photograph was told their photo
  "never leaves this phone and becomes a 128×128 sprite" — describing the implementation instead of
  answering the only question that screen raises, which is how to get rid of it. `hintFor` now
  distinguishes them, and a worn photo says **"Pick a character below if you want to remove your
  photo."**
- **Decision (selection):** the character row shows **what is worn**, so a worn photo gets a box of
  its own at the front of it, captioned "My photo", and that box holds the selection. Reported from
  the running app: previously a character was always drawn as `aria-pressed`, so a participant
  wearing a photograph was shown a character they were *not* wearing, marked as chosen. Choosing a
  character moves the selection there without taking the photo off (ADR-059) — "Remove my photo"
  commits it — and pressing the photo box again is how you change your mind, which also re-disables
  removal. Its own `data-testid` (`avatar-studio__photo-option`) matters: sharing the row's testid
  would make every existing `.first()` click in the suites hit the photo instead of a character.
- **Measured, because the screenshot suggested otherwise:** choosing a character does **not** recolour
  a worn photo. The rendered sprite is byte-identical before and after, checked in the running app.
  `personaLook` does change the *look's* backdrop, which is what the participant gets when the photo
  finally comes off, and the sprite keeps its own baked backdrop until `setBackdrop` rewrites it
  (ADR-055).
- **Impact:** `PHOTO_HINT` rewritten and `HINTS` in `e2e/photo-stubs.ts` with it (plus a `worn` entry);
  six acceptance assertions updated to the new strings; `hintFor` takes the photo rather than a
  boolean, because `check-standards.mjs` rightly bans flag parameters. One new acceptance test pins
  the selection contract end to end: photo pressed and no character on open, selection moving on a
  character click with the photo still worn, and the photo box taking it back.

### ADR-061 — Every participant is called something, and it is not "Trainer"

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-007 (the cluster catalogue this copies), ADR-019 (participant identity),
  ADR-049 (one schema file, no migrations), `fds.md` §2.1 #obj-participant.
- **Decision:** a hundred energetic words live in `PARTICIPANT_TITLES` (`@psd/contracts`), are seeded
  into a `participant_title` table at bootstrap, and one is assigned **at random on sign-up** to
  every participant. `participant.title` is `NOT NULL` and a foreign key to that table. The word is
  shown wherever the app used to say "Trainer".
- **A table, not a Postgres `enum` and not a bare text column.** A row can be added by seeding where
  an `enum` value needs a schema change; a foreign key makes a typo impossible where free text does
  not; and the words are data the organisers may want to read or extend. This is exactly the shape
  `cluster` already has (ADR-007) — catalogue in code, table in the database, seeded at bootstrap,
  not runtime-editable — so it needed no new pattern.
- **Assigned in the repository, beside `newId()`.** `createParticipant` mints the title the same way
  it mints the id, so no route can create an untitled participant and no client can choose one: a
  `title` in a sign-up payload is ignored, which has its own test. `NewParticipant.title` exists only
  so a test can ask for a predictable word.
- **Deliberately not unique.** With a hundred words and hundreds of participants expected, uniqueness
  would exhaust the pool or start handing out second choices. Two Pathfinders in different clusters
  is a coincidence people enjoy; the nickname is what identifies somebody
  (`ux_participant_nickname_lower`).
- **The list needed cleaning first.** As given it had a hundred entries but only **eighty-seven
  distinct** ones — Adventurer three times, and Hustler, Jumper, Charger, Catalyst, Navigator,
  Rambler, Roamer, Starter, Strider, Trekker and Motivator twice each. Thirteen replacements were
  supplied, so the catalogue is a round hundred. Order is the order they were given in.
- **Where "Trainer" could NOT simply become the title, and why.** The word names one participant, so
  it only fits where that participant is the subject:
  - profile card header → `{TITLE} CARD`, theirs;
  - **sign-up** → "JOIN IN". Nobody has a title before they have signed up, so borrowing one would be
    inventing it a screen early;
  - **leaderboard** → "Top scorers". The list holds many participants with many different words;
  - **landing** → "choose your **character**", which is what that sentence always meant — the drawn
    avatar, not the person.
- **Impact:** the existing dev database cannot be upgraded — `NOT NULL` with no default, and there
  are no migrations by design (ADR-049) — so a fresh `PGLITE_DATA_DIR` is required, exactly as
  ADR-050 needed. The recorded demo seed needs **no** change: the server assigns the title on
  sign-up, so replaying the dump produces titled participants without storing any. `ParticipantView`
  gains `title`, and the test harness exposes it on `ParticipantSession`.

### ADR-062 — Tap a small avatar to see who it is

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-026 (the drawn art), ADR-031/035 (photo sprites and sprite ids), ADR-061 (the
  energetic word), `fds.md` §5.5 (avatars on participant surfaces only).
- **Decision:** the 32 px avatars in the leaderboard's top scorers, the team roster and a team's detail
  page become `AvatarPeek`. Tapping one opens a card with the same sprite at 96 px plus the nickname,
  the cluster badge and the participant's title; tapping the card dismisses it. A mouse gets the same
  card on hover.
- **Why:** at 32 px a face is not recognisable and the nickname beside it is doing all the work. The
  sprite is already in the browser's sprite cache, so showing it bigger costs nothing, and ADR-061
  gave every participant a word that had nowhere to appear outside their own profile card.
- **The two input methods are deliberately implemented in two different places.** **Hover is CSS**,
  inside `@media (hover: hover)`. **Tap is component state.** A touch screen that synthesises hover
  events after a tap would otherwise open the card from the pointer event and toggle it shut from the
  click, in one gesture — so only a device with a real cursor gets the hover affordance. The card
  dismisses on its own tap because on a phone there is no cursor to move away: the way out has to be
  the same gesture as the way in.
- **Styled from `.gb-panel`'s own tokens** — `--panel-border`, `--radius`, `--paper`, `--sand`,
  `--ink-soft` — rather than new values, so it cannot drift from the theme: change the panel and the
  card changes with it.
- **Anchored to the trigger's left edge, not centred on it.** Measured at 320 px, the narrowest
  supported width: these avatars sit close to the left margin, so a centred 132 px card is clipped off
  the side of the screen. Anchored left it lands at x = 68 and fits.
- **What this needed upstream:** `title` had to reach the surfaces that draw other people, so
  `TeamMemberView` and `IndividualStandingView` carry it, along with the team query, the leaderboard
  CTE and both view builders. The viewer's own large avatars (profile, QR home) are left alone — a
  card telling you who you are is not worth a tap.

### ADR-063 — A team's own chat room, and the one tab that lights up

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the global room, whose transport this reuses), ADR-016 (`?session_token=`,
  which makes an authenticated `EventSource` possible), ADR-035 (sprite ids on the wire),
  ADR-038 (cached reads), ADR-049 (one schema file), ADR-061 (titles), ADR-062 (the avatar peek),
  `fds.md` R2 (a participant is on at most one team), §4.2.3–4 (captaincy transfer and disband).
- **Decision:** a team room in **its own table**, reached at `/api/team-chat/*` with **no team id in
  any path**, and an unread **dot** on the Teams tab rather than a count.
- **A separate table, not a `team_id` column on `chat_message`.** The argument that settled it is the
  one that started as the risk: with a shared table, one forgotten predicate leaks every team's
  private conversation into the global room, and no test is as reliable as a route that cannot reach
  the rows. There is a test asserting the global room cannot see a team message, and it holds by
  construction. The columns come out simpler too — a team room is its members, so the author is
  always a participant and the global room's three-way exclusive author `CHECK` is gone.
- **Membership is the authorization boundary, and it moves.** Resolved per request, and — the part
  that is easy to miss — **re-checked before every stream write**: a socket can outlive the membership
  that authorised it when somebody leaves or a team disbands. The bus uses one topic per team, so
  that check costs a handful of listeners per message rather than three hundred, and a stream is
  never even offered a room it did not subscribe to. Filtering in the client would have been a leak.
- **The room is also the team's history.** Joining and leaving insert `joined`/`left` rows. They carry
  **no body**: their sentence is UI copy and belongs in `messages.ts`, not as text in the database
  where `duplicated-copy` cannot see it and nobody can change it. They are published **after** the
  enclosing transaction commits — a message announced from a transaction that then rolled back would
  reach every open phone and vanish on the next reload.
- **One refinement to the agreed `joined_at` read floor.** It applies to **spoken lines only**. Roster
  events stay visible to everyone in the team, because a late joiner who could see no earlier joins or
  leaves would have no history at all — and who is on the team is already visible in the roster, so
  hiding those protects nothing while breaking the feature.
- **A dot, not a count**, and three things fall out of it: the read is an `EXISTS` probe rather than a
  `COUNT` that visits every row to produce a number nobody displays; client state is a boolean, so
  there is nothing to drift; and two phones cannot disagree about it. The cursor lives on
  `team_membership`, already one row per `(participant, team)`, which means no new table, and it
  disappears with the membership. It only ever moves **forward**, so a second phone reporting an older
  position cannot un-read what the first one saw.
- **Reads are deliberately not cached.** The key would need the team *and* the member's join time, so
  sixty teams share almost nothing and entries would be invalidated about as often as read. The
  partial index on `(team_id, id) WHERE hidden_at IS NULL` does the work instead.
- **The LED.** Its own `--led` token, because `--console-danger` belongs to the admin theme and reads
  wrong on sand and paper; visually-hidden text beside it, because a bare coloured circle says nothing
  to a screen reader and nothing to anyone who cannot pick the colour out. Only the Teams tab lights:
  team chat is small and targeted, which the global room deliberately is not.
- **Layering the standards caught, and were right about.** The first cut had a component calling the
  server (`AlertsProvider`) and a hook importing a component (`useTeamChatRoom`). Now
  `useAlertsStore` owns the fetch, the provider only shares it, and the **panel** — which is allowed
  to know about both — passes `clearTeamChatUnread` into the hook. Two named functions rather than one
  taking a boolean, because `flag-parameter` is right that "clear" and "raise" are what callers mean.
- **Impact:** schema change with no migrations by design, so a fresh `PGLITE_DATA_DIR` is required.
  `useForegroundGeneration` and `mergeById` moved to `lib/hooks/liveRoom.ts`, shared by both rooms.

### ADR-064 — The global room opened empty for anyone who had used it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the global room), ADR-038 (cached reads), ADR-019 (storage ownership),
  ADR-063 (the team room, whose design made the contrast visible).
- **Reported by a user, reproduced, and found by a peer session** reading the tree while ADR-063 was
  in flight. Three fixes, one of which was user-visible and bad.
- **The defect: a persisted cursor and an unpersisted list.** `useChatRoom` wrote the newest message
  id to local storage on every absorb, but `messages` was React state only. `/social/chat` is a plain
  route, so leaving the tab unmounted the panel and discarded the list while the cursor survived. The
  next visit asked `GET /api/chat/messages?after=<the newest id it had already seen>`, the server
  correctly returned nothing, and the room rendered its **empty state** — including the message the
  participant had just sent, because sending routes through the same absorb that moved the watermark.
  Every tab switch. Every reload.
- **Why the suite could not catch it:** `useChatRoom.test.ts` clears storage in `beforeEach`, so no
  test had ever mounted the hook with a cursor already present. That is the whole lesson — the fixture
  erased the precondition. Two tests now seed one deliberately, and were confirmed red before the fix:
  `expected [] to deeply equal [ 'someone else', 'mine' ]`.
- **The fix: the cursor lives for the life of the mount, in a ref.** A fresh mount opens on the tail;
  the cursor still serves the reconnect and poll delta *within* a mount, which is all it was ever
  needed for. Two things improve for free: the per-device cursor was never cleared at sign-out, so the
  next participant on a shared phone opened an empty room; and `readVisibleMessages` keys its cache by
  `cursor ?? 'tail'`, so three hundred phones reconnecting with three hundred distinct cursors was
  three hundred queries where opening on the tail is one. **Removing the persistence is a cost win,
  not a cost** — it restores ADR-046's stated cost model, which the cursor had quietly inverted.
- **`isLive` could only ever go false.** Neither stream module registered an `open` listener, and
  `EventSource` raises `error` on any transient drop before reconnecting by itself — so a healthy
  stream spent the rest of the mount telling the participant that live updates were off, with a
  redundant 45–75 s poll running beside it. Both modules now report recovery through an `onLive`
  handler, and `eventSourceStub` gained a `connect()` dispatcher so it is testable.
- **Id comparison now matches the server.** `mergeById` sorted with `localeCompare`, an ICU collation,
  while the server orders with SQL `>` and de-duplicates with `<=`. It agrees for fixed-format
  lowercase hex, which is why nothing broke, but it is a different comparison and a slower one.
- **Left undone, deliberately:** the backlog is still read twice on mount (HTTP catch-up plus SSE
  replay). Only the no-`EventSource` path needs the HTTP read, but `isLoading` is cleared in that
  read's `finally`, and a stream that opens on an empty room delivers nothing — so removing it would
  leave a first-time participant on a loading state forever. Fixing it properly needs a
  "replay complete" frame from the server, which is a protocol change and not this one. Also left:
  a guard on how long the page was actually hidden before bumping the reconnect generation, and a cap
  on the client-side list, which grows unbounded from live frames while reads cap at 200.

### ADR-065 — The global room opens on fifty and reaches back on demand

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the global room), ADR-038 (cached reads), ADR-024 (the jittered poll and
  the live list), ADR-064 (the per-mount cursor this builds on).
- **Decision:** the room opens on the newest **fifty** messages instead of two hundred, and older
  pages of fifty are fetched only when somebody scrolls back for them, via a `before=` cursor.
- **Why fifty:** it is the cheap end of "do not blow the database up" — four times less to serialise,
  parse and lay out on the one page every participant visits — and a room is read from the bottom.
