  Nobody arrives wanting the two-hundredth message back. The rest is still there, one scroll away.
- **`hasOlder` is a fact, not a guess.** The server reads one row past the limit and drops it, so the
  list knows to stop asking rather than making one more empty request at the end of the conversation,
  which is the flicker that "we returned a full page so there is probably more" always produces.
- **The backwards read is an index scan, not a sort.** `ix_chat_message_visible` is on `(id)`, so
  `id < before ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 51` walks the index backwards and stops. It is cached on the
  same terms as the tail read and is the most cacheable thing in the room — history only changes when
  a message is hidden, which invalidates `CHAT_TAG` anyway — so three hundred phones scrolling back
  through the same conversation share every key.
- **Three reads, one route, told apart by which cursor is present.** `after` is the forward delta a
  reconnect resumes from, `before` walks back, and neither means "open on the tail". `readCursor` now
  takes the field name so a malformed cursor's 400 names the parameter the caller actually got wrong.
- **Two client problems, both of which had to be solved or the feature feels broken.** Fetching is
  triggered by an `IntersectionObserver` on a sentinel *above* the list with a 400 px `rootMargin`, so
  the page is already longer by the time the reader arrives — waiting for a real top-of-page scroll
  would show them the end of the history and then move it. And prepending pushes everything down
  while the browser keeps `scrollY`, so the document height is measured before the prepend and the
  difference added back after paint, which leaves what they were reading exactly where it was. The
  chat list is not its own scroll container, so the anchor works on the document.
- **The button is not decoration.** An observer is an optimisation; a reader on a browser without one,
  or using a keyboard rather than a scroll gesture, still needs a way back through the history.
- **Testing note worth keeping:** the API tests seed through the repository, not the route. `POST
  /messages` is rate limited to three per two seconds, so posting fifty-five messages through it
  measures `setTimeout` rather than pagination. The walk-back test also asserts a *property* — that
  paging terminates, that pages do not overlap, and that each is strictly older than the last —
  because the test context is shared across the file and any absolute assertion about the room's
  contents is hostage to whatever earlier tests said.

### ADR-066 — A hidden message is retracted on the stream, not only on the next read

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the room and its bus), ADR-038 (the cached read this relies on),
  ADR-065 (the backwards page the frame has to agree with), `fds.md` §9.5, reported bug: "I want you
  to examine the global chat interface for potential errors."
- **Decision:** hiding a chat message publishes a second kind of frame on the room's bus, and the
  stream writes it as `event: hidden` carrying `{ messageId }` and nothing else. `subscribeToChat`
  now delivers a tagged `ChatFrame` — `{ kind: 'message' }` or `{ kind: 'hidden' }` — and the
  stream's replay buffer holds frames rather than messages.
- **Why:** moderation was reaching the database and nothing else. `POST /messages/:id/hide` soft-hid
  the row and invalidated `CHAT_TAG`, which governs what is fetched *next* — but the catch-up read
  only ever returns ids *newer* than the caller's cursor, so no later request can retract something
  already on screen. A message a superadmin had pulled therefore stayed visible on every phone that
  already had it, for as long as that phone kept the room open. On a one-day event with the room on
  a bottom-bar tab, that is the whole afternoon.
- **One topic, not two.** A message and the hide that retracts it can be published in the same tick.
  `EventEmitter` dispatches a single topic synchronously in emit order, so one topic keeps them
  ordered for free; two topics would have been ordered today and left every subscriber merging two
  buffers to keep it. A retraction that overtakes the thing it retracts leaves the message up for
  good, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed.
- **The frame carries no SSE `id:`, deliberately.** That field is the resume cursor the browser
  echoes back as `Last-Event-ID`. A hidden message's id is by definition older than everything the
  stream has already sent, so putting it on the frame would wind the cursor backwards and turn the
  next reconnect into a replay of the entire room. For the same reason the hide bypasses the
  `lastSent` guard rather than being filtered by it: every hide is about something already sent, so
  the guard would have swallowed all of them and complained about none. The guard now lives in a
  `roomWriter` closure that owns the cursor and exposes the two write paths separately, which is
  what makes "this frame does not move the cursor" a structural fact instead of a comment.
- **It carries only the id.** A retraction that quotes what was said would make the frame removing a
  message the last thing to deliver its text. The row itself still exists — the hide is soft, for
  the audit trail (AGENTS-database.md §4).
- **Hides are buffered through the replay window.** The stream subscribes before it reads the
  backlog, so a hide published in between lands in the pending buffer and is flushed after it.
  Dropping those would have reintroduced the original bug for exactly the phones that happened to be
  connecting at that moment — the hardest case to notice and the easiest to leave broken.
- **Published after the row comes back, never before.** A hide that changed nothing — a repeat, or an
  id that does not exist — tells nobody anything.
- **The client removes by id and moves neither end of the list.** `seen` is a high-water mark for the
  forward cursor, so winding it back to the new last message would re-request and re-merge everything
  said since; `oldest` may keep naming a removed id because the backwards page compares ids
  (`id < before`) rather than looking that row up. Both are asserted — one test hides the newest
  message and then checks the reconnect still resumes from it.
- **Only the stream carries the retraction, and that is a known asymmetry.** A browser with no
  `EventSource` polls the forward delta, which by construction returns nothing older than its cursor,
  so there a hidden message stays until the panel remounts and opens on the tail (ADR-064) — which
  excludes it. Retracting on that path would mean re-reading the whole tail on a cadence, which is
  the cost ADR-046 exists to avoid. `CHAT_HIDDEN_EVENT` and `ChatHiddenView` live in
  `@psd/contracts`, so the two sides share the frame's name and shape rather than restating it.
- **An unparseable frame is a transport failure, not an instruction.** The hidden listener reports
  `onError` — the room goes not-live and starts polling — and leaves the list alone. A frame nobody
  could read must never be able to empty a room.
- **Three reads, one answer.** The regression tests assert the frame arrives live and carries no
  `id:` line, that a hidden message is not replayed to a phone connecting afterwards, and that it is
  absent from an ADR-065 backwards page — that last one because the older-page read is cached under
  its own key, and only the shared `CHAT_TAG` invalidation makes the three paths agree.

### ADR-067 — The sprite stamp hashes the pictures, not the grids

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-018 (superseded by this entry), ADR-014 (the motif pipeline), ADR-008 (the
  avatar pipeline this one now mirrors structurally)
- **Decision:** `versionOf` hashes the emitted SVG of every sprite, keyed by name in sorted order,
  instead of the ASCII grids. The art moves to a pure `apps/web/scripts/motif-art.mjs`;
  `generate-motif-sprites.mjs` keeps only I/O, and builds and validates the entire corpus in memory
  before it writes anything.
- **Hashing the grids left open the exact hole the stamp was built to close.** ADR-018 exists
  because a redrawn sprite kept being served from cache under its old URL. But the hash covered
  only the grid strings, so a palette edit or a change to the serialiser produced different bytes
  under an *unchanged* stamp — the same bug, reachable two other ways. Hashing the output covers
  grids, palette, serialiser and viewBox by construction, and there is no third thing to remember.
- **Names are sorted before hashing.** Previously the hash followed `Object.keys` order, so merely
  regrouping the `MOTIFS` literal by theme moved the version with no picture changing. With a
  corpus heading for ~100 sprites, regrouping is something we will want to do freely.
- **The split exists because the old script wrote files on import.** `main()` ran at module scope,
  so *anything* that imported the generator regenerated the corpus as a side effect. That is why
  there has never been a review sheet or a test that reads the art — neither could exist.
- **Writing is now all-or-nothing.** The previous `main()` wrote inside its loop, so a throw on the
  twelfth sprite left eleven new files beside a stale version module and a stale stylesheet: a tree
  that looks generated and is not.
- **`assertGrid` is new, because there was no validation at all.** An unknown palette key rendered
  *nothing* and the run still reported success. It now checks the name charset, rectangularity and
  that every cell resolves, in the shape of `assertLayer` in `generate-avatar-art.mjs`.
- **The stylesheet rewrite checks its own work.** The reference pattern was `([a-z]+)`, which
  silently skipped any sprite name containing a digit or a hyphen — and because the file then
  compared equal, the run reported success. It is now `([a-z0-9-]+)` plus three post-conditions: no
  stale `?v=` survives, every `/motifs/<name>.svg` in the CSS names a sprite that was just written,
  and a repeating tile's CSS size is reported when it is not a whole-number multiple of its grid.
- **Impact:** `MOTIF_VERSION` moves once on adoption (`55545560` → `803ac592`) with no picture
  changing; the sixteen surviving SVG bodies are byte-identical. `apps/web/src/lib/motifSprites.test.ts`
  recomputes the stamp from the committed files, which closes the gap where nothing verified that
  `public/motifs/` matched the generator — `check-standards.mjs` scans neither `apps/web/scripts`
  nor `public/`, and `PixelMotif.test.tsx` compares two values from the same generated module, so a
  stale `motifVersion.ts` was self-consistent and passed. That test is only possible because the
  hash covers output rather than source.

### ADR-068 — Two motif sprites nobody asked for are retired

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-014 (whose decision text names eighteen sprites — that inventory is superseded
  here), ADR-022/ADR-023 (the generated panorama that took over the scenery), ADR-067
- **Decision:** `monorail` and `palm` are removed from the corpus, which is now sixteen sprites.
  `generate-motif-sprites.mjs` deletes any committed SVG that the art no longer declares.
- **They were referenced by nothing.** Neither appeared in `MOTIF_NAMES`, in `gameboy.css`, or in
  any source file — 13.9 kB of committed output that no surface could ever request. The scenery job
  they were drawn for went to the generated panorama two ADRs later.
- **Two documents claimed otherwise, and both are corrected here.** `apps/web/src/lib/motifs.ts`
  said "the wide tiles (wave, monorail, palm) are referenced from gameboy.css" — only `wave` is.
  `AGENTS-frontend.md` §4 said background scenery was CSS-only motif sprites, which the panorama
  replaced.
- **Leaving them was the worst of the three options.** Re-toning dead art to the Gameboy standard
  spends the budget on zero users; leaving them unconverted would make them the only sprites
  exempt from `assertGrid`, which is precisely the kind of exception that makes a validator
  decorative.
- **Impact:** recoverable from git if wanted. If the monorail is wanted it should return *with* a
  call site — a repeating Sentosa Express strip across the banner, mirroring the `wave` strip —
  and its own addendum. The drift test now asserts committed sprites ⊆ `MOTIF_NAMES` ∪ CSS
  references, so a future orphan fails the suite rather than accumulating quietly.


### ADR-071 — The social seeder strides across the photo corpus instead of taking its first ten

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-050 (the SHA-1 duplicate guard this explains rather than changes), ADR-039
  (the sixty-photo corpus), ADR-063 (which made the seeder re-runnable and so made the repetition
  visible), `e2e/seed-social.spec.ts`, `e2e/photo-stubs.ts`
- **Decision:** `uniquePhoto` no longer uses the caption index as the corpus index. It strides by
  `floor(corpusCount / captionCount)`, and `photo-stubs.ts` exports `socialPhotoCount()` so the
  stride is derived rather than hard-coded. The seeded archive filename now names the corpus photo
  (`SEED_<corpusIndex>_<timestamp>.png`) rather than the caption slot.
- **The symptom was reported as a dedup failure, and the dedup is fine.** A user asked why the dev
  gallery showed duplicates when the app checksums uploads. It does: the SHA-1 is computed
  server-side in `routes-gallery/upload.ts` over the received `raw` bytes, and
  `ux_gallery_photo_sha1` is unique over every row including hidden ones. What produced the
  duplicates is this seeder appending 64 random bytes to each file *on purpose* (ADR-050's note on
  trailing bytes after IEND), so the guard correctly never fires on it.
- **Ten captions bounded the loop, and the photo index rode along with it.** `CAPTIONS.entries()`
  yielded 0–9, `busyPhoto(index)` resolved `social[0…9]` on a sorted listing, and photos 11–60 were
  never seeded at all. The first ten happen to be the plainest of the set — the clean portrait
  variants — while everything with visual interest (`27-rain-umbrella`, `39-kopitiam-steam`,
  `46-stage-colour-light`, `57-colour-powder`) sits above 20. So a re-run did not just repeat, it
  repeated the dullest tenth of what was available.
- **Derived stride, not a constant, and not a shuffle.** A literal `6` would silently stop spreading
  the first time a photo is added; the division cannot. A seeded shuffle was rejected because this is
  a seeding tool — two runs disagreeing about which photos are in the gallery costs review confidence
  and buys nothing.
- **What this does NOT fix, recorded so it is not mistaken for fixed:** (a) re-running the seeder
  still adds a second set of rows — the random tail is what makes a corpus photo reusable at all, so
  idempotence needs its own guard; (b) the checksum is byte-identity of the archival original, not
  perceptual identity, so a re-encode (ADR-052), an EXIF difference or a messenger recompression
  still yields a second row for the same picture; (c) the corpus is a *face* corpus borrowed from the
  avatar studio, so captions like "Monorail over the water" still sit under a headshot. A gallery of
  real event photos is the right answer to (c) and needs its own addendum.

### ADR-072 — Cut the background by a tuned mask, and drop the pieces that are not the subject

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-033 (the segmentation model this corrects), ADR-031/032 (the colour cut-out
  it also applies to), ADR-054 (the palette ordering it relies on), ADR-056 (the retained matte
  that makes it free), reported bug: "besides her head to the right there is a small black blob …
  whether we can tune something in our background removal to remove this blob."
- **Decision:** the cut-out is governed by three numbers — `threshold`, `minIsland`, `edge` — held
  in `apps/web/src/lib/avatar/cutOut.ts`, and by default the subject is reduced to the single
  4-connected piece the face is standing in. `maskFromModel` takes the threshold as a parameter
  instead of hardcoding 128; `trimEdge` shrinks or grows the subject by whole cells; `pruneIslands`
  paints out every detached piece of `minIsland` cells or fewer. They are applied in the order
  threshold → trim → prune, and the same prune governs the colour cut-out so there is one behaviour
  rather than two. `Bitmap`, `CropBox` and `SubjectMask` moved to a new leaf module
  `lib/avatar/types.ts` to make this possible without a circular import.
- **Why:** MODNET is *portrait* matting — it mattes any person-shaped thing in the frame, not "the
  one subject". `Wei_Ling` in the recorded crowd was photographed in a hawker centre with another
  person's head directly behind her, and the model kept eighty cells of it: a lump floating in the
  backdrop with no path to her face. Nothing could catch that. `maskFromModel` thresholded each cell
  independently, and `despeckle` only rewrites cells matching *none* of their four neighbours, so an
  eighty-cell blob was invisible to both. Connectivity was the missing question.
  Measured across the recorded crowd: 22 of 75 photo avatars carried detached pieces, the largest 80
  cells and the smallest main subject 5788 — so anything in ~100…5000 means "keep the main piece
  only", and `minIsland` defaults to 512, about 4× clear of the largest observed stray and ~3 % of
  the grid. The seed is the cell between the eyes, `(size/2, 0.52 × size)`, because `locateFace`
  centres every crop it produces on the eye midpoint; where a participant placed the square by hand
  that cell can hold no subject at all — one avatar in the crowd does — so the largest piece wins
  as a fallback. Without that fallback, pruning renders them blank.
  *Rejected:* raising the alpha threshold alone. The blob has a hard boundary and eighty cells of
  area, which is a confident model, so the threshold erodes her hair edge long before it bites the
  blob. *Rejected:* swapping MODNET for a salient-object model (RMBG-1.4, BiRefNet). Both are
  larger downloads, and ADR-033 deliberately treats the model as an optional CDN upgrade that must
  be allowed to fail.
- **Impact:** every photo sprite changes, so the recorded demo seed must be re-recorded
  (`AGENTS-testing.md` §10) — and with `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1`, because the default stand-in matte is
  a single ellipse with no detached pieces and would not exercise this at all. Reversing it means
  passing `minIsland: 0`, which is a true no-op. `componentSizesOf` is exported for the regression
  suites to ask "is this person in one piece?" without re-implementing the walk.

### ADR-073 — The participant tunes the cut-out on the screen that already shows them the square

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-072 (the three numbers this exposes), ADR-036/056 (the square-confirmation
  screen it joins), ADR-059/060 (the worn-avatar state it must not disturb), gap — `fds.md` is
  silent on the photo studio.
- **Decision:** `CutOutControls` sits beneath the square in `PhotoCropper`, as its child rather than
  part of it. Three rows of named choices — `Loose · Normal · Tight`, `Keep · Remove`,
  `Trim · As-is · Grow` — with the raw numbers behind a "Fine tune" disclosure, a "Back to normal"
  reset, and its own live preview. `usePhotoTuning` owns the state, caches the resampled cells per
  square, and debounces recomputation by 120 ms. The cut-out row is hidden when there is no matte.
  The square is reported up on drag *release* only.
- **Why:** a knob is only worth offering if turning it is answerable, and it is: the matte is
  already retained (ADR-056), so nothing re-runs the model. Named steps rather than sliders as the
  primary surface because this is a beach and a wet thumb — `Tight` says what it does where `176`
  says what it sets — with the sliders kept for anyone who wants the number.
  The performance shape was measured rather than assumed, and the assumption was wrong: of ~104 ms
  for a full rebuild, resampling is 5.8 ms and painting is ~95 ms. Caching the cells therefore buys
  ~6 %, not the bulk, because the expense is quantising and the palette genuinely depends on which
  cells a knob just called subject. The debounce is what makes tuning usable; the cache mostly buys
  a `paintPrepared` that can be called on its own. At ~95 ms a frame, reporting the square per
  pointer-move would be a slideshow, hence release-only.
  *Rejected:* pushing each tuned sprite to the big preview at the top of the studio. `onPhoto` also
  means "a new photograph arrived", so it clears the fallback character (ADR-059) and moves the
  selection back onto the photo (ADR-060); choosing a character changes the backdrop, which repaints
  the sprite, which would then have fired that reset and undone the choice that caused it. Two
  acceptance tests caught it. The preview beside the controls is the live feedback instead.
  *Rejected:* holding the palette still while a knob moves. It would cut the ~95 ms substantially
  and it trades honest colour for speed nobody has asked for yet; it is the next lever if a real
  phone proves too slow.
- **Impact:** tuning is deliberately **not persisted**. ADR-031 discards the bitmap on navigation,
  so there is nothing to re-tune against later — changing your mind means choosing the photo again.
  `PhotoCropper` gained two optional props (`onBox`, `children`) and keeps every testid.
  `photoSpriteUrl` was added to `lib/avatars.ts` for the preview, deliberately *not* `avatarUrl`,
  whose unbounded session cache would grow by a few kilobytes per slider step. `.gb-range` is the
  first range input in the app, so it is styled directly rather than hidden under a label the way
  the colour wheel is, and it had to be added to the focus-ring selector list by hand.

### ADR-069 — Motif art is reviewed on a rendered sheet, not in the diff

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-139 (no browser can be fetched in this sandbox), ADR-014, ADR-067, ADR-026 (the
  avatar sheet this follows)
- **Decision:** `apps/web/scripts/render-motif-sheet.mjs`, run by `npm run motifs:review
  --workspace @psd/web`, writes `docs/screenshot/motif-sheet.png`. Every sprite is drawn on three
  fields — mid-grey, sand `#f5e2b8` and sea `#2f7dd1`. `--only=<name>` renders one sprite large
  plus a band showing it at each size it actually ships at, at DPR 1 and DPR 2.
- **A pixel grid cannot be reviewed as text.** The diff of an ASCII grid shows which characters
  changed, never whether the picture got better. Three defects in this batch were invisible in the
  source and obvious in the render: a speech-bubble tail that read as two detached blobs, a water
  bottle that all but vanished against the sea, and a whistle that read as a slipper through two
  redraws.
- **The three fields are the point, not decoration.** These sprites sit on sand panels and on the
  sea strip. A white net mesh that reads perfectly on grey disappears on sand — caught here, fixed
  by moving the mesh to `k1`.
- **The shipped-size band answers a question argument cannot.** Fourteen of the call sites render a
  16-px grid at 20 px. Rather than reasoning about whether a tone survives 1.25×, the band
  resamples the way the rasteriser does and shows it.
- **It also gives an orphan a source.** `docs/screenshot/motif-sheet.png` has existed since
  `8bf75e5` as a committed binary with no generator, while ADR-014's impact clause called it "a
  render of the shipped sprites for reviewers". It is now actually that.
- **No label font, deliberately.** The sheet is read by a human in a pull request and by an agent
  iterating on one sprite. A 3×5 glyph font is legible to neither at review size, so the sheet uses
  a fixed alphabetical grid with the reading order printed to stdout. A 5×7 font becomes worth its
  thirty-six glyphs somewhere past thirty sprites.
- **Impact:** regenerate the sheet in any commit that changes art; its PNG diff *is* the art review.

### ADR-070 — Four tones per material, and a cell is two characters

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-014, ADR-067, ADR-069, `docs/design/motif-catalogue.md`
- **Decision:** new motifs are drawn from the sixteen ramps in `apps/web/scripts/motif-palette.mjs`
  — four tones per material plus that material's own hue-shifted outline. A grid cell is
  `<material><tone>`: `g2` gold base, `g1` its highlight, `g3` its shadow, `g0` its outline, `..`
  transparent. Cell width is declared per sprite and asserted uniform, so the sixteen legacy
  one-character grids keep working untouched.
- **The old corpus was flat fills, and that was the actual gap.** `crab`, `starfish`, `shell` and
  `flag` were a single colour inside a global navy ring. Gameboy item sprites are shaded; asked for
  "pixelated gameboy styled motifs", flat fills are what was missing, not more silhouettes.
- **A per-material outline instead of one global ink.** One navy contour around a gold coin and a
  pink shell flattens both. `scene-art.mjs`'s `stoneLine` was already the precedent for shifting an
  outline toward a material's own hue.
- **Two characters per cell, for three reasons in ascending order of weight.** Sixteen ramps × five
  values exceeds the sixty-two single characters available; tone becomes a *comparable field*, so
  "is this lighter than its neighbour" is answered by reading digits rather than recalling a
  sixty-entry table — the old case-pairing convention had already collapsed at twenty-two keys,
  where `r`, `o`, `n`, `v`, `c` and `t` had no shade at all and `d` was sea-deep while `D` was PSD
  navy; and a monospace cell being roughly 0.48 aspect means one character per pixel displays the
  art 2:1 vertically stretched, so circles are authored as ellipses.
- **Cell width is per sprite rather than a corpus-wide migration.** Transcribing all sixteen legacy
  grids up front would have been one commit touching every line of art with nothing verifiable in
  it. Instead each sprite moves to the new format when it is re-toned, one reviewable commit at a
  time, and `assertGrid` enforces that a single sprite never mixes widths.
- **Impact:** eleven new sprites ship in this batch (`bellalert`, `bunting`, `chat`, `cone`,
  `crown`, `emptybox`, `medal`, `net`, `raincloud`, `waterbottle`, `whistle`). `bunting` is a
  24×6 repeating tile wired to `.gb-banner::before` at 48×12 — exactly 2×, unlike `wave`, whose two
  tiles are 1.25× and 1.5× of its grid and which the generator now warns about on every run. The
  sixteen legacy sprites are still flat and still look it beside these; re-toning them is the next
  batch.

### ADR-074 — A staff announcement is not a chat message

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the global room), ADR-047 (the console surfaces), ADR-063 (the alerts
  endpoint and the attention LED this reuses), ADR-049 (one schema file), `fds.md` §9.6 (the three
  actor languages).
- **Decision:** a superadmin can announce to every participant. The announcement appears as a
  **persistent toast over the participant's banner** and stays until they tap it. It lives in its own
  table, is delivered on the existing alerts poll, and is dismissed **per participant, in that
  participant's own browser** — see the dismissal bullet below, which records why the server-side table
  this bullet first described was replaced before release. (Corrected in ADR-081: as committed, the
  entry contradicted itself.)
- **Why it is not a chat message, which is the question that produced this.** The first proposal was
  "give staff a chat surface", and it did not survive being asked what a broadcast actually *was*: the
  answer was "a `chat_message` row with a different badge". That is worth nothing here — participants
  are at stations scanning QR codes, not sitting in a chat room, so "finals start at 4pm" as line
  eighty-three is a message nobody reads. An announcement needs to arrive **where the participant
  already is**, and it needs per-reader dismissal state, which a chat row has nowhere to put. Two
  different objects.
- **Facilitators do not announce, and that retires the original problem.** The thread began with a
  seeded staff chat line that could not seed, because `/social/chat` is wrapped in
  `RequireActor actorType="participant"` and a facilitator session is redirected to the staff home
  before `ChatPanel` mounts. Once announcing is a superadmin act, there is no facilitator use case at
  all — the seeded line had been standing in for a need nobody had. `StaffShell` keeps its three
  spartan tabs, and the canned-button design that the wet-hands persona justified dies with it: the
  superadmin console is a dense laptop surface where a textarea is the native control.
- **Send is refused while offline, and that inverts the app's usual rule deliberately.** Everything
  else on a staff surface is offline-tolerant — a station queues scans and syncs later (DC-004) — but
  an announcement is the one message where late delivery is worse than none: "finals in fifteen
  minutes" arriving an hour afterwards actively misleads people. The header already shows
  Online/Offline, so the reason is visible rather than mysterious.
- **Delivery costs nothing new.** It rides `GET /api/me/alerts`, which ADR-063 already polls on the
  jittered 45–75 s cadence and whose own comment said it was shaped so "a second kind of alert does
  not need a new endpoint". No new stream, no new poll, no new socket. Up to a poll window of latency,
  which for an event announcement is the right trade against three hundred permanently-open connections.
- **Dismissal lives in the browser, not the database — and this was built the other way first.** The
  first implementation had an `announcement_dismissal` table, a row per `(participant, announcement)`,
  and a dismiss route; it was replaced before release. Keeping it out of the server is better on three
  counts, and only the third is a real cost:
  - the server holds **no per-reader row per announcement**, so nothing accumulates as the day goes on;
  - the live read becomes **identical for every participant**, which is what lets it be a `cachedRead`
    shared by all of them — three hundred phones polling their alerts cost about one query per TTL
    window instead of three hundred. A per-reader filter would have shared nothing *and* been
    invalidated by its own reader's dismissal;
  - the cost: a second device shows the toast again. For a notice rather than a conversation that is
    arguably correct — being told twice beats missing it — which is what made the trade worth taking.

  `lib/storage/announcementStore.ts` owns the key and reaches the store only through `localStore.ts`,
  as ADR-009/019 require, so a private-mode Safari that refuses writes degrades to "dismissed for the
  life of the page" rather than breaking. Stored ids are **pruned against the live list** on every
  write, so the key cannot grow forever — a retracted announcement can never be shown again, so
  remembering it was dismissed is dead weight. There is a test asserting the dismissal **route does not
  exist**, because a leftover endpoint would be a second source of truth for the same fact.
- **One at a time, oldest first.** A 320 px screen stacked with toasts hides the app the announcement
  is about; and somebody who was away reads them in the order they were made rather than backwards.
- **A button, not a div with a handler.** The whole toast is the dismiss control — there is no small ×
  to hit with wet hands in the sun — so it has to be reachable by keyboard and announced as pressable.
- **Retraction is a soft hide**, never a delete: gone from every reader's toast, still listed in the
  console, still on the row for the audit trail.
- **Impact:** one new table, so a fresh `PGLITE_DATA_DIR` is required (ADR-049, no migrations). New
  `/admin/announce` tab — the console already has ten, so a text tab costs nothing, unlike the
  participant nav's six-column grid. `author_type = 'facilitator'` in `chat_message` is now
  deliberately unreachable from any UI; left in place because removing it is another schema change, but
  it should not be mistaken for a capability.

### ADR-075 — Sprites are one path per colour, not one rect per pixel

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-014, ADR-067 (the stamp covers the serialiser because it hashes output),
  ADR-070
- **Decision:** `motif-art.mjs` serialises each sprite as one `<path>` per colour, horizontal runs
  encoded as `M<x> <y>h<run>v1h-<run>z` subpaths, replacing one `<rect>` per painted pixel.
- **The byte count is the lesser reason, though it is large.** Measured over the 193-sprite corpus:
  per-pixel rects 1.4 MB, horizontal run-merged rects 0.6 MB, one path per colour **772 kB and
  falling to ~190 kB gzipped**. At 16 sprites nobody would care; at 193 it is the difference
  between a corpus you can keep growing and one that becomes a page-weight decision.
- **The real reason is seams.** Adjacent same-colour rects snap to the device grid independently
  under `shape-rendering="crispEdges"`, so at a fractional scale a hairline can appear between
  them. Fourteen of the call sites render a 16-px grid at 20 px. One filled region per colour
  cannot seam against itself, on either axis — run-merging rects only fixes the horizontal case.
- **Verified by decoding, not by eye.** The review sheet renders from the grids, so it is
  structurally blind to a serialiser change and cannot prove this neutral. Instead every committed
  SVG was parsed back into a pixel map and compared against its grid: 193 sprites, 18,349 painted
  pixels, every one decoding to exactly the hex its grid declares and no extra pixels anywhere.
- **Impact:** `MOTIF_VERSION` moves once with no picture changing, which ADR-067's output-hash
  makes visible rather than silent. The drift test's "paints only palette colours" assertion still
  works unchanged, because it matches on `fill="…"` and paths carry that attribute too.

### ADR-076 — A button that says it is pressed must look pressed

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** `AGENTS-frontend.md` §4 (the two UI languages), ADR-021 (the studio), ADR-073 (the
  cut-out rows, which hit this first), reported bug: "during the sign up screen, the gender buttons
  when selected do not give sufficient visual cues to let you see that a button is selected."
- **Decision:** `gb-button[aria-pressed='true']` inverts its bevel and drops the face onto it, for
  every `gb-button` in the app rather than per block. The attribute is the selector.
- **Why:** every button carrying `aria-pressed` was authored correctly and rendered identically
  whether on or off — the gender pair at sign-up, the studio's trait rows, the cut-out choices.
  `gb-avatar-option` and `gb-swatch` had their own pressed styling; plain `gb-button` had none, so
  screen readers were told which option was chosen and eyes were not. Every DOM-level assertion in
  the suite passed throughout, because they all check the attribute, which was always right.
  Keyed on the attribute rather than a modifier class so the affordance cannot drift from the state
  it describes: there is nothing for the next author to remember to add. Scoped to all buttons
  rather than to one block because an audit found only four `gb-button` call sites use
  `aria-pressed` and **all four want the affordance** — ADR-073 had scoped it to `.gb-controls` on
  the assumption that restyling the studio's rows would be an unwanted side effect, and that was
  wrong: those rows had the same defect. Pressed-in rather than recoloured, because that is what a
  Gameboy button does and it survives sunlight better than a hue change.
- **Impact:** the studio's 51 trait buttons and the gender pair now show their selection, which is a
  visible change to two surfaces nobody asked to have restyled — intended, and the point. Pinned by
  `e2e/participant-signup.spec.ts`, which asserts the *computed* `background-color` and `box-shadow`
  differ between the chosen and unchosen button. That assertion needs a real browser; jsdom resolves
  no stylesheet, so the acceptance suite structurally cannot catch this class of defect, which is why
  it survived this long.

### ADR-077 — Background removal can be turned off entirely

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-033 (the segmentation model), ADR-031/032 (the colour cut-out), ADR-072 (the
  tuned mask), ADR-073 (the controls this joins), user request: "Sometimes background removal from
  the portraits just simply doesn't work, and as a user they might want to disable it entirely."
- **Decision:** `CutOutTuning` gains `removeBackground`, default `true`. When false the mask is
  all-subject (`keepEverything`), so the sprite is the whole crop with its own background intact, no
  cell is repainted as the backdrop and no contour is inked. The control is the first row of
  `CutOutControls` — "Take it out" / "Keep my photo" — and the three numeric rows are **removed from
  the screen** while it is off.
- **Why:** the three knobs of ADR-072 assume the cut-out is fundamentally working and needs
  adjusting. Some photographs defeat every setting: a crowd directly behind the subject, a wall the
  colour of a shirt, a matte that decides an arm is background. At that point the honest answer is to
  stop cutting rather than to offer a better number, and a participant who can see their own photo is
  a better judge of that than any threshold.
  Modelled as an all-subject mask rather than a second code path, because everything downstream
  already does the right thing when told no cell is background — the palette derives from the whole
  crop, nothing is repainted, and the ink pass only inks backdrop that touches subject, so it draws
  nowhere. "Off" costs a branch, not a parallel pipeline.
  The numeric rows are hidden rather than disabled: a disabled control still claims to do something.
  Their values are deliberately *preserved* in the tuning while hidden, so turning the cut-out back
  on returns the participant to the picture they had rather than to the defaults.
  It is its own field with its own setter rather than a fourth entry in `CUT_OUT_STEPS`, because it
  is a choice about whether the others apply at all, not another value on the same footing.
  `TuningKnob` is now derived from `TUNING_BOUNDS` rather than `keyof CutOutTuning`, so the numeric
  knobs and the boolean cannot be confused by a type that spans both.
- **Impact:** a sprite made with the cut-out off still carries backdrop and ink entries in its
  palette — the format always emits sixteen colours — they are simply unreferenced, so
  `recolourSpriteBackdrop` (ADR-054) becomes a no-op on such a sprite, and offering the backdrop
  swatch for one is meaningless. Not addressed here; the studio still shows it. Reversing this
  decision means deleting the field and the row. Pinned by `cutOut.test.ts`,
  `usePhotoTuning.test.ts`, `photoSprite.test.ts` (asserting no backdrop or ink index appears in the
  painted rows) and `e2e/cut-out-tuning.spec.ts`.

### ADR-078 — The off state names the background, and greys out what it cannot do

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-077 (the toggle this refines), ADR-036/056 (the cropper whose cancel button
  caused the collision), `AGENTS-frontend.md` §5 (copy discipline), user reports: "I think the
  wording 'Keep my photo' can be a bit confusing" and "when [it] is selected, the fine tune and back
  to normal buttons should be greyed out".
- **Decision:** the pair reads **"Take it out" / "Leave it in"**, both naming the background the row
  is labelled with. While the cut-out is off, the three numeric rows are still removed from the
  screen, but "Fine tune" and "Back to normal" stay in place **disabled**, and the disclosure reports
  `aria-expanded="false"` because it has nothing to expand over.
- **Why:** "Keep my photo" was ambiguous twice over. On its own it reads as "do not delete it" rather
  than "do not remove the background" — and the cropper's own cancel button sits a few pixels above
  it saying **"Keep what you had"**, which means keep your *previous avatar*. One screen, two
  meanings of "keep", inches apart. Naming the background in both buttons removes the guesswork and
  makes the pair parallel, which is what lets the label above carry the object. Short enough that
  both fit one line at 9 px pixel type, which the longer "Remove background / Keep background" would
  not.
  On greying rather than hiding: ADR-077 hid the numeric rows on the principle that a disabled
  control still claims to do something, and that principle is right for *choices* — with nothing
  being cut out, "Loose / Normal / Tight" is a set of options that no longer exists. It is wrong for
  the panel's two fixed *actions*. Removing those would collapse the controls from five rows to two
  and slide everything else under the participant's thumb mid-tap, on a phone, on a beach. Greyed
  says "not for this" while keeping the furniture still. The distinction to carry forward: **hide a
  choice that has ceased to exist, disable an action that is merely unavailable.**
  `aria-expanded` follows the real state rather than the toggle's own memory, so a screen reader is
  never told a disclosure is open over an empty region. The remembered open/closed preference is
  deliberately *not* reset, so turning the cut-out back on returns the participant to the panel they
  left.
- **Impact:** `.gb-button[disabled]` already carried the greyed treatment (ADR-076 did not disturb
  it), so this needed no new styling. Pinned in `e2e/cut-out-tuning.spec.ts`, which asserts both
  buttons are visible *and* disabled while off, that the disclosure reports shut, and that both
  return to enabled when the cut-out is turned back on — visibility and disabledness asserted
  separately, because "greyed out" is a claim about both and hiding them would satisfy neither.

### ADR-079 — "A new photograph arrived" and "the same photograph, re-rendered" are different events

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-073 (which skipped this commit and caused the bug), ADR-077 (the toggle that
  exposed it), ADR-059/060 (the state that must not be reset), ADR-054 (the backdrop path this leaves
  alone), reported bug: "when I select 'Leave it in' the preview looks correct but when saved the
  background removal still happened."
- **Decision:** `PhotoRow` takes two callbacks instead of one. `onPhoto` still means a photograph
  arrived or was taken off, and still starts the character choice over. `onSpriteChange` means the
  same photograph rendered differently, and touches nothing but the draft. A settled tuning is
  committed through the second, from an effect keyed on `usePhotoTuning`'s new `settled` value.
- **Why:** the draft's `avatarPhoto` was written in exactly four places, and only one of them —
  `useCrop`, reached solely by pressing "Use this square" — carried the participant's tuning. Turning
  the cut-out off and pressing Save therefore saved the sprite `convert()` had produced with the
  default tuning: a cut-out photo. The preview was right the whole time, because it reads the hook
  directly, which is precisely what made it convincing.
  ADR-073 had considered pushing each tuned sprite to the draft and rejected it for a real reason:
  `onPhoto` means two things, and choosing a character changes the backdrop, which repaints the
  sprite, which would have fired `onPhoto`'s reset and undone the character choice that caused the
  repaint. Two acceptance tests caught that at the time. The mistake was to drop the commit instead
  of splitting the event — the conflation was the defect, and skipping the commit only hid it behind
  a button.
  Keyed on `settled` rather than on the sprite because `settled` is the tuning the current sprite was
  painted from: its identity changes exactly once per settled knob change. A backdrop repaint yields a
  new sprite but the same `settled`, so it does not fire here and remains ADR-054's business. That is
  also why the guard is a comparison and not a dependency list — `onSpriteChange` is an inline arrow
  in the parent, so its identity changes every render.
- **Impact:** tuning now reaches the big preview at the top of the studio as well as the controls'
  own, which ADR-073 had listed as a deliberate omission — that omission is withdrawn. `useCrop`
  still paints with the tuning, so accepting a square remains correct on its own terms.
  Pinned by `e2e/cut-out-tuning.spec.ts`, which turns the cut-out off and presses **Save without
  "Use this square"**, then asserts the sprite *the server holds* contains neither the backdrop nor
  the ink palette index. That test was written first and observed to fail before the fix. The four
  tests that already existed all passed while this bug was live: three read the preview and one went
  through "Use this square", so every one of them exercised the broken path without asking what was
  persisted. The lesson is in `AGENTS-testing.md` terms — assert on what the server ends up holding,
  not on what the screen shows.

### ADR-080 — Coverage thresholds are a ratchet the gate actually runs

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** `AGENTS-testing.md` §1.1 (what an assertion must look at), ADR-072 (the type-only
  module that made 100 % unreachable), ADR-013 (entrypoint exclusions), user request: "now boost up
  our test coverage", after "is our playwright coverage of app dropping below 100%?"
- **Decision:** both workspaces' `test` scripts run `vitest run --coverage`, so `npm run verify`
  evaluates the thresholds. The thresholds are set to **today's measured coverage**, not to 100, and
  may only ever be raised — in the same change that earns the rise. Type-only modules are excluded
  from the report.
- **Why:** both configs already demanded `{ lines: 100, functions: 100, branches: 100, statements:
  100 }` and both `test` scripts were plain `vitest run`, so **nothing ever evaluated them**. The
  declared standard was 100 %; the measured reality had drifted to 91.33 % (web) and 97.07 % (api),
  and no gate could notice. A threshold nothing runs is a comment.
  Set to the actual rather than left at 100 because the alternative was turning `npm run verify` red
  for four sessions working in one shared tree, over a gap none of them created and most of which
  belongs to features still in flight. A floor that holds today converts an aspiration nobody checked
  into a regression test everybody runs; 100 remains the target, reached by raising the floor as
  coverage is earned, which is a series of green commits rather than one long red branch.
  Type-only modules compile to an empty file, so v8 reports 0 % of 0 statements and the run can never
  reach *any* high threshold however many tests exist. `lib/avatar/types.ts` (ADR-072) had made 100 %
  arithmetically unreachable from the moment it was added, which is worth knowing before the next
  person spends an afternoon on it.
- **Impact:** floors at this commit are web `lines 91.5 / functions 92.7 / branches 98.2` and api
  `lines 97 / functions 97.9 / branches 94.6`. **Lowering one requires an addendum saying why**;
  raising one needs nothing but the tests. The gap that remains is concentrated in features other
  sessions own — `SelfieCapture` 4 %, `PhotosPanel` 7 %, `GalleryModerationPage` 7 %, `AnnouncePage`
  9 %, `ChatPanel` 10 %, `useGalleryModeration` 12 %, `useUploadPhoto` 14 % — and closing it is
  several hundred tests, not one sitting. Separately, **Playwright coverage is still not measured at
  all**: the e2e suite has 11 spec files and ~84 tests, essentially all participant-side, against 28
  facilitator and superadmin route files with no dedicated specs. Nothing in this addendum changes
  that, and a coverage percentage would not have caught any of the three defects that prompted §1.1.

### ADR-081 — What a dead export is, and what is merely unused

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** [`../cleanup/2026-09-30-orphan-cleanup.md`](../cleanup/2026-09-30-orphan-cleanup.md)
  (the mechanical inventory, written before the removals), ADR-068 (which retired two motif sprites on
  the same grounds and set the precedent), ADR-080 (the coverage ratchet this must not trip), ADR-010
  (a convention nothing checks decays), ADR-074 and ADR-064/065 (whose superseded halves produced most
  of what is removed here), user request: "remove all these, but first I want you to mechanically
  document all these removed bits into a clean up md doc, then do the cleanup".
- **Decision:** an export is **dead**, and removed, only when it has zero references outside its own
  file **and** zero inside it, and is not a deliberate test seam. Anything failing only the first test
  is over-exported, not dead, and stays. Removed on those terms: the `cursor` field on both chat page
  views and its three producers, `editCourtRequestSchema`, `findAnnouncementById`,
  `findChatMessageById`, four wire types (`ErrorView`, `MatchRosterEntry`, `ScanResultView`,
  `ListView`), four Drizzle row types, `CLUSTER_COUNT`, `SHA1_HEX_LENGTH`, `MessageKey`,
  `EmptyStateKey`, and fourteen `z.infer` request aliases nothing imported. Five false code comments
  are corrected in the same change.
- **Why the second test is the one that matters.** A scan that only asks "is this imported anywhere
  else?" flags 244 symbols in this repository, and most of them are fine: `CHAT_PAGE_LIMIT` has no
  external consumer and is used at `db/entities/chat.ts:87`. Adding "and is it used in its own file?"
  cuts that to 32 genuine ones. The remaining judgement is the seam exemption — `forgetSegmenter`,
  `resetCachesForTests`, `componentSizesOf` and their kin exist so a test can reach what the product
  reaches another way, which ADR-033/045/072 state outright. A sweep without that exemption deletes
  the testability those ADRs paid for.
- **The interesting finding is not any single symbol, it is the shape they share.** Almost everything
  here is the *residue of a superseded decision*: `cursor` is what ADR-064/065 left when the client
  stopped persisting a position; `findAnnouncementById` served the dismissal route ADR-074 replaced
  before release; `findChatMessageById` is the half of a read-then-hide pair that ADR-066's
  publish-after-the-row-returns rule made unnecessary. **A decision that supersedes another needs to
  name what the change makes dead, or the dead thing survives as a plausible-looking API.** Recording
  that here because it is a rule for writing the next addendum, not a rule for sweeping later.
- **`ErrorView` is the one that had already failed.** The error envelope is hand-built four times in
  `app.ts` while the contract type describing it was imported by nobody — the two-sources-of-truth
  trap `AGENTS.md` §3 exists to prevent, resolved in the worse direction, silently. Removing the unused
  type is the honest half; typing those four sites from the contract is a refactor of the error path
  (ADR-048's `HTTPException` handling lives there) and is deliberately left, recorded in the cleanup
  doc §4.6 rather than done badly here.
- **Two constants were removed while their constraints were not.** `SHA1_HEX_LENGTH` claimed in its own
  comment to bound the duplicate check; `snapshot.sql:348`'s `char(40) CHECK (sha1_raw ~ '^[0-9a-f]{40}$')`
  and `ux_gallery_photo_sha1` are what have ever enforced it. A constant that documents a constraint it
  cannot reach is exactly the unchecked convention ADR-010 objects to. The SQL is untouched.
- **What was reported as dead and deliberately kept, which is the more useful half of the audit.**
  `signInStaff` and `seeded.facilitatorPasscode` in `e2e/fixtures.ts` had zero callers once ADR-074
  retired the seeded staff chat line — and are kept, with a comment naming why and when to revisit
  (`ec6c119`). The twelve lines were never the cost: `signedInAt` beside them records a race that only
  appeared once the database moved off in-process PGlite onto a real Postgres server, because the
  sign-in round trip grew by the milliseconds the old check had silently relied on. Delete the helper
  and that is re-derived wrong by whoever writes the first facilitator e2e spec — and ADR-080 says 28
  route files are waiting for one. **The rule this sets: where a zero-caller export carries knowledge,
  comment it with an expiry instead of deleting it. An unexplained zero-caller export is what generates
  the next audit.**
- **Explicitly not done, and why each is a decision rather than a cleanup:** `TEAM_CHAT_PAGE_LIMIT`
  still serves both team-room reads at 200, so ADR-065 reached one of the two rooms — closing it is a
  route parameter and a contract change, so it wants its own entry. Staff authorship of chat messages
  is live, intended and test-pinned at the API (`authorization-matrix.test.ts:73-77`, ADR-046) while
  ADR-074 closed every UI path to it, so **removing either end breaks an accepted ADR or a passing
  test** and it needs a ruling. ADR-077's backdrop swatch on a cut-out-off sprite, ADR-027's missing
  scan undo and ADR-064's three stated leftovers are absent features, not orphans. `apps/api/.data/dev`
  cannot boot because `bootstrap.ts:28` probes a single sentinel, and that is 136 MB of the user's data
  and the user's call. The motif corpus — 169 of 191 `MOTIF_NAMES` entries have no call site — is
  excluded by direction: those sprites are to be placed, not retired. Participant titles likewise stay
  in full, including their two unused symbols, by direction: the feature is wanted.
- **Impact:** no behaviour changes and no schema changes. Two response bodies lose a field no client
  read. Deleting untested code raises the ADR-080 floors rather than tripping them, so they are
  untouched. Verified: `npm run typecheck` (3 workspaces), `npx eslint .`,
  `node scripts/check-standards.mjs`, `apps/api` integration against real PGlite, `apps/web` unit and
  hook suites. **E2E was not run** — Chromium cannot obtain its Mach port bootstrap under this
  sandbox, so an e2e claim from this session would be unverifiable (`AGENTS-workflow.md` §4).
  The sweep is reproducible: collect every `export` in `apps/*/src` and `packages/*/src`, count
  references in all of `apps`, `packages`, `e2e`, `scripts` **including** the declaring file minus the
  declaration itself, and report the symbols scoring zero on both counts.

### ADR-082 — Presence is a note in memory, not a write on the request path

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-01
- **Relates to:** ADR-003/043 (exactly one API process — the reason no Redis is needed),
  ADR-004 (sessions), ADR-024/034 (the polling crowd this protects the database from),
  ADR-081 (the dead-export terms under which the single-row touches were removed).
- **Decision:** `loadActor` no longer performs the two awaited UPDATEs (`sessions.last_seen_at`
  always, `participants.last_seen_at` for participants) that every authenticated request paid
  before its handler ran. Requests now add ids to two module-level `Set`s in
  `lib/presence.ts`; a 30-second interval started by `index.ts` — the only file that opens a
  port is also the only file that starts background clocks, so `createApp()` stays pure for
  `app.request()` tests — drains both sets and stamps everyone seen with ONE statement per
  table (`touchParticipantsSeen` / `touchSessionsSeen`, batch replacements for the deleted
  single-row touches). A failed flush logs, restores its ids, and lets the next tick retry;
  `flushPresence` never rejects into the timer. A `Set` rather than a timestamp map because
  the flush stamps everyone with the same moment: per-request timestamps carry no
  information the "within a minute" contract can express, and deduplication comes free —
  forty polls from one phone in an interval are one entry.
- **Why:** the touches were the app's largest write source and scaled with traffic, not with
  anything a reader wanted: at 300 phones and ~4 authenticated requests/minute each, roughly
  2,400 single-row UPDATEs per minute queued on the single serialized connection (ADR-003)
  ahead of match scores — while `sessions.last_seen_at` has zero readers (expiry is a fixed
  `validUntil` window, not sliding) and `participants.last_seen_at` reaches no wire view.
  After: at most four statements per minute, bounded by headcount (≤ ~300 rows each), and
  the request path performs no writes at all. Parallel page-load requests no longer take
  turns holding a row lock to record timestamps milliseconds apart.
- **What is knowingly given up:** per-request precision (no consumer can observe the
  difference), and up to one interval of presence on a crash or restart (the contract
  absorbs it). `sessions.last_seen_at` is kept — batched — purely as forensics: "when was
  this token last used" is a question an incident review does ask; the column's only cost
  is now two statements a minute.
- **Impact:** `src/tests/presence.test.ts` reads the real rows: three authenticated requests
  move neither timestamp, the flush moves both, only seen actors are stamped, an empty
  interval issues no query, and a failed flush loses nothing. Anyone adding a feature that
  READS `last_seen_at` at finer than flush-interval resolution must revisit this ADR.

### ADR-083 — The Social tab lights up for unread global chat after all

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-01
- **Relates to:** ADR-063 (whose "the global room deliberately does not light up" this
  reverses, and whose mechanics it reuses wholesale), ADR-046/064/065/066 (the room itself),
  ADR-024/074 (the jittered alerts poll the dot rides on), ADR-049 (schema changed in place).
- **Decision:** the global room gets the team room's exact treatment: a read high-water mark
  per participant (`participant.chat_last_read_message_id`, the participant-level twin of
  `team_membership.last_read_message_id`; NULL = never opened the room), a `LIMIT 1`
  existence probe over *visible* messages (`hasUnreadChat`) riding the existing
  `GET /api/me/alerts` response as one more boolean, and `POST /api/chat/read { upTo }` whose
  never-back guard lives in the UPDATE's WHERE clause — two phones on one account report
  different positions, and the later report must not un-read what the other saw. On the web,
  absorbing is also reading: `useChatRoom` clears the dot and names the newest id it actually
  rendered, exactly as `useTeamChatRoom` does, and the Social nav item joins Teams in
  carrying an LED (dot-not-count, visually-hidden label, per ADR-063).
- **Why the reversal:** ADR-063 reasoned the global room is ambient and not worth
  interrupting for. In practice a dark Social tab reads as a dead room — the one signal a
  quiet event app cannot afford to send — and the product call went the other way. The cost
  argument that justified the original exclusion no longer exists: the alerts poll already
  runs, so the dot costs one indexed existence probe per poll and no new request, stream, or
  cadence.
- **What is knowingly given up:** the marker moves even for messages that scrolled past
  unread on an open panel (the team room accepts the same), and a participant who never
  opens the room keeps a lit dot — that is the feature working.
- **Impact:** `chat-read-marker.test.ts` proves the lifecycle against real rows, including
  the two places this differs from the team room: the marker works with no team at all, and
  a moderated-away line puts the dot out rather than leaving it burning for something nobody
  can see. `GameboyShell.test.tsx` pins both LEDs' render contract. Anyone adding a third
  room should extract the marker pattern rather than photocopy it a third time.

### ADR-084 — Every strictness TypeScript offers about our own code, and `skipLibCheck` stays on

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-010 (the numeric half of the function-design rules), ADR-080 (the coverage
  ratchet), and the instruction "set tsconfig to use the absolutely most strictest config, then …
  ensure all tests are still good".
- **Decision:** `tsconfig.base.json` adds `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`,
  `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, `noImplicitReturns`,
  `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, `allowUnreachableCode: false` and `allowUnusedLabels: false`
  on top of the `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `noImplicitOverride` and
  `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` that were already there. All three workspaces extend it, so this is
  one edit for the whole repo. **`skipLibCheck` stays `true`.**
- **Why `skipLibCheck` stays on, having actually been tried.** Turning it off produced **107**
  errors, of which **87 were inside `node_modules`** — Drizzle's `singlestore-core`, `mysql-core`,
  `gel-core` and `sqlite-core` dialects that this app never imports, plus PGlite and Hono. Not one
  was actionable, none said anything about our code, and the only ways to silence them are pinning
  or patching a dependency. That is a worse repo than the one with the flag on, so "strictest" here
  means strictest **about code we write**, which is the thing the flag actually controls.
- **The 20 real errors it found, and how each was fixed.** No suppression, no `any`, no
  `@ts-expect-error`:
  - **13 × `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` (TS2379/TS2375).** Route handlers pass
    `c.req.query('…')`, which is `string | undefined`, into filter and insert bags whose optional
    properties were declared `?: string`. Every one of those properties is read behind a truthiness
    test, so an explicit `undefined` was always as valid as an absent key — the declarations now say
    so (`?: T | undefined`) instead of leaving it to be inferred. Where the receiving type is not
    ours — `RequestInit.body`, React Router's `NavLink.end` — the key is spread conditionally rather
    than set to `undefined`, because there the distinction is real.
  - **5 × `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` (TS4111).** `process.env.PORT`, a header map's
    `.authorization`, a `dataset`'s `.liveKey`, a CSS declaration's `.transform`, a cluster-keyed
    pool's `.BP` — all lookups into index signatures, now bracketed. This one is worth keeping
    precisely because it marks the difference between a field that is known to exist and a key that
    is hoped for.
  - **2 × unused bindings (TS6133).** Parameters that exist only to reach the next one, now
    underscore-prefixed, which `eslint.config.js` already exempts for the same reason.
- **The web workspace's errors were hidden behind the API's.** `npm run typecheck` runs contracts →
  api → web and stops at the first failure, so the first clean run was not the last: fixing
  `apps/api` revealed a further 31 in `apps/web` of the same three classes. Worth knowing before
  anyone reads one green typecheck as the end of a strictness change.
- **Nothing was loosened to make this pass.** Every fix either states a truth the code already
  relied on or omits a key that should never have been set. Full gate green afterwards: typecheck,
  lint, standards (321 files, 0 violations), API 277 passed / 3 skipped, web 676 passed, coverage
  ratchet satisfied.

### ADR-085 — A completed input is a submission

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-027 (PIN entry and `autoComplete`), ADR-041 (Safari first-class), ADR-046 and
  ADR-063 (the two chat rooms), ADR-074 (announcements), F26–F28 (the fringe station), and the
  instruction: "when the facilitator scan a QR code of a participant, I want the frontend to
  immediately act as though the submit button has been pressed. Similarly, when users are typing in
  the chat and they hit the send key on their mobile keyboard, it sends immediately as well."
- **Decision:** wherever an input can be *complete*, completing it submits. The button stays —
  it is how the action is discovered, and how a keyboard-less or screen-reader user reaches it — but
  nobody has to travel to it. Concretely: Enter sends in both chat boxes and the announcement box
  (Shift+Enter breaks the line), the fourth digit of a PIN signs a participant in, and the six
  single-field panels that had a dead Enter key are now real forms.
- **The QR half of the request was already true**, and is recorded here so the next reader does not
  re-implement it: `useQrScanner`'s `onDecoded` calls `submitScan` directly (F27), so a decoded badge
  scores without a button press. What was missing was everywhere *else* that logic had not reached.
- **One hook, `useSubmitOnEnter`, for the textareas**, with three guards that each exist for a real
  case rather than for tidiness:
  - **Shift+Enter still breaks the line**, which is the escape hatch that makes Enter-to-send fair to
    impose. Ctrl, Alt and Meta pass through untouched for the same reason.
  - **A composing IME is not a send.** Chinese, Japanese and Korean input uses Enter to accept the
    candidate being offered; sending there would post a half-finished word *and* eat the keystroke
    that was choosing it. This app runs in Singapore, so that is an ordinary case, not an edge one.
    Both `isComposing` and the older WebKit `keyCode === 229` signal are checked (ADR-041).
  - **`canSend` is asked, never assumed.** The keyboard refuses exactly when the button is disabled —
    empty, whitespace-only, over the cap, already in flight, or offline for an announcement. A
    keyboard path that skipped those would be a way around the guards the button advertises.
- **A refused send still calls `preventDefault`.** Otherwise the rejected Enter leaves a newline in
  the box and the next attempt sends whitespace the sender never typed.
- **The PIN auto-submit needed a real fix, not just a callback.** `onComplete` fires from inside the
  `onChange` that produced the fourth digit, so at that instant React state still holds **three**
  digits — the first implementation submitted a PIN one character short, and the existing test caught
  it (`expected { pin: '482' } to deeply equal { pin: '4821' }`). Two consequences, both deliberate:
  the completed value travels *with* the callback rather than being read back from state, and
  `useParticipantSignIn`'s `submit` takes an optional override for it. For the same staleness reason
  the guard is on the **nickname**, not on `form.canSubmit` — that also requires a four-digit PIN, so
  guarding on it would have meant the auto-submit could never fire at all.
- **Opt-in per surface, because completeness is not always submission.** Sign-in passes `onComplete`;
  **sign-up does not**, because it asks for a cluster and an avatar after the PIN, and submitting
  there would send a half-filled form. A PIN completed *before* the nickname also waits for the
  button rather than firing a request that could only fail — that case has its own test.
- **Three sign-in tests had to change, and that is the specification moving rather than a
  regression.** They typed a full PIN and *then* clicked submit, which is now two submissions. One
  of them asserted the button becomes enabled after a complete PIN — a state ADR-085 makes
  unreachable on success, because the form has already navigated away. It is split: the disabled rule
  is asserted on an incomplete PIN, and the enabled rule on the one path where the button is still
  the way through (PIN completed before the nickname). Per ADR-080 and ADR-081 §4.10 item 6, a red
  suite here meant the spec moved.
- **The six new forms are real `<form onSubmit>` elements, not key handlers.** Join-by-code,
  create-team, add-member-by-nickname, photo caption, the void/unvoid/winner-edit reason dialog and
  the announcement box. A form gives Enter-to-submit for free, correctly, including for assistive
  technology — hand-rolling `onKeyDown` six times would have been more code and less correct. Each
  button moves from `type="button"` to `type="submit"` and keeps its existing disabled condition, and
  each form carries a `data-testid` per AGENTS.md §3.11 (`check-standards.mjs` caught all five that
  did not).
- **The reason dialog is included deliberately, though it gates a destructive act.** A correction
  console is used at speed with one hand on the keyboard, the reason field is already required, and
  `isBusy` stops a double Enter from sending the change twice. The announcement box keeps its offline
  refusal on the keyboard path too — an announcement sent late is worse than none (ADR-074).
- **Validation:** typecheck, lint, standards (323 files, 0 violations), API 277 passed / 3 skipped,
  web 695 passed, coverage ratchet satisfied. Red-checked: removing the chat `onKeyDown` fails two of
  the four keyboard tests, and the two that still pass are the ones asserting Enter does *not* send.
  E2E not run.
### ADR-086 — The last announcement before you arrived sticks; the rest of the backlog does not

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-074 (the announcement toast and its browser-side dismissal, which this replaces
  the storage of), ADR-064 (the per-mount cursor, the sign-out leak and the cache-key regression this
  copies its lessons from), ADR-046 (UUIDv7 as a sort key), ADR-038 (the shared `cachedRead` this must
  not break), ADR-009/019 (one owner per storage key), ADR-081 §4.10 (where the gap was recorded),
  ADR-080 (the coverage ratchet), user request: "clients remember when they log on, so announcements
  sent before session are not retrieved and ignored… the timestamp of the most recent announcement that
  was read and dismissed", revised to "only the final announcement before the user login should stick,
  all the ones before that final announcement will be ignored."
- **Decision:** a participant sees **the last announcement made before they signed in**, everything
  announced after they signed in, and nothing at or before the last one they dismissed. This is carried
  by **one stored id** — `psd.announcements.floor.v1`, owned by `lib/storage/announcementStore.ts` —
  seeded on the first alerts poll of a session to the **second-newest** live announcement, advanced by
  each dismissal, forgotten at sign-out. The filter is `announcement.id > floor`.
- **Why the revision is the better rule, which is worth recording because the first version was
  specified and rejected within the hour.** "Ignore everything from before I logged on" loses
  *"finals start at 4pm"* for anyone signing in at 15:55 — the single announcement most worth arriving
  to. Keeping exactly the last one gives a latecomer the current state of the event without handing them
  the morning's backlog, which is what the cutoff was for. The rule is "the event has a current notice",
  not "you missed it".
- **Two floors collapse into one value.** "Before I signed in" and "up to the one I last dismissed" are
  the same sentence — *ignore everything at or before this point* — so they are one mark and one
  comparison, not two timestamps that have to agree. The seed being the **second-newest** id is what
  makes the newest one stick with no special case: there is no "except the last one" branch anywhere.
- **An id, not a time, and this is the load-bearing choice.** Ids are UUIDv7, so comparing them as
  strings *is* comparing the server's ordering. The specification said "timestamps", and timestamps
  would have meant comparing a locally-recorded clock reading against the server's `createdAt`: a beach
  phone whose clock is hours out would hide notices it should show, or show ones it should hide, and the
  bug would be invisible to everyone whose clock was right. No device clock takes part in this feature.
- **A high-water mark replaces the dismissed-id list rather than joining it.** That list needed
  `rememberDismissed(id, live)` to prune itself against the server's live ids purely to stop growing for
  the life of the device; a mark is bounded by construction, so the pruning is deleted rather than
  ported. One key, one id, no maintenance.
- **Seeded where the list first arrives, not at the sign-in surface.** There are four ways into a
  session — participant sign-in, sign-up, staff sign-in, a restored cookie (ADR-015/017) — and seeding
  at each would be four chances to forget one. `useAlertsStore`'s first successful poll is one seam that
  serves all of them.
  The guard is `hasAnnouncementFloor()` rather than `floor === null`, and the difference is a real bug
  rather than a style: a participant who arrives before anything has been announced has a null floor,
  and if "null" meant "unseeded" then every poll would re-seed — so the first announcement of the day
  would be treated as one made *before* they arrived and silently swallowed. "Seeded with no floor" and
  "never seeded" have to be different states.
- **Forward only, and forgotten at sign-out.** Two tabs can report positions out of order, and winding
  the mark back would resurrect announcements the reader has cleared. Sign-out removes the key beside
  the session token and the last path (`signOut()` in `lib/api/participants.ts`) — ADR-064 found exactly
  this leak one feature over, where an uncleared chat cursor opened an empty room for the next
  participant on a borrowed phone; here an inherited floor would hide notices from someone who has never
  seen them.
- **The server does not change, deliberately.** Both floors are applied client-side, so `GET
  /api/me/alerts` keeps returning one identical list and ADR-074's shared `cachedRead` survives: three
  hundred phones remain about one query per TTL window. Pushing the floor into a query parameter is the
  obvious alternative and is exactly ADR-064's regression — three hundred distinct cursors were three
  hundred cache keys, and removing that was recorded as a *cost win*.
- **A retraction still wins, by construction.** The floor decides what is too old to show, never what
  stays shown, so an announcement the server has dropped from the live list is gone whatever the floor
  says. The mark may also name a row that has since been retracted, which is fine because the comparison
  is `id > floor` and never a lookup — the same property ADR-066 relies on when its `oldest` cursor names
  a hidden message.
- **Impact:** `readDismissed`/`rememberDismissed` are gone; the key changes from
  `psd.announcements.dismissed.v1` (a JSON array) to `psd.announcements.floor.v1`
  (`{"floorId": string | null}`). **A browser holding the old key simply re-seeds** — the new key is
  absent, so the first poll seeds a floor and the reader sees the current notice; the stale key is never
  read again. No migration, and nothing to clean up on a device nobody controls.
  `check-standards.mjs` rule 8 needed no change: the module reaches storage only through
  `localStore.ts`, which is what the rule asks.
  Tests: `announcementStore.test.ts` is new (11 cases — seeding at zero, one and three live, the
  malformed and wrong-shape values, forward-only advance, idempotence, and the sign-out forget), written
  first and observed failing for the right reason. `AnnouncementToast.test.tsx` moves from ADR-074's
  contract to this one, and its old "shows the next one after the first is dismissed" case **splits in
  two**, because under this rule that scenario only holds for announcements made *after* sign-in: one
  test now pins "only the last one before I arrived", another pins the oldest-first queue for arrivals
  during the event, and a third pins that a remount does not re-seed and resurrect the backlog. Those
  tests were green against the old behaviour — per ADR-080 and ADR-081 §4.10 item 6, a red suite here
  meant the specification moved, which is the one case where editing a passing test is correct.

### ADR-087 — The team room gets ADR-065's limits too

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-30
- **Relates to:** ADR-063 (the team room), ADR-065 (the same decision for the global room), ADR-064
  (the per-mount cursor), `fds.md` §4.2 R2, and the instruction ADR-065 was written from — "in the
  spirit of not blowing up our database … the frontend only retrieves the last 50 messages … only
  when the user scrolls up we do ajax lazy loads".
- **Decision:** the team room opens on the newest **fifty** rather than two hundred, and
  `GET /api/team-chat/messages?before=<id>` walks back up the history fifty at a time reporting
  `hasOlder`. `TeamChatPageView` carries `hasOlder`, and the panel gets the same early-fetch sentinel
  and "Earlier messages" button as the global room.
- **Why:** ADR-065 was applied to one of the two rooms. `TEAM_CHAT_PAGE_LIMIT = 200` backed *both* the
  forward delta and the tail read, and there was no backwards pagination at all — so the room a
  participant opens most, because its tab lights up when something is said in it, was still handing a
  phone four times what the global room hands it. **No ADR said the rooms should differ**, which makes
  this an omission rather than a decision, and that is the whole reason it is being fixed rather than
  documented.
- **One implementation, shared.** `useOlderPages` moves out of `useChatRoom` into `liveRoom.ts`,
  generic over the message type and the fetch. The two rooms differed only in those: the guards, the
  optimistic `hasOlder` and the error path were identical, and duplicating them is precisely how the
  team room came to have no walk-back in the first place. The global room's behaviour is unchanged —
  its sixteen hook tests pass untouched, which is what makes that claim checkable rather than asserted.
- **A backwards page does not mark the room read.** This is the one way this room differs from the
  global one, and it is deliberate. `markTeamChatRead` only moves its mark forward, so old messages
  could not drag it back — but it would still be a write per scroll gesture, and a reader has read
  nothing *new* by scrolling up. The mark belongs to the newest line seen, which is what keeps the nav
  dot honest (ADR-063).
- **The walk-back is bounded by the predicate, not by the cursor it is handed.** Membership is
  resolved before the cursor is read, and `readableBy` still floors spoken lines at the member's
  `joined_at`. So a `before` naming a message in another team's room returns this caller's own
  history, and a late joiner cannot reach conversation from before they joined by scrolling. Both have
  a test; the first is this feature's wrong-party case.
- **Uncached, unlike the global room's equivalent.** Per the reasoning already recorded in
  `teamChat.ts`: a key would have to include both the team and the member's join time, so sixty teams
  would share almost nothing and each entry would be invalidated about as often as it was read. The
  partial index does the work.
- **`hasOlder` is a fact, not a guess** — one row past the limit is read and dropped, so a list stops
  asking instead of making one extra empty request at the end of the conversation. Always false for a
  forward delta, where the question does not apply.
- **Numbering note:** written as ADR-075, renumbered to 083 before landing because three other
  sessions claimed 075–082 while this was in flight. `TEAM_CHAT_PAGE_LIMIT = 200` is deliberately
  kept: it still bounds the forward `after` delta, which is a reconnect catching up rather than a
  phone opening a room.


### ADR-088 — A spoken 4-digit scan number replaces the typed nickname at the fringe station

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-01
- **Relates to:** `docs/design/scan-number-assessment.md` (the full option analysis this decision
  compresses), `docs/design/facilitator-journey-assessment.md` R-2/P6/D-5/D-6 (the frictions being
