  `@psd/contracts`; `lib/socialPause.ts` middleware and `lib/lifecycle.ts`; `PROCESS_SUPERVISED`
  in `env.ts` and in `docker/supervisord.conf`; `routes-superadmin/system.ts`; S61 `SystemPage`
  with `useSystemControls`, and an "Operations" tab last in the console. On the participant
  side, `lib/socialPaused.ts` recognises the pause from the 503 the panel's existing read
  already makes — no extra request and nothing new to poll — and `SocialPausedNotice` renders
  it. `useChatRoom` absorbed `canSend` while it was there, so the Enter key and the button can
  no longer form separate opinions about it. Six sabotages were watched to fail: hard-coding
  `canRestart` true, rendering the panels on a guess instead of waiting for the read, dropping
  the state re-read after a pause, never recording that a restart was asked for, treating the
  pause as an ordinary error, and treating every error as a pause.

### ADR-119 — a quiet stream is timed, not trusted

- **Date:** 2026-10-02
- **Status:** Accepted
- **Relates to:** ADR-046 (the global room's SSE transport), ADR-063 (the team room), ADR-064
  (`isLive` and the reconnect), ADR-024 (jittered polling, which `isLive` suppresses),
  ADR-043 (the Cloudflare tunnel whose idle timeout the heartbeat already exists to beat)
- **Status note:** implemented.
- **Context:** both rooms decide whether they are live from `EventSource`'s own `open` and
  `error` events, and `error` only fires when the *browser* notices the connection drop. It does
  not fire for a half-open socket — beach Wi-Fi vanishing, a phone changing network, a proxy
  dropping the far side without a FIN. TCP will hold such a connection open indefinitely with
  nothing arriving on it. Both rooms then behave badly, and differently. The global room spends
  `isLive` suppressing its own fallback (`usePolling(room.isLive ? noop : room.catchUp)`), so a
  lying `isLive` means no stream *and* no poll. The team room has no poll at all: a dead socket
  there is a room that never updates again, while showing none of its "live updates are off"
  hint. Meanwhile the evidence needed to detect this was already on the wire and being thrown
  away — the server writes a heartbeat every 25 s for the tunnel's benefit, and no client
  listened for it.
- **Decision:** the client times frames instead of trusting the absence of an error. A shared
  `createStreamWatchdog` (`lib/api/streamWatchdog.ts`) is touched by **every** frame — message,
  retraction, heartbeat, and the `open` event — and fires `onStale` after `STREAM_STALE_MS` of
  silence. Both rooms respond by setting `isLive` false *and* bumping a `revival` counter in the
  effect's dependencies, which tears the stream down and rebuilds it from the current cursor.
  The heartbeat's name moves into `@psd/contracts` as `CHAT_HEARTBEAT_EVENT`, beside
  `CHAT_HIDDEN_EVENT`, so the two sides cannot drift.
- **Why 70 seconds.** Two and a bit heartbeats. One lost frame is a hiccup and must not tear a
  healthy stream down; three missed in a row is not a hiccup. It is a pair with the server's
  `HEARTBEAT_MS` of 25 s, and moving one without the other reintroduces the bug — which is why
  the constant says so.
- **Why reuse the effect rather than reconnect inside the transport.** `useForegroundGeneration`
  already rebuilds a stream by re-running the effect, and that path is proven: it closes the old
  handle, re-reads the cursor, and re-subscribes. A bespoke reconnect inside `chatStream.ts`
  would have to re-acquire the cursor the hook owns, and would be a second implementation of
  something the app already does correctly.
- **Why the stale callback carries no `cancelled` guard**, unlike every handler beside it:
  closing the handle stops the watchdog, so a stale callback cannot outlive the stream that
  armed it. A guard there would be a branch no test could reach, and this repo treats an
  uncoverable defensive branch as a defect rather than as prudence.
- **Impact:** `CHAT_HEARTBEAT_EVENT` in `packages/contracts`; new
  `apps/web/src/lib/api/streamWatchdog.ts`; `chatStream.ts` and `teamChatStream.ts` gain an
  `onStale` handler and a heartbeat listener; `useChatRoom` and `useTeamChatRoom` gain a
  `revival` trigger. **No server change** — the heartbeat it already sends is simply consumed by
  a second reader. Four sabotages were watched to fail: removing the heartbeat listener (both
  rooms' "stays alive on heartbeats alone" went red), disarming the watchdog timer (both rooms'
  staleness tests and the unit test went red), and removing the `revival` bump from each hook in
  turn (each room's rebuild test went red). Web coverage floors raised to lines 98.94, functions
  98.12, branches 98.33, statements 98.94 — the minimum of six runs. Worth recording why they are
  not the prettier numbers: the suite run *alone* reports functions 98.23, but the same suite run
  inside `npm run verify` reports 98.12, because a loaded machine changes what the timing-
  sensitive surfaces execute. A floor set from the isolated reading fails the real gate.
- **Also in this change, and not part of the decision:** `security-sweep.test.ts` gained a named
  tolerance for `POST /api/admin/system/restart`, which answers 503 when the process has no
  supervisor to restart it. That is a capability answer, not a crash, and it is the correct
  reply under `app.request()` where nothing opened a port. The branch was failing `npm run
  verify` on this before any of the work above — fallout from ADR-118 landing in halves.

### ADR-120 — the two reads to fix before anything is pushed

- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Status:** Accepted
- **Relates to:** ADR-038 (`cachedRead`), ADR-094 (the tags), ADR-091 (the up-soon window),
  ADR-109/114 (the live feed and its scores), and `docs/design/sse-announcements-feed.md` §11,
  whose build order this is steps 1 and 2 of
- **Status note:** implemented.
- **Context:** the SSE design ends with a build order whose first two steps are not streaming
  at all. They are the two reads that a mass reconnect would amplify, and both are worth doing
  even if the stream is never built. The public feed asked an unindexed status scan for the
  matches in progress on every poll of every phone — the same answer for all three hundred of
  them, several times a second. The up-soon alert asked a per-team question that is not
  per-team: it scanned the whole unresolved queue, up to forty times a window, and kept forty
  memo entries that every fixture write had to void together, all to compute forty different
  `findIndex` results over one identical list.
- **Decision:** memoise the live-match list under a new `LIVE_MATCH_TAG`, and replace
  `upSoonFromDb` with a single all-teams `upSoonPicture` that `upSoonFixtureForTeam` indexes
  into. No transport change, no wire change, no behaviour change.

- **Why a new tag rather than `SCOREBOARD_TAG`, which the design document specified.** Writing
  it as designed would have shipped a bug in one of two directions. `setMatchScore` invalidates
  nothing today — correctly, because a point awards no points to anybody until the match is
  completed — so hanging the live feed off the scoreboard's tag would have frozen the public
  scoreline for up to thirty seconds at a time. Adding `invalidateTag(SCOREBOARD_TAG)` to the
  score write instead would have thrown away the leaderboard's memo on every tap of the strip,
  costing far more than the feed's cache saves. The live list needs a tag whose writes are
  exactly the four that change it: start, point, completion, cancellation. The design document
  has been corrected in place.

- **Why stale-while-revalidate is safe on a live score.** It looks reckless — a thirty-second
  tail on a number the crowd is watching — and it is not, because the tail can only ever serve
  an answer that no write has invalidated. A score nobody has changed is not stale, it is
  current. The TTL bounds how long the memo survives *silence*, never how long it survives a
  write.

- **Why the other two callers of `listMatches(in_progress)` were left alone.** The marshal's
  startable-offers and the kick-off projections read the same list, and both run for a handful
  of staff inside a decision whose inputs are all read in one breath. Routing them through the
  shared memo would save nothing measurable while putting a cache in the middle of the "is this
  team already playing" guard, which is the one answer on the day that must come from the
  database it is enforced against.

- **Why one picture beats forty entries.** The team id was never part of the question, only of
  the answer: the queue is global and the window is "the next *enabled court count* fixtures".
  Walking only that window and letting a team's first appearance win reproduces the old
  "earliest unresolved fixture, discarded if beyond the window" exactly — a team cannot have an
  earlier fixture further down the queue. The memo now holds one `Map` for the whole event, and
  it is handed out without copying: copying per reader would reintroduce the per-team cost the
  change exists to remove. It is also the shape the pushed `team.upsoon` frame needs, because a
  publisher deciding who to notify must diff the whole picture, not forty separate answers.

- **Impact:** `LIVE_MATCH_TAG` and `readLiveMatches` in `matches.ts`, invalidated at
  `startMatch`, `setMatchScore`, `completeMatch` and `cancelMatch`; `upSoonPicture` replaces
  `upSoonFromDb` in `schedule.ts` with `upSoonFixtureForTeam` keeping its signature, so both
  callers are untouched. Six sabotages were watched to fail: dropping the invalidation from a
  point and from a match start, returning the feed to an uncached read, reverting the picture
  to one cached read per team, ignoring the window depth, and letting a team's later fixture
  overwrite its earliest. The per-team sabotage is the reason the test probes a team that has
  not been asked yet in the window — the first draft of it passed happily against forty caches.

### ADR-121 — One status stream for the shell, and the poll demoted to a fallback

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Supersedes in part:** ADR-063's "a poll rather
than a permanently-open stream"

**Context.** Every signed-in participant held three repeating reads open for the whole
afternoon: `/api/me/alerts` on ADR-024's jittered 45–75 s cadence, carrying the two chat dots,
the undismissed announcements and "your team is up soon". Across three hundred phones over four
hours that is on the order of five hundred polls each, and all but a handful of them answer
"nothing has changed". The team room already pushes its messages over SSE — but only while the
room is open, which is why ADR-063 refused a socket in the first place: three hundred
connections to drive one boolean was a bad trade.

**Decision.** `GET /api/status/stream`, participant-only, one `EventSource` per phone, carrying
everything the shell knows. The repeating poll runs only when that socket is not carrying.

**The five rulings worth keeping.**

- **The socket became per-phone, not per-dot.** ADR-063's arithmetic was right for what it
  priced. Once announcements, retractions and "walk to the court" wanted the same connection,
  one socket replaced three polls rather than one boolean, and the trade inverted.

- **A snapshot on every connection, including every reconnect, instead of a replay cursor.** A
  client that missed three minutes needs the current answer, not the three minutes of frames —
  which is precisely what its poll used to fetch. So `StatusSnapshotView` is literally
  `AlertsView`, `/api/me/alerts` and the stream share one read (`lib/alerts.ts`), and the
  client applies both through one action. The snapshot **replaces** state and never merges, or
  an announcement retracted while the socket was down would survive the reconnect; there is a
  test that asserts exactly that, because the merging version passes every other test.

- **The up-soon publisher watches the answer; it does not instrument the causes.** Nine or ten
  write paths move that window — a claim, a walkover, a court enabled, a cancellation — and the
  eleventh will be forgotten. A missed publish there is not a stale number, it is a team never
  told to walk to the court. So a 5 s ticker diffs ADR-120's shared picture and publishes
  transitions only. It costs nothing extra *because* ADR-120 made the picture one read, which
  retroactively is the main reason step ② came first.

- **The two unread dots are raised client-side from bodyless frames.** A deliberate exception
  to "payloads, not signals": that rule exists so a frame does not cost a DB read per listener,
  and a dot has no payload to read. Known cost: a message arriving while the room is open can
  briefly raise a dot that the open room then clears on the same tick, via its own stream.

- **The mount read stays; only the repeating read goes.** `usePolling` waits a full 45–75 s
  before its first tick, so dropping the mount fetch would blank the dots for up to a minute on
  a browser with no `EventSource` or a socket that failed to open. The cost was five hundred
  polls an afternoon, not the dozen mount reads per navigation.

**Impact.** Server: `lib/statusBus.ts` (global and per-team topics), `lib/upSoonWatch.ts`
(`publishUpSoonChanges`, 5 s), `lib/alerts.ts` (the shared read), `routes-status/`
(`HEARTBEAT_MS = 25_000`, pending frames buffered until the snapshot is out, both topics
unsubscribed on abort). Web: `lib/api/statusStream.ts`, `lib/hooks/useStatusStream.ts`
(ADR-119 staleness, reconnect on revival and on foreground per ADR-105), and `useAlertsStore`
rewritten stream-first.

Eleven sabotages were watched to fail: on the server, a frame published to the wrong team, the
snapshot sent after the buffered frames instead of before, a missing unsubscribe, the up-soon
watcher publishing the picture rather than the transitions, and the route open to staff; on the
client, the poll left running while the socket carries, a merging snapshot, an announcement
appended twice, the handler object rebuilt per render (caught only by counting connections —
never by type or lint), a socket opened for a staff session, and a stream left open on unmount.

**Not in this change.** `feed.match` — the live result rows — waits for step 4 of the design's
build order, with the publishes at the remaining invalidation sites. Results never toast
anybody (the no-result-toast decision), so they are pure list data and the stream needs no
notion of who is watching.

### ADR-122 — The reconnect storm, and not computing for an empty room

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Builds on:** ADR-121, design §6

**Context.** ADR-121 put three hundred phones on one socket each. That trades a steady drip of
polls for a rarer but sharper failure: every one of those sockets dies at the same instant —
the Cloudflare tunnel dropping idle connections, the restart button (ADR-118), the hall's
Wi-Fi — and `EventSource` reconnects on a *fixed* interval. The metronome ADR-024 removed from
polling came back in through the transport, and the thing it stampedes is the connect-time
snapshot read.

**Decision — two guards, both cheap.**

1. **A per-connection `retry:`, jittered 3–10 s, written on the snapshot frame.** The `retry:`
   field is per connection, which is the whole reason this is a one-line fix rather than a
   client protocol: the server hands each phone its own reconnect delay and three hundred of
   them come back spread over seven seconds. It rides the snapshot rather than a hello frame,
   because a frame whose only job is to carry a header is a frame every client has to learn to
   ignore.

2. **A client-side jitter on the watchdog's revival, 1–5 s.** This is the half the design did
   not spot. ADR-119's watchdog does not let the browser reconnect — it closes the handle and
   constructs a *new* `EventSource`, and a new one starts again from the browser's fixed
   default, so the server's `retry:` never reaches the path that needs it most. Whatever
   silenced one socket silenced all of them together, so their watchdogs all fire together.
   The pending timer is cleared on teardown, which is not mere hygiene: a phone waking up
   (ADR-105) rebuilds the stream itself, and an armed revival from the dead connection would
   make that a second reconnect.

3. **The up-soon watcher does nothing while nobody is connected** (design §6 trap 3). With no
   phone subscribed there is nobody to tell, so the tick skips the read entirely — and that is
   most of the day, twice over, before the event and after it. `hasStatusSubscribers()` on the
   bus is the whole check.

**The ruling that reversed itself.** The first draft also dropped the watcher's remembered
picture while the room was empty, so that the window would be "restated" to whoever came back.
A sabotage run exposed that as work for nothing: every connection opens with a snapshot that
already says so, so restating only manufactures frames a client ignores. The memory is kept
across the idle stretch, and a returning phone hears about exactly what moved — which, when
nothing moved, is nothing. The test asserts the silence, because that is the property.

**Impact.** `routes-status/stream.ts` (`reconnectDelayMs`, `retry:` on the snapshot),
`lib/statusBus.ts` (`hasStatusSubscribers`), `lib/upSoonWatch.ts` (the idle skip),
`useStatusStream.ts` (`reviveDelayMs` and the cleared timer). Six sabotages were watched to
fail: a fixed server delay, no `retry:` at all, the watcher computing for an empty room, the
watcher forgetting its picture while idle, an immediate lockstep revival, and the revival timer
left armed across a foreground rebuild. The empty-room test has to move the queue behind the
entity layer's back to bite — with the window unchanged, a watcher that *did* read would also
publish nothing, and the test would pass against the design it forbids.

### ADR-123 — The same jitter for the chat sockets, and one membership read per connection

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Follows:** ADR-122,
`docs/design/restart-behaviour.md`

**Context.** Tracing an actual restart end to end (that document) turned up three things the
reconnect-storm work had left behind. The measured downtime is ~2 s — 250 ms of exit delay plus
a ~1.7 s warm boot — which is comfortably under the 3 s floor of the status stream's `retry:`,
so the shell's phones all come back to a server that is already up. The gaps were elsewhere.

**Decision.**

1. **The two chat sockets get a per-connection `retry:` as well**, from a shared
   `lib/reconnect.ts` rather than a constant copied three times. They were still reconnecting on
   the browser's fixed default — the exact lockstep ADR-122 removed from the shell — and they
   are the worse case of the two, because the team room's catch-up read is deliberately uncached
   (ADR-094), so their reconnects do not collapse into one query the way the shell's do. The
   field rides a heartbeat frame written before the backlog: the client already treats a
   heartbeat as "alive, nothing to do", and an empty room has no first message to hang it on.

2. **`readAlertsFor` takes the membership instead of reading it.** The stream had already looked
   it up to know which team topic to subscribe to, and then read it again inside the snapshot —
   one wasted indexed query per connection, which is three hundred of them in the wave after a
   restart. The caller now passes what it is holding; `/api/me/alerts` reads it once and passes
   it too. This is proven by construction rather than by a sabotage: the parameter is required,
   so a second read cannot quietly come back.

**Two test gaps this uncovered, both now closed.** Adding coverage *revealed* branches v8 had
never counted, which is how a green tree can lose a tenth of a point of branch coverage by
testing more. The two worth having: the team room had **no API test for its live push at all**
(a message reaching an already-open socket), and no test that a stream whose owner has **left
the team** stops being served — a security property the code implements per delivery precisely
because a socket can outlive the membership that authorised it. Also added: the superadmin as
the third author kind in the global room, and the global room's cursor guard on the push path.

**The flake that was real.** `status-stream.test.ts` timed out about one full-suite run in
three. The cause was a race no amount of waiting on `hasStatusSubscribers()` could close:
`app.request()` resolves when the response head is written, *before* the handler subscribes, and
under load the **previous** test's handler could still be mid-subscribe — so the poll saw that
listener, the test published, and the frame went to a stream nobody was reading. Tests now wait
for the connection's own snapshot frame, which is written after its subscribe and is therefore
the only honest proof that this socket is listening. `watchStream` in that file does it with one
background reader, so a test can wait, act, and wait again on one connection.

**Still open.** The `onDead` branch from `restart-behaviour.md` §5: distinguishing a transport
failure (the browser will retry) from a hard close (`readyState === CLOSED`, the browser has
given up) so the latter does not wait seventy seconds for the staleness watchdog. It needs a
stopping rule first, because the hard-close case includes an expired session answering 401, and
a quick retry on that is a loop.

### ADR-124 — Telling a dropped connection from a browser that has given up

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Closes:** `docs/design/restart-behaviour.md` §5

**Context.** `EventSource` fails in two ways and the client was treating them as one. A dropped
connection leaves `readyState` at `CONNECTING` and the browser reconnects itself, on the delay
ADR-122's `retry:` handed it. A reconnect that receives an actual HTTP response which is not
200 `text/event-stream` makes the browser *fail the connection* per the specification: `CLOSED`,
no further attempts, ever. That second kind is not exotic — it is the tunnel's 502 during the
~2 s reboot after the restart button, a 401 from a session that expired while the phone slept,
and the security sweep's 503.

Our handler did the same thing for both: drop `isLive`, resume the poll. For the retrying kind
that is exactly right and doing more would put two sockets in the air. For the hard close
nothing reopened the stream at all, so recovery fell to ADR-119's staleness watchdog — an
instrument built for the *silent* half-open socket, firing seventy seconds after the last frame.
We were sitting on an explicit "the browser has given up" signal for the better part of a minute
and then acting on a timer tuned to a different problem.

**Decision.** `onDead`, raised only when `readyState` is `CLOSED`, revives the stream on the same
jittered 1–5 s delay as staleness — **but at most three times in a row**.

**Why a budget rather than backoff.** The two causes of a hard close want opposite things. A 502
mid-reboot fixes itself in about two seconds, so retrying is right and three tries covers it with
room to spare. A 401 never fixes itself, and retrying it is a loop — three hundred phones asking
to be refused, for the rest of the afternoon. Exponential backoff would also bound that, with
more state in the hook and a slower recovery from the common case; the cap is simpler and the
401 already has an owner. When the budget is spent the socket stays shut, the fallback poll
carries the dots, and it is the poll's own 401 that signs the participant out — which is the
correct end state for an expired session anyway. The watchdog is deliberately left armed as the
long-stop. The budget resets on a connection that actually opens, so an afternoon of ordinary
blips never adds up to it.

**Impact.** `lib/api/statusStream.ts` (`EVENT_SOURCE_CLOSED`, `bindLifecycle`, the new handler),
`lib/hooks/useStatusStream.ts` (`QUICK_REVIVALS`, `reviveIfAllowed`, the resetting ref), and
`test-utils/eventSourceStub.ts`, which now models `readyState` and distinguishes `fail()` — a
dropped connection — from `die()` — a hard close. Without that the stub could not express the
difference the production code turns on, and no test could tell the branch from the old
behaviour. Four sabotages were watched to fail: removing the branch entirely, treating every
error as a death, removing the budget, and never resetting it.

### ADR-125 — Social-feed LEDs as a watermark the reader compares against

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Decides:** `docs/decisions-outstanding.md` B1–B3

**Context.** The two chat dots were computed on the server, per reader, on every alerts poll and
on every reconnect: two indexed `EXISTS` probes keyed by that participant's stored read marker
("is there anything after *yours*"). It worked, and it had three costs. The cache key was the
reader's position, so a wave of three hundred reconnects after a restart asked the question once
per distinct position rather than once. Every room visit posted a mark-read round-trip that
could fail on a beach phone with no signal. And a message landing in a room somebody had open
still lit its own dot for a moment, because the frame reached the shell before the room cleared
it (ADR-121's known wart). The gallery, meanwhile, had no LED at all — a photo arrived in
silence, which is the one social feed nobody is sitting and watching.

**Decision.** The server publishes **when each social feed last changed**; the device holds its
own **last-read timestamp** per feed and lights the LED when the feed's is the later one. Chat,
team chat and the gallery.

**Timestamps, against my own earlier recommendation, and why that is sound here.** ADR-082 chose
ids over times for the announcement floor on clock-skew grounds, and the objection looks like it
should apply. It does not, because skew only bites when the two sides of a comparison come from
different clocks — and here they do not: **the value a device stores as "read" is always a
string the server produced**, never `Date.now()`. Both sides are server-clock, so a phone two
hours out still lights correctly. `iso()` emits fixed-width UTC, so the comparison is `>` on
strings and nothing ever parses a date.

**What it buys.** `readAlertsFor` no longer takes the participant at all — nothing on the path is
keyed by who is asking, so three hundred reconnects share three cached entries (plus one per
team room) instead of six hundred keyed queries. Both mark-read endpoints and both client calls
are gone. The open-room flicker is gone by construction: the surface that renders a message is
the thing that moves the mark, so there is no dot to race.

**What it costs, stated plainly.** Dots are no longer account-wide — reading on your phone no
longer clears the dot on your tablet. For one day on one phone each, that is the right side of
the trade, and it is the same bargain ADR-074 already struck for announcement dismissal.

**The three details that are easy to get wrong.**

- **The first-sight rule.** A device with nothing stored adopts the current watermarks and shows
  every LED dark. Without it a phone arriving at four o'clock is greeted by three dots for a day
  it was not present for. This is also where the team room's `joined_at` floor now lives — which
  is what let the room's watermark query drop the floor and collapse from a key of
  `team:marker:joinedAt` to just the team.
- **Seeding happens once**, tracked by the key's presence rather than by "the marks are null". A
  device that arrived while every feed was empty holds three nulls, and re-seeding would swallow
  the first message ever sent.
- **The gallery's marker is `visible_since`, not `created_at`** (new column, defaulting to
  `now()` and moved by a restore). A photo hidden by a moderator and later restored has a
  creation time in the past, so a watermark over `created_at` would let it slide back into the
  grid without lighting anything. A *hide* lowers the watermark instead of raising it, which is
  why the client replaces the block on each snapshot rather than merging by maximum: merging
  would keep a dot burning for a line nobody can read any more.

**A latent bug this surfaced.** `AlertsProvider` was mounted *inside* `GameboyShell`, so every
surface that renders a shell — `ChatPanel`, `PhotosPanel` — sat above its own provider and its
`useAlerts()` resolved to the quiet fallback. Clearing had been a no-op for as long as it had
existed; nobody noticed because the server also cleared the dot on `POST /api/chat/read`. With
the mark on the device there is no second mechanism to hide behind, so the provider moved up to
`App`'s participant guard, where the surfaces actually are.

**Impact.** Contracts: `FeedWatermarksView`, `FeedActivityView`, `STATUS_GALLERY_ACTIVITY_EVENT`;
`AlertsView.chatUnread`/`.teamChatUnread` replaced by `feeds`. API: `latestChatActivity`,
`latestTeamChatActivity`, `latestGalleryActivity` (all cached and reader-independent), the three
activity frames now carrying the row's own timestamp, `gallery_photo.visible_since`, and the
removal of both unread probes, both mark-read routes and both entity helpers. Web:
`lib/storage/feedReadStore.ts`, a rebuilt `useAlertsStore` holding watermarks and marks rather
than booleans, one `markFeedRead(feed)` in place of three clear/raise pairs, `AlertLed` extracted
for the Social segmented control, and the gallery's first dot. Nine sabotages were watched to
fail: publishing `new Date()` instead of the row's time, restoring without moving
`visible_since`, dropping the gallery publish, removing seeding, seeding every time, applying a
frame without the forward-only guard, merging the snapshot by maximum, keeping the marks at
sign-out, and dropping the gallery's mark-read effect.

**The columns left behind.** `participant.chat_last_read_message_id` and
`team_membership.last_read_message_id` now have no reader and no writer. They are deliberately
left in place for one release rather than dropped in the same change as the behaviour.

### ADR-126 — The content-versioned art was uncacheable, and a missing file was not a 404

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Builds on:** ADR-014/067 (`MOTIF_VERSION`),
ADR-043 (one origin) · **Relates to:** `docs/decisions-outstanding.md` C2

**Context.** `webStatic.ts` decided caching with a single test — is the file under Vite's
`assets/`? — and gave everything else `no-cache`. Everything else is 223 files: **193 SVGs**
under `public/motifs/` and **30 images** under `public/scene/` and `public/scene-2x/`. Every one
of them is already content-addressed by the application, because ADR-014/067 built
`MOTIF_VERSION` precisely so that *"a redrawn motif can never be served from a stale cache under
its old name"*. The hash was there; the header told the browser to ignore it.

Worse than it first looked. `serveFile` emitted **no `etag` and no `last-modified` either**, and
`no-cache` does not mean "do not store" — it means "revalidate before use". A response with no
validator gives the browser nothing to revalidate *with*, so the revalidation is a full
re-download. These files were not slow-cached, they were uncacheable. Measured on this tree: a
participant page load re-fetches about 29 files and 38 kB of art that cannot have changed, every
load, three hundred phones, on beach Wi-Fi.

Separately, `GET /sw.js` answered **200 `text/html`** — the SPA fallback caught it, as it caught
every missing file.

**Decision.** Three changes to one file.

1. **`IMMUTABLE_DIRECTORIES`** — `assets`, `motifs`, `scene`, `scene-2x` get
   `max-age=31536000, immutable`. `index.html` is deliberately absent and must stay absent: it
   is the one file whose freshness decides whether a deploy is seen at all.
2. **Every file gets a validator** — a strong `etag` of `"{size:x}-{mtimeMs:x}"`, and
   `if-none-match` is honoured with a bodyless 304. So the files that legitimately stay on
   `no-cache` can at last be revalidated instead of re-sent.
3. **A path that names a file is answered as a file** — 404 when it is missing, rather than
   falling through to the SPA shell. The fallback exists for extensionless deep links like
   `/team/line-ups`; `/sw.js` is not one.

**Why size+mtime and not a hash of the bytes.** Hashing is stronger and would mean reading every
file on every request. Size and mtime both change when a deploy rewrites a file, and a deploy is
the only moment any of these files can change — the container is immutable otherwise. This is
what every static file server has done since 1996, and the weaker guarantee is bounded by the
same event.

**Why the third change matters even though nothing registers a worker.** Retiring a service
worker depends on its script **404ing** on re-fetch; a script that 200s forever cannot be
withdrawn. C2 is not being built (see `docs/outstanding-tasks.md`), and the reason to fix this
now is precisely that: the escape hatch has to exist *before* anyone could need it, and it costs
one line. It also stops a mistyped asset URL from arriving as a silent 200 of HTML, which is the
kind of bug that reads as "the image is broken" and debugs as anything but.

**What this does to the C2 argument.** It takes most of it. The service worker's measurable win
was "zero-request repeat loads"; this captures that for the art with no new failure mode, no
un-purgeable cache and no update ritual. What remains for a worker is true offline paint alone —
which is a real benefit, and a much smaller one than it looked like before this was measured.

**One behaviour deliberately changed.** The traversal test previously asserted that
`/..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd` returns the index shell. It now returns 404. The property under test —
a file outside the dist root is never served — is unmoved and, if anything, better served; the
test now asserts that property directly rather than through the shape of the refusal.

**Impact.** `apps/api/src/webStatic.ts` only: `IMMUTABLE_DIRECTORIES`, `validatorFor`,
`notModified`, `namesAFile`, and `serveFile` taking the caller's `if-none-match`.
`apps/api/src/tests/web-static.test.ts` grows twelve cases across three describes: immutability
per directory, `index.html` never immutable, a validator on every file, a 304 round trip, a 200
on a mismatched validator, a changed file issuing a changed validator, three 404 cases including
`/sw.js`, and the extensionless deep link still reaching the shell.

### ADR-127 — The status-stream flake was never timing, and the budget goes back

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Closes:** `docs/outstanding-tasks.md`
housekeeping, *"the `status-stream.test.ts` flake is mitigated, not diagnosed"*

**Context.** `status-stream.test.ts` failed roughly one run in five, always in the same test —
*"tells a team when it crosses into the up-soon window, once"* — and always with the same
message: no `team.upsoon` frame arrived, one frame seen, the snapshot. The mitigation was to
raise `waitFor`'s budget from ten seconds to thirty and to print the frames actually seen.

**The diagnosis, which the message itself provided.** One frame, not zero. The connection was
open and listening — it had the snapshot to prove it — and the up-soon frame simply never came,
because it was never addressed to that participant. The test chose whose socket to watch like
this:

```ts
const front = fixtures[0];
const captain = front.teamAId === fixture.teamAId ? fixture.captainA : fixture.captainB;
```

`seedTournamentReady` makes two teams, but this describe's `beforeAll` adds a **third** (the
outsider, who exists to prove that one team's news never reaches another's phone). The draw is
shuffled with `crypto`, so the front pair is genuinely unpredictable — which is the shuffle
working. When the front pair was *outsider v team A*, the ternary's condition was false and its
else-branch handed back **captain B**, who is not in the front fixture and, with one enabled
court, not inside the up-soon window either. The test then waited for a frame the server was
correct not to send.

So this was a test that asserted something false, one time in five, and a longer budget only
bought a slower red build. That is the general shape worth remembering: **a flake that always
fails the same assertion with the same evidence is not a timing flake.** Timing flakes move
around.

**Decision.**

- The test asks **who is actually at the front** rather than guessing: a `teamId → captain`
  map built in `beforeAll` over all three teams, and `captainOf(front.teamAId)` that throws
  rather than silently substituting somebody.
- **The budget goes back to ten seconds.** It was raised to mask this; with the cause gone the
  original is right, and leaving it at thirty would mean every future genuine failure in this
  file takes three times as long to report.
- The failure message **stays**. It is what made the diagnosis possible, and it cost nothing.

**Evidence.** Ten consecutive runs of the file green with the fix. Then the sabotage, which is
the half that matters: the old ternary restored and the file run ten times again — **two
failures**, both carrying the original message. The reproduction rate matches the one-in-five
originally reported, and the fixed version has not failed once.

**Impact.** `apps/api/src/tests/status-stream.test.ts` only. No production code changed, which
is itself the finding: for a month this looked like an infrastructure problem and it was an
assertion that was wrong about the data.

---

### ADR-128 — A status socket re-checks membership on team frames, and keeps the socket

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Decides:** `docs/decisions-outstanding.md` B5 ·
**Follows:** ADR-121 (the stream), ADR-123 (the same guard for team chat)

**Context.** `statusStreamResponse` read the participant's membership once, at connect, and used
it to subscribe to `status.team.{id}`. Nothing re-read it. A socket therefore outlived the
membership that authorised it: somebody who left a team at two in the afternoon kept being told
when that team was due on court for the rest of the day, over a connection that was perfectly
legitimate when it opened. Team chat has had the same hole and has re-checked per delivery since
ADR-123; this is that guard, one directory over.

B5's ruling picked this over waiting for the client to reconnect on `visibilitychange`
(ADR-105), and the reason is the stake rather than the cost: a participant who never backgrounds
their phone can sit on the wrong topic for an hour, and the frame in question is the only one on
this stream that asks a person to physically walk somewhere.

**Decision.** A `TeamGate` per connection. `authorised(frame)` returns true immediately for any
frame that is not a team frame; for `team.upsoon` and `team.chat.activity` it re-reads the
active membership and compares the team id.

**Three things that are deliberate.**

1. **Only team frames are gated.** A global frame — an announcement, a chat or gallery
   watermark — is addressed to every connected phone by definition, so guarding it would mean
   three hundred indexed reads for a frame whose audience cannot expire. The two gated kinds are
   the only ones whose authorisation is conditional, and they are rare: a handful per team per
   day, delivered to about five listeners.
2. **The frame is dropped; the socket stays open.** This is where it diverges from team chat,
   and the divergence is the point. A chat room *is* the authorisation — leave the team and
   there is nothing left on that socket, so closing it is honest. This stream also carries
   announcements and the three social watermarks, which belong to every participant. Closing it
   would confiscate those as collateral for a team the person is no longer on, and being
   teamless is a legitimate way to attend (`lib/alerts.ts` already says so).
3. **A failed check gives up the subscription on the spot.** Without this the departed member's
   socket would pay a membership read for every frame their old team generates for the rest of
   the day. `forget()` leaves the topic and clears the team id, so `authorised` short-circuits
   on the first line from then on: one read, not an unbounded series of them.

**Why a small object rather than three variables in the handler.** "Am I still allowed this
frame" and "give up the subscription" have to move together, and two loose booleans plus an
unsubscribe handle in a sixty-line stream callback is exactly the shape that drifts. It also
kept `statusStreamResponse` under the fifty-line limit without inventing a reason to.

**Impact.** `apps/api/src/routes-status/stream.ts`: `isTeamFrame`, the `TeamGate` interface and
`teamGate` factory, `deliver` replacing the direct `writeFrame` call in both the live path and
the buffered flush — a frame buffered during the snapshot read is re-checked at flush time too,
which matters because the membership can go away inside that window. Tests:
`status-stream.test.ts` gains *"stops telling a participant about a team they have left, without
closing their socket"*, which proves the socket first works, then that the team frame is dropped
after `POST /api/teams/:id/leave`, **and** that an announcement published afterwards still
arrives — the half that pins the divergence from team chat. The sabotage (the guard made to
always return true) fails that test and only that test.

### ADR-129 — The two read-marker columns are dropped

**Date:** 2026-10-03 · **Status:** accepted · **Completes:** ADR-125 ·
**Supersedes:** ADR-063's `team_membership.last_read_message_id`, ADR-083's
`participant.chat_last_read_message_id`

**Context.** ADR-125 moved the "how far have I read" mark from the server to the device, and
said so in its closing paragraph: the two columns *"now have no reader and no writer. They are
deliberately left in place for one release rather than dropped in the same change as the
behaviour."* The user has called it — drop them now rather than waiting.

**Confirmed dead before touching anything.** A grep across `apps/api/src`, `apps/web/src`,
`packages`, `scripts` and `e2e` finds no read and no write. What it does find is one site the
task list had not noticed: `listParticipantsForDirectory` still *selected*
`chatLastReadMessageId` into its projection, where nothing consumed it — so the superadmin
directory, one of the hotter admin reads, was carrying a dead column across the wire of every
query it made.

**Decision.** Remove both columns, their Drizzle mappings, the dead projection, and the
corresponding values from the recorded demo seed.

**Why there is no migration.** ADR-049: one schema file, applied whole on first boot, and no
migrations directory until there is a live deployment to migrate. A database already
bootstrapped keeps its two unused columns until it is re-provisioned, which costs nothing
because nothing reads them. `npm run standards` enforces the half that can go wrong — Drizzle
may not map a table the schema file does not create.

**Why the demo seed needed care rather than a regeneration.** `seed-demo.sql` is a recorded
artefact (ADR-102): 80 participant rows and 54 membership rows, each carrying an inline avatar
sprite, so it is not a file to hand-edit casually. Every value in both columns was verified to
be `NULL` across all 134 rows before the column was taken out of the four `INSERT` lists and the
matching `NULL` removed from each tuple. `demo-export-cli.ts` needs no change at all: it derives
its column list from `select *`, so the next `npm run db:export-demo` emits the new shape on its
own.

**Impact.** `db/schema.sql` (both columns, with a line each recording where they went),
`db/schema/identity.ts`, `db/schema/teams.ts`, `db/entities/participants.ts` (the dead
projection), `db/seed-demo.sql` (4 INSERT headers, 134 tuples), and the explanatory aside in
`lib/storage/feedReadStore.ts` is now past tense. `.env.example` lost a stale `snapshot.sql`
reference while in the area.

**Proof.** Beyond the suites: `PSD_SEED=demo npm run db:setup` against an empty throwaway data
directory — *"applied schema.sql and the default seed"*, then *"applied seed-demo.sql"*. The
recorded day still loads into the schema it was recorded against, which is the only thing a
column removal can really get wrong.

### ADR-130 — A roster line is a message in the room, so it raises the dot like one

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** ADR-063 (the room is the team's history), ADR-121/125 (the watermark and the
  device-side read mark), ADR-094 (`cachedRead`, and writes void their tags),
  `db/entities/teams.ts`, `db/entities/teamChat.ts`, audit findings A-4 and A-5
- **Decision:** `announceRosterEvent(teamId, row)` now holds all three obligations a committed
  roster line owes the rest of the system — void `teamChatTag`, publish the line on the chat
  bus, publish the watermark on the status bus — and both roster paths call it:
  `withRosterAnnouncement` after the commit, and `addTeamMember` directly.
- **Why (A-4):** `routes-team-chat` published both a `team.chat.message` and a
  `team.chat.activity`; `createTeamWithCaptain`, `addTeamMember` and `invalidateMembership`
  published only the first. The deciding evidence is in neither publisher but in the query:
  `latestTeamChatActivityFromDb` filters on `hiddenAt` **and nothing else**, so the snapshot a
  reconnect opens with has always counted roster rows. Push and snapshot therefore disagreed
  about the same room — a join lit no dot on a phone with a socket open, then lit one on the
  next poll. The bug was not that the dot was wrong; it was that two call sites answering one
  question had drifted apart, and only one of them was ever tested.
- **Why (A-5):** `createTeamChatMessage` voids the tag at insert. That is correct and
  sufficient for callers that write outside a transaction, but it cannot be *late* enough:
  inside `createTeamWithCaptain` and `invalidateMembership` the insert is uncommitted, so a
  reader arriving between the void and the `COMMIT` re-populates the memo with pre-commit state
  — and that entry then lives the full **ten-minute** TTL with no write left to clear it. The
  symptom is a team's dot stuck wrong for ten minutes, which nobody will diagnose on the day.
  `recordRosterEvent`'s own comment already explained why *publishing* must wait for the commit;
  invalidation had the same constraint and no guard. The insert-time void is kept — belt and
  braces for the non-transactional callers, and no caller can forget it.
- **Impact:** a join or a leave now lights the team-chat dot for members who do not have the
  room open, at the same instant a spoken line would. Four tests in `roster-announce.test.ts`,
  each half of the fix separately sabotaged and watched to fail (3/4 for the missing watermark,
  1/4 for the early void). The collision in A-5 needs two connections and PGlite has one, so
  that test asserts the property that closes the race rather than the race: it inserts behind
  `createTeamChatMessage`'s back to leave the memo warm and wrong — exactly the state a losing
  reader leaves — and requires `announceRosterEvent` to clear it.
- **Not done:** the publish/invalidate pairing is still a convention rather than a rule. T4
  turns it into the thirteenth `check-standards.mjs` rule, which is the thing that would have
  caught this without an audit.

### ADR-131 — The match feed and the board are pushed, and the frame is the response

- **Status:** Accepted (server half; the browser still polls until ADR-132)
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** B6's ruling, ADR-120 (`LIVE_MATCH_TAG` took the per-point traffic off
  `SCOREBOARD_TAG`), ADR-121 (the one status stream), ADR-130 (the defect this step's rule now
  prevents), `lib/statusBus.ts`, `lib/leaderboardPush.ts`, `routes-tournament/index.ts`,
  `routes-superadmin/corrections.ts`, `scripts/check-standards.mjs`
- **Decision:** two new global frames — `feed.match`, carrying a whole `MatchView`, and
  `leaderboard`, carrying a whole `LeaderboardView`. Six mutation sites publish the match
  (start, score, complete, cancel, winner-edit, void/unvoid); the three that change a *result*
  also push the board. A thirteenth standards rule, `push-pairing`, makes both obligations
  machine-checked.
- **Why the frame is the response, literally:** every mutating handler already ended with
  `matchView(await requireMatchRecord(...))` to answer the marshal. Publishing *that* object
  rather than building a second one has two consequences, and the second is the one worth
  having. It costs **no database read** — the plan's "zero reads on the publish path" is met not
  by discipline but by construction. And the socket and the HTTP body are now the same object,
  so they cannot disagree about a match; the class of bug where a phone's pushed row and its
  re-fetched row differ by a field is not fixed here, it is unrepresentable.
- **Why the board is different, and admitted as such:** standings are an aggregate, so this one
  cannot be free. Three things keep it honest. It is gated on `hasStatusSubscribers()`, because
  an `EventEmitter` makes *emitting* to nobody free but not *computing* — before and after the
  event that gate is the whole cost. It runs just after the write that voided `SCOREBOARD_TAG`,
  so it repopulates a memo the next reader would have filled anyway: the work is moved earlier,
  not added. And it is deliberately absent from the per-point path — ADR-120 left
  `SCOREBOARD_TAG` voided by completion and correction only, a few dozen times an afternoon,
  which is what retired the throttling question. There is a test asserting a score tap moves
  the feed and **not** the board, so nobody reintroduces it by accident.
- **The thirteenth rule.** `push-pairing` reads as a table of "if a region calls X it must also
  call Y": the two chat message/watermark pairs, and the six match mutations against
  `publishFeedMatch`/`pushLeaderboard`. Regions are found by line boundaries rather than by
  parsing braces — an approximation chosen in the conservative direction, because merging two
  adjacent regions can only ever *miss* a violation, never invent one. A rule that cries wolf
  gets switched off. Written before the feature, it named all six sites on its own.
- **Impact:** 8 tests in `feed-match-stream.test.ts`. Four sabotages watched to fail: the
  subscriber gate, a completion that forgets to publish, a score tap that wrongly pushes the
  board, and — against the standards rule rather than the suite — a start that forgets.
- **A test that was worthless, and the lesson.** The subscriber-gate test first asserted on the
  bus: no subscriber, therefore no frame. That is true whether the gate exists or not, because
  with no subscriber there is nobody to record a frame. Deleting the gate left it green. It now
  counts queries through a spy on `db.execute` (the standings are raw aggregates and do not
  travel by `select`). **A test for an optimisation must observe the work, not the output** —
  the output is identical either way, which is what makes it an optimisation.
- **Not done here:** the browser still polls. `useBoard` consuming these two frames, and the
  e2e that stubs `EventSource` to prove the app stays correct with the stream off, are the
  second half. The server-side acceptance test for that ruling — poll answers still correct
  with no subscriber at all — is already in place.
- **Noted, deliberately not changed** (*superseded by ADR-153, 2026-10-04 — now fixed, and the
  gap turned out to be wider than this paragraph thought*): hiding a global chat message lowers
  `latestChatActivity` but publishes no `chat.activity` frame, so a lit dot stays lit until the
  next poll. ADR-066 already reasons explicitly about a hide governing only what is fetched
  next, so this is a judgement to revisit on its own evidence, not a defect to fold into B6.

### ADR-132 — The board surfaces take the socket's word for it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** ADR-131 (the frames), B6's ruling, ADR-121 (one socket per phone),
  `lib/live/boardLive.ts`, `lib/api/statusStream.ts`, `lib/hooks/useBoard.ts`,
  `lib/hooks/useAlertsStore.ts`
- **Decision:** a module-level store, `boardLive.ts`, sits between the one socket and the board
  surfaces. `useAlertsStore` forwards `feed.match` and `leaderboard` straight into it;
  `useMatchFeed` and `useLeaderboard` read it through `useSyncExternalStore` and fold it over
  their polled answer. This completes T4.
- **Why a store and not the alerts store.** The socket is opened once, for the whole shell, by
  the hook that answers "does anything need the participant's attention". A leaderboard does
  not. Folding board payloads into `AlertsStore` would re-render every nav dot in the app each
  time a score moved on a court nobody is watching. The store also **retains** the last frame of
  each kind rather than merely forwarding it, so a participant who opens the board a second
  after the push still sees it — without that, the push closes no gap at all for anyone who was
  not already looking.
- **Why `mergeById` could not be reused.** It sorts by id, which for a chat log is chronological
  and for this list is nonsense. The feed is `[...readLiveMatches, ...readCompletedMatches]`,
  each ordered by `started_at` DESC, and **`cancelled` is in neither** — so a frame saying a
  match was cancelled has to *remove* a row. `mergeMatchFeed` mirrors those three rules, is
  named after the endpoint it mirrors, and each rule has a test of its own, because this is
  duplicated server knowledge and duplicated knowledge drifts.
- **Why the board is compared on `generatedAt` and not simply taken.** A poll already in flight
  when the push lands answers with the older truth. Taking whichever arrived last would let the
  push make the board *worse* — a rare, invisible, and entirely self-inflicted regression. The
  two are compared instead, and there is a test that an older pushed board is ignored.
- **Impact:** 23 tests across three files — the merge rules, the hooks over the store, and the
  whole path from an SSE frame through the real `EventSource` client to the rendered row. Five
  sabotages watched to fail: a dropped listener, the `mergeById` id-sort trap, cancelled rows
  left in the feed, last-write-wins on the board, and a snapshot rebuilt per call (which is the
  `useSyncExternalStore` infinite loop, and took 12 tests down with it).
- **On the acceptance test the plan asked for.** It wanted a Playwright e2e with `EventSource`
  stubbed. This workspace cannot fetch the Playwright browsers — `npx playwright install
  chromium` fails against the CDN — and `npm run verify` does not run e2e in any case, so a
  spec written here would have been committed unexecuted, which is worse than none. The same
  instrument exists one layer down: `test-utils/eventSourceStub.ts` drives the real stream
  client with a stubbed socket, and `useBoardStream.test.ts` uses it for exactly the two
  acceptance assertions — a frame reaches the rendered list, and with the socket silent
  throughout both surfaces are still correct. The e2e remains worth adding wherever the
  browsers can be fetched; it is recorded as outstanding rather than quietly dropped.
- **Correction to this session's audit (A-2).** The audit called "no headless browser in this
  workspace" a claim Playwright had falsified. Half right: the repository does have a full
  Playwright setup, two engines and an `e2e:install` script, so the claim is wrong *about the
  repository* — but it is still true of a sandbox that cannot reach the CDN, which is why the
  phrase was written in the first place. The defect is the citation, not the observation: those
  five ADRs cite **ADR-013**, which is about coverage and says nothing about browsers.

### ADR-133 — "Your team is up next" is a call, and a call is made once

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** ADR-091 (the up-soon window and its LED), ADR-118 (the restart button),
  ADR-082 (the announcement floor this is modelled on), ADR-131 (one representation of one
  fact), `packages/contracts/src/wire.ts`, `apps/api/src/lib/alerts.ts`,
  `apps/web/src/lib/storage/upSoonStore.ts`, `apps/web/src/lib/hooks/useAlertsStore.ts`,
  `apps/web/src/components/participant/GameboyShell.tsx`
- **Decision:** `AlertsView.teamUpSoon` becomes a `TeamUpSoonView` — the identical type the
  live frame already carried — and the browser raises a dismissible toast for a fixture it has
  not announced before, remembered under `psd.upsoon.floor.v1`. This completes T5 (B4).
- **Why the server had to change first.** The live frame already carried `{upSoon, gamesAway,
  fixtureId}`; the **snapshot** collapsed the same fact to a boolean. A phone that reconnects —
  or that ADR-118's restart button re-states the window to, for every team at once — could not
  tell news from a replay, so no honest "have I already said this?" was possible in the
  browser at all. `readAlertsFor` now keeps the entry `upSoonFixtureForTeam` already returned
  instead of discarding it to a `!== null`: the fact was in hand and was being thrown away.
- **One type for both, deliberately.** ADR-131's lesson, applied one endpoint over: the
  snapshot and the frame describe the same fact, so they are the same type. A second shape —
  a boolean here, an object there — is two representations of one fact, and they drift.
- **Why the floor keys on `fixtureId` alone.** `upSoonWatch`'s `Remembered` comparison includes
  `gamesAway`, so "one match to go" and "you're up next" are two frames for one fixture. Keyed
  on the pair, a participant would be interrupted twice for the same walk to the same court.
  The compare is strictly-greater on the UUIDv7 id, so the fixture *at* the floor is already
  announced, and a frame buffered across a reconnect cannot wind the mark backwards.
- **A null fixture is never announced.** That is the "left the window" frame. It darkens the
  lamp and has nothing to shout about.
- **A corrupt stored value reads as absent**, as the announcement floor's does: the cost is one
  duplicate toast, and the alternative is a phone that silently never calls its team to a
  court for the rest of the day. The floor is also forgotten at sign-out, beside the
  announcement floor and the feed marks — the next participant on a borrowed phone is in a
  different team playing a different fixture.
- **Why the floor advances on dismissal and not on display.** A phone that reconnects before
  the tap re-shows the toast already on screen, which costs nothing. Advancing on display
  would instead lose the call outright for a phone that reconnected in a pocket.
- **No sound, no vibration.** The browser notification (ADR-091) is the half that reaches a
  pocketed phone. A noise from a tab somebody is already looking at is the feature people ask
  you to turn off. The toast also yields to an announcement rather than stacking: one 320 px
  screen cannot carry two full-bleed banners, and nothing is lost by waiting, because the
  toast is floored on a fixture and not on a timer.
- **The lamp and the toast answer different questions**, which is why both exist and why only
  one of them is floored. The lamp says "true now" and a re-statement of it is simply correct;
  the toast says "newly true, and I have not said so yet".
- **An older server sending a bare `true` lights the lamp and raises no toast.** There is no
  fixture to floor such a call against, so a toast raised from it could never be dismissed for
  good — it would fire again on every reconnect for the rest of the day. One normaliser,
  shared by the snapshot and the frame, makes that the behaviour of both paths at once; it
  replaces the `teamUpSoon === true` coercion that used to guard only the poll.
- **Impact:** 994 tests (100 files), 19 of them new across four files — the floor's own unit
  tests (including every malformed stored value), the store's news-versus-re-statement cases,
  the rendered toast, and sign-out. Coverage rose to 99.01% statements / 98.42% branches and
  the gate rose with it (ADR-080). Five sabotages watched to fail: a `>=` floor compare (4
  tests), a normaliser that trusts a bare boolean (1), a sign-out that keeps the floor (1), a
  dismissal that cannot find the fixture it is dismissing (3), and a toast that overlaps the
  announcement instead of yielding (1).
- **One function extracted, not for tidiness.** `useUpSoonToast` holds the floor, the ref and
  the dismissal; `useAlertsStore` was over the 50-line lint ceiling with them inline, and the
  split falls exactly along the lamp/toast seam the decision is about.

### ADR-134 — One photo wall, cached once; "did I like this" travels beside it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** decision C3, ADR-047 (the gallery), ADR-038 (the read cache), ADR-074 (one
  global list, one per-browser overlay — the same shape), `db/entities/gallery.ts`,
  `routes-gallery/index.ts`, `views/gallery.ts`, `lib/hooks/useGallery.ts`
- **Decision:** `readGalleryPage` is keyed on the **sort alone**. `hasMyVote` leaves
  `GalleryPhotoView`; the page response gains `myVoteIds`, read uncached per viewer and folded
  onto the shared list by the browser. This completes T6 (C3).
- **What was wrong.** The cache key was `${sort}:${viewerId}`, so three hundred phones on the
  photo wall were three hundred cached copies of the same sixty rows — each costing a listing
  select plus a vote tally to build, each voided by every like anywhere in the event, and all
  of them holding identical photo data that differed in exactly one boolean per row. Two
  entries now serve the whole room.
- **Why the overlay is not cached, and why that is the point.** It is one index scan returning
  a handful of ids. A per-viewer cache entry would be three hundred entries that every like in
  the event voids through `GALLERY_TAG` — a worse hit rate than the query it replaces, at three
  hundred times the memory. **Cache what the room shares; read what belongs to one person.**
- **One response, not two** (decision C3). A second endpoint would double the request count on
  the surface that already makes the most of them, and every authenticated request costs two
  writes before the handler runs. The list and the overlay are read separately and sent
  together.
- **Ids, not a flag per photo.** A flag per photo is what made the list per-viewer in the first
  place. Ids keep the big half byte-identical for everybody — which is also what makes T7's
  shared ETag worth having, and the reason C3 was ordered before C1.
- **Folded in the hook, never in the grid.** `myVoteIds.includes(photo.id)` inside a `map` is a
  linear scan per tile, sixty tiles against a few hundred likes, re-run on every render. One
  `Set` per answer, memoised on the page, and `PhotosPanel` is untouched — it still reads
  `photo.hasMyVote`, which is now a derived field on a derived type.
- **The moderation console lost a field it never used.** `GalleryModerationRecord` carried
  `hasMyVote: false`, hard-coded, because it extended the record that needed it. A superadmin
  does not vote; the field is gone rather than preserved for symmetry.
- **The test counts queries, not photos.** The responses are identical before and after — that
  is what makes this an optimisation, and what made the obvious test worthless (ADR-131). It
  measures one viewer's read against the same viewer's read with the tag voided, and asserts
  the difference is exactly two: the listing and the tally. The absolute number is deliberately
  not asserted, because it also counts the session lookup and the uploader's quota, which this
  change does not touch and which must stay free to move.
- **Impact:** 995 tests (100 files), four new — the query count, the shared page rebuilding
  after a like, a facilitator's empty overlay, and the browser's fold. Four sabotages watched
  to fail: a page keyed per viewer again (1), an overlay that ignores whose votes it is reading
  (1), a vote that stops voiding `GALLERY_TAG` (1), and a hook that drops the overlay (3).

### ADR-135 — A poll that has to happen can still cost no body

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** decision C1, ADR-038 (`cachedRead`), ADR-112/113 (which cut *requests*),
  ADR-131/132 (`generatedAt`), ADR-134 (which made the gallery list shared), audit finding A-6,
  `lib/http.ts`, `lib/leaderboardView.ts`, `tests/conditional-reads.test.ts`
- **Decision:** one helper, `respondCached(c, body)`, answers a polled GET with a strong ETag
  and a 304 when the caller already has that exact answer. Applied to `/api/leaderboard`,
  `/api/tournament/matches/feed`, `/api/tournament/courts`, `/api/me/alerts` and
  `/api/gallery/photos`. This completes T7 (C1).
- **What it saves, said precisely: bytes, not database time.** The body must be built before it
  can be hashed, so a 304 costs the server exactly what a 200 costs — a memo hit for the
  participant surfaces, a real query for the staff ones. That is finding **A-6** carried
  forward rather than quietly dropped, and it is written into the helper's own doc comment
  where the next person to reach for it will read it.
- **Why a hash of the bytes.** These bodies are computed, not stored: there is no mtime, no
  immutable id, no single row whose version could stand in for "has any of this changed". The
  gallery's *images* can use `"{id}-{rendition}"` because a photo never changes; a leaderboard
  is an aggregate over the whole day. Hashing what is about to be sent is the only validator
  that cannot be wrong, and it makes the tag **strong**, which is what makes a 304 safe.
- **`private, no-cache`, and why that is the safe pair.** Every one of these answers is scoped
  to a session, and the URL does not say whose. `private` keeps shared caches out; `no-cache`
  means the browser may store the answer but may never use it without asking. That is what
  makes a borrowed phone safe — a second participant signing in hits the same URL, the stored
  entry is revalidated rather than served, the body differs, the ETag misses, and they get
  their own data. `Vary: authorization, x-psd-session` says the same thing to any cache that
  keys on the URL alone.
- **No client change at all.** The browser's own HTTP cache stores the response, sends
  `if-none-match` on the next poll, and hands `fetch` the stored body when the server says 304.
  `response.json()` keeps working and not one hook knows this happened. A client-side ETag
  register would have been a second cache to get wrong.
- **The leaderboard nearly shipped this doing nothing.** It stamped `new Date()` into the body
  at serialisation, so its hash could not match twice — every poll would have carried a
  validator and still re-downloaded the board. `readLeaderboardView` now builds the whole view
  **inside** a memo, so `generatedAt` means "when these standings were computed" rather than
  "when this JSON was written". It still moves whenever the board does, because every write
  that can change a standing voids `SCOREBOARD_TAG`.
- **One builder, so ADR-131's rule is now true of the bytes.** The route assembled the board
  and `pushLeaderboard` assembled it again. "Publish the same object the response returns" was
  true of the shape and false of the value; both now call `readLeaderboardView`, and the frame
  and the body are byte-identical, `generatedAt` included.
- **What is deliberately NOT ETagged.** `/api/tournament/lineups` carries `estimatedStartAt`,
  which is computed from the clock and moves between two otherwise identical reads — a
  validator there would be theatre. Fixing that means making the estimates stable, which is a
  different change with a different risk, and this one is not the place to smuggle it in.
- **The first assertion for every surface is byte stability** (amendment D), because an ETag
  that changes every request is indistinguishable from a working one unless somebody asks
  twice: nothing fails, every response carries a validator, and every poll still downloads the
  whole body. 18 tests in `conditional-reads.test.ts`, parameterised over the five surfaces —
  the tag is stable, a matching request gets a 304 with an empty body and the tag back, the
  headers are `private, no-cache`, two participants get different tags for the same alerts URL,
  an upload moves the gallery's tag, and — stated as a test so nobody misreads a 304 as a saved
  query — the work still happens behind one.

### ADR-094 amendment — the title claims a universal the code deliberately does not meet

- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Status:** Accepted (amends ADR-094; audit finding A-6, folded into ADR-135's change)
- **What is wrong.** The title reads *"Every poll-fed read goes through the cache decorator"*.
  The body enumerates the participant-facing reads and that enumeration is accurate, but the
  staff poll surfaces — `listSwagStations`, `listSwagClaimsForRound`, and the fringe station's
  round reads — have no `cachedRead` and are polled on the same 45–75 s jitter.
- **The code is right and the title is wrong.** Twenty facilitators are not three hundred
  phones, and a memo on a read that happens twice a minute buys nothing but a way to serve a
  stale answer. Read the title as *"every poll-fed **participant** read"*.
- **Why it is worth a line.** It is load-bearing for ADR-135: a conditional response on an
  uncached read still pays for the query, so "everything polled is cached" would have made the
  ETag work look like a query saving. It is corrected as an amendment rather than by editing
  ADR-094, because the register is append-only.
- **A coverage-gate correction, recorded because it is a process defect not a number.**
  `apps/web/vite.config.ts` says in its own comment to set the floor from the **minimum** of
  several runs, and notes that a run inside `npm run verify` reads lower than the same suite
  run alone. The T5 and T6 raises in this session ignored that and pinned the gate to a solo
  run's printed high; the next `verify` on an unchanged tree then failed at 98.99/98.55 against
  99.01/98.65. Two statements and one function flicker between identical runs. The floor is
  back at the observed minimum. ADR-080's ratchet is over what the suite *reliably* covers — a
  gate that fails half the time on an unchanged tree measures the machine, not the tests.

### ADR-136 — The champion bonus is read off the final, not written into the ledger

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** decision D3, ADR-005 (snapshots), ADR-006 (the board is computed on read),
  ADR-089 §5.5 (corrections against the bracket), ADR-117 (the adjustment ledger),
  `db/entities/leaderboard.ts`, `db/entities/schedule.ts`, `tests/champion-bonus.test.ts`
- **Decision:** a tournament's winning roster may be awarded a configurable bonus. It is a
  fourth branch of the leaderboard query — derived on every read from the knockout fixture
  nothing feeds from — and not a row anywhere. The only thing stored is the *amount*:
  `tournament.champion_points_snapshot`, written when the final settles. This completes T9 (D3).
- **This overrules the queue's own provisional recommendation**, which was "an adjustment row".
  Two reasons, and both are about what a stored award would quietly break:
  - ADR-006 makes the board computed-on-read *precisely so* that a void, an unvoid or a winner
    edit needs no compensating write. A stored bonus would outlive the void of the final it was
    paid for, and the day's last correction is exactly the one nobody re-checks.
  - `score_adjustment` is ADR-117's ledger of **human** decisions — who awarded it, why, and
    under whose name. A machine award with an invented `activityId` and no author corrupts what
    the ledger means, and the superadmin's correction screen would start showing entries nobody
    made.
- **Why the amount is nonetheless snapshotted.** ADR-005's rule, one table over: a superadmin
  editing the config at six o'clock must not silently rewrite what the day paid at five. So
  *how much* is frozen at close; *who won* is always re-derived from the match. The two halves
  are split along the line of what can legitimately change afterwards — a corrected winner
  should move the trophy, a corrected config should not.
- **How the final is identified: the knockout fixture no other fixture sources from.** There is
  no `is_final` column and there does not need to be one; the bracket's own shape says it. The
  bonus is paid to the ADR-005 frozen roster of whichever side `winner_team_id` currently names,
  so correcting the final moves the bonus with it — in the test, one captain swings by
  −(7 + 25) and the other by +(7 + 25), with no row written to balance it.
- **Zero is the default and zero means off.** An organiser who never opens the field runs
  exactly the day they ran before, and existing dumps load unchanged. The CTE requires
  `coalesce(champion_points_snapshot, 0) > 0`, so "no bonus configured" produces no row rather
  than a row of zeroes.
- **Three honest edges, recorded rather than patched.**
  - A tournament that ends because fewer than two teams qualified is marked `completed` with the
    snapshot left NULL. No final was played, so there is no champion.
  - A final won by **walkover** pays no bonus: a walkover has no match, so there is no frozen
    roster to pay and no `completed_at` to date it. Paying the live team roster would contradict
    ADR-005 in the one case where the roster was never verified on court. An organiser who wants
    to pay it anyway has `score_adjustment` — which is the right tool, because at that point it
    genuinely is a human decision.
  - Voiding the bonus away is unreachable: ADR-089 §5.5 blocks voiding any knockout result. The
    CTE still filters `is_voided = false`, as defence in depth against a future path that can.
- **No cache invalidation was added, and that is the interesting part.** The first draft voided
  `SCOREBOARD_TAG` inside `advanceWinner`, on the reasoning that the match's completion had
  already cleared the board before there was a champion. That reasoning was wrong: every caller
  that reaches it (`completeMatch`'s `.then`, `editMatchWinner`, `setMatchVoided`) voids the tag
  **after** its transaction commits. The extra call fired too early and bought nothing; removing
  it changed no test. A test primes the memo before the final is played and reads the board
  afterwards *without* clearing it, so the ordering is now asserted rather than assumed.
- **The tests defeat the cache on purpose.** A snapshot bug — reading the live config instead of
  the frozen figure — is invisible behind a memoised board, because the stale answer and the
  correct answer are the same bytes. The helper that reads the board drops the cache first;
  without that, the "a later config edit does not rewrite history" test passed against code that
  did exactly what it forbade. That is the ADR-135 rule again in a new costume: ask twice, and
  make sure the second ask can actually see a difference.
- **Impact:** seven new tests in `champion-bonus.test.ts`, an eight-team day played in order.
  Four sabotages watched to fail: paying the losing roster (2 tests), reading the live config
  instead of the snapshot (1), dropping the "nothing feeds from it" clause so the semi-finalists
  collect a trophy each (2), and never writing the snapshot at all (3).

### ADR-137 — The third-place match is its own stage, because the final is defined by what nothing feeds from

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-03
- **Relates to:** decision D2, ADR-089 §5.3/§5.5 (the bracket and its corrections), ADR-111
  (TBD seats name their feeder), ADR-136 (the champion bonus this must not collect),
  `lib/tournament/engine.ts`, `db/entities/schedule.ts`, `tests/third-place.test.ts`
- **Decision:** a world-cup day may play the two beaten semi-finalists off for third place.
  It is **off by default**, chosen at activation (`tournament.has_third_place`), and it is a
  fixture with its own stage — `third_place`, never `knockout`. This completes T9 (D2).
- **The hazard ADR-136 left behind, and the discriminator that answers it.** The champion
  bonus is paid to "the knockout fixture nothing feeds from", because a bracket's own shape
  says which fixture is the final without needing an `is_final` column. A third-place match
  fed by the two semis answers that description *exactly*: nothing feeds from it either. Had
  it been a `knockout` row with a flag, it would have ended the day the moment it was played
  and stamped a champion bonus on the team that came third. As a separate stage it is excluded
  by the predicate that was already there — `f.stage = 'knockout'` — and by one added clause in
  `advanceWinner`. A test plays the third-place match **before** the final and asserts the day
  is still `knockout` and nobody got paid; sabotaging either half of that fails it.
- **A semi-final now feeds two fixtures, so "the downstream" became a list.** The winner goes
  up to the final and the loser goes across. They are the same operation with a different team
  in hand, which is why `advanceWinner` walks what it feeds rather than fetching one row, and
  why `findDownstream` is gone in favour of `findDownstreamFixtures`. `cascadeWinnerEdit` had
  to learn the same plural: correcting a semi-final must move the loser out of the third-place
  match as well, or it leaves a team standing in a fixture they are no longer in.
- **The correction guard widened with it.** ADR-089 allowed a knockout winner edit while *the*
  downstream seat was untouched. Now every seat the result feeds must still be pending — once
  the third-place match has been played, its teams are in a result that counted, and the semi
  that put them there can no longer be rewritten. That is a new refusal, and it has its own
  test.
- **Which fixtures the rules bend for, and why they bend.** The third-place match may be
  **voided** (ADR-089 blocks voiding knockout results because a bracket seat cannot hold
  "nobody"; this fixture has no seat below it) and it may be **skipped** — which is the lever
  that makes offering the option safe at all. It is sequenced *last*, after the final, which
  reads oddly on the console and is right on the sand: when the light goes, this is the fixture
  that gets dropped, and the final is untouched.
- **Three qualifiers get no offer.** The round before the final must hold exactly two fixtures
  feeding exactly one. With three qualifiers the top seed byes into the final, so there is no
  pair of beaten semi-finalists — only a team that lost and a team that never played.
  `semiFinalRoundIndex` returns null and the checkbox is quietly honoured as nothing.
- **"Loser of #13", not "Winner of #13".** ADR-111 names a TBD seat after its feeder, and the
  naive reuse here would print the one team certain *not* to be in this match. The stage line
  reads "Third-place match" rather than "Knockout · round 3", because a round number reads like
  a route to the trophy.
- **A dead branch found by sabotage, not by review.** The first draft guarded the completion
  rule inside `advanceWinner` *and* only called `advanceWinner` for `stage === 'knockout'`
  fixtures — so the guard was unreachable, and deleting it changed nothing. The call sites now
  say `stage !== 'group'` (bracket fixtures advance; group fixtures feed nothing and this runs
  on every completed match), leaving `advanceWinner` as the single place that knows which
  fixture ends the day. After that change the sabotage fails, which is the only reason to
  believe the guard is doing anything.
- **Impact:** 10 new API tests and 3 new web tests. Five sabotages watched to fail: the fixture
