  with a type-guard. A switch that grows an arm per frame is the wrong shape for a mapping, and
  a table cannot be given the wrong event name by a copy-paste. The two ternaries in the
  publishers were likewise folded into one `retractionOf` helper — which also took `statusBus`
  to 100% branch coverage.
- **Four sabotages, four bites.** (1) Making `applyFeedRetraction` monotonic again — the exact
  bug this ADR exists to avoid — fails the new web test. (2) Publishing the *hidden* row's own
  time instead of the recomputed latest fails both API tests. (3) Deleting the gallery publish
  fails the gallery test. (4) Deleting the chat publish fails the standards rule. The gallery
  test deliberately goes through the **SSE socket** rather than subscribing to the bus: an
  unhandled kind would fall through the switch's default arm and be delivered under the wrong
  event name, which a bus subscriber cannot see. That also covered the new `case`.
- **Assertion scoping, again.** The gallery test first asserted `not.toContain(newer.createdAt)`
  against the whole transcript and failed — the opening snapshot on the same socket legitimately
  carries the pre-hide watermark. The assertion now reads the retraction frame's **own** data
  line by index. A transcript-wide `toContain` would also have passed had the frame never
  arrived at all, which is the ADR-131 lesson in a new costume.
- **Debt repaid in passing:** ADR-152 shipped two ESLint violations (`scoreOnce` at four
  parameters, `useAdminPointConfig` at 51 lines) because `npm run standards` is not ESLint and
  only the former was run. Both are fixed here — `scoreOnce` takes `{ side, headers }` across
  21 call sites, and the seven rate bindings moved into `pointFields`. **`npm run standards`
  passing is not evidence that lint passes.**
- **Impact:** 3 API tests and 2 web tests added (591 → 594 and 1133 → 1135), API branches 94.63 against a 94.60 floor, web branches 98.46 against 98.40, repo-wide
  ESLint clean for the first time since ADR-152.

### ADR-154 — Roster repair is a second door, and every door names what is behind it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-04
- **Relates to:** Gap #1 in `docs/outstanding-tasks.md`, the design at `docs/design/roster-repair.md`,
  ADR-005 (the roster snapshot), ADR-027 (destructive actions ask first), ADR-149 (absolute wins
  decide qualification), `db/entities/rosterRepair.ts`, `db/entities/teams.ts`,
  `routes-superadmin/teams.ts`, `routes-superadmin/directory.ts`, `lib/repair/consequences.ts`,
  `lib/hooks/useTeamRepair.ts`, `routes-superadmin/TeamsDirectoryPage.tsx`
- **Decision:** a superadmin may repair a roster from the team directory — **move** a member
  between teams, **add** an un-teamed participant, **remove** a member, **transfer the
  captaincy**, and **force-unlock** a locked team. Each action asks before it writes, and each
  confirmation states the consequence of *this* repair on *this* team, in a sentence, before
  the superadmin can agree to it.

- **Why a second door and not a replacement.** Captains manage their own rosters, and on a
  normal day that is right: the people who know who is on a team are the people on it. The
  design fails at one specific moment — the captain is on court, their phone is flat, and
  somebody has joined the wrong team off a six-character code read out across a marquee. Every
  action here exists for that moment. None of them removes a captain's own control; they are a
  way in when the first way in is unavailable.

- **The feature is the sentence, not the button.** The writes are thin. What makes the tool
  safe to put in front of a superadmin at 10:40 is that it says what will happen first, and two
  of the things that will happen are **invisible from the row they are looking at**:
  - **The team is on court right now.** Points reach a person through
    `tournament_match.team_*_roster_snapshot`, which is written at *completion* (ADR-005). Move
    somebody mid-match and they will not be credited for a match they actually played. The tool
    does not close that hole — mid-match edits are permitted by ruling — it refuses to let a
    superadmin walk into it unknowingly.
  - **This is the last member.** `invalidateMembership` disbands a team when its last member
    goes (§4.2.4). Inheriting that silently from a staff action would mean a superadmin deleting
    a team by pressing *Remove*.
  Both facts come from `GET /api/admin/teams/:teamId/repair-context`, which `askRemove` and
  `askMove` call **before** they ask. A confirmation written from the directory row alone would
  be confidently wrong, which is worse than no confirmation at all.

- **Withdrawal is not an action; it is a consequence.** The design listed it as a sixth button.
  It cannot be one: the user's ruling that a withdrawal must refuse while the team still has
  members means the only reachable state for a `/withdraw` route is a team with nobody on it,
  and §4.2.4 already disbands that team the moment its last member leaves. A `/withdraw` route
  could therefore only ever answer 409 or 404. The fixture-skipping lives where the disband
  actually happens, in `removeMembershipWithin`, and both the move and the remove routes return
  the `WithdrawalOutcome` they may have caused so the console can report it.

- **Skipped, never walkover.** A withdrawn team's unplayed fixtures are marked `skipped`.
  `foldStandings` counts played-unvoided matches and walkovers, so a walkover would hand free
  wins to everybody still on that team's schedule and feed them straight into ADR-149's
  absolute-wins qualification race. Played results stand; the remaining fixtures vanish. That
  leaves a real asymmetry — somebody genuinely plays fewer group matches than their neighbours
  — and the console **states it** rather than hiding it, because the alternative is a captain
  discovering it from the fixture list and inventing a worse explanation.

- **Why `members[]` was added to `GET /api/admin/teams`.** The directory published nicknames
  only. A nickname is not a handle: two participants may share one, and a console that posted a
  nickname would eventually repair the wrong person. The repair surface works in participant
  ids; the nickname list stays, unchanged, for the human reading the row.

- **Recorded in team chat, nowhere else.** Per ruling, repairs are written into the affected
  room — a move writes two lines, one in each — with three new chat kinds (`staff_added`,
  `staff_removed`, `captain_changed`) rather than reusing `joined` / `left`, because a member
  an organiser removed did not leave. `EVENT_SENTENCE` is a `Record`, so a kind without a
  sentence is a type error rather than a row silently labelled with the wrong verb. The copy
  says *"an organiser"*, never a staff member's name: the room is owed the fact, not the
  identity. The accepted cost is that force-unlock, which belongs to no person, is recorded
  nowhere, and that no superadmin can read back what any superadmin did.

- **What was deliberately not built.** Nothing here consults the team lock: a repair is not a
  join, so moving or adding past a lock is the point. The unlock button therefore only appears
  on a row that is already locked, and *Make captain* only on a member who is not already
  captain — a console full of buttons that can only do nothing is how the real ones get ignored.

- **Impact:** 20 API tests (`roster-repair.test.ts`) plus one directory test; 15 web tests for
  the console surface and 11 pinning the four sentences verbatim, plus three for the staff chat
  lines that had shipped with the server half unrendered by any test. Web 1166 tests, functions
  98.68 against a 98.55 floor that **had been failing since before this work** (98.38 at
  `90488e3`, confirmed by running coverage at that commit in a worktree); API 617 tests,
  branches 94.77 against 94.60. Two sabotages on the console half — a confirmation built from
  the row instead of the server read, and a dialog that wrote before it was accepted — were
  each caught by three and two tests respectively.


### ADR-155 — The captain moderates their own room, because nobody else may read it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-04
- **Relates to:** the ADR-153 audit finding (`docs/outstanding-tasks.md` §4c), ADR-063 (the team
  room), ADR-066 (moderation reaching an open room), ADR-125 (watermarks), ADR-153 (retraction
  frames), ADR-154 (roster lines as the only record of a repair), `db/entities/teamChat.ts`,
  `routes-team-chat/index.ts`, `routes-team-chat/stream.ts`, `lib/chatBus.ts`,
  `lib/statusBus.ts`, `lib/hooks/useTeamChatRoom.ts`, `components/participant/TeamChatPanel.tsx`
- **Decision:** a team's **captain** may hide a spoken line in their own room, through
  `POST /api/team-chat/messages/:messageId/hide`. It is a soft hide, it asks before it acts,
  and it is the only moderation this room will ever have.

- **Why the captain and not a superadmin.** The audit that came with ADR-153 found a room with
  the storage for moderation — a `hidden_at` column and a partial index predicated on it — and
  nothing in the codebase that ever wrote either. The obvious owner of a hide is a superadmin,
  and that is exactly who cannot have it: the roster-repair ruling, reaffirmed when it was put
  a second time, is that **no superadmin may read team chat**. Moderating a room nobody with
  authority can read is a strange power. The captain already reads the room and already has
  standing in it, so giving them the hide closes the gap without reopening the ruling.

- **Two refusals, and they are the feature.**
  - **A member who is not the captain gets 403.** If any member could hide, anybody could erase
    the thing they had just said the moment it landed badly, and the room would stop being a
    record of anything.
  - **A roster line gets 409.** ADR-154 made this room the *only* record of a staff repair —
    the organiser ruled against an audit table. A captain who could hide those lines could
    erase the record of their own team being changed. A captain may hide what was **said**,
    not what was **done**, and the message says so rather than leaving a dead button.

- **The team id is in the `WHERE` clause.** Every other route in this room resolves the caller's
  membership and takes no id at all, which is what makes a wrong-room bug impossible there.
  This route has to take a message id, so the room is re-asserted inside the UPDATE rather than
  checked beside it: a borrowed id from another team matches no row, and the captain who tries
  it gets the same 404 as for an id that never existed. A repeat hide is a no-op that returns
  200 — the room is already in the state the caller asked for, and a 404 there would read as
  "that message is not in this room".

- **Two frames, because there are two audiences.** `hidden` on `team.chat.${teamId}` reaches
  the phones with the room open, carrying only the id (a retraction that quotes what it
  retracts is not a retraction). `team.chat.retracted` on the team's status topic reaches the
  team-mates who do not, because the hidden line may have been the one lighting their dot.
  ADR-153's reason applies unchanged: the client merges activity **monotonically** on purpose,
  so the one event that legitimately lowers a watermark has to be a frame the client assigns.
  A `push-pairing` entry now makes forgetting the second one a standards failure.

- **The retraction frame carries no SSE `id:`.** The browser echoes the last id it saw as
  `Last-Event-ID` and the backlog resumes from it, so tagging a retraction with the id of the
  message it retracts would wind the cursor back to a row that no longer reads and the room
  would silently lose everything after it. It is also never buffered behind the replay: the
  backlog is read through `readableBy`, which already excludes hidden rows, so a retraction
  that waited would be retracting something this socket was never sent.

- **No unhide.** An unhide needs a view of the hidden rows, and the only actor who could hold
  that view is the one barred from the room. So the hide is irreversible from this surface and
  the confirmation says so, rather than offering a reversal that cannot exist.

- **What the sabotage pass found.** Removing the retraction publish was caught by the new
  standards rule and by **no test at all** — the existing watermark assertion reads the alerts
  endpoint, which recomputes from the database and is therefore right whether or not the frame
  was ever sent. That gap is why `status-stream.test.ts` now asserts the frame itself, per team.
  A rule that fires where a test does not is a rule describing a test that is missing.

- **Impact:** API 625 tests (8 new in `teamChat.test.ts`, 1 in `status-stream.test.ts`, a
  matrix row), branches 94.82 against 94.60; web 1174 tests (7 new on the panel, 1 on the
  alerts store), functions 98.61 against 98.55. `useTeamChatMessages` was split along a real
  seam — `useListEdits`, the three ways the list changes — when the hide made it a fourth
  concern, and `TeamChatPanel` grew a `MessageRow` for the same reason.

### ADR-156 — a drawn match says so: the result wording, the record columns, and the champion CTE re-read

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-04 · follow-ups (b) and (c) to ADR-152.

ADR-152 made a group match drawable and taught the engine to score one. It did not teach
anything downstream to *say* so. This addendum is the sweep: every surface that reports a
result was re-read against a day in which `winner_team_id` can legitimately be null, and three
of them were lying.

**1. The feed line.** `matchResultLine` had exactly two shapes — "A beat B" and "A vs B" — and
chose between them on the winner alone. A null winner meant "not finished", so after ADR-152 a
match that had been walked off level an hour earlier rendered in the finished feed wearing the
live wording. The status is the only thing at the call site that separates the two null cases,
so the status is now an argument, and a completed drawn match reads "A drew with B". The verb
is a verb, not a repetition of the score: the score sits beside it in the same row and would
disagree with it the moment a correction landed. Four call sites — the match feed, my team,
team detail and the console match list — all already had the status in hand.

**2. The record columns, which were counting draws as losses.** Two independent tallies did the
same arithmetic: `losses = played - wins`. That identity was true for exactly as long as a
finished match had a winner. `useTeamDetail` showed a team that had drawn a game a defeat it
had not suffered; the console standings table showed `P 3 · W 2 · L 0`, three numbers that do
not add up and whose quietest reading is that the missing game was a loss. Draws are now
counted directly and the remainder taken from them, so the three results account for every
game played by construction.

**3. The view boundary that was dropping `draws` on the floor.** The fold has carried a `draws`
column since ADR-152, and `standingsGroupView` and the bracket's `liveGroup` simply did not
copy it. That is why §2 could not be fixed on the page: the number was not in the payload.
`StandingRowView.draws` and `BracketSlotView.draws` now exist, which also forced the question
of what each surface should *say*:

- The console table gets a D column between W and L, so `P = W + D + L` reads across the row.
- The participant record badge grows a D **only when the team has one** — "2W · 0D · 1L" on a
  day with no draws in it is noise, while a missing D on a day with draws is a lie, so the
  shape of the badge follows the record rather than the rules.
- The hall board does the same in its two-centimetre-wide record cell: `2W 1D`, or `2W`, or
  nothing at all for a team that has not played. Dropping the D would put two teams on "2W"
  side by side when one of them has a point the other does not.

**4. The hall screen's finished rows needed nothing**, and the reason is worth recording. ADR-114
decided those rows show `A vs B  3 - 1` — the score *is* the result, with no winner badge that
could disagree with it. A draw prints `2 - 2` and reads correctly with no code. The decision to
avoid a derived verb paid out two ADRs later, in a feature it was not written for.

**5. ADR-136's champion bonus, re-read (follow-up (c)).** The CTE awards the bonus to
`CASE WHEN m.winner_team_id = m.team_a_id THEN team_a_roster_snapshot ELSE team_b_roster_snapshot END`
— an `ELSE` that hands the trophy to team B whenever the comparison is not true, and in SQL a
null winner makes it not true. The filter `AND m.winner_team_id IS NOT NULL` was already there
and already prevents it; the conclusion of the re-read is that **no change is needed, and that
line is now load-bearing in a way it was not when it was written** (it was defence in depth
against a void; it is now the thing standing between a drawn final and a crowned runner-up).
Since no reachable path can produce a drawn knockout match, the guard is pinned by a test that
writes the null directly and asserts the exact arithmetic — remove the filter and the
champion's delta loses precisely the 25 while every other assertion in the file still passes.

**That test also surfaced the snapshot hazard for free.** The champion-bonus day never
configured a draw rate, so `coalesce((snapshot->>'drawPoints')::int, 0)` resolved to zero and
both finalists were paid nothing for the match. Harmless there — the state is unreachable — but
it is exactly what a correction desk able to retire a result would do to a match recorded
before draws scored.

**Deliberately not done: `editMatchWinner` to and from a draw (follow-up (a)), which is
PARKED, not forgotten.** It was built and then backed out, because the database said no in a
way worth reporting rather than working around. `tournament_match` carries
`CHECK (status <> 'completed' OR winner_team_id IS NOT NULL OR score_a = score_b)`: a draw must
have a level score. The correction desk has never had a way to change a score — it can move a
win from one team to the other, void, and unvoid, and that is all — so "this 11-7 was actually
a draw" cannot be expressed, and the only completed-and-level-and-won match the schema permits
is the knockout 0-0, which the draw guard refuses anyway for being in a bracket. The feature as
scoped would therefore have shipped unreachable. The honest fix is a **result** correction that
carries the score alongside the winner, which is a larger change to a shipped endpoint and a
decision for the organiser rather than for the agent. The guards the attempt produced — refuse
a draw in a knockout or third-place fixture, refuse one on a match whose snapshot has no draw
rate — are recorded here so they are not rediscovered.

**Gates.** standards 467/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 625 passing (2 new — the view
boundary and the champion CTE), branches 94.82 against the 94.60 floor; web 1180 passing
(6 new), all four floors held.

### ADR-157 — one rule, both doors: the correction desk becomes a result correction

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-04 · supersedes the F43 winner edit · closes ADR-152 follow-up (a).

ADR-156 parked this with a question for the organiser, who answered it in one line: *make the
superadmin surface the same as the marshal's; if two teams have the same score it is a draw
anyway.* That ruling is larger than the draw it came from, and it is the right one.

**What was wrong.** There were two doors into `tournament_match` and they disagreed about what
a score means. The completion route has enforced ADR-114 since the beginning — the score
decides the match, and the two may not contradict each other. The correction desk enforced
nothing: it took a winner, checked only that the team was in the match, and wrote it. A
superadmin could set the winner of an 11 - 7 to the team on 7, and the row would be accepted.
Downstream, the feed line said one thing, the hall screen's `11 – 7` said another, and the
standings counted a win for a team the scoreboard says lost. Nothing anywhere could tell which
half was true, because both halves were written by the same authorised action.

The second defect was quieter and older: **no route anywhere could change a score after a match
ended.** Not the desk, not the court, nobody. A marshal's typo was permanent for the day, and
it is the reason the draw correction was impossible — the schema requires a drawn match to be
level (`CHECK (status <> 'completed' OR winner_team_id IS NOT NULL OR score_a = score_b)`) and
there was no way to level it. ADR-156 discovered this by building the feature and watching the
database refuse it.

**What now exists.** `POST /api/admin/matches/:matchId/result` takes `{scoreA, scoreB,
winnerTeamId, editReason}` — the whole result, restated, in one UPDATE so no reader can see a
half-corrected row whose score and winner disagree. `winnerTeamId` is nullable for the same
reason it is nullable at the court: null is "it finished level".

**The rule now lives in one function.** `assertResultMatchesScore` moved out of the completion
route into `apps/api/src/lib/matchResult.ts` unchanged, and both routes call it. `stageCanDraw`
and a new `readMatchOutcome` moved further, into `@psd/contracts`, because the browser needed
them too — the court console had grown its own private copy of the same four lines. Three
copies of one rule is how the doors came to disagree in the first place; there is now one, and
the court console, the completion route and the correction desk all read it.

**The desk's dialog is the court's console.** It asks for the two scores, prefilled with what
was recorded, and says what they mean in the marshal's words: "Wave Riders wins." · "Level, so
this is a draw." · the overtime sentence. **There is no winner picker** — the picker was the
input that let a result contradict its own score. The one survivor is the escape hatch the
marshal also has: 0 - 0 in a bracket names nobody and cannot be drawn, so a human still
chooses, and only then does a select appear.

**Two guards beyond the shared rule.**

1. *The bracket.* A knockout or third-place fixture cannot be corrected into a draw —
   `advanceWinner` has already seated somebody and `cascadeWinnerEdit` has no null branch. This
   falls out of the shared function (it tests the capability, not `stage === 'knockout'`, which
   ADR-137 would have made wrong), and is pinned against the FINAL, the one knockout match
   nothing feeds from and so the one the usual "already fed the bracket" refusal misses.
2. *The rate.* A draw is paid out of the rates frozen when the match was completed. A match
   played before there was a draw rate has none, and `leaderboard.ts` coalesces a missing one to
   zero — so the correction would report success and silently strip both teams of everything the
   match was worth. Refused with `drawRateMissingForMatch`. Unreachable through the API, so the
   test writes the old snapshot directly with `points_awarded_snapshot - 'drawPoints'`.

**What this costs.** Flipping a winner is no longer a one-field edit: to say "the other team won"
the desk must also give a score in which they lead. That is the ruling working as intended — the
desk can no longer record a result the scoreboard contradicts — and it is why every existing
caller in the suites had to grow a score. The snapshot still never moves, so a correction is
still paid at the rates of the day rather than today's, and still needs no compensating write.

**Verified by sabotage.** Removing the shared rule from the desk fails three tests; removing the
draw-rate guard fails one; removing the two score columns from the UPDATE fails three.

**Gates.** standards 469/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 632 passing, branches 94.85
against the 94.60 floor; web 1184 passing, all four floors held.

### ADR-158 — the admissions desk, announced on the page the superadmin is actually on

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-04 · completes ADR-149 · extends ADR-151's operations overview.

The outstanding list still carried "a warning for teams formed after the tournament was
activated" as half a day of work. It was not: ADR-149 had already built the admissions desk —
the plan, the cost in fixtures and minutes, the cutoff, the POST — and the design doc had
already struck the entry. Only the task list had not caught up. Grepping before building
turned a half-day feature into a count and a sentence.

What was genuinely missing is narrower and worse than the list described. The admissions
panel is complete, and it lives on `/admin/tournament` — a page the superadmin visits to
activate the schedule and then leaves for the rest of the day. The page they keep open is
the operations overview (ADR-151). A team that forms at 11:40 therefore appears on a screen
nobody is looking at, and plays nothing, and nobody is told. The failure is not a missing
capability; it is a capability on the wrong screen.

So ADR-158 is a **pointer, not a second implementation**: a count, one sentence, and a link.
Deciding stays where the cost estimates are.

**Why not call `planAdmissions`.** It answers a richer question — what admitting *each* team
would cost — by reading every entry, every team and every fixture. The panel would discard
all of it to render one integer, on a view that refreshes itself. `countTeamsOutsideTournament`
is a single bounded `NOT EXISTS` over `tournament_entry`, and the two cannot drift, because
an entry row *is* membership of the tournament (ADR-149).

**Why `canAdmit` travels with the count.** A count alone would drop to zero the moment the
group stage closed, and silence on an operations panel reads as *resolved*: the superadmin who
saw three outside teams at 11:00 would conclude someone had let them in. The number therefore
stays after the cutoff and the sentence changes — "they can no longer be admitted" — so the
panel reports a closed door rather than an empty room.

**Why the count takes no tournament id.** It was written scoped to one, which looks obviously
correct and is in fact unpinnable: a database holds exactly one tournament row, ever.
Activation refuses while any row exists (`tournamentAlreadyActive`), nothing deletes one, and
`activeTournamentFromDb` is a bare `LIMIT 1` with no ordering — already meaningless with two.
Deleting the filter from the `NOT EXISTS` failed no test, which is information, not a gap to
paper over: the id would have dressed the query up as multi-event support the schema does not
have, and left a branch no test could ever reach. It was removed rather than defended.

**Why a null tournament is the before-activation case.** The first draft guarded
`status === 'planned'` and failed `tsc` with TS2367 — `findActiveTournament` never returns a
planned row, so its type cannot be `'planned'`. Nothing outside the tournament exists before
activation, because nothing is inside it either; the panel stays silent, which is correct.

**Verified by sabotage.** Forcing `canAdmit: true` fails the "keeps counting once admission has
closed" test; returning 0 from the count fails two.

**Gates.** standards 469/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 635 passing (4 new), branches
94.82 against the 94.60 floor; web 1188 passing (4 new), branches 98.39 against a measured
baseline of 98.38 — the 98.55 figure carried in earlier notes was stale and never met.

### ADR-159 — a handout can be taken back, and the allowance comes back with it

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-04 · closes design-doc §5 · extends ADR-110 · reuses ADR-138's
window · adds `swagclaim` to ADR-117's ledger.

Every recorded fact on the day was reversible except one. A fringe scan had a station undo
*and* an admin void; a match result had void, unvoid and correction; points had the
adjustment ledger; a photo could be hidden; an announcement retracted. A swag claim had
nothing. `swag_claim` is immutable by ADR-110, which is the right instinct for a ledger and
the wrong outcome at a table with a queue: a wrong badge burned that participant's per-round
allowance *and* a unit of stock, and the only remedy was a points adjustment that restored
neither.

**Both reversals, not just the admin one — the organiser's call.** The design doc asked only
for `/admin/scans`-style void lines. Asked whether the counter should also get ADR-138's
ten-second undo, the organiser chose both, and the reason is physical: the person who notices
a wrong handout is the facilitator with a queue in front of them, not a superadmin on another
screen, and ten seconds is roughly how long the tote bag is still within arm's reach. After
that the item has left, and the remedy is correctly a superadmin's with a reason attached.

**The flag was the easy half.** What makes this a feature rather than a column is that
`createSwagClaim`'s allowance count now carries `NOT is_voided`. Without it a void would set
the flag, read as success in both consoles, and leave the participant unable to collect the
item they never received — a correction that corrects nothing, which is worse than no
correction at all, because someone would stop looking for the problem. Sabotage: removing
that one predicate fails **eight** of the twelve new API tests, and almost every one of them
asserts the allowance rather than the flag, deliberately.

**Two reversals, kept tellable apart.** `undone_at` is stamped only by the counter's own
undo; a superadmin void leaves it null and writes to `void_audit_entry` instead. This is
ADR-138's ruling inherited wholesale — the ledger records *a human overruling the day*, and a
counter fixing its own slip inside ten seconds is not that. A test asserts the ledger stays
empty after an undo, and the admin table marks the rows that were taken back at the counter,
so nobody hunts for a reason that was never written.

**The window lives in the UPDATE, not the route.** `undoSwagClaimAtStation` carries the id,
the facilitator, "not already voided" and `now() - claimed_at <= interval` in one WHERE, so
null collapses expired, already-voided, not-yours and raced into a single honest refusal.
Dropping the facilitator predicate left every route test green — the route's 403 refuses
first — exactly as it did for ADR-138, and the answer is the same: the statement is asserted
**directly**, in its own test, rather than left as defence in depth that nothing exercises.

**A voided row stays on both lists, marked.** Asked, the organiser chose struck-through over
removal. A line that vanished would be indistinguishable from a handout that never
registered, and those two have different next moves — the second one ends with a second tote
bag going across the table.

**One consistency repair found on the way.** `countRecentClaimsByStation` had no void filter,
because until now nothing could be voided. Its fringe twin already carried one, with a
comment about a station that spends ten minutes correcting itself reading as a station that
was busy. The swag twin now matches.

**Verified by sabotage.** Allowance ignoring the void flag → **8** API tests fail; window
predicate removed → 1; facilitator scope removed from the statement → 1 (the direct test);
the counter undo writing to the ledger → 4; the undo handle offered on a replayed claim → 1
web test; voided rows filtered off the round list → 1 web test.

**Gates.** standards 472/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 647 passing (12 new), branches
94.76 against the 94.60 floor; web 1199 passing (11 new), branches 98.37 against a measured
baseline of 98.38, statements and lines both up.

### ADR-160 — a screen key carries the scenes its screen may show

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-05 · extends ADR-140/145 · constrains ADR-141's deck · relates
to ADR-150.

The request was "let the superadmin name a key, and choose which scenes it shows". **Half of
it was already built**: ADR-140 shipped a required name at mint time — the console asks
"Where is it?" with the placeholder *Main hall*, the server refuses an empty one, and the
revoke list is keyed on it. Grepping first turned a two-part feature into a one-part feature,
which is the second time in three ADRs that reading the code before building changed the
scope.

What did not exist is any way to make two screens differ, or to change a key after minting:
the routes were create and revoke, full stop. Every projector in the building therefore ran
the same nine-scene loop, so a foyer screen that should show photographs and a court-side
screen that should show *on court* and *up next* both also showed the cluster board, the
bracket and the top players.

**Scenes only — the name stays fixed.** Asked whether the edit should cover the label too,
the organiser kept it immutable: a key's name is its identity in the revoke list and in the
`last_seen_at` troubleshooting that precedes a revoke, so "what was projecting in the hall
that day" keeps a stable answer. A projector that changes rooms gets a new key. The edit
route is correspondingly narrow, and refuses a revoked key for the same reason — a revoked
row is the record, and editing one would quietly rewrite history.

**An empty scene set is refused, at three doors.** A screen showing nothing is
indistinguishable from a projector that has died, and nobody in the room can tell which. The
schema carries a `jsonb_array_length >= 1` CHECK, the route refuses before it, and the
console disables the last ticked checkbox. Turning a screen off is what revoke is for, and
the error message says exactly that.

**Omission means "everything", but only at creation.** A key minted without an opinion gets
all nine — the behaviour every key had before this existed, so the column defaults rather
than migrating. On the PATCH it is an error: a body that silently reset a carefully-chosen
screen to all nine is the worst available reading of an empty request.

**An unknown scene id is rejected, not filtered.** Dropping it quietly would save a key with
fewer scenes than the superadmin ticked, and they would discover that from a wall in front of
an audience. Stored sets are also de-duplicated and sorted into the canonical running order,
so two consoles that chose the same scenes produce byte-identical rows.

**The screen needed its first "who am I" read.** A projector has only ever carried a token
and fetched the same public boards as everybody else, because nothing about a key changed
what appeared on the wall. `GET /api/status/screen` is answered from the key row the session
middleware already loaded, so it costs no extra query, and it is **polled** rather than read
at pairing time: a projector runs for eight hours and nobody is walking to the booth after a
change. A tick in the console reaches the hall on the next cycle.

**Until it answers, the screen shows everything.** A slow or failing profile read must never
be the reason a wall goes blank in front of a room — so the fallback is today's behaviour,
not an empty strip. Sabotaging that one branch to `[]` fails **21** tests, which is the right
order of magnitude for a mistake that would blank every projector in the building.

**The filter needed no new machinery.** A scene the key may not show simply leaves the strip,
which is precisely what already happens to a scene with nothing to say. ADR-141 built the
deck to adopt a re-laid strip at rest, so unticking a box mid-event slides the scene out at
the next pause instead of cutting an animation in half.

**The nine ids became a vocabulary.** They were literals inside `useScenes`, which was fine
while they addressed a local array; they are now written into rows and sent over the wire, so
renaming one is a data migration rather than a refactor. `SCREEN_SCENES` says so from the
declaration, and `HallScene.id` is narrowed from `string` to `ScreenSceneId` so a scene added
in one place and not the other cannot compile.

**Verified by sabotage.** Unknown ids filtered instead of refused → 1 API test; the empty-set
guard removed → 1; editing a revoked key allowed → 1; the screen ignoring its scene list → 1
web test; the show-everything fallback replaced with a blank strip → **21**; the
"never empty" rule removed from the shared toggle → 1 (asserted directly, because the console
disables that checkbox and `userEvent` will not click it — ADR-138's problem and ADR-138's
answer).

**Gates.** standards 473/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 655 passing (8 new), branches
94.77 against the 94.60 floor; web 1207 passing (8 new), branches 98.38, every metric at or
above the measured baseline.

### ADR-161 — the day leaves the building

**Status:** accepted · 2026-10-05 · closes `superadmin-event-day-gaps.md` §7, and with it §4c
· extends ADR-006/029 · obeys ADR-115 · reuses ADR-136's definition of the final.

There was no export, download or print anywhere in the console. At 15:50 the prize-giving
needs the top three individuals and the top three teams, and the organiser afterwards needs
a record; today that meant reading it off a projector or querying the database. The hall
screen is a beautiful way to *show* the result and no way at all to *keep* it.

**One read behind everything.** The page fetches a single `FinalStandingsView` and builds the
printed sheet and all three CSVs from that one object, in the browser. Three CSV endpoints
would have been the obvious shape and would have been wrong: a spreadsheet fetched a second
after the sheet was printed can disagree with it, and then the room has two answers to "who
won" and no way to tell which is real. Here they cannot differ, because they are the same
read.

**Three questions went to the organiser, and all three went the generous way.**

*Every participant, not the board's top ten.* The leaderboard carries `LIMIT 10` and a
`> 0` filter, both right for a wall that has to be legible from forty feet. A record that
silently omits everybody who scored nothing cannot answer "did my cluster turn up", which is
exactly what gets asked a week later — so the export has its own uncached query with neither
restriction. The cache was dropped with it: ADR-038's shield exists because every phone in
the building polls the board, and this is one superadmin a handful of times.

*Three separate CSVs, not one file with a section column.* Clusters, individuals and group
tables have nothing in common but a date. Forced into one table, every row carries columns
that only apply to some of it, and the file opens as a field of blanks.

*Always available, never refused.* An unclosed match at 15:50 must not be the reason nothing
prints. Instead the sheet says `PROVISIONAL — the tournament has not finished` on itself, in
a 2pt box, **in the print stylesheet as well as on screen** — because the paper is what
leaves the room, and a provisional sheet read out as the result is the worst thing this page
can cause.

**The rostrum is withheld rather than guessed.** It is empty while the final is unplayed even
though both finalists are known and every semi-final is won, which is precisely the moment a
naive "top of the bracket" reading would start naming a champion. A round robin has no final
at all, so there the table is the result — but only once every fixture has resolved, for the
same reason ADR-150 withholds a group rank before anybody has played. The third-place match
is its own stage (ADR-137) and so is its own place: the rostrum is two deep until that match
is won, which reads as a fact about the format rather than as missing data, because each
entry says how it was earned.

**The final is found exactly as the champion bonus finds it** — the knockout fixture nothing
else feeds from. Reused deliberately: a second definition could drift, and then the printed
rostrum and the points on the board would name different teams.

**Printing is its own medium.** The console is near-black and dense, built for a laptop in a
dim hall. Printed as-is, a driver either empties a cartridge over the page or drops the
background and prints pale grey on white. `print.css` inverts it to ink on paper, hides the
tabs you cannot click and the buttons you cannot press (including the Print button that
produced the sheet), and repeats table headings across page breaks — eight groups of four do
not fit on one page, and page two of a standings table without headings is a grid of
unlabelled integers. jsdom never evaluates `@media print` and nothing here renders a printer,
so the rules whose absence produces a *wrong* sheet are asserted as text. ADR-144 is the
precedent: a stylesheet nothing asserted on shipped a projector that looked switched off.

**The CSV is the one place user text is handed to something that executes it.** Excel runs a
cell beginning `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, and a nickname is whatever a participant typed, so those
cells get a leading apostrophe. A BOM and CRLF go with it: without the BOM, Excel reads UTF-8
as the local code page and every accented nickname in the record arrives mangled — and
nobody opens this file until the day is over, when it is far too late to notice.

**ADR-115 is honoured in both renderings.** A group whose matches carried no score has a
partial sum, not a difference, so the screen shows an em dash and the CSV an empty field.
A zero there would be a claim rather than a fact.

**Verified by sabotage.** Reusing the board's `> 0` filter → 2 API tests; naming a champion
from the bracket before the final is won → 2; `isProvisional` pinned false → 2; dropping the
CSV injection guard → 1 web test; dropping the BOM and CRLF → 3; the provisional banner
inverted → 2; the print sheet keeping the console's dark background → 1.

**One flake fixed in passing.** `useScreenPhotos.test.ts` failed once under a full-coverage
run. Its own comment explains why two of its waits carry a five-second window; the third had
been left on the default and was the one losing the race. Not news about the code.

**Gates.** standards 481/0; eslint clean across four roots; API 665 passing (13 new),
branches 94.68 against the 94.60 floor; web 1223 passing (16 new), branches 98.40 against
98.38, functions 98.76, statements 99.17.

### ADR-162 — the memoised membership, and the only cached authorisation decision

**Context.** The cache audit of 2026-10-05 (`docs/outstanding-tasks.md` §9) found
`findActiveMembership` to be the hottest uncached read in the system and the only one that
scales with *traffic* rather than with people. It runs once per stream connect and then again
for every team frame delivered (the status stream's gate, ADR-128) and every team chat message
(`stillAMember`, ADR-123) — roughly two indexed point-reads per member per message.

The audit recommended leaving it alone, on the grounds that a stale hit here is not a slow page
but an ex-member reading a room they were removed from, and that the invalidation surface
looked wide. The organiser pushed back: cache it, and make sure it is voided when membership
changes. That is the right call, and the premise of the objection was wrong — the surface is
**nine writes in two entity modules, funnelling through four post-commit seams**, which is
narrower than `TOURNAMENT_TAG` (thirteen) and about the same as `GALLERY_TAG`.

**Decision.** Cache it, under a coarse `MEMBERSHIP_TAG`, with three rules that follow from it
being an authorisation decision rather than a display value:

1. **Freshness comes from the void, never from the TTL.** Everywhere else in `cache.ts` the TTL
   is the safety net under a write path someone forgot to tag. Here it is a blast radius.
2. **One second** — an order of magnitude below every other TTL in the file. The deliveries
   this exists to collapse all land in the same tick as the message that caused them, so a
   one-second window captures essentially the whole burst while bounding any future missed void
   to one second.
3. **No stale-while-revalidate.** Serving a knowingly stale authorisation answer is the exact
   failure being guarded against.

**Coarse, not per-participant.** Membership changes are rare (a few hundred across an event)
and the reads are constant, so over-voiding costs a handful of point-reads. The benefit is that
no caller can get *which* participant wrong — and several writes touch more than one person: a
disband ends five memberships, a staff move ends one and creates another.

**The void happens after the COMMIT, never inside.** Otherwise a concurrent reader can be
answered from uncommitted state and pin it for the full TTL — the same hazard
`announceRosterEvent` already documents for the team-chat watermark.

**`isCaptain` is on the cached row, so captaincy changes invalidate too.** This is the part
that is easy to miss, because a handover does not change whether anyone is on a team.

**Enforcement.** Two mechanisms, because comments do not fail builds:

- A sixteenth standards rule, `membership-void`: any module writing `team_membership` must also
  call `forgetMemberships()`. File-level rather than region-level on purpose — the write is
  inside a transaction and the void must follow the commit, so demanding them in one region
  would be demanding the bug. It catches a *new* module that never learns the rule.
- Tests at all four seams, verified by deleting each void in turn. Two were already covered
  many times over (leave 51 failures, join 15). **Two were covered by nothing** and are the
  reason this entry is not just a performance note: the superadmin roster repairs through
  `announcingAll`, and the participant-facing captaincy handover. Both are now pinned, each
  warming the cache before the write — a cache test that reads only afterwards is fresh either
  way and sees nothing (the lesson from §9's K7).

**Consequence.** A membership change is visible to both SSE streams on the very next frame, as
before, and a busy team room stops re-reading the same row once per member per message. The
honest residual risk is a future write path that bypasses all four seams; the standards rule is
what stands between that and a privacy failure.

### ADR-163 — the line that says where you stopped reading

**Context.** Both rooms open on the newest fifty messages with no indication of which of them
arrived while the reader was away. On a phone, coming back to a busy team room after a match
means scrolling up through a wall of text guessing at the last line you recognise. The app
already knows the answer: `psd.feeds.read.v1` holds a per-feed watermark, and it is the same
value the nav dot is derived from.

**Decision.** Draw a `new messages` rule immediately above the first message newer than the
watermark, in **both** chat surfaces, and bring it to the top of the view on arrival. Four
rulings from the organiser shape it:

1. **Freeze the mark on entry and hold it for the whole visit.** This is the only one that is
   load-bearing in the code. Opening a room marks its feed read, which advances the very value
   the line is derived from — so a straightforward implementation draws the line, clears the
   dot, and then erases the line a tick later, in front of the reader. The mark is therefore
   captured into a ref on the **first render**, before any effect runs, and never re-read.
2. **No unread, no line.** The room opens the way it always did.
3. **The separator goes to the TOP of the view**, not the centre: everything below it is the
   new material, so the reader should be able to read downwards without scrolling back.
4. **Record it as an ADR.** (It was briefly numbered 162; that number went to the membership
   cache first.)

**The marker is a timestamp, compared as a string.** Not a message id. Two reasons: the stored
watermark *is* a server-produced UTC ISO instant, and comparing ids would lean on UUIDv7's sort
order for a purpose nobody promised it for. Compared lexicographically rather than parsed, so a
phone with a wrong clock still draws the line in the right place — the comparison is between two
values the server produced.

**A message whose time equals the mark has been read.** The watermark is how far the reader got,
not the instant before it. Off by one here puts the line above a line they have already seen on
every visit to a room they are caught up on, which is the most common visit there is.

**The line is allowed to be above the very first message.** Fifty new messages with older
history behind `Earlier messages` is an ordinary case, and is not the same as having read
nothing at all — which draws no line, because there is nothing to separate.

**It renders as an `<li>`.** The rooms are `<ul>`s; a `<div>` between two `<li>`s is invalid
markup and the rule would be mispositioned by the list's own flex rules. `role="separator"`
with an `aria-label`, so a screen reader hears it rather than meeting an unlabelled bullet.

**The scroll happens once per mount**, from a callback ref rather than an effect — the ref fires
exactly when the node exists, which an effect ordered against a list that is still arriving does
not. It is `typeof`-guarded because jsdom has no layout and therefore no `scrollIntoView`, and a
room that threw rather than rendered would be a far worse bug than a missing scroll.

**Gates.** standards 487/0; eslint and tsc clean; web tests green with 14 new (11 on the hook,
3 across the two panels), each verified by mutating `>` to `>=` in the boundary comparison.

**A finding on the way.** The first panel test placed the divider at the top of the list and
failed. The cause was the fixture, not the feature: `mergeById` sorts the room **by id**, on the
promise that a UUIDv7 sorts chronologically, so fixture ids of `older`/`newer` render in the
wrong order. Any new room fixture must use ascending ids.

### ADR-164 — The duplicate sign-up, stopped in the only second it can be

**Context.** Design-doc §8 says "a duplicate sign-up is permanent" and leaves it there. Reading
the code made the sentence worse rather than better. Identity is a nickname and a 4-digit PIN
and nothing else — no email, no phone, no pre-loaded roster — so a duplicate is **undetectable
by construction**: the only uniqueness the database enforces is `ux_participant_nickname_lower`,
which stops two people taking the same nickname and does nothing about one person taking two.
And every per-participant guarantee in the system is keyed on `participant_id`, so the second
row is a second entitlement: it can score the same activity round again
(`ux_fringe_scan_live_slot`), claim the same swag again, and join a second team. Nothing merges,
hides or deactivates — `participant` has no `is_hidden`, no `merged_into`, no `withdrawn_at`,
and `no-hard-delete` forbids removing the row. The points earned under the first nickname are
stranded there for the rest of the day.

The organiser ruled: **build the prevent remedy, not a merge and not a hide**, and accepted
that this does nothing for ghosts that already exist. Asked whether the lookup should be
restricted, the ruling was **no — these are all nicknames**.

**The trigger is a forgotten nickname, not a forgotten PIN.** A PIN can already be reset by any
facilitator, so somebody who remembers who they are can always be let back in. Somebody who has
forgotten *which* nickname they chose had no route at all, and the fastest thing to do about it
on a busy morning is to sign up again. That is the entire mechanism of the defect, and it is
the thing this fixes.

**Decision.** One anonymous read — `GET /api/participants/nicknames?clusterCode=XX` — surfaced
in three places, of which only the first is the actual prevention:

1. **On the sign-up form, above the nickname field.** This is the point. Somebody who could
   remember their nickname would already have taken "I already have a nickname" at the bottom;
   the warning has to interrupt the person who cannot, three taps before they make the
   duplicate. Below the form, or beside that link, it would be read by everybody except the one
   person it is for.
2. **On the sign-in form**, beside the existing PIN-reset hint — the two halves of "I can't get
   in", which previously answered only one of them.
3. **As a cluster filter on the superadmin directory**, which is the organiser's own worked
   example: the help desk picks the cluster and reads the short list out.

**Anonymous, and it has to be.** The only person who needs this is one who cannot sign in, so a
session requirement would make it available exclusively to people who do not need it. What it
publishes is a list of nicknames, which the leaderboard already projects onto a wall, a chat
room shows to everyone and a team roster shows to the team. It answers with **bare strings and
nothing else** — no id, no scan number, no avatar, no PIN — and that is pinned by a test that
asserts the *shape* of the response rather than the absence of particular fields, so a column
added to the row later cannot leak through here unnoticed.

**The cluster is required, not optional.** Not as a secret, since it is a dropdown on the
sign-up form, but because "every nickname at the event" is a list nobody can read down. A
missing or invented cluster is **refused with a 400** rather than defaulted to everybody —
otherwise a typo in a client becomes a scrape. The cluster is also the one fact about
themselves a participant has certainly not forgotten.

**The typed filter runs in the browser**, over the list already fetched, and matches anywhere in
the nickname rather than only at the start. Somebody at a desk trying to recall whether they
were `BeachBoss` or `Beach_Boss` must be able to try both in the same second, and the fragment
people retain is as often the end of a word as the beginning. Changing cluster clears the
filter, because a guess typed against one cluster's list means nothing against another's.

**Choosing a nickname fills the sign-in field; it does not sign anybody in.** Recognising a
name on a public list is not proof of owning it — the PIN is the only thing that proves
anything, and it is still required. The nickname is seeded into form *state* rather than held
as a prop, so from that point it is editable: recognising is not the same as being sure.

**Deliberately uncached.** Every other guest read here is cached; this one is not. It runs a
handful of times across an entire event, by definition only for people who are stuck, and the
house rule from the §9 audit is that a cached read must have an invalidation surface — adding a
tag voided by every sign-up, to save a query that happens twice a day, would be risk bought
with no benefit. `readTeamChatMessages` is uncached for the same kind of reason.

**What this does not do.** It does not detect a duplicate, merge one, or recover points
stranded under a nickname nobody can name. Those remain impossible by construction, and the
organiser accepted that when ruling for prevention.

**Gates.** standards 491 files / 16 rules / 0 violations; eslint and tsc clean across contracts,
api and web; api 690 passed / 3 skipped, branches 94.91; web 1252 passed, branches 98.41,
functions 98.69. 7 API tests and 13 web tests, with eight sabotages watched to fail: the cluster
filter dropped from the query, the 400 softened to an empty list, the PIN added to the selected
row, the filter ignored, the list fetched before a cluster was chosen, the filter left in place
across a cluster change, the sign-in prefill dropped, and the console's cluster parameter
dropped.

### ADR-165 — Apply the schema snapshot on every boot, not only to an empty database

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-05
- **Relates to:** ADR-049 (one snapshot, no migrations), ADR-102 (the three data tiers),
  ADR-061 (`participant_title`, the table that exposed this), `AGENTS-database.md` §5,
  user report: `./dev.sh` on a fresh machine dying with
  `relation "participant_title" does not exist`.
- **Decision:** `ensureSchema` reads `schema.sql`, compares **every** table the snapshot
  defines against `information_schema`, and applies the file whenever any is missing — rather
  than applying it only when one sentinel table is absent. It returns
  `'provisioned' | 'repaired' | 'unchanged'` so the boot log can say which happened, and a
  `repaired` boot logs a warning naming the likely cause.
- **Why:** the old guard asked `to_regclass('public.cluster')`, and `cluster` is the **first**
  table in the snapshot. A single probe can therefore only tell you that provisioning once
  *started*. A database built by an older snapshot has the sentinel and lacks every table added
  since, so the check reported "present", nothing was applied, and the boot died much later
  inside the seed with a bare `relation "participant_title" does not exist` — an error naming
  neither the cause nor the remedy, several frames from the decision that caused it.
  Applying the file unconditionally is safe and was always the intent: every one of its 72
  statements is `IF NOT EXISTS`, the only other statement is an idempotent `ALTER … SET
  STORAGE`, and the file carries its own `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. ADR-049's "applied whole to any
  database that does not have it yet" is better served by letting Postgres decide per object
  than by a proxy question about one table.
  **Rejected:** a first-table/last-table sentinel pair — cheaper, and still blind to a table
  missing from the middle, which is precisely the reported case. The second new test exists to
  hold that line; the pair passes the first test and fails the second.
  **Rejected:** reintroducing numbered migrations. ADR-049's reasoning is unchanged — there is
  still nothing deployed to migrate from.
- **Impact:** a dev database from an older commit now self-heals on boot instead of crashing,
  which is the difference between a working morning and a stack trace for anyone pulling this
  branch. `ensureSchema`'s return type changed from `boolean` to `SchemaOutcome`; `index.ts`
  and `db/setup-cli.ts` are the only callers. **This is still not a migration system**: a table
  or index added since is created, but a column whose type changed *in place* is not altered,
  and the remedy for that remains a clean database (`./dev-reset.sh`). The `repaired` warning
  exists so that case is visible rather than mysterious. Two new tests in `bootstrap.test.ts`,
  and the two existing assertions moved from `true`/`false` to the named outcomes. Four
  sabotages watched to fail: the single-sentinel check restored (3 tests), a first+last sentinel
  pair (2), never reporting `repaired` (2), and detecting the gap but applying only to an empty
  database (2).

### ADR-166 — An image that never answers must not freeze the hall screen

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-05
- **Relates to:** ADR-143 (decoded before shown), ADR-141 (every scene mounted at once),
  `AGENTS-workflow.md` §4b, `GREENFIELD.md` §3.2. Found while chasing an intermittent failure
  in `useScreenPhotos.test.ts`, which turned out to be reporting a live fault.
- **Decision:** `load()` in `lib/photo/imagePreload.ts` resolves on the first of load, error, or
  a **ten-second ceiling** (`IMAGE_LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS`). A timed-out URL is left *unknown* — not
  added to `broken` — so the next scene retries it. Separately, `useScreenPhotos.test.ts`
  unmounts (`cleanup()`) **before** clearing the module-level preload caches.
- **Why:** a browser does not promise to fire `onload` **or** `onerror`. A hung request — a
  stalled tunnel, a backgrounded tab, a projector laptop that lost Wi-Fi mid-fetch — fires
  neither, so the promise in `inFlight` never settled and was never deleted. Every later caller
  for that URL then awaited the same dead promise **for the rest of the event**, and because a
  scene awaits its batch with `Promise.all`, one hung thumbnail stopped the whole wall from
  ever changing photos again. Nothing logged, nothing visibly broken: the strip simply stopped.
  Ten seconds is far longer than a thumbnail on a working connection and far shorter than a
  scene cycle, so being wrong costs one photo for one rotation.
  **Not marked `broken`** on purpose: `broken` is forever and means "the server said no". A
  timeout means "we did not find out", and a recovered connection deserves another go.
  **A `try/finally` around the await was written and then removed.** With the ceiling in place
  `load` always settles, so no test could make the `finally` matter — a sabotage of it survived,
  which is the signal that it was unreachable rather than untested (ADR-013's method).
- **Impact:** `IMAGE_LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` is exported and two tests pin it; `imagePreload.test.ts`
  goes 6 → 8. Two sabotages watched to fail: removing the ceiling (2 tests) and marking a
  timed-out URL `broken` (2). The test-isolation half is the more general lesson and is written
  up in `GREENFIELD.md` §3.2: **shared module state must be reset against a quiet tree.**
  Clearing it in an `afterEach` that runs *before* Testing Library's automatic cleanup left the
  previous test's hook mounted and still able to start a preload, which then landed in the map
  after it had been emptied — so the next test awaited a promise belonging to a stub that no
  longer existed, its image was never requested, and its wait expired on a value that was never
  going to change. `useScreenPhotos.test.ts` had been "fixed" three times before this, twice by
  raising a timeout, because the symptom looked like slowness and was actually a dead promise.
  Six consecutive full-suite runs clean, against roughly one failure in three.

### ADR-167 — A sign-out the server did not confirm has not happened

- **Status.** Accepted.
- **Reported as.** "Participants cannot sign out; pressing Sign out leaves them signed in."

- **Context.** Every layer underneath this bug was green. The API invalidates the session row
  and clears the cookie, with tests for both carriers (`auth.test.ts`, `session-cookie.test.ts`);
  driving the real dev server by hand confirmed it — after `POST /api/auth/signout`, both the
  bearer token and the cookie return 401. The web tests pressed the button and asserted that
  `POST /api/auth/signout` was sent (`participant-pages.test.tsx`) and that the location trail
  was forgotten (`location-memory.test.tsx`).

  All of them asserted the **call**. None asserted the **outcome** — that the person is
  afterwards signed out, and stays signed out. Both route tables answered `GET /api/auth/session`
  with a fixed `200`, so no amount of breakage in sign-out could have failed them.

- **Mechanism.** The session cookie is `httpOnly` (`sessionCookieOptions`), which means the only
  thing in the system that can revoke it is the server's response. `endSession` ran
  `await signOut().catch(() => undefined)` — it discarded the failure, cleared the localStorage
  token, set the session to `null` and reported success. When the request did not land, the
  device kept a live cookie and the server kept a live session row, and **a cookie on its own is
  a complete credential**. The UI said "signed out"; the next page load presented the cookie and
  signed the participant straight back in. From the far side of the screen that is a Sign out
  button that does nothing.

  The same `await`-then-clean-up shape hid a second defect: every local `forget…` call sat after
  the awaited request, so a throw skipped all of them and left the previous participant's
  announcement floor, feed marks and up-soon floor on a borrowed phone.

- **Decision.**
  1. `signOut()` does its local forgetting in a `finally`, so a failed request still clears this
     device. The throw still propagates — the caller has to know.
  2. `endSession()` resolves `true` only when the server confirmed. On failure it empties the
     local caches (a borrowed phone must not keep readable data) but leaves the session standing,
     because it *is* still standing.
  3. Both Sign out buttons — participant profile and staff console — stay put on failure and say
     so, rather than navigating to a page the surviving cookie re-authenticates.

- **Consequence.** Sign-out can now visibly fail, which is the honest outcome and a better one
  than a silent lie: the participant is told they are still signed in on that phone and can press
  the button again. Nothing can be done client-side about an `httpOnly` cookie, so reaching the
  server is not an implementation detail of sign-out — it *is* sign-out.

- **Tests.** `apps/web/src/acceptance/signout.test.tsx` — the route table is stateful the way the
  real server is: the session is alive until the signout lands and dead from then on, and the
  session route never inspects the bearer token, which is exactly how an ambient cookie behaves.
  Sabotages: swallow the failure and report success → caught; drop the `finally` → caught;
  navigate away anyway → caught (and only after a second assertion was added; the first version
  of the test let that one through).

  `e2e/signout.spec.ts` covers the same ground in a real browser, where the cookie is real. It
  is **unrun** — this sandbox has no browser binary and the Playwright CDN is unreachable from
  it — so it is written to be run wherever the rest of the e2e suite runs.

- **Method note.** Asserting that a request was *sent* is not a test of a feature whose whole
  purpose is a state change on the other side. Where a fixed stub cannot distinguish a working
  feature from a broken one, the stub has to hold the state the server holds.

### ADR-168 — A column the snapshot added cannot reach a database that already has the table

- **Status.** Accepted. Extends ADR-165.

- **Context.** ADR-165 made a database built by an older snapshot self-heal, by comparing the full
  list of tables `schema.sql` defines against the ones that exist and applying the snapshot when
  any were missing. It fixed the reported crash and left a hole one size smaller.

  `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` does nothing at all to a table that already exists — including
  adding a column that was written into its definition later. So the first time the snapshot grew
  a **column** rather than a table, every existing database would be told it was complete (no
  table is missing), nothing would be applied, and the boot would die further down on a missing
  column — the same failure ADR-165 was written to end, one granularity down.

  The `ensureSchema` doc comment already said the right thing — *"apply it on EVERY boot and let
  Postgres do the deciding"* — and the code it sat above did not: an `if (missing.length === 0)
  return 'unchanged'` short-circuited before the apply. The contract and the implementation had
  quietly diverged, and nothing failed, because until a column was added there was no difference
  between them.

- **Decision.**
  1. `ensureSchema` applies `schema.sql` unconditionally, as it always claimed to. Completeness is
     computed for the **report** only (`provisioned` / `repaired` / `unchanged`), not as a gate.
  2. Every column added to a table after that table was first released is repeated at the foot of
     the snapshot as `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, in a marked section.

- **Consequence.** Additive schema changes now self-heal on boot, which is the whole of what this
  project needs while it is pre-production. It is still not a migration system: it adds, it never
  alters or drops, and a column whose type changes in place still needs `./dev-reset.sh`. The
  duplication between a column's definition and its ALTER is real and deliberate — the comment
  says to keep them identical — and is the price of having no migration tool at all.

- **Tests.** `bootstrap.test.ts` drops a column from a complete database and asserts both that the
  outcome is `unchanged` (nothing is missing, so there is nothing to *repair*) and that the column
  comes back anyway. Sabotages: restore the early return → caught; delete the ALTER lines → caught.

### ADR-169 — Which teams meet first is a choice, not a correction

- **Status.** Accepted.
- **Asked for as.** "16 teams; #1 v #2, #3 v #4 …; the winner of (1,2) plays the winner of (3,4),
  and so on until one remains."

- **Context.** Read as a request for a new tournament *format*, this looked large. It was not: the
  engine's knockout half is already general — `knockoutDrafts()` builds the whole tree with byes
  and feeder links, `stage = 'knockout'` fixtures already exist, and both the golden-point rule
  (`knockoutCannotDraw`) and the court-marshal's knockout marking key off a fixture's **stage**
  rather than off the `world_cup` format, so they apply to any knockout fixture for free.

  What the request actually collided with was one line: `bracketSeedOrder()` deliberately does the
  opposite, pairing 1 v 16 and 2 v 15 *"so top qualifiers meet late, not early."*

  These are two different tournaments, and which is right depends on what the numbers mean. If
  they are **strength ranks**, pairing 1 v 2 in the first round throws the ranking away and makes
  being seeded first a disadvantage. If they are **labels** — team number, enrolment order, a drawn
  position — then "keeping the top seeds apart" is keeping apart two things nobody ranked, and
  pairing the list in order is exactly right. Being unable to tell which from the request, the
  question was put rather than guessed, and the answer was to offer both.

- **Decision.** `knockoutPairing`, with two values, on the plan (editable) and frozen onto the
  tournament at activation:
  - `classic` — the seeded bracket. **The default**, so no day that already existed changes shape.
  - `adjacent` — the list paired in order, 1 v 2, 3 v 4.

  It decides the **first round's seating only**; everything after it is the tree, which is the same
  either way. Everything else — byes to the padding seats, late admission, a withdrawn team's
  fixtures, final standings — is deliberately untouched.

- **Consequence.** Under `adjacent` with two groups advancing two, the two group winners meet in
  the first knockout round. That is the format working as asked, not a bug, and the console says so
  under the selector in words rather than leaving "in order" to be interpreted.

- **Tests.** Engine-level for the two orders and the default; `knockout-pairing.test.ts` drives a
  real eight-team day twice and asserts the two group winners meet at once under `adjacent` and
  cannot under `classic` — an observable that needs no knowledge of the internal seeding.
  Sabotages: fall back to classic in the engine → caught; ignore the frozen value at the draw →
  caught (only after the integration test was added; the engine test alone let it through);
  flip the entity's default → **survived**, because the contract schema already defaults it, so the
  second default was removed rather than pinned.

### ADR-170 — The browser suite mirrors the jsdom areas, and runs its files in parallel

- **Context.** The e2e suite was fourteen flat spec files at `workers: 1`. Flat meant a spec's
  location said nothing about the surface it drove, and one worker meant the suite's cost grew
  strictly with its size — which is the pressure that stops specs being written at all. The jsdom
  suites had long since split by area (`routes-superadmin`, `routes-participant`, `lib/hooks`,
  `acceptance`); the browser suite had never followed.

- **Decision 1 — the layout mirrors the jsdom areas.** `e2e/{acceptance,participant,facilitator,
  superadmin}` with shared helpers in `e2e/support/`, so a spec's home is guessable from the
  surface it drives, and npm scripts exist at the same granularity as the jsdom ones.

- **Decision 2 — parallel by FILE, not by test.** `fullyParallel: false` with `workers` defaulting
  to half the cores (`PSD_E2E_WORKERS` overrides; `1` restores the old behaviour exactly). The
  rejected alternative is the tempting one: `fullyParallel: true` scatters tests *within* a file
  across workers, and many specs here are journeys — sign up in the first test, act as that person
  in the second. That setting would have converted a correct suite into a flaky one, and the flake
  would have looked like a product bug. A file whose tests really are independent opts in for
  itself with `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` — a claim its author can check.

- **Decision 3 — singleton mutators are quarantined in `e2e/exclusive/`**, run last at one worker.
  The backend is one shared stack that is not reset between files, so parallel safety rests on two
  rules: provision only through the app's own APIs under a **worker-unique** run id, and never let
  two workers touch a row that has exactly one instance — the tournament, the plan, the point
  config, the station-offline switch. `runId` was clock-derived (`Date.now()`), which collides
  precisely when the machine is fast enough to start its workers in the same millisecond; it now
  folds in `TEST_WORKER_INDEX`, kept to six characters to stay inside the 20-character nickname cap.

- **A move broke three things that no type-checker could see.** `git mv` plus rewritten imports
  passed `tsc` and eslint while three `dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))` joins still counted
  one directory too few — runtime strings, invisible to both tools, and two of them would have
  surfaced as a missing fixture file mid-run. `npx playwright test --list` caught it in two seconds
  **and needs no browser installed**, which makes it the check to run after any e2e restructure.
  The fix was not a third `'..'` but `e2e/support/paths.ts`: the count up to the repository root is
  now made in exactly one file, where moving a spec cannot make it wrong.

- **New specs, chosen for what jsdom cannot do.** `facilitator/type-anywhere.spec.ts` presses a
  **real** key: a synthetic `keydown` has no default action, so the jsdom test can prove the box
  took focus but never that the keystroke which caused the focus was then delivered into it — which
  is the entire mechanism of ADR-105, and the thing a scan gun depends on.
  `exclusive/knockout-pairing.spec.ts` stops at the plan and never activates, because activation
  writes a singleton no UI can undo and would leave the shared event database unable to run the
  suite twice; the draw itself stays proved at the API layer.

- **Honesty.** **None of this has been executed.** No browser binary exists in the environment that
  wrote it. The evidence is `playwright test --list` (122 tests in 16 files collect; the
  parallel/exclusive split partitions them 108 + 14 with nothing lost), `npm run typecheck`, eslint,
  and a deliberate `PSD_E2E_WORKERS=nonsense` that produced the intended error. The two new specs
  have never run, and the cross-talk risk that parallelism introduces — specs asserting global
  collection counts, such as the gallery and announcements — is real, unmeasured here, and has
  `PSD_E2E_WORKERS=1` as its documented escape hatch.

### ADR-171 — The second default for `hasThirdPlace`, removed on the same evidence as the first

- **Decision.** `hasThirdPlace` defaulted twice: `.default(false)` in the contract schema and
  `?? false` in `ActivateTournamentInput`'s construction. Flipping the entity's default to `?? true`
  — a change that inverts the feature — **survived all 40 tests** across the third-place,
  tournament-shape, knockout-pairing and final-standings suites. Unreachable code cannot be pinned
  by a test, so it was removed and the field made required, exactly as ADR-169 did for
  `knockoutPairing`.

- **The generalisation, now two for two.** Two defaults for one value is not redundancy, it is a
  latent divergence: with one caller the inner default is dead, and with a second caller the two
  disagree silently and the schema's answer wins somewhere the entity's comment says it should not.
  The contract schema is the single source of truth. A grep for `?? ` beside a field that a Zod
  schema already defaults is a cheap way to find the rest.

### ADR-172 — The cluster catalogue becomes editable, and the protection moves to where it bites

- **Context.** fds.md §2.2 called the sixteen clusters "not runtime-editable", §11 listed "no
  delete on Cluster" as deliberate, and §9 gave the reason: **"Cluster editability | Immutable |
  Prevents leaderboard gaming."** The request was to make the list editable anyway. Rather than
  discard that reasoning, this keeps it and narrows it to the operation it was actually about.

- **What could game the board, precisely.** Cluster standings are computed live by grouping
  `participant.cluster_code` (`clusterStandingsFromDb`). So **moving a participant moves every
  point they have ever earned**, retroactively, on a board the hall is watching. That — not
  editing a list — is the gaming risk. Adding a cluster cannot do it (a new cluster starts at
  zero) and renaming cannot do it (the code every table references does not move). Hence:

  | Operation | Frozen once scoring starts? | Why |
  |---|---|---|
  | Add | No | starts at zero; a cluster that turns up on the morning is a real thing |
  | Rename display name | No | a label, not a key; no point moves |
  | Retire | **Yes** | removes a cluster from a day that has already scored |
  | Reassign (bulk or single) | **Yes** | moves points that have already been counted |

  "Scoring has started" is asked of the database — a non-voided `fringe_scan` or a completed,
  non-voided `tournament_match`, exactly the two sources `participantPoints` aggregates — rather
  than kept as a flag, which would have been a second place for it to be true.

- **Retire, never delete.** `chat_message.cluster_code_snapshot` and
  `gallery_photo.cluster_code_snapshot` record the author's cluster permanently. A `DELETE` could
  therefore only succeed by being refused by the foreign key or by blanking somebody's history, so
  there is **no delete route at all** and a test asserts its absence. Retiring hides a cluster from
  signup and leaves every past message, photo and point exactly where it was.

- **The requested rule, and the way out of it.** Retiring is refused while the cluster still has
  members. The console does not merely report that refusal: the row carries `memberCount`, the
  button is disabled with the reason in its title, and the bulk move appears **on the same row**,
  because "move them first" is useless advice if the move is somewhere else in the console.

- **The type system was the real work, not the CRUD.** `clusterCodeSchema` was
  `z.enum(CLUSTER_CODES)`, so the valid set was a **compile-time** fact and a cluster added at run
  time would have been rejected by the very validator meant to admit it. The schema now checks
  shape only, `ClusterCode` widens to `string`, and the questions it stopped answering moved to
  where the catalogue is visible: `assertClusterUsable` at signup, `assertClusterExists` in the
  nickname finder. **Widening a type deletes checks silently** — `tsc` passed immediately and said
  nothing, and the nickname finder went on accepting `?clusterCode=NOPE`, answering 200 with an
  empty list: "nobody from there" instead of "there is no such place". A test caught it, not the
  compiler.

- **A sabotage that survived, and the test it condemned.** Removing the catalogue cache
  invalidation entirely left every test passing. The tests added the cluster and *then* read the
  list, so there was never a cached entry to go stale. A test for a cache has to **put something in
  the cache first**: priming `/api/clusters` before the edit now makes two tests fail under that
  sabotage. ADR-038 holds this list for sixty seconds, which on a signup queue is a long time to
  keep offering a retired cluster.

- **One deliberate exception to an immutability rule.** fds.md §2.1 marks a participant's cluster
  immutable post-signup; single-participant correction is allowed because the value is
  self-declared and unverified (§10 A2), so a mis-tap at signup is the most ordinary mistake of the
  day and nothing else can fix it. It is held to the same freeze as a bulk move.

- **Tests.** 15 API cases covering each refusal, including a separate context for the freeze — its
