  own because `scoringStarted` is global and one scan would have locked every other case in the
  file. 14 web cases, including that a chosen destination is the one sent rather than the first
  option. Sabotages: retire with members → caught; join a retired cluster → caught; drop the cache
  invalidation → **survived**, until the tests were fixed. Playwright was not run.

## ADR-173 — A sunburst backdrop for the avatar, two colours and two sliders

**Status:** accepted · **Supersedes:** nothing · **Touches:** ADR-021 (drawn avatar), ADR-028
(colour wheel), ADR-029 (build), ADR-031/037/054/057 (photo sprites), ADR-073 (tuning preview).

### What was asked for

After the backdrop colour row in the character customisation screen, a further backdrop option: a
hypnotic radial sunburst whose two colours are picked from the palette and whose ray count is set
by a horizontal slider. A canvas implementation was supplied as the reference for the maths.

Three questions were put and answered: it must work behind **photo avatars as well as drawn
ones**; it **moves only in the studio preview**; and **twist is a second slider**, zero included.

### The maths, moved off the canvas

The reference walks each ray's two edges outward and fills the polygon between them, bending the
angle by `θ + r · spiralForce` as it goes. That is the right geometry and the wrong mechanism for
this codebase: an avatar here is not a canvas but a 64×64 grid of role keys composed from RLE
layers and emitted as merged `<path>` rectangles in an SVG data URL. A photo sprite is the same
renderer at 128×128. There is no drawing context, and rasterising one would have to be re-indexed
back into the grid to be displayed at all, losing the crisp pixel edges the art style depends on.

So the polygon fill inverts into a point test. Every backdrop cell asks which ray it is standing
in, using the same bent angle. For a grid this small that is exact rather than approximate: no
edge-step resolution to tune, no seams between neighbouring polygons, no anti-aliasing to fight.
The 50 % duty cycle is preserved, so N rays means N rays and N equal gaps.

`twist` is carried as an integer 0–10 and multiplied by `SUNBURST_TWIST_STEP` (0.006 rad per unit
radius per step) when drawing. At maximum, the outermost ray of a 64-cell grid bends by about 2.7
radians — unmistakably a spiral, while still legible at the 32 px the avatar is often shown at.
Zero is a plain straight sunburst, which the user asked to keep reachable.

### The wire format: appended, never inserted

`avatar_look` gains three optional trailing parts — second colour, rays, twist. **The existing
backdrop becomes the sunburst's first colour**, so every code ever minted keeps meaning exactly
what it meant, and a seven-part code is a plain backdrop. This is the move ADR-029 made for
`build`, read from the other end, and it is why `parseAvatarLook` now has three back-compatibility
branches rather than a version number. A partial or out-of-range tail is **rejected**, not
repaired: a look that cannot be read is already handled by falling back to the drawn character,
and silently inventing a ray count would persist a choice nobody made.

This forced the first *change* to a CHECK constraint in `schema.sql`, a file whose rule is that it
adds and never alters. Editing the inline `CREATE TABLE` constraint only reaches a database made
after the edit; an existing one would keep the seven-part rule and reject every sunburst as a
constraint violation. An idempotent `DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS` / `ADD CONSTRAINT` pair is appended
at the tail. It is safe to re-run and safe to apply out of order, because the new rule accepts
everything the old one did.

### Photo avatars: at render time, not at save time

ADR-054 recolours a photo's backdrop by string surgery on the second-to-last palette entry. That
cannot express two colours, and a seventeenth entry would breach `AVATAR_SPRITE_MAX_COLOURS`.

The sunburst is therefore **never baked into the stored sprite**. The sprite keeps the single
backdrop colour ADR-054 put there, and the backdrop-keyed cells are split between the two colours
when the picture is drawn. Baking would have been the obvious move and is a trap: once the cells
are split there is no longer any record of which were backdrop, so moving the ray slider a second
time would have nothing coherent to recolour. Keeping the split in memory also leaves the sprite
format, the colour cap and ADR-054 itself untouched.

### Motion, confined to the preview

Everywhere an avatar appears — leaderboards, chat lines, rosters — it is the same static data URL
it was before. Only the studio preview turns, and only while a participant is choosing.

Spinning the finished image would spin the face with it, so the preview emits the same grid twice:
once with everything but the backdrop painted `fill="none"`, once with only the backdrop. The rays
layer rotates under a face that holds still. Stacked unrotated the two are pixel-for-pixel what
`avatarSvg` produces, so the preview cannot drift from what gets saved. The rays layer is drawn at
150 % and centred so a square image turning in a square frame never swings its corners into view.

The animation is CSS, which puts it under the `prefers-reduced-motion` block that already governs
every other moving part rather than inventing a second mechanism. A hypnotic backdrop is precisely
what that setting exists to stop — and unlike the cable cars, which are hidden because a parked
cable car reads as broken art, the rays are merely **frozen**: a still sunburst is exactly the
picture that will be saved.

### Also considered

- **A second colour row for colour one.** Rejected. The backdrop palette directly above already
  sets it, and two controls for one value leaves two places to disagree about which won.
- **Disabling the sliders when the backdrop is plain.** Rejected in favour of unmounting them: a
  ray count means nothing behind a flat colour, and dead controls invite the question of what they
  would have done.

### Scope

`fds.md` specifies `avatar_variant` only; the whole look format is an ADR-level extension
(ADR-021/028/029), so this needs no amendment there.

### Tests

Geometry is pinned by walking a circle and counting wedge boundaries — N rays crosses 2N
boundaries at every radius and every twist, which is the one property the slider actually sells.
Also pinned: the 50 % duty cycle, that twist 0 is straight and twist 10 is not, and that the
pattern is centred on the grid rather than half a cell off it (asserted with an *odd* ray count,
since an even one passes whether the half-cell offset is there or not). Round-trip and
back-compatibility cases cover both older formats and every malformed tail. Render cases cover the
drawn path, the photo path, and both preview layers. Two studio cases drive the select in both
directions, move both sliders and pick a second colour — without them the `onChange` handlers land
uncovered and the web gate's 98.55 % function threshold fails, the exact trap ADR-172 hit.

Sabotage: dropping the half-cell centring offset → **caught**. Playwright was not run.

## ADR-174 — A whole event day, proved twice

**Status:** accepted · **Touches:** ADR-089 (fixture claiming), ADR-114 (live scoring),
ADR-152/F-1 (draws), ADR-161 (final standings), ADR-169 (knockout pairing), AGENTS-testing.md §5–§6.

### What was missing

Every tournament test in `apps/api/src/tests/` proves one slice and provisions the rest by the
shortest route available. `final-standings.test.ts` walks its entire group stage over by
superadmin walkover; `knockout-pairing.test.ts` stops at the plan and never activates. Those are
the right calls for what each is interrogating, and together they leave one thing unproven: that
the surfaces **compose**. A participant signs up, joins a team, earns points at a fringe station
in the morning, and in the afternoon her team plays fifteen real matches — and both halves have
to arrive in the same totals, through caches invalidated along the way, with the printed export
agreeing with the wall the room is watching.

Two tests now cover that, deliberately at different layers.

### 1. The runnable journey (`apps/api/src/tests/full-event-journey.test.ts`)

One ordered narrative over the real HTTP routes: signup, join-by-code, a fringe scan and its
offline replay, activation into two groups of four, twelve group matches, two semi-finals and a
final. No walkovers; every match is started on a court, scored a rally at a time, and completed
by naming the winner the score implies, because `assertResultMatchesScore` refuses anything else.

Three things it pins that nothing else did:

- **Fringe points and match points land in the same column.** Nadia's total is derived from the
  real fixtures rather than asserted as a constant, and her captain — who did not scan — is
  exactly the fringe award behind her.
- **The export agrees with the leaderboard.** They are built from different queries, so two
  surfaces answering "who won" differently is a live risk, not a theoretical one.
- **Points are paid per MEMBER, not per team.** A first draft hardcoded the day's total and was
  wrong by exactly Nadia's share, because her team carries two people and every match it played
  paid out twice on its side. The assertion now derives it.

The `FixtureView` field is **`resolvedWinnerTeamId`**, not `winnerTeamId`. Reading the latter
yields `undefined`, which is not `null`, so a draw silently scores as a decided match. Typecheck
catches it; running vitest alone does not, which is why the gate runs both.

Sabotages, both caught: dropping `settleFixtureOfMatch` strands every fixture in `claimed`;
paying a drawn match at the loss rate breaks the export/leaderboard agreement.

### 2. The browser day (`e2e/full-event/full-event.spec.ts`)

What the API journey cannot prove is that the day is **reachable** — that every button exists, is
enabled at the moment it is needed, and leaves the console in a state the next press can act on.
Fifteen matches are played the slow way through the court console, because the failure being
guarded against is a console that works for one match and wedges on the next.

Division of labour follows `e2e/support/fixtures.ts`: the **cast** is provisioned through the
app's own APIs, the **day** is played through the UI. Eight captains filling in eight signup
forms would prove nothing `participant-signup.spec.ts` does not already prove. The protagonist is
different — she signs up on the real form and reads her four-digit number off her own QR home
screen, which is literally how it reaches a facilitator when the camera will not focus.

### A database of its own

This is the only spec that activates the tournament, and the reason it needs its own config.
`tournament` is one row per database, activation cannot be undone through any UI, and a second
attempt is refused with `tournamentAlreadyActive` — which is exactly why the knockout spec stops
at the plan and says so in its docblock.

Three options were put. A documented "reset first, skip if active" was the cheapest and leaves a
suite that silently does nothing when someone forgets. A superadmin reset route would have been a
destructive admin capability built solely to serve a test, against the retire-never-delete grain
this codebase has held elsewhere. The choice taken was the isolated one: **its own stack**.
`playwright.full-event.config.ts` boots the app on its own ports with its own PGlite directory,
wiped as part of the `webServer` command so there is no argument to forget. Nothing it does can
reach the shared dev database, and it is re-runnable immediately.

That surfaced a real defect: `_dev-common.sh` has always read `PSD_WEB_PORT` to decide where to
health-check the web server, but `vite.config.ts` hardcoded 5173 — so asking for another port
moved the check and not the server. Vite now honours it.

### What was actually verified, and what was not

Playwright **cannot execute in this sandbox** — the browser CDN is unreachable, re-confirmed. No
claim is made that the browser spec passes. It typechecks, lints, and lists its ten tests.

Its premises were verified another way: the scratch stack was booted for real, and the whole day
driven through it over HTTP as the facilitator the spec signs in as. A fixture was offered on
every one of the twelve group iterations, `upNext` reached exactly 0 afterwards (which is what
the spec asserts), the three knockout matches followed, and the day ended `completed` with a
two-deep podium and a non-provisional export. The court schedule read is also **facilitator-only**
— as superadmin it returns nothing, which would have made the match loop silently find no
fixtures had the spec signed in as the wrong actor.

## ADR-175 — The demo image and the production image are the same image, minus the demo day

The container had no opinion about data. `Dockerfile` set no `PSD_SEED`, so every image ever
built fell through to the `default` tier: schema, reference data, nothing else. That is the
correct answer for an event and the wrong one for the image a person builds first, which boots
to an empty leaderboard and cannot be demonstrated, evaluated or smoke-tested without somebody
inventing a day's worth of data by hand.

So the tiers are now split across two build files. `Dockerfile` sets `PSD_SEED=demo` and applies
`seed-demo.sql` on first boot. `Dockerfile-prd` sets `PSD_SEED=default` and never reads it.
`docker-compose.yml` — the deployment path — builds `Dockerfile-prd`, because a deployment is
the one place fabricated participants must never appear; `PSD_DOCKERFILE=Dockerfile` flips it
back for a rehearsal. Neither choice is irreversible: `PSD_SEED` is still an environment
variable, so either image can be run as the other tier, and the demo tier still refuses to
apply itself to a database that already has participants in it (ADR-102).

### Two build files is a drift hazard, so drift is now a build failure

The obvious objection to a second Dockerfile is that nobody will remember it. Someone bumps the
base image, adds a `COPY`, or fixes a build flag in one file, and the production image quietly
becomes a different artefact from the one that was tested — the failure arrives months later,
in the only environment that matters.

`check-standards.mjs` gained a `docker-twins` rule. It strips comments and blank lines from both
files and requires the remaining instructions to be identical except for exactly one line, the
`ENV PSD_SEED=` tier. A changed base image, a dropped `COPY`, or a production image that has
been handed the demo seed all fail `npm run standards`. All three were confirmed to fail before
the rule was accepted. The two files are therefore one image described twice, and the compiler
of that claim is the gate rather than somebody's memory.

### The audit found the image was already broken

Checking "is the Dockerfile up to date" turned up a defect that predates this work: **the image
could not be built at all.** Every workspace `tsconfig.json` extends `tsconfig.base.json`, the
builder stage never copied it, and Vite resolves `extends` during `vite build`. `docker build .`
died at the web build with `failed to resolve "extends":"../../tsconfig.base.json"`. It was
invisible in development because a developer's checkout always has the file.

There is no Docker in this sandbox, so the build context was reproduced by hand — the exact
`COPY` list, filtered through `.dockerignore` — and `npm ci && npm run build --workspace @psd/web`
run inside it. That reproduced the failure, and copying the one file fixed it. The runtime stage
was then driven the same way: `npm ci --omit=dev` (which `tsx` survives, being a production
dependency of `apps/api`), then the API booted from the pruned tree against a fresh PGlite
directory at each tier. `PSD_SEED=demo` logged `applied seed-demo.sql` and left **80
participants, 9 teams and 3 courts**; `PSD_SEED=default` left **0, 0 and 0**. That is the
deliverable, measured rather than asserted.

`.dockerignore` was stale in the same way and now excludes the dev-stack scripts (`/*.sh`, scoped
to the context root so `docker/app.sh` is still copied), `.dev/`, `test-results-full-event/`,
both build files, and `playwright*.config.ts` rather than only the one config that existed when
it was written. A comment in `docker-compose.yml` still referred to `snapshot.sql`, which has
been `schema.sql` since ADR-049.

### What is not covered

No image was actually built here, because there is no Docker daemon in the sandbox. The build
context, the install, the web build, the dev-dependency prune and both seed tiers were each
executed for real against the same file list the Dockerfile uses, but the `FROM`, `HEALTHCHECK`,
`VOLUME` and supervisord layers are unexercised and remain reviewed-only.

## ADR-176 — The passport bonus: a threshold, so it is derived

The day's published points table has a row the app could not compute: a completed passport —
four distinct fringe stations — is worth 20. Every other number on that table was already a
configuration field, because every other number is a *rate*: a price per match, per placing, per
turning up. The passport is not a rate. It is a count of how many different stations one person
reached, and nothing in the schema counted that.

Without it the choice on the day is to break a printed promise or to reconcile 250 paper
passports by hand in the forty minutes between the activities closing and the prize-giving,
with a closing speech in the middle of them. So it is built.

### Derived on read, for a sharper reason than the champion bonus

`fringe_passport_bonus_points` and `fringe_passport_stations` join the point config, and the
bonus is computed in the leaderboard's aggregate rather than written anywhere — the same shape
as ADR-136's champion bonus, but the argument is stronger here.

**A passport is a threshold, and a threshold can be crossed backwards.** Void one scan and a
participant who had four distinct stations has three; the 20 points have to vanish. Stored as a
row, they would not, and the compensating write would have to find every passport that void
invalidated — precisely the class of bug ADR-006 exists to make impossible. Derived, the next
read simply fails the `HAVING` and the bonus is gone. Unvoid it and the bonus returns, still
with nobody writing anything. Both directions are tested, because a bonus that only ever goes
up is not a passport.

The same property makes the config live: raise the threshold to five stations and every
four-station passport stops paying immediately. That is a consequence worth stating plainly
rather than hiding — it means the passport rule must be settled before the stamps start, since
changing it mid-afternoon silently re-prices everybody. The alternative, snapshotting the bonus
at the moment the fourth stamp landed, buys stability at the cost of the void behaviour above,
which is the wrong trade for a day with a correction desk.

`DISTINCT activity_id`, not a count of scans. Two rounds at the same station are two scans and
one stamp; a passport fillable by queueing at the same table four times is not a passport. That
is a test, not a comment.

### The bug the feature exposed

The profile card has always shown a line labelled **"Stations visited"** whose value was
`scanCount` — the number of scans. Those are different numbers the moment anybody is stamped
twice at one station, and nothing in the product cared about the difference until now, which is
exactly why it survived. The label now reads "Stamps collected", which is what the number is,
and the passport card beside it reports the distinct count that actually drives the bonus.

### What the participant sees

Nothing at all, when the bonus is zero — a day not running a passport must not show a row of
zeroes about one. Otherwise a single line that leads with what is still needed: "Passport: 2 of
4 stations. 2 more for 20 points." The ordering is deliberate. "2 of 4" is a status; "2 more for
20 points" is the sentence that moves somebody to the next table at four o'clock, and moving
people between stations is the entire reason the passport was invented.

### Verification

Eight API tests covering the forward case, the once-only case, stations-not-scans, the void
withdrawal, the unvoid restoration, progress reporting, the off switch, and a moved threshold.
Three web tests covering the unearned copy, the earned copy, and rendering nothing when off.
Playwright was not run — the browser CDN is unreachable from this sandbox.

---

## ADR-177 — The agenda: a segment, a nullable start, and no delete

The day has a run sheet — twelve rows from "before departure, have an early lunch" to "5.20pm
group photo" — and until now it lived only on a slide deck. The app could tell a participant the
score, the next fixture and who had won a sand sculpture, but not what time to be back at the
pavilion. That is the question most often asked out loud at an event, and the one the app was
silent on.

### It is a segment, not a seventh tab

The first framing was a seventh bottom-nav tab with its own motif. `docs/design/agenda-tab-plan.md`
§1 works the arithmetic out: at the 320 px floor, seven tabs give 45.7 px each, which fits five
characters at the nav's 8 px type. Six tabs was not a default, it was a decision — ADR-046 set the
count and ADR-125 fixed the naming to fit it — and a seventh costs either a rename, a raised
viewport floor, or an illegible font.

**Ruled: none of those. The agenda is the third segment of the Ball tab**, `/feed/agenda`, beside
Results and Line-ups. Three segments at 320 px is ~96 px each against a widest label of 72 px, so
it fits with room left and nothing was renamed. The deeper reason is traffic: a tab is for a
surface checked constantly, and the agenda is checked a handful of times a day. It belongs next to
the other two things a player looks up between matches, not in permanent competition with them for
the thumb. The motif was built before the ruling and is kept — a clipboard run sheet whose third
row is gold — because the hall-screen scene (G4) will want it.

### `starts_at` is nullable, and that is the whole preamble problem solved

The real run sheet opens with a line that has no clock on it: have an early lunch, no food is
provided. Two cheap answers presented themselves. Give it a nominal midday start — but then the UI
renders a time the item does not have, which is a lie told in a 92 px column. Or add an
`is_preamble` boolean — but that states the same fact twice and lets the two halves disagree.

A null start *is* "no fixed time". It sorts first, it renders as an em dash, and it is never *now*
and never *next*. One nullable column replaced a flag, a fake timestamp, and a day-level notes
field that §5.2 of the plan had talked itself into needing.

### Now and next are derived, and that is what makes three hundred phones agree

No `is_current` column, no cron. `GET /api/agenda` computes both against the server's clock on
every read, the ADR-006 lineage the champion bonus and the passport already follow. A stored flag
would be correct only at the instant it was written; derived, every phone in the field gets the
same answer because they are all asking the same clock.

Three rules fell out of writing the tests, each of which could have gone the other way:

1. **A cancelled item is never now or next.** It is still *listed* — see below — but it does not
   get to be the thing the page tells you is happening.
2. **A timeless item is never now or next.** It has no window to contain anything.
3. **An item with no end is a moment, not a block.** "1.45pm meet at the pavilion" is never "now";
   it is "next", and then it is past. The tempting alternative — treat a null end as running until
   the following item starts — would have made the fifteen-minute gap after the muster part of the
   muster. The gap after a moment is not part of it.

### There is no DELETE, and the first version was wrong about that

A `DELETE /api/admin/agenda/:itemId` was built, on an argument that reads well: *cancelled* and
*never happened* are different acts, and an item typed in by mistake should be able to vanish
rather than sit on three hundred screens struck through forever.

`npm run standards` rejected it. The `no-hard-delete` rule is absolute here — rows are invalidated,
never removed — and it caught two things at once, since the shared `setActive(db, id, isActive)`
helper behind the activate/deactivate pair also tripped `flag-parameter`. Both were honoured rather
than suppressed: the route and the entity function were deleted, and `activateAgendaItem` and
`deactivateAgendaItem` now each carry their own update.

On reflection the rule is right and the argument was not. An item added in error can be edited into
the item it should have been, or left cancelled and ignored; neither case is worth a second way for
a row to leave the database. What remains is the behaviour that actually matters: **a cancelled
item stays on the participant's page, struck through and badged CANCELLED.** Somebody who memorised
a 3pm item has to *learn that it is off*, not find it silently missing and conclude they misread
the programme. The badge is grey, not red — it is off, not an error.

### A guest read

`GET /api/agenda` sits in `mountGuestReads`, unlike every other participant feed. The run sheet is
on a poster by the registration tent; somebody checking what time to turn up may not have signed in
yet, and making them do so to read a public timetable is a login wall in front of a noticeboard.
The writes are superadmin-only, which is where the actual asymmetry is.

### Two smaller things

**An omitted optional field clears it.** The edit form can empty the location box, and it means
what it shows. The alternative — omission means "leave alone" — makes an empty box unclearable
without a sentinel.

**The admin form takes `HH:MM` and supplies the date.** The person typing a run sheet thinks in
"2.30pm", and a one-day event should not make them pick the same date twelve times. The form
attaches the day of the earliest existing item, falling back to today.

### Verification

Eight API tests: timeless sorts first and never wins now/next; the window containing now plus the
one after; a moment is never now; a cancelled item stays listed but drops out of now/next; 400 on
an end without a start and on an end before its start; an edited-away field clears; the guest read
works unauthenticated; a participant writing the programme gets 403. Six web tests: the single NOW
badge, the cancelled row surviving on the page, the timeless row without an invented clock, a
moment as one time not a range, the empty state, and all three segments present. The twelve real
rows are in the demo seed, anchored to the demo's own today so a walkthrough on any date sees a
live now and next.

## ADR-178 — The app must not need DDL rights to boot

A deployment to a managed Postgres crash-looped. Every ten seconds: `[api] failed to start
error: permission denied for schema public`, exit 1, supervisord respawns, repeat. The tunnel was
healthy and faithfully proxying to `127.0.0.1:8787`, where nothing was listening, so the symptom
reported by the person deploying was "the build succeeds but I cannot see the app".

Supervisord made it worse by being reassuring: `startsecs` is 5 and the process died at ~10, so
every cycle logged `success: app entered RUNNING state` before the crash. A container that is
entirely dead reported a steady stream of successes.

### The cause is a PostgreSQL 15 default, not a bug here

Since PG15 the `public` schema no longer grants `CREATE` to `PUBLIC`. It is owned by
`pg_database_owner` and its ACL leaves every other role with `USAGE` alone. Managed providers
hand out exactly such a role. ADR-049 has the app provision itself from `schema.sql` on boot, and
that silently assumed a role allowed to run DDL — true of the bundled Postgres container, where
the app owns its database, and of PGlite, where there is one superuser role and no one else.

### The part that makes it interesting

The obvious fix is to build the schema from somewhere holding an admin credential. That does not
work on its own, and the reason is worth knowing: **Postgres checks the privilege before it checks
`IF NOT EXISTS`.** Measured, not assumed:

```
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS foo (...)           -- table exists  -> permission denied for schema public
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_foo ON foo(a)    -- index exists  -> must be owner of table foo
ALTER TABLE foo ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS a int -- column exists -> must be owner of table foo
```

So re-applying a fully-applied snapshot fails exactly as hard as applying it to an empty
database. Without a second change, an operator would provision the database perfectly, redeploy,
and watch the identical crash loop. The whole premise of ADR-049's unconditional re-apply is that
re-applying is free; against a read-only role it is not free, it is fatal.

### What was built

**`ensureSchema` now asks before it builds.** If the role holds CREATE on `public`, behaviour is
byte-for-byte what it was — apply unconditionally, report `provisioned` / `repaired` /
`unchanged`. If it does not, the snapshot is *verified* rather than applied: a complete schema
returns the new `verified` outcome and the app boots; an incomplete one throws with the role, the
database, the count of missing tables and both remedies spelled out in pasteable SQL.

This is the one place ADR-049's contract is deliberately not honoured, and it is honoured
wherever it *can* be. The cost is real and is stated in the code rather than discovered later:
completeness counts TABLES, so a managed database missing a COLUMN added by a later snapshot
passes the check and fails at the query that wants it. The self-repairing idempotent ALTERs in
the snapshot's tail cannot run without DDL rights. The remedy — re-run the provisioner — is named
in the error rather than left to be deduced at the wrong moment.

**`./db-provision.sh`** builds a database this machine can reach and the app cannot. It takes the
connection string positionally, or reads it from a hidden prompt when given none, because a
credential passed as an argument lands in shell history and the process list. It prints
`user@host/database` and never the password. `--inspect` reports privileges and writes nothing,
which answers "will the app boot against this?" before a deploy rather than after.

**`--grant-to <role>`** is the half that is easy to miss. Tables built by an admin are owned by
that admin, so the runtime role needs privileges on them or the next error is `permission denied
for table cluster` — the same outage wearing a different hat. It also sets `ALTER DEFAULT
PRIVILEGES`, because `GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES` covers the tables standing at that instant and the
snapshot grows: `agenda_item` was added the same week as this ADR, and without default privileges
it would have been invisible to the app.

### Smaller things the outage exposed

`explainFailure` unwraps `.cause`. Drizzle replaces a driver error's message with the entire
failed query, so a refused connection or a rejected password arrives as forty lines of
`select current_user…` with the actual reason nested out of sight. `bootstrap.ts` already carried
a complaint about an error naming "neither the cause nor the remedy"; this was another one.

Role names are validated against a conservative pattern before being concatenated into `GRANT`.
An identifier cannot be a bind parameter, so the only options are proving it safe or trusting it,
and a provisioning tool that takes a role name from argv should not trust it.

### The rotating admin, which the first version of this got wrong

The platform that prompted this does not hand out a permanent admin credential. It pre-populates
a constrained string for the app and issues a **temporary, unconstrained one per maintenance
window** — `jit_107262_202610060742`, with the minting timestamp in the role name. So the admin
is a different role every time.

That breaks `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES`, which attaches to the role that ran it. Measured:

```
jit_a: CREATE TABLE made_by_a; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES ... GRANT SELECT TO approle
jit_b: CREATE TABLE made_by_b
    -> approle SELECT on made_by_a: true
    -> approle SELECT on made_by_b: FALSE
```

The first version of this ADR leaned on default privileges as the thing that would keep a growing
schema reachable. Against a rotating admin they are a bonus within one tenure and nothing more.
What carries the day is the explicit `GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES`, **re-run on every provisioning
run** — so `--grant-to` is not an optional extra, it is part of the procedure.

Relying on an operator to remember that is not a design, so the tool proves it instead.
`verifyRuntimeAccess` asks `has_table_privilege` for the *app's* role, table by table, from the
admin session — no password and no `SET ROLE` membership required — and the run exits non-zero if
a single table is out of reach. The failure mode it catches is a provisioning run that looks
completely clean and leaves the app crashing on one table it cannot read.

`--grant-to` also accepts the app's whole connection string and takes only the username from it.
Nobody has memorised `jit_107262_202610060742`; making them retype it out of a string the platform
generated is how a GRANT lands on a role that does not exist and reports success.

### The login name is not the role — confirmed against the real platform

The first `--inspect` run against the live managed database returned:

```
role prod_role_ddl on databricks_postgres (PostgreSQL 17.11; public owned by pg_database_owner;
holds USAGE+CREATE)
```

The connection string's username was `jit_107262_202610060742`. The *role* is `prod_role_ddl`.
The platform authenticates a rotating, timestamped login and maps it onto a stable role.

That vindicates asking the database rather than parsing the URL — `inspectDatabase` reports what
we got, not what we dialled, and the two genuinely differ here. It also softens the previous
section: because the effective role is stable, `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` set by `prod_role_ddl`
*does* survive a credential rotation. Re-running `--grant-to` every time remains the advice, on
the grounds that it costs nothing and does not depend on a mapping nobody here controls.

But it introduces a trap in the other direction. `--grant-to` takes the username out of the
app's connection string, and that username may likewise not be the app's role — in which case
the GRANT names a role that does not exist, which Postgres reports as an error only if you look,
and which leaves the app exactly as broken as before. So a report of "no such role" now lists the
login roles that *do* exist and points at the way to settle it: inspect using the app's own
connection string and read `current_user` off the result.

### When nobody can read the app's connection string either

The platform injects `DATABASE_URL` into the container as a hidden variable. So the advice that
closed the previous section — inspect with the app's own string and read `current_user` — is not
advice the operator can act on. They cannot see the string at all.

The database is the witness instead. Three ways, in descending order of certainty:

1. **`pg_stat_activity`.** A crash-looping app reconnects every few seconds, so its role appears
   as a live backend and is *observed* rather than guessed. `usename` is visible to ordinary
   roles even though other sessions' queries are not, so this needs no special privilege.
2. **The login-role list.** Where the survey finds exactly one role that is not the admin, it
   says so: on a dedicated managed database that is almost always the answer.
3. **The app itself.** `index.ts` now logs `[api] database: role … on … (holds …)` on every boot.
   It is the one party that can read the hidden variable, so it reports what it found. No
   credential is involved — this is `current_user`, asked of the database.

`--inspect` runs the survey automatically when no `--grant-to` was given, because an operator
inspecting a database they cannot otherwise identify is exactly the person who needs it.

And a documented last resort: **`--grant-to PUBLIC`**. It grants to every role in the database,
present and future, which on a single-tenant managed database is a defensible way to stop
guessing. It needed real support rather than falling out for free: `PUBLIC` is a keyword, not an
identifier, so quoting it the way every other role name is quoted would produce a GRANT to a
literal role named `"PUBLIC"` that does not exist. It verifies like any other grantee, because
`has_table_privilege` resolves the pseudo-role and every role inherits what it holds.

### Two things the first real deployment attempt taught

**A grant over an empty database is not a pass.** Granting PUBLIC before the schema existed
covered nothing — `GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES` applies to the tables standing at that moment — and
the verification reported `PUBLIC can read and write all 0 tables. The app will boot.` Perfectly
true and completely wrong. Zero tables is now its own message, and `--inspect` reports schema
completeness (`schema: 0 of 33 tables present — NOT fully provisioned`) as a separate line from
the privilege verdict, because the two failures look nothing alike and have different remedies.

**The stack trace is the deployment's version number.** The crash-looping container reported
`ensureSchema (bootstrap.ts:92)` and `main (index.ts:60)`, which were exactly the pre-ADR-178
line numbers for `await handle.runSql(schemaSql)` and `await ensureSchema(handle)`; in the new
code those statements are at 141 and 70. So the image predated the fix, and no amount of granting
was going to help. The `[api] database: role … on …` line now logged before the schema is touched
is the positive signal for the same question — if it is absent, the running image is old.

### Verification

Twenty-eight tests, all against PGlite — which is a real PostgreSQL, so `CREATE ROLE` and `SET ROLE`
reproduce the entire failure in process rather than mocking it. They cover both privilege states,
the verified boot, the refusal naming the remedy, the grant working for tables created *after*
it, the injection refusal, redaction of a password out of a connection string, the strict
argument parser, and a test asserting that Postgres really does refuse `CREATE TABLE IF NOT
EXISTS` on an existing table — pinned so that if that ever changes, this design can be revisited
deliberately instead of by accident. And one that creates two separate admin roles to reproduce
the rotating-credential trap end to end, then shows the re-run closing it.

## ADR-179 — A photo owns its backdrop's style, not just its colour

ADR-173 built the sunburst against the studio's drawn-character branch, and the photo branch was
never revisited. The renderer was always ready for both — `avatarPreviewLayers` has an explicit
`paintSpriteSunburst` path for a photo sprite, lifting the backdrop onto its own rotating layer
exactly as it does for a drawn face. Only the control was missing.

The result was a trap with no way out of it. `sunburst` lives on the end of `avatarLook`, so it
survives putting a photograph on; the rays therefore kept rendering behind the photo, while the
one control that could change or remove them had vanished with the branch. A participant who
chose a spiral as a drawn character and then wore a photo was stuck with it.

`BackdropStyleRow` now sits directly under the backdrop palette in the photo branch, which is
where ADR-054's reasoning already pointed:

> The backdrop is the exception, and it is offered. Once the cut-out model has taken the real
> background away there is a genuine backdrop behind the person […] so it is a colour the
> participant really does own.

If they own the colour, they own what is done with it. The alternative — clearing `sunburst` when
a photo goes on — was rejected because it silently discards something the participant chose, and
because it would have to be undone again the moment the photo came off.

Unlike the colour, the style needs no sprite repaint. A backdrop colour is baked into the sprite's
own palette, which is why `setBackdrop` exists and has to move the look and the photo together in
one `onChange`. The rays are composed from `look.sunburst` at render time instead, so the ordinary
`setLook` is both sufficient and correct here — reaching for `setBackdrop` would have been the
easy mistake.

Pinned by a test that wears a photo *and* a sunburst at once, asserts the control opens showing
what is actually worn rather than a default, and then takes the spiral off and checks the saved
look is the plain one. It fails on the previous build with `Unable to find an element by:
[data-testid="avatar-studio__backdrop-style"]` — the stuck state exactly.

## ADR-180 — A verified boot proves more than it says

The managed deployment came up:

```
[api] database: role prod_app on databricks_postgres (PostgreSQL 17.11 (fcae950);
  public owned by pg_database_owner; holds USAGE)
[api] schema verified (this role cannot run DDL; provisioned elsewhere)
[api] listening on http://0.0.0.0:8787 (driver: postgres)
```

`holds USAGE` reads like a warning and is not one. USAGE is the whole of what the app needs:
ADR-178 moved CREATE to a separate, temporary credential precisely so the runtime role would
never hold it. `holds USAGE` without `+CREATE` is the designed end state, not a shortfall.

The second line turns out to carry a guarantee nobody designed. `tablesMissingFrom` reads
`information_schema.tables`, and PostgreSQL filters that view by privilege — a role sees only
the tables it holds *some* privilege on. Measured here: a role granted `SELECT` on one of two
tables sees exactly one in `information_schema.tables` and both in `pg_catalog.pg_tables`; a role
with schema USAGE and no table grants at all sees nothing.

So `schema verified` on a DDL-less role is not a catalogue count. It is proof that the runtime
role holds a privilege on every one of the tables the snapshot defines — which is exactly the
question `--grant-to` exists to answer, answered for free at boot. Had the earlier `GRANT … TO
PUBLIC` landed on an empty database and covered nothing, this check would have reported every
table missing and refused the boot, rather than serving a site that fails on first query.

That makes the choice of catalogue load-bearing and entirely accidental. `pg_catalog.pg_tables`
is the unfiltered equivalent and the obvious swap for anyone who notices information_schema is
the slower of the two; making it would convert a refused boot into a server that answers every
request with `permission denied for table …`. Both the source and a test now say so.

What is still NOT proved, and still needs `--grant-to` to establish:

- **Which** privileges. "Some privilege" is not SELECT+INSERT+UPDATE+DELETE — a table carrying
  only SELECT appears here exactly like a fully granted one.
- **Columns.** ADR-178's limitation is unchanged: completeness counts tables, so a database built
  from an older snapshot passes and fails later at the query wanting the new column.
- **Sequences.** Nothing in this view covers them, and an INSERT into a table whose sequence is
  ungranted fails on the default.

## ADR-181 — The spiral stands still, and is chosen by a square

Two changes to the sunburst, both asked for after seeing it running.

**The preview no longer turns.** ADR-173 split the studio preview into a backdrop layer that
rotated under a face layer that did not, so the rays could spin without the face spinning with
them. It glitched — two separately encoded SVGs, the rays drawn at 150% and `crisp-edges`
pixelated, both re-rasterised on every keystroke — and the decision was to delete the mechanism
rather than tune it.

That was the right trade twice over. The spin was never in the product: the saved avatar is one
still picture everywhere it is ever shown, so the animated preview was the only place a
participant saw something they could not keep. `avatarSvg` already paints the sunburst into the
finished image for both drawn characters and photo sprites, and `avatarUrl` memoises it, so the
preview is now literally the image that gets saved — the strongest guarantee a preview can offer,
and it arrived by removing code. Gone with it: `avatarPreviewLayers`, `AvatarPreviewLayers`,
`onlyKeys`, `exceptKeys`, `maskedPalette`, `svgUrl`, `DRAWN_BACKDROP_PAINT`, the
`.gb-avatar--spun` / `.gb-avatar__rays` / `.gb-avatar__face` rules, `@keyframes gb-avatar-spin`,
and the `prefers-reduced-motion` exception that existed solely to park it. Nothing moves, so
nothing needs stopping.

The tests moved with it. `avatar-studio__preview-rays` was how a test asked "is the sunburst on?",
and with the rays no longer their own element the answer would otherwise require decoding a data
URL. `data-sunburst="on|off"` on the preview image replaces it.

**The dropdown became a square.** A two-option `select` of "Plain colour" / "Sunburst" is a worse
control than a toggle in every respect that matters: it costs a tap to discover what the options
are, it cannot show what either looks like, and it reads as a separate setting rather than as
something done TO the colour above it. It is now one `aria-pressed` swatch sitting at the end of
the backdrop palette, wearing the backdrop colour with the rays drawn over it in a
`repeating-conic-gradient` — the square shows the effect it turns on. Pressing it reveals the
second colour, the rays slider and the twist slider; pressing it again puts them away.

`backdrop` is the last entry in `AVATAR_COLOUR_AXES`, so the square lands directly after the
palette in the drawn branch as well as the photo one, with no reordering.

## ADR-182 — The worker still waits, but now it says so

ADR-147's worker deliberately does not call `skipWaiting()`:

> Swapping code under a running page yields a half-old app the moment anything is lazily loaded,
> and a facilitator mid-scan is the worst possible moment to find out.

That stands. What it cost was discoverability, and the bill arrived in the form of a debugging
round: a new build sits in `waiting` until every tab is closed, nothing says so, and a hard
refresh does not help — the waiting worker keeps waiting while any client is still controlled.
The symptom is indistinguishable from a deployment that never happened, which this project has
now misdiagnosed more than once.

So the wait stays and becomes visible. The page polls for a held-back worker, shows one line and
a Reload button, and only that press sends the worker a message telling it to stand down. The
unsafe thing about `skipWaiting()` was never the call; it was calling it without asking. This is
the only path to it in the app, it runs from a human's press, and the page reloads immediately
afterwards, so there is no running session for the new code to appear underneath.

Two details worth keeping:

- **`waiting` alone does not mean "update".** It is also set while the first worker a device ever
  installs finishes up. Without a live `controller` there is nothing the new worker could be newer
  *than*, and greeting a first-time facilitator with "a new version is ready" would be both wrong
  and alarming. Both conditions are required; a test pins it.
- **The reload is unconditional.** Two tabs share one worker, so whichever presses Reload first
  activates it and the second finds nothing to message. Waiting on a `controllerchange` that will
  never arrive would hang that tab on "Reloading…" forever.

`navigator.serviceWorker` does not exist in jsdom, so every function here takes its container as
an argument and the component accepts one as a prop. That is the only reason any of it has tests.

## ADR-183 — Alerts stack downwards; the queue hid the newest news

ADR-074 showed one announcement at a time, and ADR-133 had the up-soon call yield entirely to
any undismissed announcement. Both were defended by the same sentence — a 320 px screen covered
in stacked full-bleed banners hides the app they are about — and that worry was real. The remedy
was not.

What it actually produced: `AnnouncementToast` rendered `announcements[0]`, the OLDEST
undismissed message. So the newest thing the organisers had said was the thing a participant
could not see, behind something they had already chosen not to dismiss. A notification surface
whose failure mode is hiding the most recent notification has inverted its own purpose. And
because `.gb-announce` was `position: absolute; top: 0` on every instance, anything that did
slip through the queue painted exactly on top of its neighbour rather than beside it.

Alerts now stack. `.gb-announce-stack` owns the positioning that used to sit on each banner —
full-bleed, absolute against the viewport-locked shell, above every other layer — and each alert
inside it is an ordinary block, so they lay out downwards in DOM order. Oldest first, newest
nearest the content, every one of them reachable.

ADR-074's objection is honoured rather than overruled: the COLUMN is capped at 70% of the frame
and scrolls, with `overscroll-behavior: contain` so a flick inside it does not scroll the page
underneath once it reaches the end. The stack can never swallow the screen — which is what was
being prevented — without the queue that meant only one could ever be read.

**The up-soon call leads the column.** It is the only alert here with a deadline: it says walk to
your court now, and it expires by itself whether or not anybody read it. An announcement is
read-and-dismiss and keeps indefinitely, so it can afford to wait a row. Pinning it to the top
rather than giving it its place in arrival order is the one deliberate exception to the ordering,
and it is the opposite of what it used to do — yield completely to anything older.

Every banner after the first wears its own top border. Without it, two gold announcements stacked
together read as a single tall block with one garland, and the number of separate things the
organisers have said stops being countable at a glance.

## ADR-184 — `facingMode` is a suggestion, so give people a switch

Three surfaces open a camera: the fringe station and swag station scanners ask for
`facingMode: 'environment'`, the selfie viewfinder asks for `'user'`. Both were written as if
that settled it. It does not.

A bare constraint value is an **ideal**, not a requirement. Only `min`, `max` and `exact` are
mandatory; everything else the browser treats as a preference with gravity, and it is never
obliged to honour it or to say that it didn't. So `getUserMedia({ video: { facingMode:
'environment' } })` can return the front camera and resolve successfully. There is no error, no
warning, and nothing in the promise to check — just a marshal looking at their own face.

This is not theoretical. Many webcam drivers do not expose `facingMode` as a constrainable
capability at all, which is common on Windows 2-in-1s: Chromium cannot resolve the hint to a
device and returns the same lens whatever is asked for. The usual library workaround — catch
`OverconstrainedError` and retry with the other direction — never fires, because an ideal
constraint does not throw.

**`{ exact: 'environment' }` is not the fix.** It makes the constraint mandatory, and then it
rejects outright on every laptop and desktop with only one camera, turning a working-but-wrong
viewfinder into no viewfinder at all. The facing hint stays a hint.

The fix is to stop guessing and ask the stream. On every successful open, the track's
`getSettings().deviceId` says which lens actually opened — the one identifier that cannot be
wrong about itself. That is recorded, `enumerateDevices` supplies the rest, and a **Switch
camera** button cycles them with `deviceId: { exact }`, which is mandatory on purpose: if the
remembered camera has gone, that must fail loudly enough to catch rather than silently opening
something else.

**Always visible, not revealed on failure.** There is no failure to reveal it from. The whole
problem is that the browser reports success, so the control has to already be on screen for
someone who can see that it is wrong. It hides only when the device genuinely has one camera.

**Remembered per surface**, in two keys. The scanner wants the back lens and the selfie camera
wants the front, so one shared preference would be wrong for one of them by construction. A
remembered id can go stale in entirely ordinary ways — a borrowed phone, an unplugged webcam, a
browser that rotated its ids after a permission reset — so a failed open forgets the preference
and falls back to the hint rather than leaving a marshal with a dark screen and a queue.

Two things turned up while wiring it, and both are real rather than test artefacts.
`getVideoTracks`, `getSettings` and `deviceId` are each absent from some combination of browser
and stream, and `enumerateDevices` is not universally present either; every one of them is
guarded, and "this browser will not say" resolves to null rather than to a guess that would be
persisted and then demanded. Switching restarts the stream rather than calling
`applyConstraints`, which is patchily supported and fails in precisely the drivers that make
this necessary.

## ADR-185 — an SSE carve-out that is a shape, not a list

`compress()` buffers, and a buffered event stream is a stream that does not arrive. ADR-046
answered that with `UNCOMPRESSED_EXACT`, a hand-kept list naming `/api/chat/stream` and
`/api/status/stream`.

Team chat then shipped its own SSE endpoint at `/api/team-chat/stream`, and nobody added it. For
the whole life of that feature its frames have been going into the gzip buffer instead of to the
phone — the exact failure the carve-out exists to prevent, reintroduced by the carve-out being a
list that a new stream can be added without touching.

So the rule is now a pattern over the shape every SSE route in this codebase already follows:
`/stream` at the end of its own group. A pattern cannot be forgotten by the next stream, and the
test asserts the shape rather than the membership, so it keeps holding as routes are added. The
same class of miss as `publishChatHidden` — a rule applied to the room it was written for and
not to the room added afterwards — and closed the same way.

## ADR-186 — an agenda time is a date and a time

The programme editor held `HH:MM` strings from `<input type="time">` and grafted them onto a day
it INFERRED: the earliest item already on the programme, falling back to `new Date()`.

That fallback is why times did not stick. On an empty programme the first item was dated today;
edit it tomorrow and the same clock reading was re-grafted onto tomorrow, so the entire run sheet
walked forward with the calendar. Nothing ever looked wrong on screen, which is what made it hard
to see — the TIME was right every time, and the date underneath it had moved.

The original reasoning is in the record and was not unreasonable: the person typing a one-day
programme thinks in "2.30pm", and making them pick a date twelve times is a worse form. But the
thing it bought that convenience with was a GUESS about which day the user meant, and a guess
that silently rewrites saved data is not a convenience. Start and end are `datetime-local` now
and there is nothing left to infer.

## ADR-187 — a spent reconnect budget backs off; it does not surrender

The status stream allowed three quick reconnects after a hard close and then stayed shut for the
rest of the session, leaving the client on its fallback poll. The reasoning was sound as far as it
went: a 502 during a reboot fixes itself and is worth retrying, a 401 from an expired session
never does and retrying it fast is a loop.

What the reasoning missed is what the fallback costs. That poll runs on a jittered 45–75s
interval, so a phone that has given up on the socket is making requests at the SAME RATE it would
have been anyway. The surrender bought no saving whatsoever, and charged for it in latency: every
announcement arriving up to a minute late, for the rest of the afternoon, for anyone whose first
three attempts happened to fail. Three failures at start-up is not exotic — a tunnel that buffers
the opening bytes, or a proxy mid-restart, will do it — and nothing existed that could bring the
stream back afterwards.

The budget now governs the PACE of retrying rather than whether to retry. Past it, revival slows
to the poll's own window. The 401 loop it was written to prevent is unchanged in cost, because
the poll was already making exactly that request, and the session layer still owns signing out.

## ADR-188 — a swag station is editable, name included

The `PUT /:stationId/items` route had been implemented and no UI ever called it, so in practice a
station was immutable from the moment it was created. There was no rename route at all, which
meant a name typed with a typo at eight in the morning was permanent for the day and the only
remedy was a second station standing beside the wrong one.

Screen keys refuse renaming, and that precedent was worth testing against rather than assuming.
It does not transfer: a screen key is a VALUE other configuration points at, so renaming it
breaks the thing holding the reference. A station name is a LABEL on a table that people read.
Nothing points at it except the unique index on `lower(station_name)`, which answers a collision
with the same 409 that creating a duplicate already gets.

One `PUT /:stationId` saves name and items together, and the list's Edit button loads a station
into the existing create form rather than growing a second copy of the same fields inline.

## ADR-189 — the demo fixture's clock

Two defects in one file, both of which made the demo look wrong in ways that had nothing to do
with the app.

`scripts/seed-demo.mjs` drives the real HTTP API, deliberately (ADR-040): every row it makes is
reachable by a human doing the same clicks. The API stamps `created_at` with `now()`, correctly,
and the script posts a hundred and twenty messages in a tight loop — so every message in a room
shared one instant and the demo rendered eighty people speaking simultaneously.

The seeding script cannot fix this without writing behind the API's back, which is the one thing
it exists not to do. So the spread lives in the EXPORT, the step that turns a live database into
a frozen fixture, because the silences between messages are a property of the fixture and of
nothing else. Order is preserved exactly; only the gaps are invented, from a seeded LCG so that
re-exporting the same database twice gives the same file.

Separately, `atClock` built the programme with `setHours`, which reads the clock of whatever
machine ran the seed. Exported from a UTC box, "12:50" became 12:50Z — twenty to nine at night in
Singapore. Anchored to a fixed +8, which the event has no DST to complicate.

`seed-demo.sql` was re-timed in place rather than regenerated. A full re-export rewrites all 11MB
of sprite blobs and every uuid in the file for a change that touches two columns, and the result
was verified by applying it to a scratch database.

## ADR-190 — hand-ordering, confined to the items with no clock

ADR-177 derived agenda order from `(starts_at, created_at)` and said no `display_order` column, on
purpose: an order that can disagree with the clock is a second source of truth, and the one it
disagrees with is the one the participant is standing in.

That argument is still right about everything with a clock. It says nothing at all about the items
WITHOUT one — the timeless preamble rows — which were therefore stuck in the order they happened
to be typed, with no way to change it short of recreating them.

So the column exists and the sort consults it BETWEEN the two existing terms. Anything with a
`starts_at` has already been placed by the first term and never reaches it, which is what confines
hand-ordering to the rows where there is no clock to contradict. Asking to move a timed item is a
400 rather than a silent rewrite of its time: the form already has a better input for that, and a
surprise edit to the programme is worse than a refusal. Every timeless item is renumbered densely
on each move, so a NULL arrival or a gap from an earlier edit cannot accumulate.

## ADR-191 — courts as processors, fixtures as a queue

The programme requires the knockout to be DECIDED by 4.30pm, and until now the only way to know
whether it would be was to watch the line-ups tab and feel anxious. This answers it.

The model is the simple one and is meant to be: each court is a server holding one match at a
time, each fixture still needing a court is a job, and a job starts when a court frees up AND its
feeders are settled. No cleverness about which court — the queue takes whichever frees first,
which is what the marshals do.

The feeder dependency is why this is simulated rather than divided by the number of courts. A
semi-final cannot start until both quarters feeding it are done, so opening a fourth court stops
helping at exactly the point the bracket narrows. Those rows are flagged, because the remedy for
them is not another court and a list of start times alone would not say so.

It is a FORECAST, so it carries its input in the open: one number drives everything, it is
measured from matches actually played today rather than typed into a config screen in March, and
the page says when it has no history yet and is assuming. A projection whose assumption is hidden
gets believed for longer than it deserves.

A friendly — a match the marshals started that no fixture claimed — appears in its lane too. It
occupies the court whether or not the schedule knows about it, and a lane showing nothing while
two teams are visibly playing there is worse than no lane at all.

Read-only, deliberately. The schedule still decides what is played next; a second place to decide
it would be a second source of truth sitting next to a marshal with a whistle. What was missing
was not control but sight.

### ADR-192 — Two things nobody could see: a socket and a swallowed rejection

Both halves of this round are the same mistake in different clothes. Something was failing in
plain sight, and the only reason it stayed a mystery is that nothing drew it.

**The stream indicator.** ADR-187 chased a late announcement and ended by fixing a real defect —
`QUICK_REVIVALS = 3` meant the client gave up reconnecting permanently — without ever
establishing that this was *the* cause. It could not be established, because an announcement
that arrives a minute late and an announcement that was *sent* a minute late produce the same
complaint from the same person on the same beach. The thing that separates them is whether the
socket was carrying at that moment, and the client has known that all along: `useAlertsStore`
computes `isLive` and uses it to decide whether the fallback poll runs. It simply never told
anybody. `isLive` is now on the `AlertsStore` and `StreamHealth` renders it.

Drawn as an **absence**, not a presence. A healthy socket renders no element at all, so the
normal case costs nothing and the indicator cannot decay into wallpaper the way a permanent
green dot would. It appears only after `STREAM_GRACE_MS` (10 s) of disconnection — longer than
any healthy connect, so it never flashes during the ordinary mount-then-connect of a page load,
and far shorter than the 45–75 s fallback poll, so it is up for the whole window in which the
participant is genuinely looking at stale data. The wording is "Reconnecting — updates may be up
to a minute behind" rather than anything shorter, because "Reconnecting" alone reads as *broken*
and sends people to a marshal who can do nothing; the feed **is** still updating, just by poll.

Placed in the participant shell and nowhere else, because that is where the symptom was. A
superadmin session is `viewer: 'staff'` and opens no status stream at all, so an indicator on the
console would have had nothing to report.

**The flake was never timing.** The station-pages flake had outlived several rounds. It did not
reproduce: eight runs of the file alone and three full web-suite runs, all green. ADR-127 settled
what to do here — mitigating a flake you have not diagnosed buys a slower red build — so instead
of touching timeouts, the question became *why would a failure land on a test that did not cause
it*, and that has a precise answer.

`installFetchStub` throws on a route it does not recognise. It throws **inside an async
function**, so what actually escapes is a rejected promise, and a great deal of real client code
starts a request without awaiting it: a refresh on mount, a drain on a timer. Nothing catches
those. The rejection floats until the runner notices and is attributed to whichever test is on
screen at that moment. Run the file alone and it is fast enough that the miss lands inside the
test that made it, harmlessly swallowed; run it inside a loaded full suite on two cores and it
slides into a neighbour. **That is the entire mechanism, and it explains both the wandering and
the failure to reproduce in isolation.**

So the stub now *records* every miss as well as throwing, and `expectNoUnstubbedCalls` asserts
in `afterEach` that a test made none. Applied to station-pages it immediately named the cause:
`CourtPage` reads `GET /api/tournament/schedule` and `GET /api/tournament/courts/:id/recent-teams`
on mount and **neither was ever listed**, so both rejected on every render in the file. They are
now stubbed empty — which is exactly what the component already saw when the request failed, so
no assertion changes — and the file is clean.

**The finding is bigger than the file.** A one-off probe over the whole web suite counted **157
unstubbed requests across 16 routes**, led by `GET /api/status/screen` (40), `GET
/api/staff/participants` (21), `GET /api/admin/participants` (17) and `GET /api/me/alerts` (14).
Every one is a floating rejection able to fail an unrelated test. The named target is fixed and
the instrument now exists; the sweep across the remaining suites is deliberately left as its own
piece of work rather than folded in here, because each route needs a body shape checked against
its reader and a wrong one would trade a flake for a test that passes for the wrong reason.

**A friendly scores if you record it.** Noted while settling the exhibition-match question: the
leaderboard counts every `tournament_match` that is `completed` and not voided, with no join to
`tournament_fixture`. An exhibition opened on a court console and scored normally therefore pays
30 and 10 and shows up in standings ten minutes later. The ruling — the exhibition is a friendly —
is consequently an instruction to marshals, not something the app enforces. Recorded in the
assessment doc as an operational warning rather than built, because a non-scoring match flag was
not asked for.

### ADR-193 — A photoreal backdrop, built and left switched off

Asked for: look at how backdrops work, generate photoreal art for every element, implement a
high-resolution lifelike backdrop, **and do not wire it in**. The last clause is the interesting
one, and it shaped everything else.

**What the scene actually is.** Not a picture — fifteen layers over a 480x270 art space, every
one positioned in percentages so the whole thing scales to any width. Three contracts are
load-bearing and none of them are obvious from looking at the result:

- `.gb-scene__drift` (clouds, waves) sits in a 200%-wide box with `repeat-x` at `50% auto` and is
  translated by exactly one tile. The art **must** tile seamlessly or a vertical seam walks
  across the sky every cycle.
- `.gb-scene__foam` and every `.gb-scene__frame` layer are **two-frame sheets** stepped by
  `steps(2, jump-none)`: the box is one frame wide, the sheet is at 200%.
- Everything renders under `image-rendering: pixelated`.

A generative model satisfies none of these. It does not produce seamless tiles, and asking it for
a sprite sheet yields two unrelated pictures rather than one subject in two poses. So the renders
supply *subjects* and `generate-real-scene.mjs` supplies the *contract*: drift tiles are made
seamless by mirroring, so the join and the wrap are the same edge by construction; frame B is
**derived** from frame A by a small deterministic transform — the surf rolls half a tile, the
palms shear, the gull drops its wings — which also guarantees the pair belongs to one subject.

**Geometry is derived from the art, not inherited from it.** A photoreal cut-out does not have
the aspect ratio its hand-drawn counterpart had. Forcing the render into the old box would squash
or letterbox it, so each sprite declares one dimension and an anchor and the other dimension is
computed from the finished file's measured aspect. Palms and players anchor by their **feet**,
because the thing that must not move when proportions change is where they stand. The palms are
the one deliberate departure: the drawn version was a 58x38 crown tucked in a corner, the render
is a whole tree, so it is sized by height and stood on the sand as a foreground frame.

**The bug the preview caught.** ImageMagick resizes RGBA without premultiplying, so a *fully
transparent* pixel still contributes its colour when the image is scaled down. Key magenta,
shrink a palm from 1024px to 464px, and every gap between the leaflets averages green with the
magenta still sitting invisibly behind it: the frond comes back wearing a bright pink halo,
invisible at full size and unmissable in composite. `-alpha background` repaints the transparent
region in a colour taken from the subject — but **only where alpha is zero**, so the
partial-alpha ring around each frond kept its magenta and stayed pink. The fix that worked is a
green despill: `min(channel, green)` in red and blue, correct for foliage and therefore opt-in
rather than applied to the volleyball.

That bug is the argument for `renderPreview`. The scene is fifteen transparent layers that only
ever meet in a browser; without a flattened composite the only way to discover that a palm is
pink, or standing in the sea, is to wire it in — the one thing this change must not do. The
preview is `_preview.png`, gitignored and regenerated on demand.

**Why a second component and not a third branch.** `<BeachScene>` keeps drawing every
participant surface. `<RealBeachScene>` is identical in layer structure and differs in one
property: `gb-scene--real` sets `image-rendering: auto`. Pixelated is load-bearing at 480x270,
where a smoothed half-pixel is a visible smear; applied to 3840x2160 of photograph it aliases
every frond and cable into a sawtooth, because there is now real sub-pixel detail to throw away.
That is a property of the art, not of the layer, so the two scenes stay apart and neither can
quietly regress the other.

**Left switched off, on purpose.** `backdropChoice` does not know the word "real" and no route
imports the component. Turning it on is a third `BackdropChoice` and a branch in `<BeachScene>` —
a line each — and it is left undone because the art is a judgement call that should be made by
someone looking at it. Tests exist anyway, and they are the point of an unreferenced component:
they hold it to the same named layer set as the drawn scene, so the day it is switched on, it
switches on working.

**Honest costs.** 14 MB of assets against roughly 20 kB for the drawn scene, and the panorama is
JPEG precisely because 3840x2160 of photoreal PNG is 11 MB of alpha channel nobody reads. Nothing
ships it today; if it is ever adopted it wants responsive sizes and almost certainly WebP, and
that is a second piece of work, not a footnote to this one.

### ADR-194 — The net goes in front of some players and behind others

ADR-193 built the photoreal set and left it switched off. This finishes it: the four players
exist, they are Singaporean, and the volleyball net is no longer part of the backdrop.

**The problem, stated exactly.** The net was painted into the panorama. The panorama is the
bottom layer. Therefore every player was in front of the net — including the two standing on the
far side of the court, who should be behind it. No amount of better art fixes that, because it
is not an art problem: a sprite that must be both in front of and behind moving things cannot
live in the backdrop. It has to be its own layer, with the movers split either side of it.

**The scene already knew this.** `portal` is a clump of foliage whose entire purpose is to sit in
front of the Sentosa Express so the train disappears behind it instead of blinking out at the
edge of its travel. That is the same device, and it had been sitting in the codebase as a
one-off. The net generalises it: an occluder is not decoration, it is the only way a flat stack
of layers acquires a front and a back. So there is now a `PLACED` category — single-frame
sprites positioned rather than animated — and the draw order carries three load-bearing
adjacencies: **far players before the net, the net before near players, and the palms last of
all**, because the palms are the closest thing in frame and must crop everything, players
included.

**Occlusion alone is not depth.** Two figures of the same height either side of a net read as a
sticker sheet. The far pair are 25–27 art units tall with their feet higher up the sand; the near
pair are 42–44 with their feet near the bottom of the frame. The size difference is doing as much
work as the layering, and the geometry module now carries a `depth` on each player so the
generator can emit `REAL_PLAYERS_FAR` and `REAL_PLAYERS_NEAR` as separate lists — the component
never decides depth, it just draws two lists with the net between them.

**Two tests exist purely to stop this being flattened again.** One walks the rendered children
and asserts the far players' indices are below the net's and the near players' above it. The
other asserts the far pair are both higher in frame and smaller. A later edit that moves the net
back into the panorama, or sizes all four players alike, fails loudly instead of quietly looking
wrong.

**Why the panorama was re-rendered.** The net had to come out of it, so the backdrop was
regenerated from the original by edit rather than from scratch — the composition, which the
foam, ball and palm geometry had been tuned against, survived intact. Nothing else moved out of
the panorama: the "adds exactly one part" test pins that, so the next person who splits something
has to mean it.

**The despill needed a second mode.** ADR-193's green despill clamps red *and* blue toward green,
which is right for foliage and catastrophic for people: human skin is legitimately R > G > B, so
clamping red turns every player grey-green. Skin gets a blue-only clamp instead — blue is the one
channel magenta spill raises that skin does not. The net uses the full clamp, because a white
tape band has R = G = B and the clamp only bites where the pixel actually went magenta.

**One number is overridden rather than measured**, and it is worth naming because ADR-193 made a
principle of deriving geometry from the art. The net render frames the mesh with a generous
length of post above and below, giving it a natural aspect of 1.83 where a real 8 m net on 2.8 m
posts is nearer 2.9. Measured, the net stood four metres tall and reached the island. The box is
therefore forced, which squashes the mesh squares into slightly wide rectangles — invisible at
this size, where the wrong height was not.

**Players are Singaporean** — Chinese, Malay and Indian — rather than the model's defaults, which
came back uniformly Caucasian for an event on Sentosa.

### ADR-195 — Splitting things that nothing passes behind

ADR-194 lifted the net out of the panorama because it had to be in front of some players and
behind others. This splits out the Merlion, the ferry terminal, the umbrella, the deck chair and
the near sea, and **none of them is an occluder** — nothing passes behind the Merlion. So the
justification has to be different, and it is worth stating plainly because it is the more general
one of the two.

**The reason is editability, not depth.** While those objects were painted into the backdrop, the
only way to move the Merlion a few metres, re-time the sea, or put the chair somewhere else was
to re-render the entire panorama — and then re-tune every other layer against it, because a new
render moves the shoreline and the shoreline is what the foam, the players and the net are
positioned against. ADR-194 paid that cost twice already. Separated, each object is a line of
geometry. **The cost of the split is paid once; the cost of not splitting is paid at every future
edit.**

That is also why the panorama now exists as a chain — `panorama.png`, then `-nonet`, then
`-base` — each one its predecessor with another object painted out. All three are kept, because
each was produced by *editing* the one before and an edit is not reproducible: re-running the
same instruction gives a different picture. The chain is the only record of how the backdrop was
stripped, and the generator simply takes the most-decomposed one that exists.

**The sea needed a mode of its own.** Clouds, surf and water glints were all rendered as
white-on-black and keyed by turning their own luminance into alpha, which is what preserves the
soft edges a chroma key would hack off. The sea is an ordinary photograph with no luminance to
spend, so strips now carry a `mode`: `luma` or `opaque`. It also only covers the band between the
sailboats and the shore — a layer spanning the whole sea would have painted over the boats, and
near water is the only place where motion is legible, since a drifting texture at the horizon
reads as a rendering fault. Both its edges fade, which is what stops it being a rectangle of sea
pasted onto sea, and it drifts at 110s against the glints' 26s: equal periods would lock the two
together and slide the whole sea sideways like a conveyor.

**Despill is now per-subject, and the direction depends on the subject's own colour.** The
magenta key raises red and blue. Foliage, pale stone and white netting can take the full clamp of
both channels toward green. Skin, timber and a red parasol are legitimately R > G > B, so
clamping red turns them grey-green — they get blue alone. A blue-and-white striped deck chair is
legitimately B > G, so for that one the clamp runs the other way and only red is pulled back.
Three different answers to one artefact, decided by what the object actually is.

**Heights are specified for all four landmarks**, which continues to override ADR-193's rule that
geometry is measured from the art. Each render frames its subject with its own margins, so the
measured aspect describes the *photograph*, not the object — a pier twice as tall as it should be
is worse than a pier whose pavilion roofs are slightly flattened. The rule earns its exceptions
where a sprite was shot rather than drawn to a box.

**What is still fused into the backdrop**, deliberately: the sky, the distant city skyline, the
island with its clock tower and dome, the sailboats, and the sand. Nothing moves relative to any
of them and nothing passes behind them, so splitting them would buy only the ability to move
them, which nobody has wanted to do. The "exactly these parts are decomposed" test pins the list
so the next split is a deliberate act with a test to update.

### ADR-196 — Making the island actually be Sentosa

The photoreal backdrop was a correct tropical beach and the wrong one. Three faults, each of
a different kind, and it is worth separating them because they do not have the same remedy.

**A landmark that exists nowhere.** A large white geodesic dome sat on the right of the island.
It is not on Sentosa, or anywhere else; it is the image model's idea of what belongs on a
