skyline. Nothing can be done with a plausible invention except delete it, so it is painted out
and replaced with more jungle. The lesson is that generated backdrops fail *confidently* — the
dome was rendered as well as everything around it, which is exactly why it survived three
rounds of review.

**Absence, which is harder to see than error.** Nothing in the frame said Sentosa. The cable car
was already there, and the Merlion; neither is enough, because both also read as "Singapore
generally". So the Universal Studios globe and the island's observation tower are now layers in
the treeline. Reviewing art for what is wrong is natural; reviewing it for what is *missing*
takes a deliberate second pass, and this one took an outside eye.

**A thing named as another thing.** ADR-195 called a sprite `ferryTerminal` and it was a jetty.
A pier is the structure you walk along; the terminal is the building you walk through to reach
it. The scene had only the first, and the name hid that it was incomplete — nobody looks for a
missing terminal in a layer already called `ferryTerminal`. The jetty is renamed `ferryJetty`
and a terminal building added beside it. **Naming a part after the thing you wish it were is how
a gap stops being visible.**

**The terminal is the scene's second occluder.** It is drawn after the Express, so the train
runs along the island shore and passes *behind* it. That is the ADR-194 argument again, now
arrived at for free: the building had to exist for correctness, and placing it in the train's
path costs nothing and buys the Express a second place to arrive rather than switch off.

**The yachts are gone and ferries replace them.** Two sailboats is not what the channel off
Siloso looks like; it is what stock photography looks like. One ferry crosses the open water and
one is berthed at the jetty — and a terminal with nothing tied up at it reads as closed. Both
are the same render, the moored one flopped, because asking for a second ferry would have
produced a different vessel and two visibly different ferries in one small bay is a busier claim
than the scene needs. The crossing ferry **fades in and out** rather than cutting: unlike the
Express there is nothing in open water to hide behind, and at that distance a fade reads as haze,
which is what it would actually be. It travels at 74s, hidden entirely under
`prefers-reduced-motion` along with the cable cars and the train — a boat parked mid-channel at
half opacity is broken art, not stillness.

One pre-existing test had pinned that reduced-motion rule as **exact CSS text**, so adding the
ferry to it failed the gate. The rule's content is not the contract; "everything that travels is
hidden rather than frozen" is. It now asserts membership, which is the thing actually worth
defending and does not break the next time the list grows.

### ADR-197 — Researching the landmark instead of imagining it

ADR-196 added a "ferry terminal" that was a modern building with a swooping white roof. It is
not the Sentosa Ferry Terminal. It is not any building. It is what the words *ferry terminal*
average out to across an image model's training data, which is a different thing from a place.

The real one, per the National Heritage Board's record of it: designed by **Lee Coo**, opened
October 1987, three storeys, a white colonial mansion with a **red-tiled roof** and a **32-metre
clock tower**, built for 5,000 visitors an hour and three ferries at a time. Photographs show
what the description leaves out — a **central rotunda** ringed with white classical columns
under a curved balustraded terrace, wide orange tile hipped roofs stepping down to long low
wings, and ornate white pierced fretwork along every roof edge. It was demolished for Resorts
World, and for the two decades before that it *was* the image of Sentosa.

**The find that matters is not the building. It is what was already in the panorama.** The white
clock tower with the red-roofed colonial building beneath it, which three rounds of review had
been reading as a generic island clock tower — and which the previous ADR all but proposed
deleting as "arguably not a Sentosa landmark" — was a half-remembered Sentosa Ferry Terminal.
The model had got the right building and blurred it. So ADR-196 did the worst available thing:
it left the half-right version in place and set an invented one down next to it.

Three lessons, in descending order of how much they cost:

1. **A wrong landmark is cheaper than a vague one.** An obviously wrong building gets deleted. A
   vaguely-right one gets accepted, reasoned about, and built on. The dome of ADR-196 was spotted
   immediately; this tower survived longer precisely because it was closer to correct.
2. **Not recognising a landmark reads exactly like the landmark not being there.** The remedy for
   both is the same and it is not more looking — it is going and finding out what the place
   looks like. Five minutes of research would have saved the whole of ADR-196's terminal.
3. **Deleting is a real option.** The fix was to paint the approximation out of the backdrop
   entirely and put one accurate, decomposed building in its place, rather than to patch around
   something that was nearly right.

The terminal is deliberately the largest element in the scene. In every photograph of 1990s
Sentosa it dominates the shoreline, and a polite building tucked into the treeline would have
been the previous mistake in a new size. It keeps its ADR-196 job as the Express's second
occluder, and the train's start was shifted left so it has somewhere to emerge from before it
reaches it. Its despill runs on blue alone: cream walls would prefer red clamped and an orange
tile roof very much would not, and the roof wins, because a terminal with a grey roof stops
being the terminal.

One accident worth keeping: the Merlion stands in the foreground with the terminal behind it.
That is the composition on every Sentosa postcard of the period, arrived at by placing two
sprites independently and noticing afterwards.

### ADR-198 — Variety as a roster, not as more slots

The scene had one cable car drawn three times with staggered delays, one ferry render used
twice (once flopped), and four players. The ask was more of each. The interesting part is not
the new art; it is that "more of each" was the moment the structure had to change.

**Three identical cabins read as one cabin.** The eye catches a repeat long before it counts
instances, so the cheapest crowd is also the least convincing. Three liveries — the original
red cabin, a glass-bottomed gold SkyOrb and a teal cabin — cost three files, and the repeat
simply stops existing. The same went for the ferry: a flopped duplicate at the jetty became a
genuinely different two-deck vessel, because the point of a berth is that something *different*
is tied up at it. A bumboat joined the crossing traffic, differing from the ferry in size, pace
and height in the frame at once rather than being one silhouette at two scales.

**Every repeated thing is now a roster.** A sprite declares the item type it is one of, and the
generator groups them and emits one list per type. The component iterates those lists; it no
longer names slots. The staggering moved with it: each cabin carries its own `delay` and each
boat its own `duration` as data, so the component's hardcoded `CABINS = ['0s', '-11s', '-22s']`
is gone. A fourth cable car is now a line of geometry and a PNG.

**The generator had three hidden copies of the player list** — the spill colour, the despill
channel and the build loop — and adding four players meant finding all three. They are derived
from the roster now. **A roster the generator still has to be told about is not a roster.**

The flip periods also moved. The real scene had been importing `PLAYER_PERIODS` from the drawn
scene's generated module, a dependency with no reason behind it; there are eight figures now and
they have their own list, deliberately non-harmonic so no two drift into step.

**The find of the turn came from the review tool, and it was a bug nobody could see.** The
flattened preview draws every layer at t=0. Three cabins sharing one position therefore landed
exactly on top of each other, and the preview had been reporting one cable car where there were
three. Giving the preview a `previewX`/`previewY` offset — applied only by the compositor, never
shipped — spread them, and that instantly exposed something real: `gb-scene-cable` lifts the
cabins 24.565% across the run because the *drawn* panorama's cable climbs to the right, while
the photoreal wire **descends** to the island. On this backdrop the classic keyframes walk the
cabins steadily off their own cable. The error is exactly zero at t=0, which is the only frame
the preview had ever drawn, so the bug lived entirely in the frames nobody could see.
`gb-scene-cable-real` flips it.

**Two tests changed in ways worth recording.** The keyframe-liveness test read only the
`animation:` shorthand and so reported a keyframe reached through `animation-name` as dead; it
now reads both. And the new roster test asserts on distinct `src` values rather than on counts —
which is what makes it a *variety* test rather than a quantity one. Padding a roster by
duplicating a sprite fails it, which is precisely the thing this ADR exists to prevent.

### ADR-199 — A live review page, without wiring anything in

Asked for the link to view the backdrop, the honest answer was that there is not one. That is
the task constraint working exactly as intended — no route reaches `<RealBeachScene>`,
`resolveBackdrop` does not know the word "real", nothing imports it but its own test. But "you
cannot see it" is a poor answer when the thing is finished, and the substitute on offer,
`_preview.png`, is **one frame at t = 0**.

That single frame is not a small limitation. ADR-198 found a cable car that had been travelling
steadily off its own wire for several turns, and the reason nobody saw it is that the error is
exactly zero in the only frame the preview ever drew. A still cannot show drift, period beats,
fade-in and fade-out, or anything that goes wrong on the way between two keyframes.

So the generator now also writes `_preview.html`: the real layer stack as plain HTML, next to
the art, linked against the real `gameboy.css`. It is served as a static file from the repo and
can be watched moving. It is **not** wiring the scene in — there is no route, no React, no
import from any shipped module, and nothing in the app can reach it. Like the PNG it is
gitignored, because it is a tool rather than an artefact.

**The thing that had to change first.** A second renderer of the same nineteen-layer stack is a
second place for the z-order to live, and two hand-written copies diverge the first time one is
edited — with the copy nobody runs tests against being the one that goes wrong. So the CSS class
each part is drawn with moved out of `<RealBeachScene>` and into the geometry, and is emitted on
every part. The component now renders `<Layer part={…} />` and reads `part.className`. The review
page reads the same field. They cannot disagree.

The z-order itself stays written out longhand in the component rather than looping over `ORDER`.
**The order is the design** — far players, net, near players, palms last — and a loop would hide
the three adjacencies the whole scene rests on behind an array index.

Two small things fell out. Writing `player1` through `player8` into the class map by hand would
have been the fourth hardcoded copy of the player list, after the three ADR-198 removed from the
generator, so it is derived from the roster. And the generator's closing size report ran
`identify` over everything in the output directory, which made ImageMagick try to rasterise an
HTML file through `html2ps`; it now reports non-images by size alone.

### ADR-200 — Switching it on: `?backdrop=life`

Seven ADRs built the photoreal scene under a standing instruction not to wire it in. This
wires it in, and the way it went is the point worth recording: **the switch was three lines.**

`BackdropChoice` gains `'life'` beside `'classic'` and `'fine'`, `isChoice` accepts it, and
`<BeachScene>` returns `<RealBeachScene />` when it is asked for. Not one assertion in
`RealBeachScene.test.tsx` changed. That file was written in ADR-193 against a component
nothing rendered, on the argument that an unreferenced component rots and the tests are what
stop it; the bill came due here and the claim held.

**It dispatches rather than branching.** The obvious cheap move was a third `parts` table
alongside `SCENE_PARTS` and `SCENE_PARTS_FINE` — those two are the same scene at one and two
pixels per art unit, so swapping tables is all they need. The photoreal scene is not a third
resolution of that art. It has eight players rather than four, three different cable cars, two
vessels crossing and one berthed, and a net that must be drawn *between* two groups of players.
None of that fits `<BeachScene>`'s fixed z-order. So the test asserts the pixel scene is **gone**
— `queryByTestId('beach-scene')` is null — rather than that it has different files.

**It is opt-in and stays opt-in.** Eighteen megabytes of photograph against a few hundred
kilobytes of pixel art is never a default, and nothing in the UI offers it: you reach it by
typing the parameter. It is still *remembered* like the other two, because a comparison you have
to re-request on every navigation is not a comparison — and remembering is safe here for a
reason that is structural rather than lucky: `.gb-scene` is `display: none` below 760px, and
browsers do not fetch background images inside a hidden subtree. A phone that once visited the
URL downloads none of it.

**Two near misses are rejected deliberately.** `?backdrop=real` is null and so is `?backdrop=Life`.
The parameter has been `real` in seven ADRs of prose and in every internal identifier, so the
wrong word is the likely typo; landing on eighteen megabytes by near-miss is worse than being
told nothing matched, and an unrecognised value falls back to classic rather than erroring.

What this does **not** do: change the default, add a UI control, or touch the classic and fine
variants. The spiral preview is still static and the backdrop style is still not a droplist.

## ADR-201 — Things that travel need something to travel on, and the way to align a sprite with the backdrop is to stop having a backdrop to align with

**Status:** accepted · **Date:** 2026-10-07 · **Supersedes in part:** ADR-198 (cable direction), ADR-200 (`?backdrop=life`)

### Context

The photoreal backdrop went live in ADR-200 and a human looked at the running app for the
first time. Three faults, all of the same kind, plus one change of mind:

1. The cable cars were not on the cables.
2. The Sentosa Express had no track — it slid along the shoreline on nothing.
3. The jetty did not reach the ferry terminal; it floated beside it.
4. The photoreal scene should be the exception, not the default, and should be reached by
   `?backdrop=real`.

Faults 1–3 all survived every preview, both the still and the ADR-199 motion page. That is
worth more than the fixes. A flattened still and a live HTML page both answer *is each
sprite where the geometry says it is*, and the geometry said yes every time. None of them
could answer *is where the geometry says it is the right place*, because the right place
was defined by a photograph nobody can query.

### Decision

**The cable is ours now.** The wires were painted into the panorama, so the cabins were
positioned by eye against them: two numbers tuned separately, one of them inside a JPEG.
ADR-198 had already found the cabins climbing while the painted wire descended and fixed it
with a second measurement, which got closer without getting right — "close" is visibly not
"on" when the line is three pixels wide. So the wires are painted out of the panorama (a
new link in the edit chain) and the cable is drawn by the generator from `CABLE
{x0,y0,x1,y1}`. The cabins hang from those same two points and travel that same vector.
**They cannot disagree, because neither of them is measured.**

This is the net and the ferry terminal argument (ADR-194/195) applied to a line one pixel
wide: anything a sprite must line up with cannot live in the backdrop.

The cabins became `__frame` boxes with computed `left`/`top` rather than width sprites,
because a background clips at its layer box and the run starts off the left edge. The
keyframe now reads `translate(var(--gb-cable-dx), var(--gb-cable-dy))` with per-cabin
values: a percentage transform is relative to the *element*, so three differently sized
cabins need three different pairs to cover one shared distance.

**The Express got a guideway**, drawn immediately before it so the train sits on it. Its
run is now bounded at both ends — round the headland, finishing hidden behind the terminal
— because a vehicle that starts and stops in open air is the same fault as one with no
track. The viaduct runs off the right edge of frame on purpose: the beam sits lower than
the terminal's footings so the building cannot hide its end, and **a viaduct that simply
stops in open water is a worse fault than the missing track it was added to fix.**

**The jetty overlaps the terminal** instead of abutting it, and is drawn first, so it reads
as running out from behind the building.

**`?backdrop=real`, and it is not remembered.** `classic` and `fine` still persist. The
asymmetry is deliberate: those two exist to be *compared*, and a comparison you must
re-request on every navigation is not a comparison. `real` is eighteen megabytes you go and
look at, and the cost of forgetting you left it on is paid by whoever opens the laptop next.
Anyone who already has `'life'` in storage is healed for free — an unrecognised stored
value has always fallen back to classic.

### Consequences

A new rule for this scene: **if a sprite must align with something, generate the something.**
The remaining alignments that are still eyeballed against the photograph — the Merlion
against the waterline, the umbrella and deck chair against the sand — are all static, so a
still frame genuinely can check them. Every *moving* alignment is now derived.

The test for the cabins does not assert they are on the line, because that is no longer a
property anything can get wrong. It asserts the thing that can: that each cabin's
element-relative travel, multiplied back out by its own size, is the same distance.

Playwright was not run.

## ADR-202 — A face beside every name in both chat rooms, resolved by id because ADR-046 said it would be

**Status:** accepted · **Date:** 2026-10-07 · **Builds on:** ADR-035 (sprite store), ADR-046 (the global room), ADR-062 (the peek card), ADR-063 (team rooms)

### Context

Both chat rooms showed a nickname and a badge and no face, while the team roster and the
leaderboard beside them showed a face you could hover or tap for a card (ADR-062). In a room
of three hundred people, the nickname is the only thing identifying anybody, which is the
exact argument ADR-062 made for the roster — it simply had not been applied to chat.

Three questions had to be settled before any code:

1. **Live or frozen?** Chat rows are snapshots by design (`authorLabelSnapshot`,
   `clusterCodeSnapshot`, non-negotiable #7): a nickname change must not rewrite what the
   room saw an hour ago.
2. **What goes where there is no participant?** The global room carries facilitator and
   superadmin messages, which have no avatar at all.
3. **Roster events?** A team room renders `joined` / `left` / `captain_changed` as sentences.

### Decision

**The avatar is live.** Non-negotiable #7 forbids lazy-joining a *historical* value, and an
avatar is not one: it is not part of what was said. Nicknames are immutable (task 48) and
titles are fixed, so the avatar is the only identity field that can move at all — and the
peek card is a *find this person on the beach* tool, not a record. Somebody who restyles
themselves at lunch should be one person in a scroll, not three. The snapshot fields still
drive the message's own header; the live identity drives only the face and the card.

**The transport was already decided, in 2026, by ADR-046.** That interface says:
`authorParticipantId` is an id, never a sprite body, *"so a busy room does not re-send the
same avatar three hundred times"*. Taking it at its word, **not one field was added to either
chat view, either chat table, the chatBus or the SSE paths.** A new
`GET /api/participants/identities?ids=…` answers who those ids are, and a
`PeopleProvider`/`usePeopleStore` pair — the same shape as ADR-035's sprite store — resolves
each person once per device. Forty people talking three hundred times is forty rows on the
wire.

The alternative, joining four identity fields onto every message, was rejected for being
both larger on the wire and larger in the codebase: it would have had to be threaded through
eight call sites across six files, including two publish paths that do not have a database
handle at the point they build their view.

**Staff get a mark, not a face.** Organisers are in the room but are not participants;
inventing an avatar for them would be a lie about who is speaking. The slot keeps its width
and holds a solid block in the same colour as the STAFF badge at the other end of the row.

**Roster events get nothing.** They are the room's own history rather than somebody
speaking, which is why ADR-063 already styles them as prose. A face would make "Wei_Ling
joined the team" read as a remark.

### Consequences

The slot is always the same width whatever is in it — participant, staff, or not-yet-fetched
— because a list that indents differently depending on who is speaking, or on whether a
request has landed, reads as broken rather than as varied.

`usePeopleStore` deliberately does **not** write to the on-device cache that
`useSpriteStore` writes to. A sprite id is a hash of its own body, so a cached sprite can
never be stale; a participant id is a stable handle to a mutable person. A tab's lifetime is
as long as this may safely be held.

An id the directory cannot place is marked as asked and never retried: a missing face must
cost one request, not one per render for as long as the room is open.

`ChatAvatar` renders `AvatarPeek` rather than a chat-flavoured copy of it, so hover-to-peek
on a mouse and tap-to-peek on a finger stay decided in exactly one place and a room cannot
drift away from a roster.

Playwright was not run.

## ADR-203 — The demo day starts before the first whistle, and the default pairing is `adjacent`

The demo day used to arrive with the tournament already played. That is a fine way to show a
leaderboard and a terrible way to show a tournament console: the console's whole first screen —
format, group size, advance count, third place, pairing — is unreachable once a tournament
exists. Three decisions and one bug fix follow from rewinding it.

**1. Seeding is a claim about relative strength, and this day cannot make one.** `classic` seeds
1v8, 2v7, 4v5 — a bracket built to keep the strongest apart until the final. That is the right
shape when the ranking means something. Here the qualifiers come out of three small groups that
never played each other, so "second in group B" and "second in group C" are closer to labels than
to a measurement, and the classic bracket spends its structure protecting an ordering it does not
have. `adjacent` pairs the list straight down and makes no such claim. It is now the app's
default and is listed first in the console; `classic` is one click away, listed second. The
default lives in the application — `packages/contracts`, the Drizzle schema, `schema.sql`,
`bracket.ts`, `useAdminTournament.ts` and `knockoutDrafts`'s own parameter, seven places that
must stay in step — not in the seed row, so every new day gets it and not just the demo.

**2. Activation is a one-way door, so the demo has to arrive before it.** `TournamentPage.tsx`
renders `SetupPanel` only when `tournament === null`. There is no "unactivate", by design: the
fixtures are real the moment they exist. So the only way to demo the setup knobs is a day with no
tournament row at all. Teams and courts stay seeded, so activation is still one click from a cold
open — the rewind is tournament-only, and the fringe history, passports, swag, photo wall, chat
and agenda are all untouched. The day is therefore deliberately not clock-consistent: the fringe
and the tournament both start at 2.30, and the demo now shows a 2.25pm tournament beside a 4pm
fringe. Demo value beat coherence, knowingly.

**3. The seed file is generated, so the rewind went in the generator.** The 102 lines of
`playTournament`, `rallyTo`, `GROUP_RESULTS` and `LIVE_SCORES` came out of `scripts/seed-demo.mjs`
and the SQL was re-exported — 593 rows across 24 tables. Leaving dead seeding code behind would
have left the repository describing a day the demo no longer has.

**4. Changing a default is a behavioural change to every path the default now reaches.** This is
the part that was nearly missed. `adjacent` had been selectable but unselected since ADR-169, and
it was broken in two ways that only a non-power-of-two field exposes. `adjacentSeedOrder` returned
the plain identity `1..size`, so six qualifiers in an eight-seat tree paired `(1,2)(3,4)(5,6)(7,8)`
— and seats 7 and 8 are both padding, which is **a fixture with no teams on either side**. Nobody
got a bye at all. Six qualifiers is exactly what a nine-team day with two advancing from three
groups produces, so the demo would have shipped a phantom match on the first click. With seven
qualifiers the single bye went to seat 7, the *lowest* qualifier.

The function's doc comment claimed byes "land on the top of the list" and walked through the
six-team case to prove it. The code had never done that. The comment's confidence is precisely why
the fault survived three years of being one option in a droplist; a two-minute probe printing the
actual round-one fixtures found in minutes what the prose had hidden. **Read the comment, then
check it against what the code prints.**

The fix seats the top `size - teamCount` qualifiers opposite padding seats and pairs everyone else
straight down — and spreads those byes across *even* round-one slots, because round two pairs
slots (0,1), (2,3), …, and clumping the byes produces a semi-final between the two teams that did
not play and another between the two that did. Full fields are unchanged: `a,b,c,d` is still
`(a,b)(c,d)`.

Giving the byes to the top of the list is not a strength claim, which would contradict the reason
`adjacent` exists. It is that a bye is an advantage, the list is the only order in the room, and
handing an unearned advantage to the *bottom* of it is the one distribution indefensible under
either reading of what the list means.

**5. The same default change exposed a second unreachable disagreement.** `plannedBracket` —
the "what the draw will look like" picture ADR-150 put on the hall screen — called
`knockoutDrafts(seeds)` with no pairing, so it drew a classic bracket however the knob was set.
While `classic` was the default this was invisible; the moment the default moved, the wall and
activation disagreed, which is the precise failure ADR-150 exists to prevent. The pairing now
comes in from the plan at both call sites. Two latent faults, both found by changing one literal
and reading what broke: a default is not a preference, it is the only path most code ever takes.

Playwright was not run.


## ADR-204 — The spiral is the last square of the backdrop palette, not a setting of its own

The spiral selector has now moved three times, and each move removed a layer of indirection
between the participant and the thing they are choosing. ADR-173 made it a two-option dropdown,
"Plain colour" / "Sunburst". ADR-181 made it a pressed-state square, because a two-option
dropdown costs a tap to discover what the options even are and cannot show what either one looks
like. ADR-204 takes away the last layer: the heading.

A `<span class="gb-label">Spiral</span>` above a single square announces a **setting**, and a
setting is a thing you decide about separately — you read the word, work out what it governs,
and then go back to the colour you had already chosen to see whether you still want it. The
square is not a separate decision. It is one more thing that can be picked for the backdrop, in
the same sense that a colour is, and the way to say that is to put it in the row of backdrop
colours rather than to write a heading explaining the relationship. It is now the last child of
that row, after the colour wheel, and the word "Spiral" survives only on the square's accessible
name and in the hint line underneath that says what it is currently doing.

Mechanically this is two slots on `ColourRow`: `trailing`, rendered inside `.gb-swatches` after
the wheel, and `children`, rendered after the row's hint. Slots rather than a `kind` flag, so a
generic colour row never has to know what a spiral is — the shirt palette passes neither and is
unchanged. The CSS needed no edit at all, which is the tell that this was the right place for it
all along: `.gb-swatch--spiral` was always styled as a swatch and has finally been put where
swatches live.

The test asserts the arrangement structurally rather than by snapshot — same `.gb-swatches`
element as the backdrop colours, last child of it, and no `.gb-label` anywhere containing the
word. What regresses here is somebody moving it back out into a row of its own, and a snapshot
of the markup would record that it changed without recording why it was wrong.

Playwright was not run.

## ADR-205 — The look code's trailing group says what it is

ADR-173 appended the spiral to the end of `avatarLook` and decided whether there was one by
**arity**: no trailing parts means a plain backdrop, three means a spiral, anything else is
malformed. That is the same move ADR-029 made when `build` arrived, and it is genuinely good —
every code ever minted keeps its meaning and nothing needs a migration.

It works exactly once. A chevron wants seven numbers and a radial wants eight, and the first time
two patterns want the same count the format has no way to tell them apart. The failure would not
be an error: the code would parse, and draw the wrong pattern, on somebody's face, with nothing
in the logs. There is no good time to discover that.

So the trailing group now opens with a one-letter tag naming the pattern — `…-1d5b8c-s-f7d154-12-4`
— and the reader dispatches on it instead of counting. **Doing this while there is still only one
pattern is the entire point.** There is nothing to disambiguate yet, so there is no migration to
run, no half-populated column, and no ambiguity to resolve later under pressure with real looks
already in the database. The cost today is two characters per code and one branch; the cost of
doing it after the second pattern ships is a format that cannot be read without guessing.

The back-compatibility rule is one line and fully decidable: **if the first trailing part is a
six-digit hex colour it is a pre-ADR-205 spiral, otherwise it is a tag.** A tag is a single
lowercase letter by construction and a colour is six hex digits, so `asAvatarColour` separates
them with no overlap and no lookahead. Stored codes are never rewritten in place; a look is
re-minted in the tagged form the next time its owner saves, which means the two forms coexist
indefinitely and that is fine.

That rule is proved by **exhaustion, not by sampling**. Legacy spiral space is rays 3…24 by twist
0…10 — small enough to enumerate outright — and the test walks all of it, asserting that each
legacy code parses identically to its tagged twin and re-mints to it. Parse equality is the whole
proof, because the rendered avatar is a pure function of the parsed look: two codes that parse the
same cannot draw differently, so there is no need to render anything. Checking three by hand would
have left the rest resting on an argument, and ADR-203 is a standing demonstration of what an
argument about a property a loop could settle is worth.

Writing that loop immediately paid for itself in an unrelated way: the count is **242**, and the
prose in three places said 220. Nobody would have caught that by reading.

The other thing the tag buys is that an unknown pattern is now an **error**. Before, three
trailing parts were read hopefully as a spiral whatever they were; now `-q-f7d154-18-7` returns
null and the display path falls back to the default look rather than drawing a confident
misinterpretation.

Playwright was not run.

## ADR-206 — Bands: a count, not a palette

The renderer split backdrop cells into exactly two buckets, `{ ray, gap }`. Bargello and the
seventies eco-logo both get their identity from a graded run of related hues, so a two-tone
version of either is a perfectly nice graphic and is not the thing. `splitBackdropCells` now
takes a list of keys and `bandOfCell` returns an index into it.

**The participant still chooses two colours.** The bands between the ends are *interpolated*,
and the control is a slider labelled "Shades" that goes from two to four. Offering four colour
wells would have been the obvious generalisation and is the wrong one: it is three extra
decisions to solve a problem nobody has, and three extra chances to pick something that fights
with a face. Two endpoints and a count produce a ramp that cannot clash with itself.

Interpolation is done in **linear light**, not straight down the sRGB numbers. Halfway between a
dark blue and a bright gold in sRGB is a muddy olive; in linear light it is the colour a person
expects in the middle. `mix` already existed and is left alone — it tints skin towards a blush,
where the sRGB behaviour is the right one — so `mixLinear` sits beside it rather than replacing
it.

The band limit is **four**, read off the contact-sheet probe rather than chosen. The probe also
produced the finding that argues for bands at all, and it is the opposite of what was expected:
at 32px, **more bands read better, not worse**. At a band height of four cells, two bands is the
worst tile on the whole sheet — hard moiré — and six is the cleanest. Because the bands are
interpolated, adding one puts neighbouring colours *closer together*, so the aliasing that
remains reads as shading rather than as noise. Interpolated bands are an anti-aliasing mechanism
that happens to also be a bargello feature.

`DEFAULT_SUNBURST` stays at **two** bands anyway. The new patterns will default to three on the
probe's evidence, but this is the look that participants already wearing a spiral see, and
changing what a stored code draws is not a default change — it is an edit to somebody's face.

Three keys had to be invented and the rest did not. `B`/`b` (backdrop and its vignette shade) and
`R`/`r` (second colour and its shade) keep exactly the colours they have always had, because band
0 is always the backdrop and the last band is always `colourTwo` whatever the count; only the
middles are new. For photo sprites the extra keys are `z`, `y`, `x`, chosen because a sprite
palette is indexed by hex digits and so can never mint them.

What makes this safe to do at all is the same move as ADR-205: **prove the old behaviour by
exhaustion**. `avatars.test.ts` renders all 242 legacy spirals through the real `avatarSvg` and
asserts the output is byte-identical to the two-band form — not "looks the same", identical. A
generalisation that quietly moves one cell has edited a face, and three hand-picked examples
would never show it. The counterweight test matters just as much: proving nothing changed is
only worth having alongside proof that something *can*, so a sibling asserts each extra band
adds a fill, and another that the interpolated colour really lands between its two ends on every
channel rather than beside them.

One deliberate softness: a caller that asks for four bands but supplies two keys gets the last
colour it supplied, not a hole. An unpainted cell in a face is a worse answer than a slightly
flat pattern.

Playwright was not run.

## ADR-207 — concentric radiating shapes: the second pattern, and the first proof the first one generalised

**Status:** accepted, 2026-10-07. Implements step 4 of the task-63 build order (probe → tag → bands
→ **concentric** → chevron/bargello → psychedelic).

🌀 Concentric radiating shapes — the seventies eco-logo — are bands of constant **shape** distance
rather than constant radius. Two standard pieces of maths, neither invented here:

- the **Minkowski p-norm** `(|u|^p + |v|^p)^(1/p)` decides what "distance" means, and its unit ball
  is a diamond at p=1, a circle at p=2, a squircle at p=4 and a square as p→∞;
- a **rose term** `1 + depth·cos(lobes·θ)` modulates that distance with the angle, which is what
  turns plain rings into petals.

**Shape is four stops, not a slider.** The contact sheet from ADR-205's probe is unambiguous: the
four named shapes read as four different things at 32px and the exponents between them do not. A
continuous control would be offering precision the picture cannot show. p=∞ is `max(|u|, |v|)`,
which is not a limit we approximate with a large exponent — it is cheaper *and* exact.

**The wire format is fixed arity, unlike the spiral's.** The spiral's band count is optional because
codes exist that predate bands and must keep meaning what they meant; ADR-205's tag made that
decidable. A pattern minted *after* ADR-205 has no history to be compatible with, so `c` writes
every part every time. The asymmetry is deliberate and worth stating out loud, because the tempting
move is to copy the shape of the thing next to it — which would have imported a back-compatibility
concession into a format that has nothing to be back-compatible with, and left a second leniency
rule to get wrong when the third pattern lands.

**`kind` is a stored field, not a sniff.** A reader could tell the two apart by looking for `rays`
versus `ringWidth`. Structural sniffing is exactly what ADR-205 replaced, three weeks after it was
written, and re-introducing it one layer down would be the same mistake in a smaller font.

**One switch in the codebase.** `bandOfCellFor` is the only place that knows which patterns exist,
and it switches over a discriminated union, so adding a pattern without wiring it in will not
compile. Each generator is a pure function that knows nothing of the others — which is the point of
the user's four-literally-named-patterns ruling: tuning the rings cannot move the spiral, and the
test that asserts so is three lines long.

**The field is still called `sunburst`.** Renaming it was proposed, declined, and the decision has
aged well: the honesty lives in the *type* names (`AvatarBackdropPattern`, `AvatarConcentric`) and
the wire tag, and nothing in the new code is called a sunburst unless it is one. A rename would have
touched every call site to deliver no behaviour.

**ADR-204's placement passed its test.** A second pattern cost exactly one more swatch at the end of
the Backdrop palette and one more CSS rule — no new row, no heading, no dropdown, no mode. That a
change generalises for free is the only real evidence that it went in the right place; the first
time you add the second thing is when you find out.

**Defaults:** three bands, on the probe's evidence that interpolation buys legibility at 32px.
`DEFAULT_SUNBURST` stays at two — a new pattern may take the better default, but changing an
existing one is an edit to somebody's face, not a preference.

**A test balanced on a knife edge is not a test.** The radial-symmetry case first sampled radius 20
with the default petal depth still on, giving a constant rose factor of 1.2 and a distance of
exactly 24.0 — precisely a band boundary, where floating-point noise picks the answer. It failed,
correctly, and the fix was to move the sample off the edge rather than to loosen the assertion.

**A flake was investigated rather than retried.** `court-queue.test.ts` failed once under the
coverage-instrumented gate and passed alone, twice. Rather than re-running until green, the full API
suite was run with the change stashed (800 passed) and again with it applied (800 passed), which
separates "unrelated flake" from "my change" with evidence instead of hope. It is unrelated; it
remains unexplained and is worth a look when the 157-rejection sweep happens.

## ADR-208 — chevron & bargello: one pattern, two waveforms

**Status:** accepted, 2026-10-07. Step 5 of the task-63 build order; step 6 (psychedelic) remains.

⚡ Chevron and bargello are straight bands displaced sideways by a wave:

    band = floor((v − amplitude·W(u / period)) / bandHeight) mod bands

**`W` is the only difference between the two looks** — a triangle wave gives the chevron its
corners, a sine gives the Florentine flame stitch its rounded crests. They ship as **one pattern
with a waveform knob**, not two patterns, because two functions differing by one line is two places
to fix every future bug and two sets of knobs to keep in step. This is not in tension with the
four-self-contained-patterns ruling: waveform is a knob *within* a named pattern, exactly as shape
is within the concentric one. The test that the brief is satisfied is that the user can ask for a
chevron and get a chevron, which they can.

The needlework literature backs the merge rather than a split: bargello is defined by **stepping** —
each upright stitch offset from its neighbour by a fixed amount, with colour following the profile.
A per-column offset applied to a stack of bands *is* stepping. The two crafts differ in the profile
they step along, which is the one term parameterised here.

**Amplitude is a percentage of the period, never a number of cells.** This is the probe's most
important finding about this pattern and the single thing a participant could never learn by
fiddling: the settings that turn to mush at 32px fall on a line of constant amplitude-to-period
ratio, so a cell-valued slider is safe at one wave width and ruined at another, with the control
giving no hint that the two interact. Exposing the ratio makes the dangerous region unreachable
instead of merely documented.

**Amplitude zero is plain stripes, and is named as such on screen.** The probe recommended shipping
stripes by name. They are not a guarded special case — they are what the same expression does when
the wave is multiplied by nothing. A pattern whose extreme setting is a *different good-looking
thing* is worth more than one whose extreme setting is a warning.

**The negative-modulo bug that would have shipped.** `v − offset` is negative over the top half of
every avatar and JavaScript's `%` keeps the sign of the dividend, so the naive remainder returns
negative band indices for half of each face. The fix is the standard double-mod, and it lives in the
generator rather than the caller because a band index is this function's output and should be in
range when it leaves. The test walks every row of the grid at the maximum amplitude rather than
asserting one sample, because the failure is regional, not pointwise.

**The open question behind ADR-206 is now closed.** Bands were introduced partly on Wikipedia's
point that bargello uses many hues of one colour, with the worry that four interpolated bands would
not be enough. At 32px, four is enough: the flame reads, and a fifth band would be finer than the
grid can quantise. That worry can stop being carried forward.

**Function coverage caught three dead sliders.** The gate dropped to 98.49% against 98.55% and
named three `onChange` arrows — concentric petal depth, wave width, band height — that no test ever
moved. Rather than nudging them to make a number go up, each is now driven to a distinct value and
asserted in the saved look code, which turned a coverage complaint into a real test that the wire
format puts every knob in its own slot. A code with wave width and band height transposed would
still have parsed.

## ADR-209 — psychedelic swirls: a domain warp, and the seam that would have shipped

**Status:** accepted, 2026-10-07. Step 6 of task 63 — the last of the four patterns.

🌀 Psychedelic swirls & groovy waves is the only **warped** pattern. The other three evaluate a
formula at the point they are given; this one moves the point first:

    u' = u + w·sin(2πf·v)      v' = v + w·sin(2πf·u)
    D  = r'/scale + arms·θ'/2π     band = floor(D) mod bands

Domain warping is the whole technique behind the liquid Y2K-poster look. The searches for the
style itself returned stock-image listings and vocabulary — *twirl, liquid, distorted* — and
nothing implementable; the usable description came from treating it as warping a regular field.
The **regularity is what keeps it from being noise**, the displacement is what keeps it from
looking drawn with a compass.

**The seam is the thing that would have shipped broken.** `θ` jumps by 2π across the negative
x-axis, so a running total that mixes radius and angle jumps by the arm count there, and
`floor(D) mod bands` shows a hard radial line straight through the face unless that jump is a whole
number of colour cycles. Arms are therefore `swirl × bands`, which closes the cycle at every
setting. The spiral never had this problem because `rays` is an integer and it takes the phase
*within* a sector — this is the same observation applied to a pattern whose radial and angular
terms share one total. The test walks the wrap at all 21 combinations of swirl and band count.

**Testing a seam means straddling the seam.** The first version of that test compared the cells at
`y = 31` and `y = 32` and failed. Both are on the *same* side of the cut: the centre line is
`y = 31.5`, and `atan2(0, negative)` is `+π`, not `−π`. Worse, comparing two adjacent cells proves
nothing anyway — neighbours may legitimately differ wherever a band ends. The honest test samples
`31.5 ± 1e-6`, two points that differ **only** by the wrap, so any difference in band is the seam
and nothing else.

**A test asserted the opposite of the truth and was right to fail.** A case claiming the field
"curls rather than shears" asserted that transposing x and y changes the answer. It does not: the
displacement pair is symmetric under swapping u and v, and so is the radius, so the pattern has a
**mirror line along y = x**. The code comment was overclaiming, not the code. Both were corrected —
the comment now states the precise property (each displacement is read off the *other* coordinate,
so a band is bent along its length rather than slid sideways) and the mirror is asserted
deliberately, so it stays a known property instead of a later surprise.

**One rule, reached twice from separate measurements.** ADR-208 exposed wave amplitude as a
fraction of period; this exposes ripple as a fraction of the frequency-dependent ceiling
`w·f² ≤ 0.8`. Two patterns, two couplings found independently by the probe, one rule worth stating
in general: **never expose the member of a coupled pair that is only meaningful relative to the
other.** It makes the unusable region unreachable rather than merely documented.

**Going last paid off as predicted.** The ripple ceiling was already measured, the
fraction-of-maximum control was already a proven idea, and the only genuinely new problem was the
seam. Had this been built first, the seam would have been debugged alongside three other unknowns.

**Task 63 is complete.** Four literally-named, self-contained patterns — Spiral, Concentric,
Chevron & Bargello, Psychedelic — each a pure function with its own knobs, behind one swatch row,
one two-colour band control, and one `kind` switch that will not compile if a fifth is added
without wiring it in.


## ADR-210 — correcting ADR-209's commit: the draw is random, nothing is unstable

**Status:** accepted, 2026-10-07. A correction to the reasoning recorded in `4f9dcad`, whose code
change stands.

That commit fixed the intermittent `court-queue.test.ts` failure and attributed it to "standings
that are identical after a round of walkovers, so the order is tie-broken unstably". **That
diagnosis is wrong.** The standings ranking is deterministic by construction and has been since
ADR-106: cohorts keyed on wins *and* draws, ranked inside by head-to-head, then a mini-league,
then point difference, then entry seed — specifically so that no tie is ever resolved by engine
internals. There is no unstable tie-break to find.

The real cause is one line in `activateTournament`:

    const groups = dealGroups(shuffle(input.teamIds), knobs.groupSize);

**The draw is randomised, deliberately and correctly.** Which teams land in which group, and
therefore who meets whom in the bracket, is a Fisher–Yates shuffle. The test was a coin flip from
the day it was written. That also disposes of the secondary story: it was never "load-dependent"
or "only under the coverage-instrumented gate" — it passed three times in isolation because three
coin flips went its way, and the coverage runs simply gave it more chances to fail.

**What was actually wrong with the method.** The first failure was dismissed as a flake. The
second prompted a diagnosis, which is right — but the diagnosis was reached by *reading* the
ranking code, finding it plausible that identical records could tie, and stopping there. The
shuffle is four frames further up the call stack and one `grep` away. A mechanism that explains
the symptom is not the same as the mechanism that causes it, and the test for the difference is
whether you went and looked.

The remedy is unchanged and remains correct: the test searches for two teams with no pending
fixture between them instead of assuming teams 0 and 1 are unpaired. A search is the right shape
precisely *because* the draw is random — a deterministic-shuffle injection would have worked too,
but it would test one draw out of many, and this way the test holds for every draw.

Also checked, since the same assumption could hide elsewhere: of the nine API test files that
close the group stage, **no other one indexes `teamIds` to assert a pairing.**

**Nothing is outstanding from this.** The "unstable standings tie-break" listed as a known defect
in PR #5 does not exist and has been struck from the list. Leaving it there would have cost the
next person a hunt for a bug that was never written.

## ADR-211 — the unstubbed-request sweep, and why the safeguard had to stop being optional

**Status:** accepted, 2026-10-07. Closes the sweep ADR-192a deferred.

ADR-192a diagnosed the failure mode exactly: the fetch stub's "No stub for …" throws inside an
`async` function, so a miss becomes a **rejected promise**; plenty of real callers start a request
without awaiting it (a refresh on mount, a drain on a timer), nobody catches it, and the runner
blames whichever test is on screen when it lands. It then supplied the remedy —
`expectNoUnstubbedCalls(stub)` in a suite's `afterEach` — **as something each suite had to opt
into.**

**Two suites out of sixty-seven did.** That is not negligence, it is the predictable yield of any
safeguard that must be remembered: the files most likely to need it are the ones nobody revisits.
So the check moved into the global `afterEach` in `test-setup.ts`, over a register every
`installFetchStub` adds itself to. One change covers all sixty-seven files, and a file written
next month gets it without knowing it exists. **A guarantee that can be forgotten is a guarantee
you do not have.**

Switching it on produced **117 failing tests across 17 files**.

**The catch-all was the wrong fix and was tempting.** Answering any unrecognised request with `{}`
would have made the suite green in one line, and thrown away precisely the signal just built: a
test that quietly calls an endpoint nobody listed is a test whose author did not know what their
component does. Instead, `test-utils/ambientRoutes.ts` offers **named, typed, opt-in bundles** —
`participantShellRoutes`, `facilitatorShellRoutes`, `adminConsoleRoutes`, `courtConsoleRoutes`,
`screenRoutes`, `teamChatRoutes`, `identityRoutes`, `fringeStationRoutes`. A file spreads in the
ones it needs, so the admission stays visible in that file's own route table, and anything outside
a bundle still fails loudly. Every body is typed as its contract view, so a fixture that drifts
from the wire format fails the typecheck rather than a test.

**An empty default is not always the neutral one.** `screenRoutes` first returned
`enabledScenes: []` and broke twenty-one `ScreenPage` tests. ADR-160 is explicit that a key minted
without an opinion shows *everything* — the feature is subtraction. A default that contradicts the
domain's own default is not a default, it is a second opinion. It now returns
`ALL_SCREEN_SCENE_IDS`.

**A harmless-looking default can shadow a real stub.** `matchRoute` tries the path *without* its
query before the path with it. Dropping `adminConsoleRoutes` into `TeamsRepairPage.test.tsx`, where
tests key `'GET /api/admin/participants?search='`, made the query-less entry win and handed those
tests an empty directory — two passing tests broken by a stub meant to be inert. Where a file
already keys by query, leave it alone and stub the prefixes it is missing. This is recorded in the
helper itself, next to the thing that does it.

**What the misses actually were.** Almost none were bugs: they were the shell doing its job —
alerts polling, the team you belong to, the identity resolver behind every chat avatar, the court
console's `recent-teams` (the original ADR-192 culprit), a directory combobox firing one search per
keystroke with a different query each time. One class deserves a note: `fetchParticipantIdentities`
ends in `.catch(() => ({ items: [] }))`, so those fifteen misses never floated as rejections. They
are stubbed anyway — "harmless" was a property of one call site's error handling, and the register
exists to record what the app asked for, not what it got away with.

**157 was the wrong number to have carried.** The earlier probe counted 157 unstubbed *requests*
across 16 routes. The real unit of work is 117 failing *tests* across 17 files, and the real cost
was not the count but the seventeen different reasons. A number copied forward three times is
worth re-measuring before planning around it — the same lesson the 242 legacy look codes taught in
ADR-205.

## ADR-212 — the cut-out scorer, and the two objectives that pointed the wrong way

**Context.** Participants' photographs go through auto-cropping and MODNET background removal, and
the removal sometimes takes a chunk out of the subject. `DEFAULT_TUNING` is one fixed setting for
every photograph ever uploaded. The question asked was whether the eighteen settings a participant
can reach by tapping could be swept, scored and the best one offered as the opening position
instead. `docs/design/cutout-auto-tuning-assessment.md` is the assessment; this is what was built
from its step 1.

**Decision.** `apps/web/src/lib/avatar/cutOutScore.ts`, pure, tested, **wired to nothing**.
`scoreSettings` measures every setting in a swept grid; `chooseTuning` returns one tuning plus its
reasoning and every candidate it looked at. Nothing in the studio calls it yet, on purpose: the
assessment's step 2 — a report over the recorded demo crowd — is the gate that decides whether
this chooses a default or merely raises a flag, and that report cannot be produced in this sandbox
(the matte needs MODNET's weights and there is no route to huggingface.co from here).

**Why it is shaped this way.** Cost was never the obstacle: the matting model runs once, so each
setting is flood fills over 4,096 cells at ~0.6 ms. The objective function is the whole problem,
and the probe caught **two** objectives that optimised in the wrong direction.

**The first was bite measured globally.** MODNET mattes every person in frame, so the stranger at
the next table is confident subject too. "Confident subject that this setting dropped" therefore
read ~4 % on every setting that prunes a bystander — correct behaviour, scored as damage. A tuner
minimising it learns never to prune bystanders: worse product, better number. Bite is now measured
inside the face-connected component only, found through the loosest possible mask so that the
definition of *who the subject is* does not depend on the setting being judged.

**The second was the tie-break, and it was invisible.** With bite and leak both zero across a
clean matte — which is what a good photograph looks like — the winner was whichever candidate the
generating loops emitted first. That is `Trim`. So the chooser shaved a cell off every
well-photographed participant and the probe printed a perfect score while doing it. Bite is
measured on *confident* subject and a soft edge is by definition not confident, so neither of the
first two keys was defending the subject's outline at all. The third key is distance from
`DEFAULT_TUNING`: **a default moves only when it is measurably better.** After it, the chooser
agrees with the shipped default on a clean matte and moves to `Loose` only where a region is
ambiguous, which is exactly the step-2 criterion.

**The structural prior.** Between alpha 32 and 224 no label can exist — that is what ambiguous
means — and that band is precisely where the chunks get bitten out. So the score appeals to
something other than the matte: **enclosed background, with no path to the frame border. People
are not perforated.** It costs one flood fill, reads 0 at all eighteen settings on a clean matte
and 108–220 on one with a shirt the colour of the wall, and it rises as the threshold tightens, so
it points at `Loose` on its own. It is a *refusal* with a tolerance rather than a cost, because
railings and a hand on a hip are real holes in real photographs.

**The plateau, not the argmax.** With no ground truth the maximum of a hand-built score is a
statement about the score. The chooser sweeps eleven thresholds rather than the three on offer —
density is nearly free — takes the centre of the widest run that all behave alike, and snaps the
answer back onto `CUT_OUT_STEPS` so the default remains something the participant can reach by
tapping and therefore undo.

**When every setting is refused**, the answer is ADR-077: stop cutting and keep the photograph.
A matte that cannot hold a face together is not one to pick a least-bad mutilation from.

*Rejected:* a weighted sum. Two hundred cells of leak are an untidy edge and two hundred cells of
bite are a missing forearm; no set of weights trades those honestly, so the score is a priority
order with refusals at the top.

*Rejected:* painting the candidates. At ~95 ms a paint that is 1.7 s, and it is unnecessary —
everything the score needs is in the mask.

*Still open:* every number behind this module comes from synthetic mattes. They proved two
objectives wrong, which is more than most fixtures earn, and they are **not** evidence about
photographs. `HOLE_TOLERANCE`, the 224/32 bands and the plateau width are all provisional until
the demo-crowd report exists.

**Addendum — the step-2 report exists now, as a dev-server page.** `/cutout-report.html`, with
`apps/web/tools/cutoutReport.ts` behind it. The blocker was never the corpus, which is real and in
the repository at `images/ingest/`; it was that the matte needs MODNET's weights and the agent's
sandbox reaches no CDN. The browser pointed at the dev server does, and that is where this model
has always run — so the report runs there, through `photoFileToSprite` → `refineWithModel` →
`chooseTuning`, which is the path that ships rather than a re-implementation of it. Given two
scoring designs that have already pointed the wrong way, a re-implementation would have been the
wrong instrument.

It is dev-only by construction and not by a flag: not a route, outside `src/`, and `vite build`
takes `index.html` alone. The photographs come from an `apply: 'serve'` middleware rather than
`public/`, because a fixture has no business in the shipped bundle.

It also states its own verdict rather than leaving it to whoever reads the table — *moved only
where the default does damage* passes, *moved on photographs the default handles cleanly* means
keep the scorer as a detector and leave `DEFAULT_TUNING` alone. Writing the criterion into the
tool before seeing the numbers is the only way it stays a gate instead of becoming a rationalisation.

## ADR-213 — the scene contained a building that no longer exists

**Context.** ADR-197 verified the ferry terminal against photographs and found the generated
asset confidently wrong in its details. The same check was run over the two remaining landmarks,
and `skyTower.png` turned out to be wrong in a way a likeness check does not usually catch: the
**Tiger Sky Tower closed on 28 December 2018 after three breakdowns and was dismantled.**
SkyHelix Sentosa, an open-air rotating gondola, opened on the same part of Imbiah Lookout in
December 2021. The backdrop has been rendering a structure that has not existed for seven years.

**This is a different class of error from a wrong colour.** A generated landmark fails
confidently — that was ADR-197's lesson — but a *historical* failure cannot be found by looking
harder at the picture. Both questions have to be asked: is this what it looks like, and **is it
still there.**

**Decision — redraw it as SkyHelix.** Offered three times as a choice (SkyHelix / drop the layer /
keep it as deliberate nostalgia) and not taken up, so the call is recorded here as the author's:
of the three, dropping the layer leaves a hole in the treeline and keeping it requires everyone
who ever notices to be told it was on purpose, while the redraw is the only one that leaves the
skyline both populated and true. Nostalgia is a defensible reading, but it is not available by
*default* — it has to be a decision somebody made, and nobody had made it.

**The geometry is the ride, not the old box.** SkyHelix is **79 m** against the tower's **131 m**,
so the layer's height drops **54 → 33** art units. A 12 m gondola on a 79 m mast is 0.15 wide
where a disc on a column was 0.22, so the width drops **12 → 5**. It keeps the same centre line
(250) and the same ground line (150): it replaces the thing in the place the thing stood.

**The part is renamed `skyTower` → `skyHelix`** across the geometry table, the despill table, the
draw order, the generated art table, the component and its test. A layer named for a demolished
building is how this survives being noticed once and forgotten.

**Verified against a photograph before and after.** The reference shows a white open-steel
hyperboloid lattice — curved struts crossing, flared at the base — with a flattened grey saucer
gondola under a shallow domed canopy. The first render came back far too squat (aspect 0.6 against
the real 0.15) and was redone with the proportions pinned in the prompt; the second measures 0.129
trimmed. It was then composited over the panorama at scene scale and looked at, because an asset
that is correct at 1400 px and a smudge at 20 px has not been checked.

*Honest note:* `sceneArtReal.ts` says "GENERATED — do not edit", and it was edited by hand. The
generator cannot be run: it reads `.scene-src/`, and no render in that directory has ever been
committed. The hand edit reproduces exactly what the generator would emit from the updated
geometry — including a fresh `REAL_SCENE_VERSION` — so a future regeneration converges rather than
conflicts. `.scene-src/` is now explicitly ignored to stop pretending otherwise: the reproducible
artefact is the **prompt**, and this one is recorded below.

> Tall narrow portrait-format photoreal architectural render of the SkyHelix Sentosa observation
> tower, isolated on flat pure magenta with no ground, sky, scenery or shadow. Straight-on
> eye-level side elevation. Very tall and slender — roughly five times taller than wide — filling
> the full height of the frame. An open white-painted steel lattice mast: slim curved vertical
> struts crossing in a narrow hyperboloid cage, slightly flared at the ground, tapering to a
> narrow waist, open enough to see through to the magenta behind. At the top a small flattened
> circular grey-and-white saucer gondola with a shallow domed canopy, only a little wider than the
> mast. Clean bright daylight, crisp edges, no text, no logos, no people, no vegetation.

**Still outstanding on the same sweep:** `uss.png`. The real globe is a **sphere** with **gold**
continents inside a tilted ring of freestanding gold letters; ours is egg-shaped with **silver**
continents and a solid dark band reading "UNIVERSAL STUDI…". At its render size (≈26 × 32 px) the
silver-for-gold is the only one of those that reads, and the fountain base is already correct.

---

## ADR-214 — the globe was an egg, and the despill table had no answer for it

**Context.** The third landmark in the ADR-197 sweep. `uss.png` rendered the Universal Studios
Singapore entrance globe as an **egg** with **silver** continents, wrapped in a solid dark band
carrying the text "UNIVERSAL STUDI…". Checked against photographs the real monument is a
**sphere** of cobalt perforated panels with continents in raised **gold**, encircled on a tilt by
a ring of **freestanding** gold capitals — separate solid letters you can see the sphere between
and behind — standing in a low circular pool. The fountain base was already right.

**Which error actually mattered.** At a render size of roughly 26 × 32 px the lettering is three
or four pixels tall and no reader resolves it; the shape and the colour are the whole of what
reads. So the ranking was: egg → sphere first, **silver → gold** second, and the band-versus-ring
third — fixed because the redraw was happening anyway, not because anyone would have caught it.

**The despill table could not express this sprite, and that is the finding.** Magenta keying
leaves spill that raises red and blue, and the existing remedies clamp one or both back toward
green. The globe carries **legitimate gold (R > G > B) and legitimate blue (B > G) in the same
image**: clamping red greys the lettering, clamping blue greys the sphere, and clamping both
leaves a monochrome paperweight. The old entry was `uss: 'R'`, with a comment explaining that
blue was spared for the oceans — written when the continents were silver and nothing in the
sprite depended on red.

So a third mode, **`M`**, clamps a pixel **only where it is actually magenta-ish**: where R and B
*both* exceed G. Gold cannot satisfy that (its blue is low), blue cannot satisfy it (its red is
low), and white mist blended with a magenta backdrop satisfies it exactly. The general rule is
worth more than the entry: **an unconditional channel clamp is only safe while the subject sits
on one side of the colour wheel.** The fountain's mist is what exposed it — a soft translucent
edge keys to pink, which `-fuzz 30%` does not catch and `Erode Octagon:1` does not reach.

**The box changed shape because the monument is a different shape.** A sphere inside a ring of
letters inside a pool is **landscape (1.3)**; an egg on a pedestal was **portrait (0.81)**. The new
box is **23 × 18** against the old **26 × 32**, chosen so the *sphere* keeps the apparent diameter
the egg had — the point is to correct the landmark, not to enlarge it. Same ground line (152),
same centre line (209).

**Checked at size, twice.** The first composite over the panorama showed a bright magenta fringe
around the mist and a monument about twice the mass of its neighbours; both were visible only
because the layer was placed in the scene at scene scale and looked at. A landmark that is
convincing at 1400 px and wrong at 20 px has not been checked — the same discipline ADR-213 used
and the reason both of these were caught before they shipped rather than after.

*Still hand-edited:* `sceneArtReal.ts`, for the reason ADR-213 gives — `.scene-src/` has never
been committed, so the generator cannot be run. The edit is what the generator would emit.

> Photoreal render of the Universal Studios Singapore entrance globe, isolated on flat pure
> magenta, no sky, scenery, people or shadow. Straight-on eye-level, whole monument in frame. A
> perfectly spherical globe — round, not egg-shaped — of deep cobalt-blue perforated mesh panels
> in a latitude-and-longitude grid, continents raised on its surface in warm metallic gold and
> bronze. Encircling it on a slight tilt, a ring of large freestanding three-dimensional polished
> gold capitals spelling UNIVERSAL, each a separate solid object standing clear of the globe so
> the sphere shows in the gaps between and behind them. It sits in a low circular fountain pool
> of pale grey stone with a plain rim and fine white mist. Bright even daylight, crisp edges, no
> additional text, no logos, no signage.

**The ADR-197 landmark sweep is now closed:** ferry terminal (ADR-197), sky tower (ADR-213),
globe (ADR-214).

## ADR-215 — suites for an experiment this environment cannot run

**Context.** ADR-212 built the cut-out chooser and deliberately wired it to nothing, because the
decision about whether it may pick a participant's default belongs to a report over real
photographs. That report needs MODNET's weights and BlazeFace's, both fetched at run time, and
this environment has no outbound network and no browser engine. The work could have stopped at
"blocked".

**Decision.** Write the suites anyway, in full, with the acceptance criteria fixed in advance, and
document them so that an agent in a different environment can run and judge them without having
been here. Three runners, one runbook: `docs/design/cutout-chooser-validation.md`.

- **`e2e/participant/cutout-chooser.spec.ts`** — the gate. Drives `/cutout-report.html` in a real
  browser so the measurement runs through `photoFileToSprite` → `refineWithModel` →
  `chooseTuning`, **the path that ships**. Gated on `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1`, the switch
  `model-available.spec.ts` already uses for the one test in that file that is not stubbed.
- **`apps/web/scripts/cutout-corpus-report.ts`** — headless screening for a host with network but
  no browser. Marked as a screen rather than a gate *in its own header*, because there is no
  BlazeFace outside a browser and it must fall back to the skin-colour crop: a different crop
  means the sweep sees different cells.
- **The page itself** — unchanged in purpose, now also publishing `window.__CUTOUT_REPORT__` and a
  `data-state` attribute so a machine can read it.

**Why the criteria are written before the numbers.** A criterion written afterwards is a
rationalisation, and this particular experiment is unusually easy to rationalise: the scorer is
ours, the corpus is ours, and the constants are adjustable. So the runbook says in advance what
counts as a pass, what counts as "demote it to a detector", and — the part that matters most —
that the constants may be set from the first run **once**, because setting them repeatedly until
the gate goes green is fitting to the test.

**The gate re-derives its verdict from the raw rows rather than reading the page's `gate` field,
and a sixth test asserts the two agree.** A tool that grades its own homework is not a gate; two
definitions of "damage" drifting apart is a defect in itself.

**Three criteria exist only because this feature has already been wrong twice.** Criterion 3 (never
choose a tighter threshold) and criterion 4 (never worsen a photograph by its own metrics) cannot
fail while the scorer is correct. They are there because the scorer has twice produced a tidy,
plausible report while optimising backwards — once measuring bite globally so that pruning a
bystander scored as damage, and once letting the array order break a universal tie so that every
well-photographed participant got a cell shaved off their outline. **An inverted objective does
not look like a bug; it looks like a result.** Assertions that are redundant against correct code
are the cheapest defence against that, and they say what they are for in their failure messages.

*Rejected:* adding `@huggingface/transformers` to `package.json` so the headless runner works out
of the box. The library is loaded from a CDN at run time precisely so that onnxruntime's
WebAssembly stays out of the bundle of an app whose main job on the day is showing a QR code on a
beach (ADR-033). A dev dependency for one script would undo that, and its postinstall reaches a
host this sandbox cannot resolve anyway. `npm install --no-save` is in the header instead.

*Rejected:* replaying the recorded crowd offline. `demo-participants.dump.json` holds painted
sprites, not alpha mattes, so it can say what one setting produced and nothing about a sweep.
`seedIslands.test.ts` already extracts what it can from those sprites; the rest genuinely needs
the model.

**Stated as unrun.** The runbook's §9 lists everything still untested, starting with "every runner
above". Writing a suite and reporting it as coverage is how ADR-054 shipped on a green suite that
was defending a defect.

## ADR-216 — synthetic street photographs join the crowd folder, numbered from 61, and go into git

**Context.** The demo crowd's adversarial photographs are in `images/ingest/social/`: sixty tracked PNGs, numbered `01-` to `60-`. The gate walks only the 26 top-level files, so `social/` sits outside the gate (defect C1; ADR-215 and the handoff). `corpus()` in `e2e/support/photo-stubs.ts` does read `social/`, and `photo-sprites.spec.ts` converts every photo it returns. The user asked for thirty synthetic photographs of busy Singapore scenes to join the crowd folder, numbered from 61, five men and five women in each batch, and for new photographs to go into git from now on.

**Decision.**
- Add thirty synthetic PNGs to `images/ingest/social/`: `61-front-…` to `70-front-…` (frontal, booth-style portraits) and `71-selfie-…` to `90-selfie-…` (selfie-style). Names follow the existing `NN-descriptor.png` convention.
- Track them in git. This is an exception to AGENTS-workflow §3, which says never to commit generated artefacts. It is made by the user's explicit instruction and recorded here, so it is not an unexplained deviation. Later batches of generated photographs go into git the same way.
- Every image is synthetic: AI-generated, with no real person. The provenance, with per-file detail and known problems, is in `docs/design/synthetic-social-photos.md`.
- No code changes. The gate corpus (26 top-level files) and the demo personas (80 entries, each `sourceImage` fixed) are unchanged.

**Consequences.**
- `socialPhotoCount()` is now 90, up from 60. Indices 0–59 still resolve to the same files, because the new names sort after `60-`.
- `corpus()` returns the whole adversarial folder by default, so it now returns thirty more photos. `photo-sprites.spec.ts` converts each of them, and its timeout grows with the count (90 s plus 25 s per photo). Its runtime rises by roughly thirty conversions per test. For quick local runs, `PSD_E2E_PHOTO_SAMPLE=8` keeps the corpus small, as AGENTS-workflow.md describes.
- `seed-social.spec.ts` derives its gallery stride from the count, which goes from 6 to 9. The seeded gallery therefore picks different photos.
- Git history grows by about 72 MB of PNG. Replacing or removing a photo later adds history; it does not remove it.
- This ADR takes the number the handoff reserved for the C1 decision. If the walk is extended to `social/`, that decision is ADR-217.
- Known problems, recorded and not fixed here: `71` is landscape (1408×768); `71` to `78` show the phone in frame, which the brief rules out; `79` and `80` show no outstretched arm; no image yet has the booth camera look (they are sharper and more saturated than the booth references).

**Validation.** Ran: vitest on `apps/web/src/lib/avatar/cutoutCorpus.test.ts` (4 of 4 pass: the walk and the crowd fixtures); file checks (count 90; PNG; 1024×1024 except `71`; the first seventy sorted names unchanged). Not run: the Playwright suites (`photo-sprites`, `seed-social`, `gallery`, the cut-out gate) and the headless screen, which need browsers and model hosts this sandbox cannot reach. `npm run verify` was not re-run, because no code changed.

## ADR-218 — the bus-and-coach batch joins the crowd folder, and the adversarial set sorts by number

**Context.** ADR-217 planned ten bus and coach selfies, numbered 91 to 100. They were generated as planned: five men (91 to 95) and five women (96 to 100), each taken inside a Singapore bus or a tour coach, with the corrected framing. The helpers in `e2e/support/photo-stubs.ts` index the adversarial set by position in a plain string sort. In that order `100-…` sorts between `10-…` and `11-…`, so every photo from `11-…` upward would move one index. That breaks the stable-index promise in ADR-216 and ADR-217, and it would change which photo `busyPhoto(k)` returns and which photos the seed-social stride picks.

**Decision.**

- No other helper changes. `corpus()` keeps its existing sort, so its iteration order changes only where the new `100-…` file falls.
- Everything else is as in ADR-216 and ADR-217: the gate corpus (26 top-level files) and the demo personas are unchanged, and each new batch goes into git as it is made.

**Numbering.** ADR-217 said the C1 decision would be ADR-218. This ADR takes that number, so the C1 decision is now ADR-219 if it is taken.

**Consequences.**
- `socialPhotoCount()` is 100, up from 90. The seed-social stride goes from 9 to 10, so the seeded gallery picks different photos.
- `busyPhoto(k)` for k from 90 to 99 returns 91 to 100. For k from 0 to 89 it is unchanged.
- `photo-sprites.spec.ts` converts every photo from `corpus()`, so it now converts ten more than before, as ADR-216 described for the earlier additions.
- Git history grows by about 28 MB for the bus-and-coach batch.
- Known problems, recorded and not fixed here: 65 and 70 have white borders, carried from the first booth batch, and regeneration is pending. The cheap-camera look is still not achieved in any of the 100.

**Validation.** Ran: a one-off check of the comparator, transpiled from `e2e/support/photo-stubs.ts`, on the real 100 filenames (the existing 90 keep positions 0 to 89, `91-…` is at index 90, and `100-…` is last); eslint on `e2e/support/photo-stubs.ts` (clean); vitest on `apps/web/src/lib/avatar/cutoutCorpus.test.ts` (4 of 4 pass); file checks (100 PNG files; 91 to 100 are 1024×1024 RGB).
