## ADR-220 — 61 to 100 follow Singapore's citizen mix, not one group

**Context.** On 2026-10-08 the user asked that the images from 60 onward all depict "native Singaporeans, ie south asian". Singapore's citizens are not mainly South Asian. The 2025 citizen shares are about 75.5% Chinese, 15.1% Malay, 7.6% Indian (the South Asian group) and 1.8% Eurasian and others (Wikipedia's "Singaporeans" page; the 2020 census as reported by the Straits Times). ADR-194 records that Singaporean players are "Chinese, Malay and Indian". The forty generated photos, 61 to 100, showed 16 Chinese, 8 Malay, 8 Indian and 8 Eurasian subjects, by the prompt record. Asked to choose, the user picked a census match for 61 to 100, and asked that image 60 be left unchanged until its source is confirmed.

**Decision.**
- The forty generated photos, 61 to 100, follow the citizen mix: 30 Chinese, 6 Malay, 3 Indian (South Asian) and 1 Eurasian or other.
- Fourteen subjects are changed. Each becomes a Chinese subject with the same gender, setting and framing: 65, 67, 68, 70, 72, 74, 79, 82, 85, 87, 89, 94, 97 and 98. The headscarves in 67 and 97 are dropped.
- The other 26 stay as they are: Chinese 61, 64, 66, 69, 71, 75, 76, 80, 81, 84, 86, 90, 91, 95, 96 and 100; Malay 62, 73, 78, 83, 88 and 93; Indian 63, 77 and 92; Eurasian 99.
- Image 60 is unchanged. It belongs to the original 1 to 60 set, and its source is not recorded.
- File names, numbering and sort order are unchanged. Each batch keeps five men and five women.
- The replacements use the blocks in the provenance doc, with the full-bleed, no-border opener from ADR-219.
- The generated files are committed under the exception to AGENTS-workflow §3 recorded in ADR-216.

**Consequences.**
- The folder still holds 100 photos at the same names and positions. The gate corpus (26 top-level files) and the demo personas (which use images 1 to 60) are unchanged.
- The 14 PNGs add about 38 MB to git history.
- The ethnicity in each row is the prompt's specification. It was not checked by eye, and appearance is not a reliable basis for judging ethnicity. If the mix needs verifying, a person should check the faces.
- Several frames show legible background signs (for example GEYLANG BAZAAR in 67), against the prompt. Recorded as a known problem in the provenance doc. Not fixed here.
- Numbering: ADR-219 gave the C1 decision the number ADR-220. This ADR takes that number, so the C1 decision is now ADR-221 if taken.

**Validation.** Ran: file checks on all 14 (PNG, RGB, 1024×1024; the 100 names match HEAD, and the other 86 files are unchanged); a border check (near-white edge fraction 0.002 to 0.023, against 1.0 for the old 65); a side-by-side visual check of old and new frames for framing, clothing, setting, the no-border rule and the selfie rule (arm from the bottom edge, no phone in view); a count of the provenance table (30 Chinese, 6 Malay, 3 Indian, 1 Eurasian; 20 men and 20 women). Not run: an ethnicity check (not possible from images, see above); vitest (no code changed); the Playwright gate and the headless screen (hosts unreachable from this sandbox); `npm run verify`.

## ADR-221 — the cut-out model runs on WebAssembly, never WebGPU

**Supersedes ADR-045's device ladder** (the rest of ADR-045, that a failed device must not poison the next, stands but no longer has a second device to protect).

**Context.** A participant took a selfie on a real webcam and the sprite came back with chunks of their face missing: forehead, both cheeks, jaw. The hint said "Background removed", so MODNET had answered and the colour fallback was not involved. The captured frame (640×480, well lit, face large in the frame) was saved from the `toBlob('image/png')` call and run through the shipped pipeline in Chromium, once with `navigator.gpu` hidden and once with the browser left alone:

| device | mean raw alpha over the face rectangle | face-rectangle background cells at threshold 128 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WebAssembly | 232 / 255 | 375 |
| WebGPU (Chromium's default on this Mac) | 157 / 255 | 1735 |

Same crop box, same code, same fp32 weights (`Xenova/modnet` resolves to the 25.9 MB `model.onnx`). The WebGPU matte put holes through the forehead, cheek and nose; `trimEdge` and `pruneIslands` left the count unchanged, so nothing downstream removed the face. The matte arrived damaged. The same frame measured in plain Node (onnxruntime-node, CPU) read 98.9 % of face pixels ≥ 128, which agrees with the WebAssembly figure.

**Decision.** `devicesToTry()` in `segmentPhoto.ts` returns `['wasm']`. WebGPU is not asked for, and the browser is no longer asked for an adapter. A correct cut-out beats a fast wrong one, and no threshold can recover a face the model already scored low.

**What was not established.** *Why* WebGPU is wrong: reduced precision in an fp32 operator on this GPU, a Transformers.js WebGPU kernel, or Chromium's backend. Only the symptom is measured, on one machine and one frame. Other GPUs may be fine; this decision does not claim otherwise, it declines to find out on a participant's face.

**Cost, measured** (`apps/web/scripts/cutout-timing.ts --headed`, Google Chrome, Apple Metal 3 adapter, the same webcam frame, 5 warm runs): WebAssembly **1282 ms** per photo once the model is loaded (4.7 s the first time, which is mostly the download); WebGPU **81 ms** (4.3 s first). That is about 16 times slower per photo, roughly 1.2 s more on a one-off selfie. The same run reproduced the damage on the real GPU (mean face alpha 139 on WebGPU against 198 on WebAssembly), so it is not an artefact of a software adapter. An earlier headless-Chromium run read 44 s for WebGPU; its adapter was almost certainly a software fallback and that figure should be ignored.

**Consequences.** About 1.2 s slower per photo on devices that had WebGPU (measured above). Every Mac and Android phone that was on WebGPU is now on the same path as everything else, which also removes a device-dependent bug class. `model-available.spec.ts`'s three WebGPU tests now assert one WASM call whatever the browser offers; the "refused WebGPU costs one retry" test (ADR-041) is rewritten as "never reached", because the refusal can no longer happen.

**Rejected.** Keeping WebGPU and re-running on WASM when the face looks wrong (a second inference, plus a heuristic that is itself a guess). Worth reopening if WASM latency proves unacceptable. Also rejected: adding threshold, feather, input-size or normalisation controls. The library already uses fp32, mean/std 0.5 and a 512 short edge; the face alpha on WASM is already ≥ 232 on average; the loss was the device.

**Also fixed, found by the same measurement.** `ambiguityOf` in `cutOutScore.ts` indexed the alpha plane with the raw crop box. `locateFace.ts` builds its box from eye-distance arithmetic and never rounds, so every real box is fractional and every real call threw "Missing matte alpha". It had never been called with a real box (ADR-212 is unwired, and its fixtures use integers). It now rounds the box the way `maskFromModel` already does. `ambiguity` is a diagnostic field read only by the reports, so this cannot change what `chooseTuning` picks. Two tests in `cutOutScore.test.ts` pin it.

**Bite checks watched to fail.** Removing the `Math.round` calls from `ambiguityOf` turns both new `cutOutScore.test.ts` cases red with `Missing matte alpha`. Restoring `['webgpu', 'wasm']` turns the two rewritten `segmentPhoto.test.ts` cases red (the adapter is requested, and `device: 'webgpu'` is asked for).

**Not run.** The rewritten `model-available.spec.ts` tests load (`playwright --list`) but could not be executed here: the participant sign-in form stays disabled in this environment, which also fails the unchanged tests and the original code, so it is not caused by this change. `npm run verify` was not run in full.

**Tools left behind** (dev-only, outside `src/`): `apps/web/tools/cutoutHook.ts` + `apps/web/cutout-hook.html` expose `window.__PSD_CUTOUT_RUN__`; `apps/web/scripts/cutout-full-report.ts` walks all 86 corpus photographs in Chromium and writes a before/after page; `apps/web/scripts/cutout-probe.ts` runs one image with WebGPU hidden and not, and prints where face cells vanish. `/corpus/social/*` in `vite.config.ts` serves the sixty photographs `listCutoutCorpus` does not reach; that walk, and defect C1, are unchanged.

## ADR-222 — the references after the squash and the WASM renumbering match the register

**Context.** Three things left references in this register and in the docs out of step with each other.

1. Five commits, `6d97e00`..`861f3dc`, were squashed into one, `81809c5`, on top of `53440fa`. The tree is the same. The pre-squash commits are no longer on the branch, but their objects are still in the local object store. ADR-217 (`6d97e00`) and ADR-219 (`c10c097`) point at them.
2. The WASM cut-out commits `5b5d10f`, `274f306` and `2d8751e` name ADR-216 in their messages. The decision they record was renumbered to ADR-221 in `bbdc7eb`. ADR-216 is the synthetic-photo decision. Commit messages are not rewritten.
3. ADR-216 to ADR-220 each gave the C1 decision a fixed number. Each of ADR-217 to ADR-220 took the number the entry before had reserved, and reserved the next one. ADR-220 reserved ADR-221, which is now the WASM decision. Four docs gave a stale next number: the ADR-212 handoff and the cut-out chooser validation named ADR-216 for a pending decision, `docs/outstanding-tasks.md` named ADR-170, and the 2026-10-08 snapshot named ADR-216 as the next free number.

**Decision.** No accepted entry is edited. The references are corrected in the docs, and this entry records the mapping.

- **Pre-squash SHAs.** `6d97e00`..`861f3dc` is now `81809c5`, and `861f3dc` is the pre-squash head. To read a removed or bordered file, use `git show 861f3dc:<path>` or `git show c10c097:<path>`.
- **ADR-216 in the WASM commits.** In `5b5d10f`, `274f306` and `2d8751e`, "ADR-216" means ADR-221.
- **C1.** The C1 decision takes the next free number when it is taken. The fixed numbers that ADR-216 to ADR-220 gave it are void.
- **Pending decisions.** A pending decision takes the next free number when it lands. `docs/design/adr-212-handoff.md` (lines 243 and 281), `docs/design/cutout-chooser-validation.md` (line 101) and `docs/outstanding-tasks.md` (lines 17 and 517) no longer name a number.
- **Snapshot.** `docs/outstanding-adrs-2026-10-08.md` is a dated snapshot. It gets a status note, and its body is not updated.
- **Provenance.** `docs/design/synthetic-social-photos.md` says the bordered files are in the pre-squash history at `c10c097`.

**Consequences.**
- ADR-210 to ADR-221 are unchanged. A reader who follows an old C1 number finds this entry.
- A clone that does not have `861f3dc` cannot read the pre-squash files. That is the cost of the squash. The pre-squash head is recorded here, so the objects can be recovered while they exist.
- No code, data or test changes.

**Validation.** Docs only. Ran: every `ADR-NNN` reference outside this register matches a heading in the register (`^#{2,3} ADR-`), and every backticked hex string of seven or more characters in the docs and the register resolves with `git cat-file -e`, except four that are not commits: the `MOTIF_VERSION` digests `55545560` and `803ac592`, the `ART_VERSION` digest `8222f306`, and an all-digit test string. Not run: `npm run verify`, because no code changed, and the lint step on `bbdc7eb` already fails on `apps/web/scripts/cutout-preview-report.ts`. Not run either: Playwright, the headless screen and the demo recording.

## ADR-223 — the demo personas gain one entry for each of photos 61 to 100

**Context.** The demo crowd is seeded from the personas in `scripts/demo-personas.json`, and `npm run demo:record` records each one as a real onboarding (ADR-040). The file named 80 personas: the 20 top-level `social-NN-*` photos, and the 60 photos in `images/ingest/social/` numbered 01 to 60. ADR-216 to ADR-220 added the 40 photos numbered 61 to 100, and none of them had a persona. The user asked for every corpus avatar to be a seed user, for each photo persona's ethnicity to be assessed, and for each image to get a suitable name.

**Decision.**
- Add one persona for each of photos 61 to 100, in photo order, after the existing 80. The 20 top-level personas are kept. The file now holds 120 personas: 100 for `social/` and 20 top-level.
- **Ethnicity.** For 61 to 100 the ethnicity is the word in each photo's subject line in the generation record (`docs/design/synthetic-social-photos.md`, Files table): 30 Chinese, 6 Malay, 3 Indian and 1 Eurasian. It was not judged from the faces. The names follow it.
- **Names.** Each nickname is `First_Last`, unique across the 120 (case-insensitive), and within the contract's rules: 3 to 20 characters, letters, digits and underscores, not all digits. The Personas table in `docs/design/synthetic-social-photos.md` lists each one with its label, gender, ethnicity, cluster and variant.
- **Gender** follows the photo's subject line: 20 male and 20 female. **Cluster** cycles through the 16 seed clusters. **Avatar variant** cycles through 1 to 5. **PIN** continues the 1000 + 37 × n sequence, from 3960.
- **Persona labels.** 26 of the 40 reuse one of the 20 labels the existing 80 use. The other 14 each have a new label, so the file has 34 labels in all.
- **The existing 80 are unchanged.** Their names, PINs, clusters, variants and labels stay. The repo has no ethnicity record for photographs 01 to 60 or the top-level 20, and this ADR does not assess them from their faces. Naming them needs a stated identity for each photo, from a source.

**Not done.** The recorded dump is not updated. `scripts/demo-participants.dump.json` still holds the 80 recorded participants, so `npm run seed:demo` seeds 80 until `npm run demo:record` runs on a host that can reach the model hosts (`huggingface.co`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `storage.googleapis.com`, `cdn.playwright.dev`). The dump is recorded, not written (ADR-040), so the 40 cannot be added by hand. After the re-record, these need updating: the header of `scripts/seed-demo.mjs` ("80 recorded participants", "eighty real onboardings"), `AGENTS-workflow.md` (line 83) and `.env.example` (line 67).

**Consequences.**

## ADR-224 — the cropper's photograph shows the backdrop behind the person

**Context.** `AvatarStudio` is the one avatar control that sign-up and the profile's look editor both use. When a participant uses a photograph, the studio shows it in three places: the 128-pixel preview at the top, the square cropper over the photograph, and the "My photo" thumbnail in the character row, close to the characters. The preview and the thumbnail already showed the photograph cut out onto the chosen backdrop. The cropper showed the raw photograph, so a participant placing the square was looking at a picture that did not match the one they would get.

**Decision.**
- The cropper shows the photograph with the chosen backdrop behind the person: the colour, and the pattern when one is on. `apps/web/src/lib/avatar/backdropPreview.ts` paints the whole frame at the photograph's own size.
- It reuses the saved sprite's functions rather than copying them. The background decision is `backgroundCells`, the first half of `paintPrepared` moved out unchanged. The pattern is `paintSpriteSunburst`, now exported from `avatars.ts` without change.
- It follows the settled cut-out tuning, which is the tuning the saved sprite is painted from. "Leave it in" shows the raw photograph, as the thumbnail does.
- It is an overlay laid over the raw image, not a new source for it. The raw image seeds the square when it loads. Changing its source would re-seed the square each time a backdrop was tapped.
- `useBackdropPreview` builds the picture after the tap has painted, encodes it as a PNG blob URL, and revokes each URL when it is replaced or the cropper goes away. Where the browser cannot encode, the cropper shows the raw photograph, as it did before.

**What differs from the saved sprite.** The saved sprite decides inside the crop square, on a 128-cell grid. The picture decides over the whole frame, which is resampled onto a 256-cell square first, because the cut-out rules are written for square grids. Where the square's edge would change what the matte or the colour rules decide, the two can differ. The saved sprite is not changed: the refactor is a move, and the `photoSprite` suite passes.

**Consequences.**
- The change is visible on both screens that contain the studio: sign-up (`#surf-signup`, F1 `#feat-signup`) and the profile look editor (`#surf-profile`, F4 `#feat-profile`).
- Nothing that is saved changes, so the recorded dump (ADR-072, ADR-223) is not regenerated.
- The cropper still dims everything outside the square, as it did for the raw photograph. The backdrop outside the square therefore looks darker. That is existing behaviour and is not changed here.
- With a real matte the picture will follow the person more closely than it does with the stand-in, which is an ellipse with a rectangle for shoulders.

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-224. The real-model rebuild that was planned as ADR-224 takes ADR-225 when it lands.

**Not done.** The recorder's photo-less branch still drops a photograph by clicking `profile__persona` with `.first()`, which selects the first character. That is the cause of the four variant rows recorded as character 1 in the current dump. It is a separate decision, and this entry does not change it.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- Unit, `apps/web` vitest on the touched suites: `backdropPreview.test.ts` (7), `useBackdropPreview.test.ts` (12), `PhotoCropper.test.tsx` (12), `photoSprite.test.ts` (15), `cutOut.test.ts` (23) and `sunburst.test.ts` (11). 80 of 80 pass.
- Typecheck of `apps/web` and ESLint on the changed files: clean.
- E2E in Chromium with the stand-in matte and face finder, `e2e/participant/photo-backdrop-preview.spec.ts`, on `desktop-chrome` and `mobile-chrome`: 3 tests, 6 runs, all pass. The tests read the picture's pixels in the browser. The corner is the backdrop colour, within 2 per channel. The square's placement does not change when the backdrop does. "Leave it in" removes the picture and "Take it out" brings it back. The sign-up screen shows the same picture.
- Existing studio suites (`cut-out-tuning`, `participant-signup`, `photo-sprites`, `selfie`, `signout`) on `desktop-chrome` with video off: 3 pass and 24 fail. The unmodified commit gives the same 24 failures with the same titles. Twenty-three are timeouts in the UI sign-in helper, and one is the sign-out test missing its landing button. The studio code is not reached in those runs, so they give no signal here.
- Recording walk: `PSD_DEMO_LIMIT=3 npm run demo:record`, in stand-in mode. 1 passed, in 12.7 s. The walk signs up through the real form and uses the studio. It ran before two edits that do not change behaviour (a comment, and `required` in place of a fallback), which the final verify and the browser spec both cover. The dump was restored afterwards, byte-identical to the committed file.
- Screenshots of the cropper on mobile and desktop, checked by eye.
- `npm run verify`: passes on the final tree (exit 0): typecheck, lint, standards (560 files, 17 rules, 0 violations), `build:web`, API tests (800 passed, 3 skipped), web tests (1,485 passed), and coverage above all four thresholds (branches 98.47%, against 98.4%).
- Not run: the real models (`huggingface.co`, `storage.googleapis.com` and `cdn.jsdelivr.net` are unreachable from this sandbox), WebKit (not installed), real phones, and the full 120-persona walk.

## ADR-225 — the small picture beside the cut-out choices wears the backdrop pattern

**Context.** ADR-224 made the cropper's picture show the chosen backdrop behind the person. The studio shows the same photograph in four places. Three already wore the pattern: the 128-pixel preview at the top (`avatar-studio__preview`), the "My photo" thumbnail in the character row (`avatar-studio__photo-option`), and the cropper's overlay (ADR-224). The fourth is the 96-pixel picture beside "Tap a choice to see it change." (`cut-out-controls__preview`), which shows the cut-out while the participant tunes it. It was painted by `photoSpriteUrl(sprite)`, which had no pattern argument. It therefore showed the plain backdrop colour whichever pattern was chosen, while the other pictures showed the pattern.

**Decision.**
- `photoSpriteUrl(sprite, sunburst)` paints the backdrop pattern with `paintSpriteSunburst`, the call `avatarSvg` already makes for a photograph. `sunburst` is a required argument, not a defaulted one, so leaving the pattern out is a compile error.
- `CutOutControls` takes the pattern as a `sunburst` prop. `PhotoRow` reads it from the look it already holds, `readAvatarLook(props.avatarLook).sunburst`, the same source the thumbnail and the preview use.
- Nothing is saved differently. The stored sprite still holds one backdrop colour, as ADR-173 requires, and the pattern is painted when the picture is drawn. The saved sprite, the committed dump (ADR-072, ADR-223) and the seed are not regenerated.

**Consequences.**
- For any pattern, the 96-pixel picture, the thumbnail and the top preview are one picture. `photoSpriteUrl(sprite, look.sunburst)` gives the same address as `avatarUrl` for the saved avatar with that look, and a unit test pins it.
- The change shows on sign-up (`#surf-signup`, F1 `#feat-signup`) and on the profile look editor (`#surf-profile`, F4 `#feat-profile`), the same screens as ADR-224.
- No earlier decision is renamed or removed, so the supersession index (ADR-139) needs no row. ADR-073 still describes the tuning preview, which now also shows the pattern. ADR-224 stands.

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-225. ADR-224 says the real-model rebuild takes ADR-225 when it lands. The rebuild now takes ADR-226. ADR-224 is not edited.

**Not done.** The cropper's overlay (ADR-224) and the saved picture centre the pattern differently. `backdropPreview` lays the pattern over the whole photograph, so its centre is the photograph's centre. The saved sprite and the thumbnail lay it over the crop square, so their centre is the square's centre, because the pattern centres on `size / 2` of whichever grid it is given (`avatar/sunburst.ts`). In the desktop screenshot taken for this entry, the overlay's centre sits about 30 px below the square's centre, on a frame about 276 px across. Matching them needs the crop box, which changes on release, so it is a separate decision. The overlay is unchanged here.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- E2E, red then green: `e2e/participant/photo-backdrop-preview.spec.ts`, Chromium 153 with the stand-in matte and face finder, video off. The new test, "the small picture beside the cut-out choices wears the pattern as well", failed on the code before this change, at its first pattern check. After the change the spec passes on `desktop-chrome` and `mobile-chrome`: 4 tests × 2 projects = 8 runs, all pass. The new test reads the three picture addresses from the page. It requires the square to equal the thumbnail and the preview for each of the four patterns, and to differ from the plain colour.
- Unit, `apps/web` vitest, targeted: `avatars.test.ts` and `CutOutControls.test.tsx`, 80 of 80 pass. The three new tests are the parity test (`photoSpriteUrl` gives the saved picture's address), the pattern-in-the-square test, and the plain-colour test.
- `npm run verify`: exit 0. Typecheck; lint (`eslint .`) clean; standards 560 files, 17 rules, 0 violations; `build:web`; API 57 files and 800 tests pass, 3 skipped; web 139 files and 1,488 tests pass (1,485 before this change). Coverage: web statements and lines 99.14%, branches 98.47% (threshold 98.4%), functions 98.67%.
- E2E, `e2e/participant/cut-out-tuning.spec.ts` on `desktop-chrome`: all 5 fail in the UI sign-in helper, with `signin-form__submit` never stable, before the studio opens. This is the sandbox problem recorded for ADR-224. It does not reach the changed code and is not counted as a pass.
- By eye: desktop screenshots of the cropper and of the 96-pixel picture, with the spiral on. The small picture now shows the spiral behind the person. The screenshots are not kept in the repository.
- Not run: the real models (`huggingface.co`, `storage.googleapis.com` and `cdn.jsdelivr.net` are unreachable from this sandbox), WebKit (not installed), real phones, the recording walk (saved data does not change), and the full 120-persona walk.

## ADR-227 — removing a photo needs no character first, and the removal waits for the save

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. Supersedes ADR-059 in part: its gate on Remove, and only that. The row is in the supersession index above.

**Context.** ADR-059 kept "Remove my photo" disabled until a character had been picked since the photo went on, because an avatar is never nothing. The disabled button said nothing on its own, and the reason sat in a hint. A participant who had not yet picked a character could not take their photo off at all (F5, observed in the Turn 3 walkthrough). Pressing Remove also dropped the photo from the draft at once, so there was no way back before the save (N4, observed). Recolouring a worn photo on a character change did not happen either: `setPersona` moved the backdrop and left the photo in the old colour (F4, observed).

**Decision.**
- "Remove my photo" is enabled whenever a photo is worn. Pressing it moves the selection to the next character, and that character's kit comes with it, as choosing a character does. The next character is `nextVariant`: the next in the row, and the last one wraps to the first. The gender does not change.
- The photo is held, not dropped. It stays on the row as "My photo", unselected, with the hint "Your photo will be removed when you save. Press My photo to keep it." Pressing "My photo" brings it back, recoloured to the backdrop chosen at that point.
- While a removal is pending the draft carries `avatarPhoto: null`, so Save sends the removal and nothing else. The held picture is view state. It lasts while the editor is open and goes when the editor closes, on save or on cancel.
- A new photograph replaces a pending removal.
- Choosing a character still does not take a worn photo off (ADR-059). A worn photo now wears the new character's backdrop in the same change (F4), as `setBackdrop` already did.

**Why.** Rejected: keeping the gate and putting its reason on the button. A participant wearing a photo would still have to pick a character they did not want before taking the photo off, which is the obstacle the request removes. Also rejected: dropping the photo at once, as before. It cannot be undone before the save, and nothing tells the participant it is going. Holding the picture in view state needs no server change: the save already sends an explicit `avatarPhoto` (ADR-031), so the database and the API see exactly the request they saw before.

**Consequences.**
- The save path is unchanged. Profile and sign-up still send an explicit `avatarPhoto`, null or the sprite. The server side of a removal (cache and phone) is ADR-228.
- The worn-photo hint changed. The old copy told the participant to pick a character to remove the photo. It now reads "Your photo is on. Remove my photo takes it off when you save." Copy is a default; the owner has not signed it off.
- Sign-up and the profile look editor both behave the same way, because both use `AvatarStudio`. The FDS anchors are `#surf-signup`, `#feat-signup`, `#surf-profile` and `#feat-profile`. The spec is silent on removing a photo, so this is a gap the register fills rather than a deviation from a stated rule.
- Also in this change, with no decision of its own: the original photograph's object URL is released when a newer one replaces it and when the studio unmounts (N6). Nothing revoked it before.

**Not done.**
- Wrap-around at the last character (five goes to one) is a default, not confirmed.
- The pending copy and the "My photo" label are defaults, not confirmed.
- The phone and the server still keep the removed face until ADR-228 lands in the same branch.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- Unit, `apps/web` vitest. `AvatarStudio.test.tsx` (new, six tests: removal with no character picked; the wrap from five to one; the held photo brought back; choosing a character keeping the photo; the backdrop recolour on a character change; the recolour on restore), `avatars.test.ts` (`nextVariant`, two tests), and the gate expectations in `acceptance/signup.test.tsx` and `routes-participant/participant-pages.test.tsx`, which were rewritten for the new rule. The N6 test in `signup.test.tsx` checks the release. Targeted run: four files, 163 tests, all pass before the N6 test was added; the N6 test passes on its own.
- E2E, `e2e/participant/photo-removal.spec.ts` (new), Chromium 153 from the `@sparticuz/chromium` tarball, `desktop-chrome`, video off. The participant is signed up and given a saved photo through the API, so the sign-in form is not involved. Two tests pass: removal with no character picked, pending until save, and genuinely gone after the reload; and "My photo" keeping the photo through the save. The server-side check after the save belongs to ADR-228, so it is not in this commit.
- Not run here: `e2e/participant/photo-sprites.spec.ts`, `model-available.spec.ts` and `e2e/acceptance/demo-onboarding.spec.ts` need the UI sign-in helper, which fails here (the submit button detaches, as recorded for ADR-224 and ADR-225). Their edits in this commit (the character click before Remove is gone, and the worn-hint copy in `e2e/support/photo-stubs.ts`) are not checked in a browser.
- Typecheck, lint and standards: pass. Full `npm run verify` is run before the push.
- Not run: the real models (`huggingface.co`, `storage.googleapis.com` and `cdn.jsdelivr.net` are unreachable from this sandbox), WebKit, and real phones.

## ADR-228 — a removed photo leaves the server and the phone at the save, and a save that omits the photo keeps it

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. Supersedes in part ADR-035 (a removed face stays on the device) and the ADR-038 cache comment (a face taken off may still be served). Both rows are in the supersession index above.

**Context.** The API probe that found N1 (observed, Turn 4) showed the server still serving a removed face from its cache after the save cleared the row. A save that carried a photo and then failed wrote the whole sprite into the error log (N2, observed): drizzle's failed-query error puts the bound values in its message, and the handler logged the error object. The server also took a photo off whenever the save omitted it, because it wrote `input.avatarPhoto ?? null` (N5). The studio always sends the field, so nothing had been lost, but the contract was a trap. On the phone, a removed face stayed in `psd.sprites.v1` (N3). The cap there is 150 faces (`MAX_ENTRIES` in `spriteCache.ts`), not the 400 ADR-035 mentions, and the plan's figure of 400 is corrected here.

**Decision.**
- **Server.** A save that replaces or takes off a photo forgets the replaced face in this process's sprite cache, after the save has committed. The old photo is read under a row lock in the same transaction, so the face taken off is the face the row actually held.
- **Race guard.** A read takes the cache epoch before it queries, and writes its results back only if the epoch has not moved. A read that was in flight when a face came off cannot put it back (`rememberSpriteBody`).
- **Three-valued photo at the API.** `avatarPhoto` as a sprite replaces the photo, `null` takes it off, and an omitted key keeps whatever is worn. The response shape does not change.
- **Logs.** An unhandled error is logged as a report (`describeUnhandledError`), not as the error object. The report has the name, the message with the bound values left out, the SQL text with its placeholders, the database's code, constraint, table and column, the cause chain without its `detail`, and the stack frames. Any sprite that still appears in a logged string is replaced by `[photo]`. The demo export CLI logs the same report. Other log sinks checked: the setup CLI prints DDL and role advice, and the export CLI prints row counts. Neither carries participant data.
- **Phone.** The phone that removes or replaces a photo forgets that face in `psd.sprites.v1` and in the provider's memory, once the server has accepted the save. A failed save keeps it, because the server still has the face. Only the removing device does this.

**Why.** Rejected: a time-to-live on the cache. It leaves a window after the removal, and a purge at commit is immediate in the process that saved. The deployment is one container (ADR-043), so that process is the one that serves. Rejected: a lock around every avatar read. The epoch is one counter, and a missed write-back costs one extra query. Rejected: pruning faces on other phones. The server cannot reach them, and what to prune is an owner's call (plan N3). Keeping the original image so a saved photo can be re-framed is not recommended (plan section 5.3).

**Consequences.**
- `GET /api/avatars` answers for a face only while a row holds it, in this process. The Turn 4 probe's steps 5 and 6 are now a test.
- The log line `[api] unhandled error` receives a report object. Anything that greps the log for an `Error` object's fields must read the report instead.
- A save that omits `avatarPhoto` no longer removes the photo. A client that means to remove a photo must send `null`. The studio and sign-up both do.
- Known limits, stated and not fixed: another process's cache would still hold a face (one container is assumed; ADR-043); other phones keep the faces they already fetched; backups and screenshots are not controlled (plan section 5.4, rows g and h); a read in flight at the moment of the save can still return the old face to that one request.

**Not done.** Pruning ids that no loaded data refers to, on any phone (owner's call, plan N3). Backup retention (owner's call). The 150 against 400 discrepancy is recorded here, not changed.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- API, vitest against the real schema: `avatar-removal.test.ts` (new, four tests: a removed face is not served from a warm cache; an omitted photo is kept; a replaced face is forgotten and the new one served; a face another participant still wears is still served after one participant takes theirs off). `avatar-error-log.test.ts` (new): one report for an injected failure that carries a photo, the photo absent from the logged text, the constraint named; and unit tests of `describeUnhandledError` using drizzle's own error class. `cache.test.ts`: the epoch guard. The four files pass, 35 tests.
- Mutation check: with the purge call disabled, the two N1 tests fail. The call was restored afterwards and the file matches the commit.
- Web, vitest: `spriteCache.test.ts` (forgets one face and keeps the others and their order; does nothing for an unknown id), `SpriteProvider.test.tsx` (forgetting drops the face from memory and from the device, and keeps the rest), and `participant-pages.test.tsx` (unchanged, passes).
- E2E, `e2e/participant/photo-removal.spec.ts`, Chromium 153, `desktop-chrome`, video off: after a removal is saved, the server serves nothing for the face and the phone's cache does not hold it (N1 and N3, in a browser). After a kept photo is saved, both still hold it.
- Typecheck, lint and standards: pass.
- Not run: real phones (iOS Safari, Android Chrome), processes other than the one that saved, and the sign-in-helper specs (the same sandbox limit as ADR-227).

## ADR-229 — the photo is taken, framed and cut out in a dialog; Done commits it, Cancel discards it

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. Supersedes in part ADR-056 (the square confirmed inline), ADR-073 (the controls beneath the square, on the studio screen) and ADR-079 (the tuning reaching the draft at each settled knob turn). The three rows are in the supersession index above. ADR-079's guarantee stands: the saved photo carries the tuning.

**Context.** Observed in the Turn 3 walkthrough: six cut-out groups and 36 controls shown together beneath the square (F7); a studio 1,413 pixels tall on a phone (F16); contradictory hints after "Choose the square myself" (F9); "Keep what you had" left the square open (F6); and no way to re-frame a saved photo, because the original is not kept (F10). Read from code: a conversion wrote the draft as soon as the picture was ready (`onPhoto(quick.sprite)`), before the participant had confirmed the square, so there was nothing to discard.

**Decision.**
- The photo's own screen is a dialog, `PhotoDialog`, portalled to the document body. It opens when a picture is taken, chosen or replaced, and it holds the whole conversion: the picture, the square, the cut-out controls and the selfie camera.
- Done ("Use this square") is the only thing that writes the photo to the draft. Cancel and Escape discard the conversion and its object URL. A conversion that finishes after a Cancel is ignored.
- A worn photo is replaced through "Replace my photo", which opens the dialog at its first step. The original is not kept, so a saved photo is never framed again in place (ADR-227, plan 5.3).
- The dialog meets the four things a dialog owes its user: focus moves in on open and returns to what opened it on close; Tab stays inside; Escape cancels; the page under it is covered. It is a `div` with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`, not a native `<dialog>`, because the unit environment has no `showModal`, and the focus rules are short enough to write here.
- One hint and one set of actions per stage (F9). Manual framing has no separate state, because the square is always there in the dialog, so "Choose the square myself" is gone. The cropper's "Keep what you had" is "Cancel" (F6).
- The sign-up dialog is portalled out of the sign-up form, and every control in it has an explicit type.

**Why.** Rejected: a full-page photo step (plan alternative B), which needs draft persistence across navigation and a way back, so it is more change. Rejected: keeping the square inline and collapsing the groups (plan alternative C), which leaves the studio tall (F16). Rejected: committing at each knob turn (ADR-079's timing). A dialog that writes as it goes cannot be cancelled, and Cancel has to mean discard.

**Consequences.**
- The draft's photo changes only at Done. Sign-up and the profile save the same thing the dialog shows at Done.
- Escape and Cancel discard. A participant who wants the photo they had keeps it by pressing Cancel, not Done.
- Chromium confirms the flow. Safari, VoiceOver, TalkBack and the camera prompt over the dialog on a phone are not checked.
- E2E specs that converted a photo and expected it worn now press Done or check that the dialog closed.

**Not done.**
- F7 is partly addressed. The three chooser rows (How much to cut away, Stray bits, Edge) still show together under the square. Moving them behind "Fine tune" would change the main controls, which was not part of this decision. The sliders are already behind "Fine tune", closed by default.
- F16 is not re-measured: the studio's height on a phone was not measured after this change.
- The overlay's centring is unchanged; the user has not asked for a change.
- F8 labels and F14, F15 wording are deferred (ADR-232 covers F8's hex; the wording is a decision for the owner).

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- Unit and acceptance, vitest (apps/web): `acceptance/signup.test.tsx` (the photo flows now press Done; two new tests: Cancel discards and the dialog stays outside the form; Replace opens with focus inside, Escape closes it and the photo stays worn; N6 is now release on Cancel). `components/participant` (AvatarStudio, CutOutControls, PhotoCropper, SpriteProvider and the rest) and `participant-pages.test.tsx`. 235 tests across 14 files pass, before the two new dialog tests were added, and those two pass on their own.
- E2E, Chromium 153, `desktop-chrome`, video off. `e2e/participant/photo-dialog.spec.ts` (new): a real corpus photo is converted inside the dialog; Cancel leaves the saved photo on the server; Done replaces it at the save and the old face is gone. `e2e/participant/photo-removal.spec.ts`: still passes. 3 tests pass in total.
- Typecheck, lint and standards: pass.
- Not run: the sign-in-helper specs (`cut-out-tuning`, `photo-backdrop-preview`, `photo-sprites`, `selfie`, `model-available`, `demo-onboarding`). Those that refer to the old hint were edited, and none of them ran here. The sign-in helper fails in this sandbox.
- Not run: the real models (`huggingface.co`, `storage.googleapis.com` and `cdn.jsdelivr.net` are unreachable here). The browser run refuses the cut-out model, so the colour cut-out is what was exercised, and cut-out quality was not judged.

## ADR-230 — pattern looks are saved, and a look the database refuses is a 422 that names the look

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. Supersedes in part ADR-173 (the look check): the check now accepts the tagged patterns. The row is in the supersession index above.

**Context.** The check on `participant.avatar_look` was written for the untagged look and the untagged sunburst (ADR-173). ADR-205 to ADR-209 then added the tagged formats (spiral, rings, waves and swirls), and no later change widened the check. The API accepted those looks (the contracts parser reads them) and the database refused them, so every save of a pattern look failed with a server error (F1, observed in the Turn 3 walkthrough and reproduced at API level in Turn 4). The failure also logged the photo (N2, fixed in ADR-228).

**Decision.**
- The check is widened to the tagged format in both places the schema states it: the column definition and the idempotent drop-and-add at the foot of `schema.sql` (ADR-173's pattern). The new regex accepts every canonical look the contracts writer produces, and it is a superset of the old one, so every row already stored still passes the `ADD CONSTRAINT`.
- A look the database refuses is a 422 with the field named (`avatarLook`) and a message the participant can act on. It is not logged, because the request may carry a photo. The 422 is a safety net: with the widened check the API's own parser agrees with the database on every look it writes.
- The schema is applied on every boot when the role can create objects (ADR-178). An older database is migrated by its next start. A managed database whose role cannot create objects receives the widened check only after `db-provision.sh` is re-run with admin credentials (ADR-178), because `verifyWithoutDdl` checks tables and not constraints.

**Why.** Rejected: refusing the pattern looks with a 422 and leaving the check alone. The owner chose to widen it, and the parser already reads these looks. Rejected: a second column for patterns. The format already carries the tag (ADR-205), so the database only needs to read it.

**Consequences.**
- Every pattern kind saves: spiral, spiral with bands, rings, waves and swirls. The look check and the parser agree.
- A database built before this change accepts the pattern looks after its next boot. Until then, a pattern save is a 422 that names the look, and nothing is logged.
- The regex is the one place a new pattern format must be added. A future format needs its own ADR and its own check, the same way.
- The widened check is re-applied at every boot, so the drop-and-add must stay idempotent.

**Not done.** The managed-database provisioning for the widened check is not run here. A deployment whose role cannot create objects must re-run `db-provision.sh` with admin credentials before pattern looks save there (ADR-178).

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- API, vitest against the real schema: `avatar-patterns.test.ts` (new, six tests). Each of the five pattern looks saves (200), and each is a code the contracts parser reads, which the test checks. A database with the old check refuses a spiral as a 422 that names `avatarLook`, logs nothing, still saves a plain look, and then saves the spiral after `ensureSchema` runs on it. That is the migration path, on a fresh database that has no pattern rows, as an older one would be.
- The rest of the API suite runs in `npm run verify` before the push.
- Not run: the managed database and a database built by an older release of the app (only the constraint state was reproduced); the real models do not enter into this change.

## ADR-231 — Skipper is the sign-up's character, and no figure is drawn until a gender is chosen

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. Fills a gap: no earlier decision set the sign-up's default character, which was an on-screen fallback over a blank state.

**Context.** The form started with no character (`avatarVariant: null`), but the studio drew Skipper with `?? 1`. Skipper looked chosen while the form said "Please select an avatar." (F2, observed R-6). And while the gender was blank, the studio drew a male figure (`gender === '' ? 'male'`), which showed a choice nobody had made (F3, observed G-1).

**Decision.**
- The form starts with Skipper (variant 1) in its own state, so what the studio shows is what the form sends. The avatar check stays in the validation, but an untouched studio no longer fails it.
- The studio is not drawn until a gender is chosen. In its place is a hint: "Choose a gender to see the characters."

**Why.** The owner chose Skipper as the real default, over an empty selection that needs a tap. Rejected: a neutral placeholder figure while the gender is blank. It would still draw something the participant did not pick, and no neutral art exists for it.

**Consequences.**
- A participant who never touches the characters signs up as Skipper, and the card shows Skipper.
- The gender is chosen before the characters, so the photo cannot be taken before a gender either.
- The `avatarRequired` message stays in the contracts, for any path that sends no character.

**Validation.** Acceptance, vitest (apps/web): the new test "draws no figure until a gender is chosen, and sends Skipper when no character is picked (ADR-231)" passes. The beard-row test now chooses the gender first. `participant-pages.test.tsx` and `useAuthForms.test.ts` pass. The sign-up e2e specs are not run here (the sign-in helper fails in this sandbox).

**Not done.** The neutral placeholder (see Why). Whether a new participant should see the chosen character announced on the card is not decided here.

## ADR-232 — studio corrections: the hex leaves the visible text, the picker shows focus, the studio's targets are 44 px, and the toggle names what is behind it

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09.

**Context.** Four findings from the Turn 3 walkthrough, all observed. F8: the visible text wrote colours as hex ("First colour: #1D5B8C — set by the Backdrop palette above"). F11: the "Use a photo" control is a visually hidden file input under a label, and the focus rule matched the label, which never takes focus, so keyboard focus was invisible. F12: thirteen studio controls were 40 px tall on a phone, and the corner handle 24 px. F13: the toggle "Customise hair, skin and colours" did not name Build or Beard.

**Decision.**
- A colour is named in visible text: its palette name when it has one, otherwise "a custom colour". The hex stays in the colour inputs, which are where the participant reads it.
- The focus ring is drawn on the picker's label when its input has focus (`.gb-file:focus-visible + .gb-button`).
- Studio buttons and avatar choices are at least 44 px tall. The corner handle keeps its 24 px look and gets a 44 px hit area.
- The toggle names what is behind it: build for everyone, and beard for a man.

**Why.** The hex is a value the participant can read in the colour input, so the visible text names the colour instead. Rejected: a new name for every custom colour, since no palette exists for them. The 44 px figure is the repo's own reference (`docs/design/agenda-tab-plan.md` 32, citing WCAG 2.5.5).

**Consequences.**
- Visible copy changes: "a custom colour" replaces the hex for custom colours, and the toggle's text is different.
- The pattern labels ("Rays", "Twist", "Ring width", "Petal depth") are unchanged. Whether they should read more plainly is a wording decision for the owner, and it is not made here.
- The failure messages (F14, F15) are unchanged. Their wording needs the owner.

**Validation.** Unit, vitest (apps/web): `AvatarStudio.test.tsx` (two new tests: the toggle names build for everyone, and beard for a man only); `participant-pages.test.tsx` (the pattern row names the colour and no longer writes its hex, and the custom colour reads "a custom colour"). `components/participant` and the sign-up suites pass. The CSS (the focus ring, the 44 px targets and the handle's hit area) is not unit-tested and was not checked in a browser.

**Not done.** The 44 px targets, the focus ring and the handle's hit area are not measured in a browser. Pattern-control labels (F8 wording) and failure messages (F14, F15) need the owner's wording.

## ADR-233 — the photo dialog's panel is the shared dialog body, and it scrolls inside the centred overlay

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09.

**Context.** ADR-229 moved the photo's conversion into `PhotoDialog`: an overlay (`psd-modal`, the shared dialog of ADR-027) that holds the square, the cut-out controls and the selfie camera. The panel was given the class `gb-photo-dialog__panel`, and no stylesheet defined that class or `gb-photo-dialog`. Observed in the `cut-out-tuning` browser spec at 1280×720 (a failure screenshot): the panel had no background, so the studio behind showed through the controls and its text overlapped them; the square was clipped at the top edge; and the Fine tune button sat below the viewport. Read from code: the overlay centres its child (`align-items: center`), and nothing bounded the panel's height, so a panel taller than the screen overflowed both ways and could not be scrolled.

**Decision.**
- The panel uses the shared dialog body, `psd-modal__body` (paper background, ink border, shadow and width, as ADR-027 sets them for the confirmation dialog). `gb-photo-dialog__panel` stays for the photo dialog's own rules.
- The panel is at most as tall as the overlay and scrolls inside it (`max-height: 100%`, `overflow-y: auto`). The overlay keeps `align-items: center`, so the centring is not changed.

**Why.** Reusing the shared body makes the photo dialog look like the other dialogs. A bounded panel that scrolls keeps every control reachable on a short screen, and it leaves the overlay's centring as it is, which the owner has not yet asked to change. Rejected: top-aligning the overlay (`align-items: flex-start`), because that changes the centring and was not asked for.

**Consequences.**
- On a short screen the photo dialog scrolls inside its own panel. The page behind it does not scroll.
- The centring is the same as before. Top alignment is a separate decision for the owner.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- Browser, Chromium 153, desktop-chrome at 1280×720, video off: `cut-out-tuning.spec.ts`, "the fine-tune sliders reach the same numbers, and reset puts them back", passes. It clicks Fine tune, which the page could not reach before this change.
- A temporary probe, deleted after one run, measured the panel at 460×688 px, centred from y 16, with a paper background, `overflow-y: auto` and a 4 px border. Its screenshot shows the title, the square, the buttons and the Background row inside the panel. The probe was read from the browser, not from the code.
- Not run: mobile sizes, and the layout is not unit-tested (vitest does not lay out the page).

**Not done.** The centring is unchanged. The height bound was checked at one desktop size only.

## ADR-234 — the backdrop picker is used in the studio only, before the photo, because the photo dialog covers the studio

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. It supersedes ADR-224 and ADR-225 in part: the live repaint while a backdrop or pattern is picked with the square open. The index at the top of this file has the rows.

**Context.** ADR-229 put the photo's square, the cut-out choices and the selfie camera in `PhotoDialog`, an overlay over the studio. While the dialog is open the studio is under it, so the Backdrop swatches cannot be pressed. ADR-224 and ADR-225 were written for a picker that could be used while the square was open: a tap repainted the square (`useBackdropPreview` builds the picture after the tap has painted), and a pattern tap repainted the small picture beside the cut-out choices. Observed in the Turn 5 browser batch, all four `photo-backdrop-preview.spec.ts` tests failed. Three pressed a swatch that the open square covered. The fourth, the ADR-225 test, never found its three pictures matching while the square was open. Where the picker belongs while the square is open was put to the owner with `ask_user` (`backdrop_picker`).

**Decision.**
- The owner chose the studio only. The Backdrop colour and pattern are picked in the studio, while the square is closed. The photo dialog has no backdrop picker.
- The square and the small picture show the backdrop and the pattern the studio had when the photo was chosen. They cannot change while the dialog is open, because the studio is under it.
- After Use this square, a new colour or pattern recolours the worn photo (plan F4, `docs/design/avatar-studio-fix-plan.md`).
- The cut-out choices in the dialog (Leave it in, Take it out and the tuning) are not backdrop picks, and they are unchanged.

**Why.** The owner's choice, given as `in_studio`. The other option put to the owner was a picker inside the dialog. It was not chosen.

**What this leaves of ADR-224 and ADR-225.** The pictures they describe stand. The cropper shows the photograph with the chosen backdrop behind the person (ADR-224). The small picture beside the cut-out choices wears the pattern, and it is the same picture as the thumbnail and the preview once the square is committed (ADR-225). What no longer happens is the live repaint while the square is open: a tap on a backdrop cannot reach the studio then, so the square does not repaint in response to one. The checks that depended on it are replaced by the checks under Validation.

**Consequences.**
- A participant who wants a colour or a pattern behind the person picks it before the photo, or after Use this square. After Use this square the change shows on the worn photo.
- Sign-up and the profile look editor both behave this way, because they share the studio.
- The dialog does not say where the colour is picked. Its cut-out line, "We will put a colour behind you.", is unchanged.
- Nothing saved changes. The stored sprite, the committed dump (ADR-072, ADR-223) and the seed are not regenerated.

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-234. ADR-226 is still reserved for the real-model rebuild.

**Not done.** The wording of the dialog's copy, which should say that the colour is picked in the studio, is the owner's call (plan F14 and F15 are still deferred). The overlay's centring is unchanged (ADR-233).

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers. The matte and face finder are the stand-ins, so cut-out and framing quality were not judged.
- Browser, Chromium 153, video off, `e2e/participant/photo-backdrop-preview.spec.ts`, rewritten for the studio-first order: `desktop-chrome` 4 of 4 pass (18.2 s), and `mobile-chrome` 4 of 4 pass (18.1 s). The four tests: a backdrop picked in the studio is in the square (the corner is the backdrop, within 2 per channel); Leave it in removes the picture and Take it out brings it back; the sign-up screen shows the same picture; and for each look (plain, then the four patterns) the small picture is a picture of its own, and after Use this square the thumbnail and the preview at the top show the same picture the square showed.
- Mutation, `desktop-chrome`: with the pattern removed from the small picture (`CutOutControls` passes `null`, the ADR-225 bug), the pattern test fails. The saved thumbnail wears the spiral and the square shows the plain colour. The mutation was reverted, and `CutOutControls.tsx` has no diff.
- ESLint on the rewritten spec: exit 0.
- Not run: the real models (`huggingface.co`, `storage.googleapis.com` and `cdn.jsdelivr.net` are unreachable from this sandbox), WebKit, real phones, `demo-onboarding.spec.ts` (it runs only through `demo:record`), and the real-model specs.
- `npm run verify` on this tree (log read in full, exit 0): typecheck; eslint (clean); standards (568 files, 17 rules, 0 violations); `build:web`; API 60 files pass and 1 is skipped, 816 tests pass and 3 are skipped; web 141 files and 1,519 tests pass; web coverage branches 98.46% (5,439 of 5,524, gate 98.4%). The two comment-only edits (`PhotoCropper.tsx`, `useBackdropPreview.ts`) are on this tree. `verify` does not run e2e, so the browser results above are the only e2e evidence.

## ADR-235 — the demo nicknames are drawn from name pools by label and gender, once, with a fixed seed

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. It supersedes ADR-223 in part: the nicknames of the 94 photo personas that have a usable label. The index at the top of this file has the row, shared with ADR-236.

**Context.** ADR-223 gave each of photos 61 to 100 a `First_Last` nickname, and left the 80 earlier personas unchanged. The owner asked for each name to fit its photo: names from ethnicity-by-gender pools, randomised, with no duplicates. The labels come from the lookup table `docs/design/demo-identities-worksheet.csv` (ADR-236). The owner approved the pools in `scripts/demo-name-pools.json` as drafted, and approved keeping the current names where a photo has no usable label.

**Decision.**
- A persona whose photo is labelled Chinese, Malay, Indian or Eurasian takes a nickname from the pool for that label and the persona's gender: one first name and one last name, drawn at random. This covers 94 personas: 54 of photos 01 to 60, and 40 of photos 61 to 100.
- The top-level 20, photos 05, 20, 30, 38 and 60 (labelled Eurasian / Other) and photo 29 (labelled Uncertain) keep the nickname they have. The pools have no group for these labels, so no name is drawn for them.
- `scripts/draw-demo-names.mjs` does the draw. It uses the fixed seed 20261009 with a seeded pseudo-random generator, so the same inputs give the same names. It is a dry run unless `--write` is given. `--write` changes only the nickname in `scripts/demo-personas.json`, the nickname column of the lookup table, and the nickname cells of the Personas table in `docs/design/synthetic-social-photos.md`.
- A nickname is 3 to 20 characters, letters and underscores only, and unique across all 120 personas, case-insensitively. The kept names are reserved before the draw, so a drawn name cannot repeat one of them. A candidate that repeats a name or is out of range is rejected, and another is drawn.

**Why.** A draw from the label alone means no name depends on anyone's view of a face. A fixed seed makes the names reproducible, so a reviewer can run the draw again and get the same result. Rejected: naming each photo by hand, which brings judgement from appearance back in; an unseeded random draw, which cannot be reproduced or checked; a pool for the Eurasian / Other and Uncertain labels, because there is no group for them and the owner asked to keep their names. The draw's rule is stricter than the contract's, which also allows digits (`NICKNAME_PATTERN` in `packages/contracts/src/schemas.ts`). The pools contain no digits, so the stricter rule never rejects a pool name.

**Result.** The draw changed 94 nicknames: Chinese female 27, Chinese male 25, Malay female 9, Malay male 9, Indian female 11, Indian male 12, and Eurasian female 1. It kept 26. One candidate was rejected by the length or uniqueness check, and another was drawn. Gender, PIN, cluster, avatar variant, persona label and photo are unchanged. Compared field by field with HEAD, the only changed field in the file is `nickname`.

**Consequences.**
- The persona file, the lookup table and the Personas table now carry the new names.
- The recorded dump, `scripts/demo-participants.dump.json` (80 participants), and `apps/api/src/db/seed-demo.sql` still hold the old names. 54 of the dump's nicknames differ from the file now, and the other 40 personas are not in the dump. `npm run seed:demo` reads the dump, so it seeds the old names. Its closing line, "every nickname in scripts/demo-personas.json works", was already untrue for the 40 personas the dump does not hold (ADR-223), and it is untrue for the 54 renamed ones until the re-record. Neither file is regenerated here. The owner's real-model recording (`PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1 npm run demo:record`, reserved under ADR-226) writes a new dump. `apps/api/src/db/seed-demo.sql` is then regenerated by `npm run db:export-demo` after the seed is replayed, as its header says.
- `scripts/seed-demo.mjs` still says "80" in its header. That changes with the re-record (ADR-223).
- A label change alters every name drawn after it, because one seeded sequence serves the rows in order. Label changes should be made together, with an entry.

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-235. ADR-226 is still reserved for the real-model rebuild. ADR-236 records the labels this draw uses.

**Not done.** The real-model recording, which the sandbox cannot run because it cannot reach the model hosts. The top-level 20 and the six photos with no usable label keep their names until the owner gives identities for them.

**Validation.** What ran, and what each result covers:
- `node scripts/draw-demo-names.mjs`, a dry run before any write: 120 personas, 94 drawn, 94 nicknames changed, 26 kept, 1 candidate rejected. After `--write`, the dry run was run again and exited 0 with 0 nicknames changed. That is the determinism check. Before the fix in this change, the second run exited 1, because the doc-sentence check expected the old text. The check now accepts the text that `--write` applied.
- Read-only checks on the written tree, from a script outside the repo: 120 personas, with 120 nicknames unique case-insensitively and none breaking the rule. Each drawn name's first and last name is in the pool for its label and gender (94 of 94). The lookup table's nicknames and genders match the file. The 40 Personas rows in the design doc match the file on nickname and gender. No field other than `nickname` differs from HEAD.
- `eslint scripts/draw-demo-names.mjs`: exit 0.
- `npm run verify` on this tree, exit 0, log read in full: typecheck; eslint; standards (568 files, 17 rules, 0 violations); `build:web`; API 60 files pass and 1 is skipped, 816 tests pass and 3 are skipped; web 141 files and 1,519 tests pass; web coverage branches 98.46% (5,438 of 5,523; gate 98.4%). Across the last four full runs on this branch, the web branch total ranged from 5,523 to 5,526 and the percentage stayed at 98.46%, so the margin over the gate is about three branches.
- Not run: the real-model recording, `e2e/acceptance/demo-onboarding.spec.ts` (it rewrites the dump and runs only through `demo:record`), and the real-model specs. No seed was regenerated, so cut-out and framing quality are not judged.

## ADR-236 — the labels for photos 01 to 60 are the owner's adopted audit table, recorded as appearance estimates, not a record

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. It supersedes ADR-223 in part. ADR-223 left the 80 earlier personas unchanged, because the repo had no ethnicity record for photos 01 to 60 or the top-level 20. The owner now adopts a table for photos 01 to 60. The index at the top of this file has the row, shared with ADR-235.

**Context.** The register's rules are that naming photos 01 to 60 needs a stated identity for each photo, from a source (ADR-223), and that appearance is not a reliable basis for judging ethnicity (ADR-220). The owner then pasted a per-photo audit of all 100 `social/` photos, with a gender and an ethnicity estimate and a note for each. Its branch note names `arena/baca76e5-special-fiesta`, which is not this session's branch. The owner said "Use table as provided" and then "Just update the lookup table as instructed". The assistant did not judge any label.

The checks compare the table's own entries with the repo, not with the people. For photos 01 to 60 the table's gender matches the persona file in 60 of 60. For photos 61 to 100 the table's gender and ethnicity match the generation record in 40 of 40 each. The table covers none of the top-level 20. Nothing checks the table's ethnicity for photos 01 to 60, because the repo holds no record of it.

**Decision.**
- The ethnicity labels for photos 01 to 60 in `docs/design/demo-identities-worksheet.csv` are the owner's table, as given: 22 Chinese, 12 Malay, 20 Indian, 5 Eurasian / Other and 1 Uncertain (photo 29). Each row's `identity_source` reads "user-adopted visual audit: appearance estimate, not a record", with the instruction.
- Photos 61 to 100 keep the labels from the generation record (ADR-223): 30 Chinese, 6 Malay, 3 Indian and 1 Eurasian.
- The top-level 20 have no label. Their rows say "identity needed", and their `identity_source` is blank.
- This departs from ADR-223's requirement of a stated identity from a source, for these 60 labels only, on the owner's instruction. The source is the table itself, an appearance estimate. The departure does not let the assistant add a label from appearance. Any other label needs the owner's statement or a record.
- Photo 60 keeps its name. Its source is not recorded (ADR-220), and the table flags mixed appearance.

**Why.** The owner decides the identities in the demo. The table is an appearance estimate, so it is recorded as one, with its source, and not as a record. Rejected: calling the table a record, which none is; leaving photos 01 to 60 unnamed, since the owner asked for every corpus avatar to be a seed user with a name that fits its photo; changing the labels the table caveats, since the owner said to use the table as given.

**Consequences.**
- The labels reach the seed only through the names drawn from them (ADR-235). The persona file has no ethnicity field.
- Some labels carry caveats in the table, and they are used as given. Photo 47 (Indian) is marked "table caveat flags it", and photo 55 (Malay) is marked "table flags it: ambiguous Malay/Indian". Their names come from a caveated label, and the owner should know that.
- Photos 05, 20, 30, 38 and 60 (Eurasian / Other) and photo 29 (Uncertain) carry the table's caveats and keep their names (ADR-235).

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-236.

**Not done.** The sources of photos 01 to 60 are not recorded. If the owner has a record for any of them, it would replace the estimate in a new entry. The table's branch note is not reconciled with this session's branch.

**Validation.** The checks on the table's entries are those described under Context, run from a script outside the repo. The lookup table holds 60 adopted rows (22, 12, 20, 5 and 1), 40 record rows (30, 6, 3 and 1) and 20 blank rows. That matches the table's totals.

## ADR-237 — one script regenerates the demo seed: record, replay onto a new database, export, check

**Status.** Accepted, 2026-10-09. It supersedes nothing. ADR-040 (the demo seed is recorded, not written) stands.

**Context.** `apps/api/src/db/seed-demo.sql` is the demo seed. It comes from the recorded dump in three steps that were run by hand: record the dump (`npm run demo:record`), replay it onto an empty database (`npm run seed:demo` on a server that has only the schema), and export that database (`npm run db:export-demo`). The steps are easy to get wrong, as observed in this session:

- The recording does not fill the database the export reads. It uses `.data/demo-recording` and writes only the dump, so exporting straight after a recording gives no participants.
- `db:export-demo` has no row guard. On a schema-only database it writes a 0-row seed and exits 0. On a database with no tables it fails with `relation "participant" does not exist`.
- The replay is the only step that fills the export's database.

**Decision.** `./refresh-demo-seed.sh`, at the repo root, runs the steps in order and stops at the first failure:

1. **Record** with `PSD_E2E_REAL_MODEL=1 npm run demo:record`. `--skip-record` skips this and uses the dump already in `scripts/`. The recording always uses the real model.
2. **Check** the dump against `scripts/demo-personas.json`: same count, same nicknames, same order. It refuses otherwise.
3. **Replay.** Delete `apps/api/.data/demo-export`, start the stack on it with `PSD_SEED=default`, and require the server log to say `empty database: applied schema.sql`. Then run `npm run seed:demo`, which must report the dump's count. The stack is stopped by process group.
4. **Export** with `npm run db:export-demo` against that database.
5. **Check** that the new `seed-demo.sql` holds the dump's participants (count and nicknames). If not, the previous file is put back.

It refuses to start while port 5173 or 8787 is in use, or when `DATABASE_URL` is set, because the database would then be a Postgres server and not the directory this rebuilds. It commits nothing. Logs and backups go to `.data/refresh-demo-seed/`, which is git-ignored. The developer database `apps/api/.data/dev` is never touched.

**Why.** One command, in the order the data needs: the recording writes the dump, and only the replay fills the export's database. Recording first means that a failed recording stops before the seed is touched. Rejected:

- Replaying into `apps/api/.data/dev`. It would mix demo data into the developer database, which `dev-reset.sh` would then have to clear.
- `dev.sh --detach` for the stack. `_dev-common.sh` hard-codes `PSD_DEV_DATA_DIR`, so the script manages its own process group, as `AGENTS-workflow.md` requires.
- Adding `seed-social.spec.ts` to the refresh. It signs personas in through the browser against a running server and is gated by `PSD_SEED_SOCIAL=1`. It is left out for now (see Not done).

**Consequences.**

- Every refresh changes every row of `seed-demo.sql`. IDs, timestamps, scan numbers, team codes and participant titles are generated on replay. Review the change by content. The script checks the participants only; the other tables are not compared.
- With `--skip-record` the script cannot tell whether the dump came from the real model. Before committing, check the record log for the five no-face photos (ADR-056).
- The recording needs Chromium and access to the model hosts, so it runs on the owner's machine. ADR-226 reserves the real-model rebuild for the owner.
- `apps/api/.data/demo-export` stays after a successful run. It is git-ignored and replaced on the next run.
- Written for bash 3.2, the macOS default. Not run under bash 3.2.

**Numbering.** This entry takes ADR-237. ADR-226 stays reserved for the owner's real-model rebuild.

**Not done.**

- The owner's real-model recording and the push of the dump (ADR-226). `seed-demo.sql` is not regenerated in this change.
- `scripts/seed-demo.mjs` still says eighty in its header and its closing line. Those change with the first 120-entry refresh.
- Whether `seed-social.spec.ts` joins the refresh is the owner's decision.
- The window between the export's write and the check is not exercised. A failure there is covered by the same restore trap.

**Validation.** Run in the sandbox on 2026-10-09:

- `bash -n` and shellcheck 0.11.0 (`-x`): clean.
- `--help` prints the header. An unknown option exits 1.
- The committed 80-entry dump with `--skip-record`: refused before any server started. Ports free. No tracked file changed.
- The default run, with no Playwright browser in the sandbox: the recording failed with `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist`. The script stopped before the replay. The dump backup was kept. Ports free. No tracked file changed. The real-model recording was not run.
- A synthetic 120-entry dump (a test file, restored by git afterwards): the first run exposed a parser fault. It read only the first of the three 40-row `INSERT` blocks, so it found 40 of 120. The script put the previous SQL back, as designed. After the fix the run exited 0 with 120 participants whose nicknames equal the persona file's set. The database held 120 rows with 120 distinct nicknames.
- Interrupt during the replay (SIGTERM to the script): the stack stopped through the trap, the ports were freed, no dev process remained, and `seed-demo.sql` was unchanged.

### ADR-238 — a face the device already holds is in the store on its first render

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-09
- **Relates to:** gap — spec is silent; amends the stand-in rule of ADR-035
- **Decision:** A participant's sprite store starts from this device's own sprite cache (`psd.sprites.v1`), read once when the store mounts. An avatar whose face is already on the device paints that face on its first render. The drawn character stands in only while a face is still being fetched, or for a person with no photo.
- **Why:** The store used to start empty on every mount. `GameboyShell` mounts one `SpriteProvider` per participant page, so each visit to the badge page began with no faces. The device copy reached the avatar only in an effect, which runs after the first paint. The stand-in was therefore painted for a frame and then replaced by the photo. Rejected: (a) reading the cache inside each avatar's render. Every read parses the whole cache (up to 150 faces, under 2 MB), so a 30-face list would parse it 30 times per render. (b) Dropping the stand-in while a face is in flight. That reverses the "no hole in a list" reason in ADR-035, and an existing test pins the stand-in. It needs the owner's decision, not a bug fix.
- **Impact:** Each mount of a participant page parses the device's sprite cache once. A face the device has never fetched still shows the stand-in until the request returns. If the request fails, the stand-in stays for the rest of that page visit; the test "draws the character while a face is on its way, and if it never comes" pins this. Bite check: with the store's initial state put back to `{}`, `SpriteProvider.test.tsx` "has a face this device already holds on the very first render, before any effect" fails with `expected null to be '64:…'`. With the fix restored, all 126 tests in the seven avatar and participant suites pass.

### ADR-239 — the passport tab lists every station, and one counted scan completes a station

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-09
- **Relates to:** gap — spec is silent on a passport tab; builds on ADR-176 (the passport bonus) and ADR-006 (derived on read, not stored)
- **Decision:** Scan History gains a Passport tab at `/me/scans/passport`, beside the list of scans. It lists every fringe station the day has, in the order the facilitators see them. A station is completed once the participant holds at least one counted scan there. A counted scan is one that is neither voided nor undone at the station, the same rule the points and the passport bonus already use. The read is `GET /api/me/passport`, participant only and bound to the session, returning `{ stations: [{ activityId, activityName, isCompleted }] }`.
- **Why:** A list of visited stations cannot show what is left, so every station gets a slot, and a completed station gets its chop (ADR-241). "Completed" is the participant's own word for having taken part in at least one round, and two rounds at one station are one station, as ADR-176 counts them. Rejected: (a) building the tab from `/api/me/scans` on the client, because that list holds scans, not stations, and cannot show a station never visited; (b) reusing `GET /api/fringe/activities`, which is facilitator-only and exposes round state; (c) storing completion as a row, because a void or an undo would then have to find and rewrite it, which ADR-006 rules out. Derived on read, the next read is correct. The station name is the station's current name, not a snapshot: the passport is a view of the day's stations, not a record of a scan, and the scan rows keep their own snapshot names.
- **Impact:** The route is classified participant-only in `authorization-matrix.test.ts`, and `passport-stations.test.ts` holds its positive and wrong-party tests. A station added during the day appears at once as an open slot, with no backfill. Inactive stations are listed too, so a station closed for the day keeps its place. The passport asks the server on every visit (warm start, ADR-113), like the scans beside it, so a station stamped on a facilitator's phone shows at the next visit. The end-to-end journeys in `e2e/participant/passport-stamps.spec.ts` run on the real stack. Bite checks watched to fail: (a) a voided and an undone stamp counted, with the `isVoided` filter removed: `passport-stations.test.ts` fails 2 of 6, "does not complete a station for a stamp that has since been voided" and "does not complete a station for a stamp the station undid"; (b) a chop on every station, completed or not: the hook and page tests fail, 2 failures in all; (c) a 60-second TTL on the passport cache: `usePassport.test.ts` fails "paints the device copy at once, then asks the server again on every visit".

### ADR-240 — the chop a station shows is drawn once per device and kept on that device

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-09
- **Relates to:** gap — spec is silent; ADR-019 (one owner per browser key); ADR-112 (the data cache is purged on sign-in and sign-out, so this key is kept outside it)
- **Decision:** The first time a completed station's chop is shown, a random 32-bit seed is drawn and kept under `psd.passportChops.v1` as `{ "<stationId>": seed }`. Every later visit from that device reads the seed back, so the same station keeps the same impression. Only the seed is stored. The look is computed from it (ADR-241).
- **Why:** The participant asked for variants that the frontend determines and stores locally, so that one device always shows one look. Rejected: (a) a new random look on every render, which changes on every visit; (b) storing the rendered look, its markup or its parameters, which copies the recipe into every device's storage and freezes each stored look at the code of the day it was drawn; a seed is a few bytes and the recipe stays in one place; (c) a seed per participant, which would give a shared phone a different chop per sign-in, where the request is per device; (d) a seed derived from the station id, which would give every device the same chops and so no device variation at all; (e) the data cache, which sign-in and sign-out purge, so the look would reset with each sign-in. Where the browser refuses writes, `localStore` keeps the value in memory and `chopSeeds.ts` keeps this page's seeds too, so one page visit shows one chop; a later visit on such a device draws again.
- **Impact:** The look belongs to the device. A new phone draws new chops, and clearing site data redraws them. The map holds one entry per completed station, so it stays the size of the day's station list. A change to the recipe in `lib/passport/chop.ts`, to a range or to the order of its draws, redraws every chop already stamped on every device, so each such change needs an ADR of its own. `chop.test.ts` pins the generator with mulberry32's reference value for seed 1. Reversal: store the look and migrate the key, or move the seed to the server, which would make the look follow the participant across devices. Bite check watched to fail: (a) the stored seed never read back, so every call draws again: `chopSeeds.test.ts` fails 3 tests and `usePassport.test.ts` fails 2.
