### ADR-241 — the passport chop is SVG drawn from a seed: one fixed die, a different impression for each seed

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-09
- **Relates to:** gap — spec is silent. A deliberate exception to AGENTS-frontend.md §4 ("art is generated and committed, never drawn at runtime"), which the pixel motifs of ADR-014 follow.
- **Decision:** The chop is an SVG drawn from a pure function of its seed, `buildChop` in `apps/web/src/lib/passport/chop.ts`. The die is fixed: the word `Completed` inside a double frame. Each impression varies its rotation (±11°), skew (±2.5°), scale, placement (±8 by ±5 view-box units), one of three reds, ink opacity (0.9 to 0.98), the height and turn of each letter, an edge roughened by a displacement filter, patchy ink starvation from a noise mask, uneven pressure from a gradient mask, an optional gap in the outer ring (about 60% of impressions) and an optional fainter second strike (about 40%). `PassportChop` draws the spec and nothing else. The mark is `role="img"` labelled with the word.
- **Why:** The variants must differ by station and by device, and a committed set of image files cannot hold that without a file for every look. SVG stays resolution-independent, costs a few kilobytes of markup per list, and needs no image pipeline. The word is live text, so it is always exact, and every impression can be reproduced from its seed. Rejected: (a) a generative image model, whose output cannot be reproduced from a seed and whose lettering is unreliable; (b) canvas drawing, which tests cannot inspect and which is harder to make accessible; (c) the pixel-art motifs of ADR-014, whose language reads as a game badge rather than a rubber stamp. The exception is deliberate: the choice is made per device (ADR-240), and no committed files can hold those choices.
- **Impact:** Tests pin the ranges, determinism, the difference between seeds, the appearance of the ring gap and second strike only when the spec has them, and mulberry32's reference value. They cannot judge the look, which was tuned by eye on rendered sheets. The filter frequencies are in user units of the 200 by 120 view box, so they were tuned at the list size of 120 px wide. Browsers draw SVG filters slightly differently, so impressions look alike rather than identical. The mark uses `mix-blend-mode: multiply` so the ink sits on the paper. A rendered sheet of twelve impressions is `docs/design/passport-chops.png`; it is a render of the component, not a screenshot of the app. A committed raster set would replace the generator and redraw every stored chop, so it would need a new storage key. Bite checks watched to fail: (a) `Math.random` in place of the seed: `chop.test.ts` fails "draws the same impression from the same seed, every time"; (b) the ring never drawn: `chop.test.ts` and `PassportChop.test.tsx` fail 3 tests between them.

### ADR-242 — a station holds a die: nine chop designs, chosen by the station and worn by the device

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-10
- **Relates to:** extends ADR-241 (its fixed die becomes one of nine, chosen per station; the generator's promise is unchanged), ADR-240 (a station-derived *die* is not the station-derived *seed* that entry rejects), ADR-239 (the tab that lists every station)
- **Decision:** The design of a chop belongs to the station and its wear to the device. `dieForStation` folds the activity id with FNV-1a and indexes nine registered dies in `chopDies.ts`: an immigration band, a union circle, a thick frame, a crown oval, a postal canceller, a hexagon customs die, an engine-turned vignette octagon, an over-inked slab with the type knocked out, and corner brackets left for somebody else to date in pen. Each die owns its geometry and ornament, its pair of inks, its own wear ranges (`DieRanges`) and whether a serial line exists; the impression owns everything ADR-241 listed, drawn from the device's own seed. A die returns primitives — frame, panels, paths, lettering, knockouts, arcs — and never markup, and `PassportChop` draws those and applies the wear in one place for all nine. Straight type is capped at 22 characters and a rim or narrow line at 15, cut with an ellipsis.
- **Why:** The owner asked for styles that differ the way different countries' chops differ, and for many variants of each. A chop is pressed from a die: the shape is a fact about the office and the wear is a fact about the press and the paper, so two designs that differ only in wobble are one design printed twice. Choosing the die by station means two participants comparing phones at one counter see the same shape, and the impression still differs device to device. Rejected: (a) choosing the die by device, which would put a different shape on the same station on two phones and make the die a second copy of the wobble; (b) choosing it by the activity id's hash *as the seed*, which is what ADR-240 rejects — a seed carries the variation, so deriving it from the station gives every device the same chop, while a shape carries none; (c) nine committed raster designs, which ADR-241 already rejects, and which would freeze the recipe and need a file per style; (d) a column naming the design, which would have to be kept in step with a code list by hand for no benefit — a hash of an id that already exists is derived on read (ADR-006).
- **Impact:** Nine designs, one renderer. A die is added by describing a shape in `CHOP_DIES` — inks, ranges and a `draw` — with no change to the component, the API or what is stored; `CHOP_DIE_IDS` is derived from that list, so the assignment and the tests cannot disagree with it. The wear ranges moved from the generator onto the die, because one global set suited a 176-unit band and not a 40-unit ring: the die decides how heavily it is struck (`slab-knockout` starves at 0.26 to 0.36, `union-circle` at 0.14 to 0.2) and how far it turns (4° on the thick frame, 13° on the pen brackets). Stored seeds stay valid and no storage key changes, because the die is drawn after the wear is drawn: a redraw gives each chop the same wobble on a new shape, which is a cosmetic change and not the recipe change ADR-241 requires a key for. Cosmetic continuity: impressions stamped before this entry no longer look as they did — the same character, not the same pixels — so the numbers ADR-241 quoted for a seed are not reproducible. `docs/design/passport-chop-dies.png` (nine rows of six impressions) and `passport-chop-list.png` (the tab at 390 px) supersede `passport-chops.png`; the old sheet stays in the repo because ADR-241 cites it, and it no longer matches what the code draws. `fitArcLabel` is a second cap on purpose: a name spilling over a ring is a bug, a name cut with an ellipsis is a chop being read. Nine dies over the eight stations of a normal day cannot all differ — measured over 2,000 eight-id days of UUIDv7s, five or six distinct shapes in 74% of cases, all eight in 1% — and that is accepted rather than fixed; `docs/design/passport-chop-styles.md` holds the alternatives and why each was left. `apps/web/scripts/render-chop-sheet.ts` renders both sheets through `renderToStaticMarkup` with the real stylesheets over Playwright's Chromium, and is a review harness outside the typecheck like the other scripts, because the look of a stamp is not assertable. Bite checks watched to fail: (a) `dieForStation` pinned to the first die: `chopAssign.test.ts` fails 2 of 6, "uses every die across a day of stations" and "does not hand a run of ids the same die"; (b) the octagon's radius pushed from 60 to 72, past the cell: `chopDies.test.ts` fails 1 of 12, "keeps every shape of every die inside the cell"; (c) the frame-gap share widened to 0.05–0.9 with `MAX_GAP_SHARE`'s clamp removed: `chop.test.ts` fails "gaps the outer ring only on the dies that have one, and never for a quarter of it" with a gap of 436.4 units against a limit of 26.3, where the same widened range passes with the clamp in place.

**Validation.** Run in the sandbox on 2026-10-10:

- `npm run verify` at the root exits 0: typecheck, lint, `standards` (591 files, 17 rules, 0 violations), the web build, 822 API tests with 3 skipped, and 1614 web tests in 149 files. The chop work is 90 tests across seven files: `chop.test.ts` 16, `chopGeo.test.ts` 21, `chopType.test.ts` 9, `chopDies.test.ts` 13, `chopAssign.test.ts` 6, `chopSeeds.test.ts` 7, `PassportChop.test.tsx` 12, plus the 6 in `usePassport.test.ts`.
- Coverage with the enforced floors: statements 99.52% (98.99), branches 98.47% (98.4), functions 98.89% (98.55), lines 99.52% (98.99). The branch floor has 0.07 points of room, so a die added without a test for it will fail the run rather than pass quietly.
- The sheets in `docs/design/` are renders of `PassportChop` through `renderToStaticMarkup` with `tokens.css` and `gameboy.css` inlined, shot by Playwright's Chromium (153.0.8010.0). The first pass was reviewed and rejected on the spot — the round dies read as faint rings at 152 px — and every die was redrawn larger and heavier before the second pass, which is what the committed sheets show. `apps/web/scripts/render-chop-sheet.ts` is run from `apps/web`, like the other scripts, so the repo's `react-jsx` setting applies.
- The passport journeys run against the real stack: `PSD_E2E_ENGINES=chromium npx playwright test e2e/participant/passport-stamps.spec.ts` passes 6 of 6 (three journeys on two Chromium projects), including "the same device shows the same chop after a reload, because it kept the seed" — the test that would catch a redraw invalidating a stored chop. The rest of the Playwright suite was not run (no WebKit in the sandbox), and the demo seed's 120-person dump is untouched by this change. `e2e/acceptance/signout.spec.ts` still fails as it does on the base commit.
- Not reviewed by eye: the marks on a real device. Both sheets are renders of the component, and `Arial Black` is absent on the sandbox, so a phone's small print is a little lighter than what the sheets show.

### ADR-243 — the SHIP-HATS pipeline files live in the repo inert, and their consistency is a standards rule

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-11
- **Relates to:** gap — `fds.md` §8 deploys the app and says nothing about CI; ADR-052 (no deployment automation in this repo); ADR-001 (`GREENFIELD.md` is kept unmodified — this entry adds a section to it, see **Why**); ADR-015 + AGENTS-function-design.md §8 (a rule with no check is a paragraph); ADR-237 (an owner-facing procedure is one command)
- **Decision:** The file set the SHIP-HATS webapp E2E template prescribes is committed **inert** — `.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats`, `BUILD.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats`, `TEST.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats`, `DEPLOY.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats` — and the only supported way to turn it on is `./shiphats-activate.sh`, which prompts for the 39 values the repo cannot answer, substitutes them into the files' `@@PLACEHOLDER@@` slots and renames them; `--revert` goes back. Its shape follows from what the platform documents: shared runners are Docker runners with no DinD and no privileged mode, so the image is built by Kaniko (`ship_docker`, `non_privileged`) and pushed by Crane (`cstack`, `non_privileged`); the artefact the compliance jobs sign, scan and publish is the image **tarball** itself (`--no-push --tarPath`), which is also what `docker load` on a host runs; the template's stages are not renamed and `deploy-final-job` keeps its name because the framework's verification jobs attach around it; the included templates are pinned to a version tag (`v1.1.0`) rather than a branch, because the E2E set is documented as no longer actively maintained; and no credential appears in any of these files, inert or live — `COSIGN_PASSWORD`, `SONAR_*`, `FOD_*`, `NEXUS_IQ_*` and `NEXUS_REPO_*` are GitLab CI/CD variables, and the compliance framework itself is attached in project settings. The discipline is then generalised: `GREENFIELD.md` §9.3 with checklist item 19, so a new project starts with an inert set plus an activation script rather than discovering this at adoption time. Enforcement is the 18th rule in `scripts/check-standards.mjs` (`shiphats-pipeline-set`): the four files come as a set or not at all, every placeholder in them has a prompt in the script's schema, a live pipeline file has no placeholder and has not dropped one of the three local includes, and neither the activator nor the record doc (`docs/design/ship-hats-pipeline.md`) may go missing while the set exists.
- **Why:** Adopting a platform pipeline is a decision that cannot be finished in one sitting — the included templates sit behind an SGTS login, the registry and deploy hosts do not exist yet, and the values that decide the shape belong to an onboarding e-mail. A live `.gitlab-ci.yml` that is sixty percent right is worse than none, because every red pipeline after it reads as the app's fault; a file GitLab cannot read costs nothing and still gets reviewed, versioned and tested. Rejected: (a) committing the live config, which buys a broken gate for the sake of looking adopted; (b) keeping the proposal in the design doc only, which makes adoption a day of transcription and leaves the doc's claims with no relationship to any file a machine can check; (c) a committed `.shiphats.env` or answers file holding the hosts and repository ids, which is a second source of truth for configuration whose only reader is the pipeline — the values belong in the YAML variables where they are diffable, and the credentials belong in masked CI variables, which is why the script has no secret prompt at all; (d) a `templates/ship-hats/` directory of generic copies to copy into new projects, which is 700 lines duplicated with nothing to run it and every change to make twice — the transferable part is the prose rule in `GREENFIELD.md` and this repo is its worked instance, as with the eighteen items before it; (e) a vitest test instead of a standards rule, rejected because repo-structural checks live in `check-standards.mjs` (ADR-015) and adding a layer that runs in the same gate would split where such rules are found. The `ALPINE_IMAGE` placeholder left dangling while these files were written is the failure mode the parity half of the rule exists for: it was found by hand once, and now it is found on every commit.
- **Impact:** The four `.shiphats` files are not dead code and are not cleanup: they are the adoption path, and `docs/design/ship-hats-pipeline.md` says which of their contents was measured, which was read from the platform's docs, and which is `CONFIRM:`-only because it could not be verified from here — the three likeliest first-run failures being the template project path, a stage the template does not declare, and a runner tag the project was not given. Activation is reversible with one command, and no pipeline has ever run in this repo: `npm run verify` remains the gate. A greenfield project that adopts `GREENFIELD.md` now inherits the requirement to write the set, the script and the record doc in the same change as the platform decision, and to verify generated pipeline files by parsing them and syntax-checking every shell snippet under each shell the runners use — which is where the `set -u` reads and the heredoc terminator that a YAML block scalar eats were caught here. Because the parity check is a gate rule, adding a variable to the YAML without adding its prompt fails `npm run standards` in the same commit that adds it. `docs/outstanding-adrs-2026-10-08.md` and the older addendum entries still quote "17 rules" for the runs they observed; those are records, not claims about today.

**Bite checks watched to fail.** All six against the tree with the rule in place; each restores the file it moved before the next case.
(a) `.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats` moved away → `missing from the set`.
(b) an unknown `@@NOT_IN_SCHEMA@@` appended to `TEST.gitlab-ci.yml.shiphats` → `has no prompt in the activator's schema`.
(c) a live `.gitlab-ci.yml` containing a placeholder → `still carries a placeholder`.
(d) a live `.gitlab-ci.yml` including only `BUILD.gitlab-ci.yml` → `no longer includes TEST.gitlab-ci.yml`.
(e) the record doc moved away → `the set ships without its record`.
(f) `scripts/ship-hats-activate.mjs` moved away → `nothing can answer their placeholders`.
With everything restored the run is `591 files checked, 18 rules, 0 violations`.

**Validation.** Run in the sandbox on 2026-10-11:

- `npm run standards` on the final tree: 591 files, 18 rules, 0 violations, with the six sabotages above each producing exactly one named violation. `npm run typecheck` and `eslint .` clean. The four pipeline files and the activator are untouched by this entry, so the measurements in `docs/design/ship-hats-pipeline.md` §6 still stand: all four files parse inert and activated, 12 jobs, 0 placeholders left, and all 23 multi-line shell snippets valid under bash, dash and busybox ash.
- `./shiphats-activate.sh` exercised end to end in a temp copy: `--list`, `--defaults`, `--dry-run`, `--answers` with a bad value rejected, and `--revert`; closed stdin mid-ask exits 1 with the non-interactive modes named.
- Docs and code agree: `AGENTS-workflow.md` §2 states the inert-by-name rule and the secrets rule, `AGENTS-function-design.md` §8 lists the new rule among what the gate checks, and `AGENTS.md` §7 answers item 19 for this project.
- The first full `./verify.sh` after this change went red on `apps/api/src/tests/scan-number.test.ts` — a pre-existing one-run-in-330 flake in a staged uniqueness collision, unrelated to anything here, diagnosed by reproducing it with the collision forced and fixed in ADR-244. The rerun on the fixed tree is green in all six stages: typecheck, lint, standards (591 files,
18 rules, 0 violations), `build:web`, 822 API tests with 3 skipped, 1614 web tests with web coverage
99.52 / 98.47 / 98.89 / 99.52. Playwright was not run — no app source, route or spec changed. The
`one run in 330` figure is arithmetic on the test's own numbers (30 draws over 10,000), not a
measured rate.

### ADR-244 — a staged scan-number collision asks the database what is free, not arithmetic

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-11
- **Relates to:** ADR-088 (the insert-and-retry mint this test stages), ADR-243 (found while validating it), `AGENTS-workflow.md` §4b and `GREENFIELD.md` §3.2 (a flaky test is an unread defect report)
- **Decision:** `apps/api/src/tests/scan-number.test.ts`'s retry test no longer computes the collision-free second number as `taken + 1`; it asks the database for the first neighbour of `taken` that has not been issued (`freeScanNumber`). The stub's contract is unchanged — it still fails loudly when the code under test asks for a number the test never staged.
- **Why:** The file's first test signs up thirty participants, and each takes a random 4-digit number from the real mint into the same database. So `taken + 1` is about a 30-in-10,000 chance of being already issued — and when it is, `createParticipant` collides a second time, mints a third time, and the run dies as `mint sequence exhausted` inside the test's own helper. The message names nothing that is wrong, which is why this class of failure survives: it reads like a broken test rather than like a test whose premise was false. Rejected: (a) widening the staged sequence to five numbers, which hides the collision the test exists to force and lets a real regression pass silently; (b) ordering the tests so the 30-signup run happens in another file, which pays a database for a fact the database can answer in one read; (c) seeding the random mint in that test, which changes what the first test proves — it is about real randomness under concurrency.
- **Impact:** One more read per retry test, and a rule worth keeping in mind for every test that stages a uniqueness collision: *the number you need to be free is only free relative to the rows that exist when you ask.* Anything a sibling test mints is part of that set. `SCAN_NUMBER_ATTEMPTS` (5, `apps/api/src/db/entities/participants.ts:53`) already has its own test — "dies loudly after five attempts rather than looping" — so the give-up path is pinned by a permanent mint (`() => stuck.scanNumber`) rather than by a fixed stub, which is the right shape for a budget test; no new test was added for it.

**Bite checks watched to fail.** Both run against the real database in the same file, with the squatter inserted only for the experiment and removed afterwards.
(a) Old helper (`taken + 1`) *plus* a participant deliberately holding that neighbour → the test fails with `mint sequence exhausted`, which is the sandbox's exact observed error — the mechanism, not a guess.
(b) The same squatter with `freeScanNumber` in place → the test passes, because the helper skips the taken neighbour and stages a genuinely free number.
The 12 tests in the file pass on the restored tree, and `npx tsc -p apps/api/tsconfig.json --noEmit` is clean.

**Validation.** Run in the sandbox on 2026-10-11: `npx vitest run src/tests/scan-number.test.ts`
→ 12 passed, and again after a comment-only edit to the same file → 12 passed. The full
`./verify.sh` then ran green in all six stages on the tree holding both entries (822 API tests with
3 skipped, 1614 web tests); its numbers are recorded in ADR-243's entry.

### ADR-245 — the day's stages are rows beside `stage`, not a second name for it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-12
- **Relates to:** ADR-089 (the schedule the stages sit around), ADR-152 (the draw rule `stage` still owns alone), ADR-136/137 (the champion bonus, whose predicate is untouched on purpose), ADR-168 (the additive section this table needed no part of), ADR-246 (what the rows are for), `docs/design/tournament-phases-assessment.md` §13
- **Decision:** `tournament_stage` — one row per stage of a tournament's day, keyed on the pair a fixture already carries (`kind` = `MatchStage`, plus `round_number`, where NULL means every round of that kind), carrying `label`, `ordinal`, `promote_count`, `promotion_points`, the three rates (NULL each = inherit `point_config`), `pays_standings`, and the close record (`is_current`, `closed_at`, `closed_by_superadmin_id`, `close_reason`). No table gains a pointer to it: `tournament_fixture` keeps `stage` and `round_number` and nothing else, and `db/entities/stages.ts` is the only place that maps a fixture to a row (a numbered row outranks the kind-wide one). `activateTournament` writes one row per kind its format will actually play, in the activation transaction; `closeGroupStage` closes the pool row and opens the next in the transaction that draws the bracket. A tournament with no rows resolves to `null` everywhere, which is the legacy day, not an error case.
- **Why:** The facilitators' mode is several phases with the match-ups under manual control, points rising as the day goes on, and a bonus for teams promoted out of each one. The obvious build was a `tournament_phase` table with its own `stage` column pointing at the fixtures; the owner's own correction — "I used phases because I didn't know the word stage; use `stage` as it is and don't replace it" — found the better shape, because `MatchStage` has three values and a day has more than three stages: quarter-finals, semi-finals and the final are all `'knockout'`, distinguished only by `round_number`. Keying on that pair means unlimited stages with no new enum value, no wire change, and no column anywhere that could disagree with the stage it names. Rejected: (a) the phase table with a `fixture_stage` declaration and a test pinning them equal — two sources for one fact, defended by a test instead of by the schema; (b) `phase_id` on the fixture, which needs a third non-additive backfill statement in the ADR-168 section; (c) extending `MatchStage` with `quarterfinal`/`semifinal`/`final`, which would put the new vocabulary in the draw-legality rule and the champion-bonus predicate for a naming benefit.
- **Impact:** One table, four indexes, 213 lines of logic in `db/entities/stages.ts` (296 with its doc block), and the day's `advance_count` now *seeds* a row rather than being the only place the number lives. The plan's `group_size`/`advance_count` CHECK ranges (`2 AND 8`, `0 AND 4`) are looser than what the wire schema will accept (`3–6`, `1–2`, `schemas.ts:874–877`), so widening them is only meaningful together with the zod bounds — the surface stage owns that, not this one. Nothing here changes how a point is scored: the rates resolve at completion (`requirePoints` → `stageRates`) and are snapshotted on the match as they always were, which is why no history is re-priced when an organiser edits a stage.

**One CHECK the tests corrected.** The design proposed `CHECK ((closed_at IS NULL) = is_current)` — "open exactly while it has no close". The first world-cup activation refused it: a seeded knockout row is neither current nor closed, and the biconditional has no way to say *not yet started*. What the table enforces now is the one real contradiction, `CHECK (is_current = false OR closed_at IS NULL)`, with "at most one open stage" left where the repo puts such facts: the partial unique index `ux_tournament_stage_one_open`, beside `ux_tournament_stage_single_schedule` and `ux_tournament_match_live_court`. A day that sets no bounds on how many stages it uses gets six kinds-worth of them and unbounded rounds, which is the "no hard constraints" the owner asked for, bought with a `timestamptz` rather than with a rule nobody can lift.

**Bite checks watched to fail.**
(a) The old biconditional CHECK, restored → `a world-cup day > activates two groups of four and twelve group fixtures` fails with `violates check constraint "tournament_stage_check"`, the observed error, and it fails at *activation*, which is how a constraint that cannot express "not yet started" announces itself.
(b) `pays_standings` flipped to `false` on the seeded pool row → the day's standings go empty and `tournament-schedule.test.ts` fails its ADR-115 points test, proving the standings read the rows and not the old hard-coded kind.
(c) `ux_tournament_stage_one_open` without its `WHERE` clause → the staged day's own test refuses the second open row and the *seeded* day fails to activate, because two rows are inserted before either is closed.
`countUnresolvedStageFixtures` narrowing from six fixtures to two when handed a round-numbered row is the scope test that makes (c) more than a unique-index trivia question.

**Validation.** Run in the sandbox on 2026-10-12: `./verify.sh --fast` green on the finished tree —
typecheck, lint, standards (593 files, 18 rules, 0 violations), 831 API tests with 3 skipped, 1614 web
tests; `npx vitest run --root apps/api src/tests/tournament-stages.test.ts src/tests/tournament-schedule.test.ts
src/tests/tournament-shape.test.ts` → 97 passed. Playwright was **not** run — no browser in this sandbox
(`AGENTS-workflow.md` §4), and nothing in this change reaches a surface. The standards half was watched to
fail three ways before it was trusted: a mapped column renamed to something `schema.sql` never creates, an
enforced FK with its `.references()` deleted, and a `.references()` on a column the database does not
constrain — one violation each, and 0 violations on the restored tree over all 33 tables. That the widened
rule found *only* the three unmirrored FKs the assessment had predicted by reading is the useful outcome:
a drift rule that reports nothing on arrival but fails when drift is staged is doing its job. One more
fact worth recording, because it is the reason no migration was needed: `bootstrap.test.ts`'s "creates
tables an older snapshot never had" passes, so `ensureSchema` carries a new table into a database
provisioned before it existed, which is the ADR-168 trouble this change does not have.

### ADR-246 — which results feed a table is a stage's setting, not a hard-coded kind

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-12
- **Relates to:** ADR-245 (the rows that hold the setting), ADR-089 (the pool table this used to be), ADR-152 (the draw rule deliberately not generalised here), ADR-161 (the export that prints these tables)
- **Decision:** `feedsStandings(index, fixtureKey)` in `db/entities/stages.ts` is the only expression of "does this result belong to a standings table", and `groupResults` and `countUnresolvedGroupFixtures` both go through it. A row with no stage rows above it means the pool, exactly: `if (!index.hasRows) return key.stage === 'group'`. The column's default is `false` and the seeded pool row is `true`, so a day that changes nothing aggregates as it did.
- **Why:** Win and draw rates rising per stage (the owner's "the number of points for a win or draw increases as the phases progress") is decoration while the standings query says `stage = 'group'`: a semi-final worth +4 paid nothing to the table because no knockout fixture fed one. Per-stage *rates* alone were already half-useful — the leaderboard counts every completed match through `points_awarded_snapshot` regardless of stage — so what was missing was the table, and it is now a setting per stage rather than a kind. Rejected: (a) seeding a `pays_standings = true` row for the knockout stage too, which would move every existing day's standings; (b) a `stage IN (...)` list widened to include `'knockout'`, which is the same hard-coded rule with more words; (c) resolving the draw-legality rule the same way (`schedule.ts:318`, `:444`), refused because "may this match end level" is ADR-152's decision about a *kind* of stage, not an organiser's preference, and moving it would put a wire-level rule in a per-day row.
- **Impact:** The pool's table becomes a cumulative one for any day that wants it — a bracket result folds into the group table of whichever pool its teams came from, which is what "the day's table" means when a day has phases. Read on every standings computation, so flipping the column changes what the board says with nothing replayed (`tournament-stages.test.ts` asserts exactly that, before and after the same played fixture). The `readStages` call adds one query to `groupResults`, which reads a day's whole fixture list and filters in memory rather than letting SQL do it — bounded by the field size the FDS caps at 8–32 teams, and the alternative was the same predicate in three places. ADR-161's export inherits the setting without a change of its own: `buildFinalStandings` asks `computeStandings`, so the day's printed record and the live table cannot answer differently about which phases counted.

**Validation.** Same tree, same gate. The behaviour is pinned by
`tournament-stages.test.ts`: with the knockout row at its default the pool table does not move when a
bracket result is played; the row alone is then updated and the *same* played fixture is seen in the table,
with no result replayed in between — the assertion that the rule is read rather than baked. Watched to
fail in both directions: `paysStandings: false` on the seeded pool row makes `a round-robin day > ADR-115:
a scored match lands its points on the standings table` and its neighbour fail (2 of 73), and the same
flip on the knockout row moves nothing until the table is asked to count knockouts.
### ADR-247 — a stage's pairs may be re-made by hand, and a day may be closed on the organiser's word

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-12
- **Relates to:** ADR-245/246 (the rows, and what they own), ADR-089 (the schedule these levers edit), ADR-149 (the admission this deliberately is not), ADR-136/137 (the champion bonus and the third-place match, which between them decide how far a claim may be scoped), `docs/design/tournament-phases-assessment.md` §13 R3
- **Decision:** Three changes, all on the facilitator's side of the day, and none of them a new column.
  - **The claim is scoped.** `claimFixtureForMatch` may bind a hand-started match only to a pending fixture of the tournament being played and, within it, of a kind the day is currently playing (`claimScope`, `db/entities/schedule.ts`) — `third_place` riding along while the bracket is live, because that is the only window in which its seats exist to be played (ADR-137). A day with no stage rows keeps the tournament bound and drops the kind bound, so an existing day behaves as it did; with no active tournament the claim finds nothing, which is the honest answer to "which fixture of today does this match belong to".
  - **A stage's pending fixtures can be re-paired.** `POST /api/admin/tournament/stages/:stageId/fixtures` hands `planRepair` (`db/entities/stagePairing.ts`, new) the pairs each fixture should hold. The decision is a pure function over rows the route already read; `applyRepair` obeys it inside one transaction in which every UPDATE carries `status = 'pending' AND match_id IS NULL`, so a match started while the dialog was open is a refusal rather than an overwrite. `sequence`, `round_number` and `group_code` are never touched: the slot stays, the teams move. A *closed* stage may still be re-paired, because what a close froze is the bracket drawn from it, not the table, and the fixtures worth repairing after a close are exactly the ones nobody played.
  - **A day can be closed early, out loud.** `close-group-stage` takes `{ force, reason }`. The count of unresolved fixtures moved out of the route into the entity (`refusalForClose`), asked through `stageFixturePredicate` of the row being left rather than through the string `'group'` — which retires `countUnresolvedGroupFixtures`, the helper ADR-246 named. `force` answers that count; `reason` (1–200, matching the column's CHECK) is required with it and lands in the row's `close_reason`, beside the `closed_by_superadmin_id` ADR-245 put there. A forced close skips nothing and invents nothing: the fixtures left pending stay pending, which is both the record of what was not played and the reason they can still be walked over, skipped, or re-paired afterwards.
  - **Not built:** re-staging a fixture between stage rows (§13 R3's third bullet). On a day whose rows are kind-wide there is exactly one row per kind, so a same-kind move has nowhere to go, and a cross-kind move would have to rewire the bracket's feeder links, which is `advanceWinner`'s contract rather than a repair's. It returns with per-round rows, and §14 says so where the rest of R3 landed.
- **Why:** The owner's constraint was "no hard constraints during field conditions", and the day has two failure modes that a schedule cannot solve by itself: a pool that loses a team at 11:00, and an afternoon that the rain takes at 16:00. For the first, the console's only lever was free-play, and free-play is the split the assessment spends §3 describing — a match that pays points and moves a table while belonging to no fixture, so the schedule and the standings drift apart and only the referee knows which games were "real". Re-pairing keeps the fixture and changes who is in it, which is why nothing downstream needs a new case: `planCourtDispatch`, the hall screen and the export were never reading team ids out of a formula, only out of these rows. For the second, the gate was a hard refusal with no escape, so the day could not be closed at all and the bracket was never drawn. Both answers are the same shape: the organiser is never *blocked*, they are made to say so, and the saying is the audit trail. The scope of a refusal is what keeps this from being a free-for-all — the field cannot change (that is ADR-149's admission, with its cap on how much play the day has left), a group fixture keeps both teams in its own pool (standings are per pool, and a cross-pool result would move a rank in a table that cannot account for either side), and a knockout seat is filled by the round before it rather than by a dialog.
- **Impact:** Two routes' behaviour changes for existing callers, in one direction each: a hand-started match that today silently consumes a bracket seat now claims nothing and becomes a friendly (this is the only place in the design where *adding* a predicate removes a hazard — `tests/court-queue.test.ts` has carried a comment about that coin flip since ADR-089, and its workaround of searching for a pair with no pending fixture anywhere becomes unnecessary rather than wrong); and `closeGroupStage` now takes one input object and returns an outcome code, so a close refused for a reason reaches the console as a sentence instead of an exception. `messages` gains nine strings and the route maps every `RepairCode` through a table typed `Record<Exclude<RepairCode, 'ok'>, () => HttpError>`, so adding a twelfth refusal in the entity without a sentence is a type error rather than `undefined` in front of a user. The console has no control for any of this yet: the request shape is deliberately a table of three columns, and the dialog is the next surface's job. No new gate had to be registered for the routes — `authorization-matrix.test.ts` already classifies every `/api/admin/` path as superadmin-only, and the file's coverage assertion is what proves a forgotten negative is impossible for a route in that namespace.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** Two sabotages on the committed tree, both in
`tournament-stage-pairing.test.ts`, 4 failures between them:

- Dropping `scope` from the claim's WHERE: the third-place seat seeded during the pool stage gets taken by
  a hand-started friendly (`expected { …14 columns… } to be undefined`), and so does the pool fixture the
  forced close left behind after the day had moved on.
- Deleting the `force` escape from `refusalForClose`: the forced close answers 409, and the two stories
  that run after it cascade, which is the shape of a day that cannot be closed at all.

The third one found the tests rather than the other way: with `fixtureState` reading `status` before
`match_id`, a fixture under a live match was refused with "This fixture has already been resolved" — true
enough to be harmless and wrong enough that the operator goes to look at a played result instead of the
match in front of them. The order in the function is now the one the sentence needs.

**Validation.** `apps/api/src/tests/tournament-stage-pairing.test.ts`, 14 tests: the eleven refusals and two
acceptances of `planRepair` (including the two the pure half is the only place to prove — a numbered row
owns only its round, and a closed stage can still be re-paired), then a played day. `./verify.sh`:
`apps/api/src/tests/tournament-stage-pairing.test.ts`, 17 tests: 7 pure over `planRepair` (every refusal,
both acceptances, and the contrast that one request is `ok` for a knockout stage and `pool` for a group
one), 9 on a played day, and 1 on a second day whose stage rows are deleted so the legacy shape is seen
refusing a force it has no row to record. `./verify.sh` on the finished tree: typecheck, lint, standards
(595 files, 18 rules, 0 violations), web build, 848 API tests passed with 3 skipped across 63 files, and
1614 web tests. The API coverage thresholds the gate enforces (94.6% branches, 98.9% functions) came in at
94.76% and 99.36% — the first version of this work missed them, by eleven unmapped error thunks in a route
table and a defensive branch no HTTP test could reach, which is why the repair now reads its rows
`FOR UPDATE` and answers a lost race with an ordinary refusal instead of a rolled-back write..


### ADR-248 — a day's awards are posted as one batch, and the batch is the thing that gets taken back

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-117 (the participant ledger the batch reuses instead of duplicating), ADR-005 (the roster snapshot, and why it is frozen), ADR-006/ADR-038 (computed-on-read, and the tag an award invalidates), ADR-009/ADR-116 (the client key, and the silent discard a guarded-free write invites), ADR-031 (the void/unvoid pair this copies), ADR-245/247 (the stage row an award is stamped with), `docs/design/tournament-phases-assessment.md` §13 R4
- **Decision:** One header over the two ledgers that already exist, and no third ledger.
  - **`award_batch` owns the decision; the rows own the money.** `schema.sql:835–886`: the header carries `client_batch_uuid uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE`, an optional `stage_id`, `label` (1–40), `reason` (1–200), its author, and the four reversal columns; `team_award` carries `team_id`, `batch_id NOT NULL`, the denormalised `stage_id`, `points` under the adjustment ledger's own CHECK (`<> 0 AND BETWEEN -100 AND 100`), and `roster_snapshot jsonb NOT NULL`. There is no `note`, no `kind`, and no reason on a row: D8's batch-level reason only, so a row cannot disagree with the header about why it exists.
  - **A participant award is an adjustment with a `batch_id`.** `score_adjustment.batch_id` is nullable — NULL keeps meaning "posted one at a time at the desk", which is every row the ledger already held — and each batch row copies the batch's reason into its own, because `score_adjustment.reason` is NOT NULL and this file adds, it never relaxes. The board has one place to look for what a person was given by hand either way.
  - **Reversible, never editable.** `reverseAwardBatch` and `reinstateAwardBatch` are two names over one `stampReversal`, which is a guarded `UPDATE … WHERE` on the flag plus one `void_audit_entry` row in the same transaction — `'void'` one way, `'unvoid'` the other — so there is no window where the flag moved and the register did not. `void_audit_entry.target_type` gains `'awardbatch'` as its fourth value, widened by ADR-173's drop-and-re-add pair as well as in the `CREATE TABLE`, because the CHECK of 2024 is standing on the databases this has to work on.
  - **The filter is written once, in the board.** `leaderboard.ts` gains a `team_award_points` CTE that pays each award to the roster the batch froze (`CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements`, the same reader `roster_points` uses) and adds one arm to `tournament_points`; the adjustment arm left-joins the header and drops what it reversed. A reversed batch is not paid, and its rows are not deleted, and the day's export follows without being touched — `readFinalStandings` reads `readAllIndividuals`, so it was always going to agree with the projector.
  - **`created | retry | conflict`.** An identical re-arrival of the same key is acknowledged with the batch it already stands for (200, `replayed: true`); a *different* payload under a key already held is a 409, decided by comparing the stored batch's rows to the ones asked for — the pre-read the retry needs is the same read, so the check is free. §13 R4 listed `created | retry` only; its own contract sentence ("one key, one payload") needs the third, and the offline queue is unaffected either way (§14 correction 6).
  - **Registers mark; readers that count filter.** The batch list, a team's ledger and a participant's adjustment list all show a reversed batch's rows, labelled and flagged; only the two CTEs that turn rows into points leave them out. Hiding them would have deleted a decision from the record of decisions, which is the one thing ADR-117's append-only rule exists to prevent.
  - **Not built:** the console dialog (the request shape is a table of five columns and the preview's "+12 already on the books" line is `GET /api/admin/teams/:teamId/awards`'s to feed, which is why that read exists before its button does), and any automatic award from a stage row's `promotion_points` — R5 keeps that derived on read, outside the batch, so a close still needs no write here.
- **Why:** Because a day's awards are decided in one breath — "the 3:40 promotion award, all four pools, 15 each" — and undone in one breath, "the field was flooded, take that back". Everything before this could only be said one row at a time by someone standing at a desk, which meant the undo was a second round of typing with no guarantee of reaching the same rows, and the record of both was nowhere. The batch makes the unit the human thinks in and leaves the ledgers alone: neither existing table is widened into something it was not for, and the reversal is one flag rather than a compensating write. `client_batch_uuid` exists because a twenty-row insert has one failure mode a single-row insert does not: a timeout *after* the rows landed. Without the key the operator's remedy is to post it again, which pays everybody twice.
- **Impact:** Five files carry the whole point: `schema.sql`, `db/schema/awards.ts` (the Drizzle mirror), `db/entities/awards.ts`, the two CTEs in `db/entities/leaderboard.ts`, and one rule in `scripts/check-standards.mjs` that had to be fixed before it could see this column; everything else is a caller. `matches.ts`'s `rosterSnapshot` is exported rather than copied, because two spellings of "who was on the team" is how a board and a ledger start to disagree, and `team_award.roster_snapshot` is deliberately the same jsonb grammar rather than a shape this feature invented. `db/entities/adjustments.ts` grows `listAdjustmentsForBatch` and three fields on every adjustment view (`batchId`, `batchLabel`, `batchReversed`), which is the widening that makes the participant's own detail page the honest place to look at a reversed batch. `audit.ts` takes `VoidTargetType` from `@psd/contracts` for both its entry and its filter, so the fourth value reaches the register's query instead of being stored and unreachable; the web console fetches the audit log unfiltered, so no screen needed a new option. `packages/contracts` gains `src/awards.ts` — `schemas.ts` had reached the 800-line cap `max-lines` exists to notice, and the fix was the package's own per-domain split rather than a compression — and `createAdjustmentRequestSchema` now reads its bounds from there, which is what "the same object with a team for a subject" is worth in code. `routes-superadmin/awards.ts` adds six routes under the `/api/admin` prefix the existing matrix already classifies as superadmin-only, and `POST /award-batches` resolves every team, participant, activity and stage before it writes, so a batch either pays whom the operator named or refuses with the field that was wrong. One lesson for the next table here: the snapshot is applied in order, so a column on an *older* table that points at a *newer* one cannot carry its `REFERENCES` inline — `score_adjustment.batch_id` is declared bare and gains `score_adjustment_batch_id_fkey` at the foot of the file, next to the `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` the additive section requires. Both paths end at the same named constraint; the first version of this had the inline form and rolled the whole snapshot back, which is how a schema error arrives as `relation "award_batch" does not exist` in 57 test files. The drift rule had to be repaired before it could check this column at all: rule 11's `parseMappedColumns` is handed the text *between* a `pgTable` call's braces and terminated each entry on the closing brace, which is not in that text — so the last mapped column of every table in the repository escaped both directions of the FK agreement, and `batch_id`, being appended last, was one of them. It has the sentinel now (601 files still green, which is the evidence the hole was not hiding anything else) and reads a named `ALTER … ADD CONSTRAINT … FOREIGN KEY` at the foot of the snapshot as the enforced key it is, single-column only.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** Four sabotages on the committed tree: three in `award-batches.test.ts`, one in the standards script:

- Dropping `WHERE NOT coalesce(ab.is_reversed, false)` from the board's adjustment arm: the two tests that pay people stop coming back — a total stays 5 down after the reversal — while the participant's ledger keeps showing the row, which is exactly the disagreement this design exists to avoid: a register that is right about a ledger being wrong.
- Dropping `WHERE NOT ab.is_reversed` from `team_award_points`: the team's 20 stays on the board after the batch is taken back, and the export carries it into the day's record in the same failure — one line missing in one CTE, and the printed result disagrees with the ledger it was printed from.
- Deleting the `not(awardBatches.isReversed)` guard from `stampReversal`: the second reverse answers 200 instead of 409 and writes a second audit row for one decision.
- Deleting the `ADD CONSTRAINT … FOREIGN KEY (batch_id) REFERENCES award_batch (id)` pair from `schema.sql`, which is a standards check rather than a test: `fringe.ts:80  schema-source  score_adjustment.batch_id mirrors an FK to a table schema.sql does not reference`. It only fired *after* `parseMappedColumns` was given its sentinel — before that, the same deletion and a mirror pointing at a table nobody references in that column were both invisible, which is the finding worth more than the feature's own line count. A second sabotage with the sentinel in place (a mapped `inventedColumn` as the last line of `award_batch`) fails the same way, and reverting the sentinel hides both again.

The last sabotage passed, and it is worth knowing which one: deleting `onConflictDoNothing` leaves all 17 tests green. A retry on a database nothing else is writing to never reaches the insert — the `client_batch_uuid` pre-read answers it first — so what the conflict clause is for is the two tabs that pre-read an empty table in the same instant, which is not a state a single-connection test can create. The idempotence has two halves and only one of them is testable from here; `resolveLostRace`'s twin in `scans.ts` has carried the same asymmetry since ADR-009.

**Validation.** `apps/api/src/tests/award-batches.test.ts`, 17 tests: the board moving and moving back, a batch that pays people only, both ledgers paid by one batch and un-paid by one reversal, the export following (read through `/api/admin/standings/final`, not from the CTE), the register listing a reversed batch marked with its counter's name and empty on a day that has posted nothing, the replay-then-clash pair on one key, four 404s for ids the day does not hold (team, participant, activity, stage) and seven refusals of shape (empty, label twice, reason, zero points, 101 points, 65 rows), the 404s and 409s of both reversal directions including a reversal of a batch that is not there, the `void`-then-`unvoid` audit rows read back through the widened `targetType=awardbatch` filter, a team's ledger with its live total and its 404, the field rule on a staged day (a team that formed after activation is refused with `field: 'teams'`, an un-stamped batch pays anybody), and a facilitator refused both routes. `security-sweep.test.ts`, which walks every registered endpoint with hostile shapes, covers the six new ones without being told about them. `./verify.sh` on the finished tree: typecheck, lint, standards (601 files, 18 rules, 0 violations), web
build, 865 API tests passed with 3 skipped across 65 files, and 1614 web tests. The API coverage thresholds
the gate enforces (94.6% branches, 98.9% functions) came in at 94.91% and 99.38%, with 99.07% lines. The first version missed the
branches threshold by two. Four tests closed it — the register of a day that has posted nothing, the empty
side of each of the register's two half-queries, and the four 404s the route owes for ids the day does not
hold — and one defensive re-read of a header its caller had just written was deleted rather than tested,
because a branch that no caller can reach is not a behaviour worth a gate. Separately, rule 10 refused three
`coalesce(…, false)` spellings inside SQL strings as flag arguments, and they are written as the conditions
they mean now: `batch_id IS NULL OR NOT is_reversed` says a row that was never in a batch has nothing to be
taken back, which is both the better sentence and the same truth. Playwright was not run: no
browser in this sandbox, and nothing on the web side changed — there is no console surface for a batch yet,
which is stated in the commit message as `AGENTS-workflow.md` §4 asks. One repair came out of running the
gate at all: its first web phase failed `FindNicknamePage.test.tsx`, a test that awaited the cluster
`<select>` and then chose an option in it — a race with the request that fills that element, won or lost on
how busy the machine was, and green again on a quiet re-run. It is fixed rather than re-run, because a gate
that goes red for an unrelated reason teaches the next person to ignore the gate: the file's nine selections
now go through one `chooseCluster` helper that waits for the `<option>` to exist. Nothing in `apps/web`
changed but that test file, and the API surface of this ADR is not involved in it.

### ADR-249 — `DB_INIT` provisions the database `DATABASE_URL` names, and the demo mode is `db-provision.sh`

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-049 (the app already provisions on boot), ADR-102 (the three data tiers and the "only into a database with no participants" guard), ADR-175 (the demo and production image twins), ADR-178 (`db-provision.sh`, and why it exists)
- **Decision:** One optional variable, `DB_INIT`, in `env.ts`, with two values.
  - **`schema`** — `schema.sql` plus the default seed (clusters, titles, the initial superadmin), in the app's own process, before the server opens a port. Schema + minimum.
  - **`demo`** — the same, then the recorded demo day, by spawning `bash db-provision.sh --demo --no-install` rather than calling `applyDemoSeed` in-process. The app and an operator at a terminal now go through one code path, so they cannot provision differently.
  - **Unset or empty does nothing extra**; the boot is exactly what it was. `DB_INIT` set without `DATABASE_URL` is refused at startup, naming both — it would otherwise provision the embedded PGlite directory and report success.
  - **The connection string reaches the script on stdin, never argv.** An argument is visible in the process list. `db-provision.sh` already reads the URL from stdin when none is given; the app uses that door. `SUPERADMIN_INITIAL_PASSCODE` goes in the child's environment, and `demo` refuses to start the script without it, because the script would otherwise stop to ask on a terminal that does not exist.
  - **A failed script stops the boot.** Non-zero exit rejects `runDbInit`, `index.ts` exits 1, and the platform's restart policy applies. Swallowing it would serve an empty database as if it had been provisioned.
  - **`db-provision.sh` gains `--no-install`**, consumed by the script and not passed on: its `ensure_deps` preflight runs `npm ci`, which is right on a laptop and wrong inside an image whose `node_modules` is already pruned.
  - **`db-provision.sh` now runs `node_modules/.bin/tsx` directly instead of `npx tsx`.** `npx` prints the command it runs, and that command line carries the connection string with its password. On a laptop that was scrollback; with the app calling the script it would have been the container log. Found by running the script against an unreachable URL, not by reading it.
  - **Both Dockerfiles** install `bash` (Alpine has none) and copy `db-provision.sh` and `_dev-common.sh`; `.dockerignore` un-ignores those two (it ignored `/*.sh` wholesale). The twins stay identical but for `PSD_SEED` (`docker-twins` rule).
- **Why:** Because a managed Postgres arrives empty and the only ways to fill it were a laptop run of `db-provision.sh` or knowing that `PSD_SEED=demo` exists and combining it with a first boot. `DB_INIT` says what is meant, in one variable, in the platform's environment panel. `PSD_SEED` is unchanged and still decides the demo tier on every boot; `DB_INIT=demo` is the explicit, once-stated version for a database that is being set up.
- **Not done, and why:** The managed-database case (ADR-178), where the app's role cannot run DDL, is not helped by `DB_INIT=schema` — the app is then asking itself to do what it cannot. `DB_INIT=demo` runs the script with `DATABASE_URL` as both the admin and the runtime credential for the same reason. That case still needs `./db-provision.sh ADMIN_URL --grant-to APP_ROLE` from somewhere holding an admin credential.
- **Impact:** `env.ts` (the variable, the DATABASE_URL rule, `inheritedEnv()` because that is the one file allowed to read `process.env`), `db/dbInit.ts` (new), `index.ts` (one call before `ensureSchema`), `db-provision.sh`, both Dockerfiles, `.dockerignore`.

**Validation.** `db-init.test.ts`, 6 tests, with the script runner as the seam: unset does nothing; `schema` builds the schema and seed and the clusters and superadmin are read back from the database; `demo` calls the script with `--demo --no-install`, the URL on stdin and not in argv, and the passcode in the environment; missing passcode refuses before running anything; a failing script rejects; no `DATABASE_URL` refuses. `bootstrap.test.ts` gains the parsing test (closed set, empty is unset, needs `DATABASE_URL`). `tsc`, ESLint and `npm run standards` (646 files, 18 rules, 0 violations) clean. `db-provision.sh --demo --no-install` run by hand against an unreachable URL fed on stdin: prints `connect ECONNREFUSED`, exits 1, and the password appears nowhere in the output. **Not run:** the script against a real Postgres (none in this sandbox), the Docker build (docker daemon down), and the full `./verify.sh`.


### ADR-250 — provisioning is a critical section across instances: one Postgres advisory lock, taken by the boot, the script and `DB_INIT`

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-049 (provisioning on every boot), ADR-102 (the demo day only into an empty database), ADR-178 (`db-provision.sh`), ADR-249 (`DB_INIT`)
- **Decision:** `DatabaseHandle.withProvisionLock(work)` runs `work` while holding `pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('psd-active-day:provision'))`, on one dedicated pooled connection (`db/advisoryLock.ts`).
  - **Why it was needed.** Every provisioning step is idempotent, and that is not the same as safe to interleave. An orchestrator starts several instances together; each runs `ensureSchema`, `seedDatabase` and `ensureDemoData`. Two instances can both read `participant` as empty and both load the demo day, because ADR-102's "only into an empty database" is a read followed by a write. That race existed before `DB_INIT`; it is just more likely when a fresh database and N replicas start together.
  - **What takes it.** The boot's whole provisioning block in `index.ts` (schema, seed, `PSD_SEED` demo), `DB_INIT=schema` in `dbInit.ts`, and `setup-cli.ts`'s provision run, which is what `db-provision.sh` executes. An operator's run and a booting instance therefore serialise with each other too.
  - **The loser waits, then finds the work done.** Polled with `pg_try_advisory_lock` every 500 ms rather than the blocking form, so the wait has a 5-minute deadline, a log line (`[db] waiting for another instance to finish provisioning`) and an error that says how to find the holder in `pg_locks`. A blocked instance that hangs silently is worse than one that fails loudly and is restarted by the orchestrator.
  - **Session-level on a dedicated connection.** The lock belongs to a connection; releasing through a pool could unlock on a different one and strand it. Session-level also means an instance that crashes mid-provision cannot leave the lock held, because Postgres drops it when the connection dies.
  - **PGlite runs `work()` directly.** One process, one connection; there is nothing to serialise.
  - **`DB_INIT=demo` does not hold the lock across its spawn.** The script takes the lock on its own connection, so a parent holding it would deadlock against its child. The child serialises itself; the parent's later boot block takes the lock afterwards, in sequence.
  - **Not re-entrant**, stated on the type: a nested call from the same handle waits on itself until the deadline.
- **Not done:** It does not make a schema CHANGE safe during a rolling deploy — old and new instances running against one database at once is a migration problem, and there are no migrations (ADR-049). It also does not cover work after provisioning: the presence flusher and the up-soon watcher run in every instance, and whether they are safe to run N times is a separate question this entry did not examine.
- **Impact:** `db/advisoryLock.ts` (new), `db/client.ts` (the handle member, both drivers), `index.ts`, `db/dbInit.ts`, `db/setup-cli.ts`.

**Validation.** `advisory-lock.test.ts`, 5 tests: free lock acquires without sleeping; a held lock is polled, announced once, and acquired when it frees; a lock that never frees fails with the lock's name and the `pg_locks` hint after exactly the expected number of polls; release unlocks the same key; PGlite just runs the work and propagates its error. `tsc` and ESLint clean. **Not run, and it matters:** two real instances against a real Postgres. There is no server in this sandbox and the postgres-driver suite is opt-in, so the claim that a session lock serialises two connections rests on Postgres's documented behaviour and not on a run here.


### ADR-251 — a failed database boot says where it stopped, why, and what to check; and a multi-host URI is accepted

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-178 (the boot already names the role), ADR-249 (`DB_INIT`), ADR-250 (the provisioning lock)
- **Decision:** Four additions, all in `apps/api/src/db/`, none of which prints a credential.
  - **A multi-host connection URI is reduced to its first host** (`connectionString.ts: normaliseConnectionString`). libpq accepts `postgresql://u:p@primary:5432,read:5432/db`; Node's `URL` does not (the port `5432,read` is not a number), so `pg` died with `ERR_INVALID_URL` and a redacted log. A managed platform issued exactly that shape: a primary and a read replica in one authority. The first host is the primary, the right one for an app that writes. The app logs that it dropped the others. Applied in `openNodePostgres`, the connectivity probe, and `describeTarget`.
  - **A malformed `DATABASE_URL` is refused at startup by `env.ts`, with a sentence naming the cause** (`diagnoseConnectionString`): an unresolved `${NAME}` reference, a blank value, stray whitespace or quotes, no `postgresql://` prefix, another scheme, an unparseable URL, a malformed `%` escape. The value is never quoted; the only text echoed back is the variable *name* inside an unresolved reference. `env.ts` prints one `KEY: reason` line per issue instead of Zod's escaped JSON dump. Skipped when `DATABASE_DRIVER=pglite`, which ignores the URL.
  - **Reachability is probed before anything queries** (`connectivity.ts: waitForDatabase`): a `connectionTimeoutMillis` of 10 s (the pool default is to wait forever, so an unreachable host looked like a hang), then up to 6 attempts with 1/2/4/8/8 s backoff, one log line each. Only *transient* failures retry — `ECONNREFUSED`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `ECONNRESET`, `EAI_AGAIN`, `57P03`, `53300`. A wrong password, a missing database or an unresolved host name is permanent and fails on the first attempt, because waiting would only delay the message that says so. Also run by `setup-cli.ts`, so `db-provision.sh` gets the same behaviour.
  - **Boot is a sequence of named steps, and a failure carries its step** (`bootLog.ts`): `reaching the database`, `opening the connection pool`, `identifying the database role`, `DB_INIT`, `provisioning`, `schema`, `default seed`, `demo seed`. Each logs a start line and an end line with a duration; the failure report starts `FAILED TO START during: <innermost step>`. The configuration the app received is printed first, with credentials as `set` / `NOT SET`, plus warnings for an *empty* `DATABASE_URL` (the app falls back to the embedded database on a filesystem that dies at the next deploy) and for `DATABASE_DRIVER=pglite` overriding a URL.
  - **The failure report replaces the raw exception** (`failureHints.ts: describeFailure`): `reason:` is the deepest cause, `chain:` is every link, `check:` is advice for the failures a managed Postgres actually produces (bad password, missing database, missing privilege, missing table, DNS, refused, timed out, TLS trust, TLS mismatch, `pg_hba`). Drizzle's `Failed query:` message — the whole SQL statement — is collapsed to its first line; every other message is printed whole, because several are multi-line instructions. The report is run through `redact`, which masks the known passwords and any `scheme://user:password@` it meets, since an error message is where a connection string leaks. `setup-cli.ts` and the script use the same report.
- **Why:** The failure that prompted this was a deploy that crash-looped with a 47-line Drizzle dump, `input: '*****REDACTED*****'`, and nothing naming the cause. It took two guesses and a screenshot to find that the URL was a multi-host list. A log should answer "what was it doing, what was wrong, what do I check" without a second person.
- **Not done:** `sslmode=require` in `pg` 8.23 is currently treated as `verify-full` (it prints a deprecation warning at every connect). A managed database with a self-signed certificate will therefore fail with `self-signed certificate`; the hint says to use `?sslmode=no-verify` or the provider's CA, but the app does not choose for the operator. The warning itself is `pg`'s and is left in the log. Read replicas are ignored, not used.
- **Impact:** new `connectionString.ts`, `failureHints.ts`, `connectivity.ts`, `bootLog.ts`; `env.ts`, `client.ts`, `provision.ts`, `dbInit.ts`, `index.ts`, `setup-cli.ts` changed.

**Validation.** `connection-diagnostics.test.ts`, 47 tests, with a fixture in the shape of the URL that failed (made-up credentials): Node cannot parse it; it normalises to the primary; every diagnosis names its cause and none quotes the value; `redact` masks a password, its decoded form, and a URL it was never told about; every hint fires for its code or message; the chain walks Drizzle → `AggregateError` → errno and survives a cycle and a non-`Error` throw; `waitForDatabase` connects first time, retries a refusal with backoff and succeeds, gives up with the cause kept, and does *not* retry a wrong password; a step failure carries its innermost step. `bootstrap.test.ts` adds the two startup refusals. Run by hand: the app and `db-provision.sh` against `127.0.0.1:1` with a multi-host URL and a dummy password (primary host chosen, five retry lines, one report, password absent from output), an unresolved `${…}` reference, and a bare secret. **Not run:** a real Postgres, so the success path through `pg` with the normalised URL, the `sslmode` behaviour against the provider, and the exact error codes a real Northflank database returns are untested here.


### ADR-252 — `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` provisions the database; `DATABASE_URL` runs the app

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-178 (a runtime role that cannot build), ADR-249 (`DB_INIT`), ADR-250 (the provisioning lock), ADR-251 (diagnostics)
- **Decision:** An optional `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` overrides `DATABASE_URL` for the `DB_INIT` step, and only for it.
  - **Provisioning runs as the admin role.** `DB_INIT=schema` opens a second connection with `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` (reachability-probed and retried like the primary), takes the provisioning lock on it, applies the schema and default seed, and closes it. `DB_INIT=demo` hands the admin URL to `db-provision.sh` on stdin.
  - **The app role is then granted and verified.** Tables belong to whoever builds them, so what the admin built is unreadable to the role in `DATABASE_URL` until granted, and the failure — `permission denied for table …` — would otherwise arrive at the first request, long after the boot log said all was well. `grantRuntimeAccess` runs on the admin connection, then `verifyRuntimeAccess` reads the catalogue back; if the role still cannot reach every table, the boot fails with `describeAccess`'s explanation. For `demo` the role name goes to the script as `--grant-to` (a role name is not a secret; the passwords are never on argv).
  - **The running app still connects as `DATABASE_URL`**, so it can hold the least privilege that works: read/write on tables, no DDL. The ordinary boot path (`ensureSchema` under the lock) then takes the `verified` branch of ADR-178 instead of trying DDL it cannot run.
  - **Same role in both URLs is a no-op grant**, not an error.
  - **Requires `DB_INIT`.** Set without it, the boot log says `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN is set … NOT being used`, because an admin credential sitting in an environment doing nothing is something an operator wants to be told. It is validated at startup (ADR-251) only when `DB_INIT` will use it, and an empty value is unset.
  - **Redacted everywhere.** Its password joins the secrets that `redact` masks in failure reports, and the boot config prints only `user@host/db`.
- **Why:** On a managed platform the application role usually cannot create objects in schema `public` (ADR-178), and the credential that can is exactly the one that should not be running the event. Separating them lets the init use the powerful one once and the app live on the weak one, without a laptop run of `db-provision.sh` between deploys.
- **Not done:** The admin credential is still present in the app's environment for as long as the variable is set, so the container holds it. Removing it after the first successful deploy is the operator's step, and the boot log warns when it is set without `DB_INIT`, which is the state to leave it in once `DB_INIT` is removed too. Nothing here rotates credentials or revokes the grant. A role that is only *named* the same in both URLs but is a different login on a different server is treated as the same role.
- **Impact:** `env.ts` (the variable, and the database rules moved into `databaseIssues`), `db/dbInit.ts`, `db/bootLog.ts`, `db/provision.ts` (`roleNameFrom` accepts a multi-host URI), `index.ts` (secrets), `.env.example`, `AGENTS-workflow.md`.

**Validation.** `db-init.test.ts` adds 7 tests on a real PGlite role: the script gets the admin URL on stdin and `--grant-to app_rt`, no password on argv; same role means no grant; schema mode builds on the admin database and not the runtime one, grants, and closes the admin exactly once; the app role is checked in the catalogue to reach every table; a missing role fails loudly and still closes the admin. `bootstrap.test.ts` and `connection-diagnostics.test.ts` cover the startup validation and the boot-config lines. **Not run:** against two real Postgres roles on a server, so the grant path through `pg` rather than PGlite, and the claim that a managed provider lets its admin role `GRANT` on the schema, rest on Postgres's documented behaviour.


### ADR-253 — the provisioning lock is transaction-level, says who holds it when it waits, and `--inspect` reports it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-250 (the lock *mechanism*; its purpose and call sites stand)
- **Decision:**
  - **Transaction-level, not session-level.** ADR-250 took `pg_try_advisory_lock` in one statement and released it with `pg_advisory_unlock` in a later one, on a checked-out pooled connection. Anything between the app and Postgres that may hand those two statements to different backends — a transaction-mode pooler, a failover proxy — takes the lock on one backend and unlocks on another, which leaves it held by a session nobody owns, and every later boot waits on it. `withAdvisoryLock` now runs `begin`, `set local idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '15min'`, `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`, the work, and `rollback`. A transaction pins every statement in it to one backend, and commit, rollback, a dropped connection and the idle limit each release the lock, so there is no path that leaves it held. The idle limit is what lets the server itself reap a holder whose process vanished without closing its socket (a SIGKILLed container behind a half-open TCP connection can otherwise be believed alive for hours).
  - **A waiting boot says who it is waiting for.** Every ten seconds the wait logs the holder from `pg_locks` joined to `pg_stat_activity`: backend pid, application name, state, seconds in that state, seconds connected, client address, and the `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` statement to end a stranded one. The statement is offered and never run: the holder may be a healthy slow provisioning, and ending it half-way is what the lock exists to prevent. If the role cannot see the other session's details the report says so rather than printing blanks. The give-up error carries the same report.
  - **Connections are named.** `application_name` is `psd-active-day@<hostname>`, so a session in `pg_stat_activity` is attributable to a container, and a leftover from one that no longer exists is recognisable by a name no running container carries.
  - **`db-provision.sh … --inspect` reports the lock** (`free`, or `HELD` with the holder). It only looks and never takes it, so inspecting cannot cause the stall it diagnoses.
- **Why:** A deploy with ONE instance still sat at `waiting for another instance to finish provisioning`, which a lock whose only job is to serialise instances cannot do unless something other than a live instance holds it. The wait gave no way to tell what.
- **Not known:** Which of the causes above held the lock in that deploy has not been established. The old code was session-level, so a lock stranded by it will still block the new code (same key), and needs one `pg_terminate_backend` by an admin to clear; the new log names the pid. Whether this provider's database sits behind a pooler is the thing to find out.
- **Impact:** `db/advisoryLock.ts`, `db/client.ts`, `db/setup-cli.ts`, `db/connectivity.ts`.

**Validation.** `advisory-lock.test.ts`, 13 tests: the wrapper's exact statement order (`begin`, idle limit, xact lock, work, `rollback`); rollback on a failing work; a failed rollback not hiding the work's error; the work never running when the lock is unavailable; the holder report for a visible, an invisible and an absent holder; and, against a real PGlite catalogue, that the `pg_locks` key arithmetic finds a held lock whose hash is negative (`psd-active-day:provision` hashes to -459877932, the case where a plain shift selects the wrong half). **Not run:** against a pooler or a real multi-session server, so the claim that this fixes the stall rests on Postgres's documented transaction semantics, and the holder query's `pg_stat_activity` columns were not exercised on a server (PGlite has one session).


### ADR-254 — a lock holder with no heartbeat is dead, and a waiting boot ends it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-250, ADR-253
- **Decision:** A booting instance that cannot get the provisioning lock looks at the holder every ten seconds and **ends it if it is provably stale**.
  - **Idle alone proves nothing.** The holder is idle by design while the real work runs on other connections, so `state = idle` / `idle in transaction` looks the same for a live provisioning and for one whose process was killed. Ending on idleness would cut a healthy run half-way, which is exactly what the lock exists to prevent.
  - **So a live holder proves it is alive.** `withAdvisoryLock` runs `select 1` on the holder's connection every 5 s while the work runs. That moves the session's `state_change`, so a live holder is never more than a few seconds idle. A holder idle for **120 s** (24 missed beats) therefore has no owner.
  - **The kill re-checks inside the statement.** `select pg_terminate_backend(pid) … where pid = $1 and state like 'idle%' and now() - state_change >= $2` — so a holder that woke between our look and our kill (a slow start, a late beat) is left alone. It returns whether a backend was signalled.
  - **It never ends the wait.** A role not permitted to signal that session gets a logged reason (`could not end stale holder pid …: <why>`) and the wait continues to its deadline; the holder is then named in the give-up error as before. After a successful kill the next poll is immediate.
  - **Only the holder lookup's own scope.** The query now filters to the current database and excludes the looker's own backend, so another database's lock on the same key, or this process's own session, cannot be mistaken for a holder.
  - **Heartbeat failure** stops the timer and logs `lock heartbeat failed, so the lock is lost`: a failing `select 1` means the connection is gone, and with it the lock.
  - Applies to the app's pooled boot path only. `db-provision.sh` takes the lock without reclaiming: a person at a terminal sees the holder and decides.
- **Not covered:** A holder that is `active` (a query stuck on a lock of its own) is never ended; it needs a person. A *live* holder whose heartbeat is starved for 120 s (a process frozen, not dead) would be ended and its provisioning cut — the 15-minute `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` is the server-side backstop for the other direction. Holders from the pre-ADR-253 code are session-level locks with no heartbeat, so they are `idle` and stale after 120 s and are reclaimed by this too, provided the role may signal them (same role, or a member of it).
- **Impact:** `db/advisoryLock.ts`, `db/client.ts`.

**Validation.** `advisory-lock.test.ts` is now 22 tests. New: the kill statement carries both guards; an active holder, a briefly idle holder and an unreadable one are never ended; nothing is ended unless asked; a refused termination and a holder that woke are reported and the wait continues; the lock is taken straight after a kill with no extra poll; `isStale` at its boundaries; the heartbeat fires on schedule while the work runs, stops after, reports a dead connection once, and can be turned off. **Not run:** against a real server with two sessions, so `pg_terminate_backend`'s permission rules and `state_change` behaviour are Postgres's documented behaviour and not something observed here.

**Amendment to ADR-249 / ADR-252 (found in a live deploy).** `DB_INIT=demo` spawned `db-provision.sh`, which unsets `DATABASE_URL` so a stale one cannot redirect it, but left `DB_INIT` and `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` in place. The script runs the app's own `env.ts`, whose rule "`DB_INIT` requires `DATABASE_URL`" then refused it, and the log showed only `database setup failed` after `schema already present`. Two changes: `db-provision.sh` now unsets `DB_INIT` and `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` as well (it names its target on stdin and none of the three configures it), and the app builds the child's environment without `DB_INIT`, `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN`, `DATABASE_URL` and `DATABASE_DRIVER`, so a direct caller is covered too. Pinned in `bootstrap.test.ts` (the one test file allowed to touch `process.env`). The unit test that stubbed the runner had the right arguments and could not see this; it needed the environment, which is what the new test asserts. The log line that hid the cause — the script's failure printing only a heading — is the thing the earlier diagnostics work was meant to prevent; the failure text itself was cut from the pasted log, so what the script printed beneath `database setup failed` is not known, and this cause was reproduced by running `env.ts` with the same variables rather than read from the deploy.


### ADR-255 — a role that can create but does not own the tables verifies the schema instead of altering it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-049, ADR-178 (the same idea, one privilege down), ADR-252 (`DATABASE_URL_ADMIN`)
- **Decision:** `ensureSchema` now asks two questions before applying `schema.sql`: may this role CREATE in schema `public` (ADR-178), **and does it own, or inherit ownership of, the tables already there**. If it can create but owns none of what exists, it verifies instead — `verified` when every table is present, a refusal naming `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` / `db-provision.sh --grant-to` when some are missing.
