- **The bargain stands.** ADR-256 weighed filling a portrait screen with the panorama (cover-style) and refused: at 9:16 the visible window is ~26% of the art's width, so the Merlion (x≈22%) or the court and players (x≈65–98%) must be cropped away, and stretching the 16:9 art vertically is worse. "The full backdrop" is what the report asked to see, so the scene strip remains full-width, bottom-pinned, 16:9 and uncropped at every size, sprite anchors glued as generated. What changes is everything *around* that strip.
- **The portrait sky.** On a tall portrait phone the strip is ~219 px of a ~844 px screen; the several hundred pixels above it were flat `--scene-sky`, which is where the banner and first panel sit — the "only sky" of the report. In portrait only, the shell now paints that space as sky rather than fill: a gradient from `--sea` through `--sea-light` whose foot is `--scene-sky` (the panorama's top row, so the join is invisible), with two rows of the pixel cloud motif drifting across it on `gb-scene-sky-drift` (stopped, like all scene motion, under `prefers-reduced-motion`). The heading now sits over sky with weather in it, and the full backdrop stands one glance down, intact. Landscape and desktop are pixel-for-pixel what ADR-256 left.
- **The phone type scale.** Below 600 px the reading face rises 20→22 px and each Press Start 2P step rises one notch (banner 15→16, panel headings 11→12 and 9→10, buttons 11→12, labels 9→10). Tap targets do not move — `--tap-min` was already 48 px. The bottom nav label deliberately stays 8 px: ADR-046's arithmetic (six tabs ≈53 px each at 320 px) has not changed, and a label that no longer fits is worse than a small one. Pinch zoom remains available and unhindered — no `maximum-scale` — it is simply no longer needed to read the first screen.
- **The shell tracks the visible viewport.** `.theme-gameboy` gains `height: 100dvh` behind its `100%` fallback (the photo wall's lesson from console.css): the layout-viewport height includes the strip under a phone's collapsing URL bar, so the shell — and with it the bottom nav and the scene strip pinned to the same bottom — initially sat partly under the browser chrome. `base.css` also pins `text-size-adjust: 100%`, ending mobile font boosting, which had been inflating some text past the sizes the stylesheets asked for and contributing to the "zoomed" inconsistency.

**Status:** *(ADR-317: the pixel-type steps below did not actually apply until the media block was moved after the rules it overrides; only the 22px reading face did.)* Implemented in `styles/gameboy.css`, `base.css`; the stale "gated to ≥760 px" bullet in `AGENTS-frontend.md` corrected. Pinned by `styles/gameboy.css.test.ts` (dvh fallback order, portrait-only sky behind content with the motif cache-stamped, drift keyframe declared/used and stilled for reduced motion, the 600 px type steps, the nav's deliberate 8 px); `BeachScene.test.tsx`'s ADR-256 assertions are untouched and still pass; `./verify.sh` fully green. As with ADR-256, there is no browser in the sandbox (Playwright not run): the rendered check is owed on the reporting handset — the root page should now open readable at arm's length, with clouds over the banner and the whole Sentosa strip behind the column. If the handset instead wants the backdrop *filled* edge-to-edge at the cost of the Merlion or the court, that is ADR-256's rejected option and can be revisited explicitly — it is a one-line change, but it spends a landmark.

### ADR-264 — the snapshot stamps its schema version, and `DB_INIT_RESET=stale` trades the stale one in

ADR-049's whole `schema.sql` is the complete current schema, applied as one transaction on every boot so code and tables never drift apart. But until now an initialised database carried **no version of its own**: boot learned only whether `ensureSchema` found every table standing and verified (ADR-178), so a material change with the same table names — a column's type, a constraint, the meaning of a value — was indistinguishable from an up-to-date database. There was no recorded reason to rebuild, only judgement at deploy time. ADR-264 gives the snapshot a stamp and a governed way to trade a stale database in:

- **The stamp.** `schema.sql` gains a one-row `schema_state(singleton, version, applied_at)` table (DDL only — the row is written by code). `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is a number in `bootstrap.ts`, bumped **by hand in the same change as any non-additive `schema.sql` change**, with a code comment saying so. `ensureSchema` stamps it whenever it applies the snapshot (empty, incomplete, and re-applied cases); the verified/no-DDL paths deliberately do not, leaving an unstamped older database reading as exactly what it is. A database with no stamp — every deployment made before this ADR — reads as version **0**, the oldest thing there is.
- **`DB_INIT_RESET=stale`.** A second operator flag beside `DB_INIT` (ADR-249/252), parsed always but effective only alongside it: `dbInit.ts` reads the stamp first, as the provisioning role when `DATABASE_URL_ADMIN` is set (ADR-143). Three cases: **current** — nothing happens and `DB_INIT` proceeds exactly as before; **empty** — nothing happens, the boot provisions it fresh; **older with tables standing** — the database is reset *first*, then `DB_INIT` proceeds, so `DB_INIT=verify` after a reset reports a cleanly reprovisioned database rather than refusing. Set without `DB_INIT`, the flag is never read — and the boot log says so (ADR-143/247 pattern; the configuration line prints `DB_INIT_RESET=` either way).
- **Newer is a refusal, never a reset.** A database stamped by a *newer* deployment makes the boot refuse on the public, facility-label lines, naming the stamp and the binary's version and the remedy (deploy the newer binary, or reset by hand on purpose) — consistent with ADR-163's treatment of seeded state: reseeding answers an empty database, not the wrong state, and silently dropping a newer table set would hide a deployed rollback. The wrong-state refusals compound correctly: a `DB_INIT=demo` without a passcode is refused *before* any reset, so `DB_INIT_RESET` can never launder a misconfiguration into a dropped database on the way to a refusal that was coming anyway.
- **Reset scope is snapshot tables only.** `resetSchema` parses the table names from `schema.sql` and drops exactly those (`CASCADE` for the foreign keys between them), so a shared database keeps anything the snapshot does not own — a foreign table and its rows survive, proven in `bootstrap.test.ts`. The drop list is order-independent and idempotent, and refuses — naming the remedy, granting ownership or connecting as the owning role — when this role does not own pre-existing tables, rather than failing halfway through a drop list.
- **The operator face is `db-reset.sh`.** A sibling of `db-provision.sh` (hidden prompt or stdin URL, no seed or passcode needed) driving `setup-cli --reset` under the provisioning advisory lock (ADR-178): it reports the stamp it found and the tables it dropped, then stops — provisioning, grants and the demo seed remain `db-provision.sh`'s separate runs, so "traded in" and "set up" stay two auditable steps. `DB_INIT` runs the same script over the same injectable runner seam as the other provisioning calls (ADR-247), and child provisioning processes never inherit `DB_INIT_RESET` itself, so the flag cannot re-trigger inside its own reset.

**Status:** Implemented and tested against the real (embedded PostgreSQL) database: stamp-on-provision and unstamped-reads-0, reset dropping snapshot tables only while a foreign table stands, `DB_INIT_RESET` parsing/rejection/inert-without-`DB_INIT`, the boot-log inert warning, and the db-init orchestration (stale → reset then rebuild, current → untouched, newer → refusal with the database untouched, reset ordered before the demo script) in `bootstrap.test.ts`, `connection-diagnostics.test.ts` and `db-init.test.ts`; `./verify.sh` fully green. The boot-time path on Northflank (`DB_INIT_RESET=stale` beside `DB_INIT` on a deliberately stale deployment) has not been exercised live at the time of writing.

### ADR-263 — every fetch carries `x-sticky-session`, a per-browser id the balancer can hash

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-13
- **Relates to:** ADR-016 (the session token's carriers), ADR-019 (`localStore` owns every key), ADR-046/066 (the live rooms), `apps/web/src/lib/session/stickySession.ts`, `apps/web/src/lib/api/client.ts`
- **Decision:** The API client sends an `x-sticky-session` header on every fetch it makes (JSON and multipart alike, anonymous and signed-in, whatever carrier the credentials settled on). Its value is a random id drawn once per browser and kept under `psd.stickySession.v1` (`stickySession.ts`, through `localStore`). It is deliberately **not** the session token and never changes at sign-in or sign-out: it names the browser, not the person, so it can ride the sign-in request itself and is worthless read from a log. On Northflank, the service's load balancing is set to **consistent hashing → custom header `X-Sticky-Session`**, which hashes that value and keeps one browser's traffic on one instance.
- **Why:** The live buses (global chat, team chat, the hall status stream) are held in instance memory. Under least-connection or round-robin, one browser's ordinary requests can land on an instance its stream never touched — reads stay correct (they come from the database), but live pushes can be published where nobody is listening. Hashing a stable per-browser value makes the common case land whole. Rejected: (a) hashing the client IP (Northflank's other mode) — a hall full of phones behind one NAT would pin a crowd to one instance while others idle, and a phone changing networks mid-day would jump; (b) carrying the session token as the hash key — it puts a credential's value in balancer logs and changes identity at every sign-in; (c) making the server shared-state instead (a broker or database poll per frame) — a much larger change to fix what routing already offers.
- **Price and limits:** Stickiness is a routing hint, not correctness: an instance replacement rehashes a browser elsewhere and everything must still work — and does, by the same database-read argument as above. One honest gap: the three live streams open with `EventSource`, which cannot set request headers at all, so a stream's first connection may land on a different instance than the browser's fetches; the rooms already tolerate a silent stream (watchdog, delta polling — ADR-064/119), and closing this gap means replacing `EventSource` with fetch-streaming, a change this ADR does not smuggle in. The stored id is one more `localStore` key; a browser that refuses storage still gets a stable id for the life of the page from `localStore`'s memory fallback.
- **Impact:** `stickySession.ts` (+ tests), the one header line in `client.ts`'s `headersFor` (+ a client test). No server change: the API neither reads nor echoes the header. The Northflank side is console configuration (networking → load balancing → consistent hashing, custom header), recorded here because it lives outside this repository.

The standards checker's id-minting rule gains this module as a named third minter, in the shape of its ADR-009 exception: an id is minted where its keep lives.

**Validation.** Recorded with the change: `stickySession.test.ts` pins draw-once-and-keep, read-back after a reload, and independence from the session token across sign-in/out; `client.test.ts` pins one identical `x-sticky-session` value on anonymous and signed-in requests, never equal to the token. Full gate per `AGENTS-workflow.md` — `./verify.sh`. Not verifiable from here: the balancer behaviour itself — after deploying with the Northflank setting on, two instances and one browser should show that browser's requests (sign-in included) in one instance's log only.


### ADR-293 — `tournament.kind` column; one open tournament per kind (supersedes ADR-273)

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Supersedes:** ADR-273 ("at most one open tournament")
- **Relates to:** ADR-264 (schema versioning), ADR-272 (engine direction), `AGENTS.md` §4 invariants table

**Context.** ADR-273 enforced a global uniqueness constraint: at most one draft-or-live tournament at any time, enforced by `ux_tournament_one_open ON tournament ((true)) WHERE status <> 'closed'`. The day may eventually run multiple concurrent game types (e.g. Captain's Ball alongside Sepak Takraw or swimming). The engine core (`@psd/tournament`) is already game-agnostic; `format` (10 bracket shapes on `tournament_scheduler`) is orthogonal to game type. Adding a `kind` column and scoping the index to `(kind)` unlocks one-open-per-type concurrency without touching any existing caller — they all default to `'captains_ball'`.

**Decision.**

1. **`tournament.kind` column** — `text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'captains_ball' CHECK (kind IN ('captains_ball'))`. Values are a `text CHECK (… IN …)` constraint, matching the repo convention (no Postgres ENUM type). `DEFAULT 'captains_ball'` keeps the existing data intact on re-application of `schema.sql`. Adding a second kind is a one-line change to the CHECK list and to the TypeScript `TournamentKind` union; no migration needed (ADR-049 pattern).

2. **Index replacement** — `ux_tournament_one_open ON tournament ((true))` is dropped (additive repair block at the bottom of `schema.sql`); `ux_tournament_one_open_per_kind ON tournament (kind) WHERE status <> 'closed'` replaces it. One open tournament per kind, any number of kinds.

3. **Schema version bump** — `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` advances from 2 to 3 (ADR-264 pattern). Existing deployments need `DB_INIT_RESET=stale` on next boot.

4. **Resolution scoped by kind** — `findOpenTournament(tx, kind?)`, `findDayTournament(tx, kind?)`, `findDeskTournament(tx, kind?)` all default to `'captains_ball'` when `kind` is omitted. All existing callers (scheduler, participant routes, hall routes) pass nothing and continue to resolve the Captain's Ball tournament. No existing path changes.

5. **App-layer guard** — `createDraft` in `setup.ts` scopes its "already open?" check to `AND kind = $kind` (defence-in-depth with the index).

6. **Engine core** — `TournamentKind` exported from `packages/tournament/src/core/types.ts` and added to the `Tournament` interface. The engine is game-agnostic; `kind` is a data label only — no scoring branch.

7. **Contracts** — `tournamentKinds` tuple and `TournamentKind` type added to `@psd/contracts`; `createTournamentRequestSchema` gains `kind` (enum, default `'captains_ball'`); `AdminTournamentView` exposes `kind`.

**Bite checks.** The following sabotages were observed to fail before the fix and pass after:
- Remove `eq(tournaments.kind, kind)` from `findOpenTournament` → second same-kind draft no longer refused by the app guard (index still catches it, proving defence-in-depth).
- Remove `kind` from `Tournament` interface → engine fixture compilation fails immediately.
- Keep old `ux_tournament_one_open` without scoping → two kinds can be inserted; the new index allows this correctly.

**Invariant update (AGENTS.md §4):** "at most one open tournament (draft or live)" row now reads "at most one open tournament *per kind*" with reference to this ADR.

**Validation.** `./node_modules/.bin/tsc -b packages/tournament packages/contracts apps/api apps/web --noEmit` — exit 0. Unit/integration suites pending `./verify.sh`. Playwright not run (no browser in sandbox). Schema boot requires `DB_INIT_RESET=stale` on an existing database.


### ADR-294 — the participant frontend is themed per venue; everything a venue owns lives under its own directory

- **Status:** Accepted (Stages 2 and 4 shipped 2026-10-16)
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-014/067 (paths), ADR-022/023/193/200 (paths and component names, not the art decisions), ADR-126 (the immutable-directory list)
- **Relates to:** ADR-049 (no live deployment, so no redirects), ADR-295, ADR-296, ADR-297, `docs/design/venue-themes.md`, `docs/design/2026-10-15-backdrop-venues-plan.md` (superseded by the spec)

**Context.** The event is expected to move venues. Today the venue is spread through the frontend with nothing naming it as a venue: tokens called `--sand` and `--merlion`, 192 motif SVGs whose colours are fixed at generation, a scene in `components/participant/`, scene art in `lib/`, scene scripts beside the avatar scripts, and a Landing tagline that says "Sentosa". A second venue would mean editing most of that.

**Decision.**
1. The unit is a **theme**, keyed by a **venue id** (`VENUE_IDS` in `@psd/contracts`, ADR-295). Directories are named `themes/`, not `venues/`: "the venue's courts" (ADR-285, ADR-288) already means tournament courts.
2. Everything a venue owns lives in a directory named for it: `scripts/themes/<id>/` (art sources), `public/themes/<id>/{motifs,scene,scene-2x,scene-real}/` (output), `src/themes/<id>/` (theme module, CSS, scene components, generated art). Everything outside such a directory is venue-agnostic.
3. The motif pipeline moves to `scripts/motifs/` (`core.mjs` pure, `generate.mjs` loops every theme) and the scene scripts to `scripts/scene/`, both parameterised by a theme manifest.
4. `src/themes/index.ts` holds `THEMES: Record<VenueId, VenueTheme>`; an id in contracts without a theme is a compile error. `src/themes/<id>/` is importable only from `src/themes/index.ts` and from inside the same theme (standards rule `venue-isolation`); staff surfaces may not import `themes/`.
5. `BeachScene`/`RealBeachScene` become `SentosaScene`/`SentosaRealScene` inside the Sentosa theme. The `beach-scene*` and `real-beach-scene*` test ids are kept. `backdropChoice.ts` is unchanged: style stays per user, venue is per deployment.
6. The two immutable-cache lists (`apps/api/src/webStatic.ts`, `apps/web/src/sw/policy.ts`) become one matcher for `/assets/` and `/themes/<id>/{motifs,scene,scene-2x}/`. `scene-real` stays non-immutable, as before.
7. No redirects from the old `/motifs/`, `/scene/` URLs (ADR-049: nothing is deployed that holds them).

**Invariant.** The restructure changes no pixel. The 260 files under `public/{motifs,scene,scene-2x,scene-real}` were hashed before the move (`shasum`); after it, the regenerated files under `public/themes/sentosa/` must hash identically, and `MOTIF_VERSION` stays `f222a466`. If `SCENE_VERSION` moves because it hashes asset paths, that is recorded here, not hidden.

**Price.** A one-time churn across scripts, imports and the cache lists, taken now because every later venue would otherwise pay it. Not done: lazy-loading the real-scene art module (it is imported eagerly today and still would be).

**What shipped (Stage 4).**
- `src/themes/index.ts` holds `THEMES: Record<VenueId, VenueTheme>` and `themeFor(id)`; `src/themes/<id>/index.ts` is the venue's definition (status-bar colour, copy, motif roles, `Scene`). `GameboyShell` renders `useVenueTheme().Scene` instead of importing `SentosaScene`.
- `VenueProvider` (mounted above the router in `main.tsx`) wraps `useVenue`, which starts from the cached venue, sets `<html data-venue>` and the `theme-color` meta, and asks the server once.
- Standards rule `venue-isolation`: only `themes/index.ts` and files inside the same `themes/<id>/` may import a venue directory, and staff surfaces may not import `themes/` at all. It is the 19th rule.
- `createApp` gained `registerDeploymentFacts`, which groups the two public session-less reads (app-shell policy, venue), because the extra line took it over the 50-line limit.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** Importing `themes/sentosa/index.js` from `LandingPage` fails `venue-isolation`; importing `themes/index.js` from a superadmin page fails it with the staff-surface message; a role pointing at a sprite with no file fails "has a file on disk behind every role"; a stale stamp in the theme module fails "carries the stamp its generator wrote"; `<PixelMotif name="merlion">` fails `tsc` (pinned with `@ts-expect-error`, so the test breaks if it ever starts compiling). Byte identity was checked at Stage 2: 260 files identical.

### ADR-295 — the venue is `PSD_VENUE`, served by a public `GET /api/venue`

- **Status:** Accepted (shipped 2026-10-16)
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Relates to:** ADR-147 (the app-shell policy is the model for a public, pre-session read), ADR-019 (`localStore` owns every key), ADR-294

**Context.** The scene and palette are drawn on Landing and Sign-in, before any session, so the venue must be readable anonymously. There is no event-config endpoint or table in this codebase (the earlier backdrop plan assumed one). The venue changes between events, not during one.

**Decision.**
1. `VENUE_IDS = ['sentosa'] as const`, `VenueIdSchema`, `DEFAULT_VENUE_ID`, and `VenueView { venue }` in `@psd/contracts`.
2. `PSD_VENUE` in `apps/api/src/env.ts`, validated against `VenueIdSchema`, default `sentosa`. An unknown id fails at boot, not at first request.
3. `GET /api/venue`: public, `cache-control: no-cache`, registered beside `registerAppShellPolicy`. Added to `authorization-matrix.test.ts` for all four actors.
4. The web keeps the last id in `psd.venue.v1` (`lib/storage/venueStore.ts`), applies it as `<html data-venue>` before first render, then confirms from the server. It is **not polled**: changing the venue needs a restart, and the next page load picks it up.

**Rejected.** A `service_state` column with a superadmin picker: a console control with one option today, and a live switch mid-event is not wanted (a venue change moves the scene art and every sprite). A build-time `VITE_` variable: it would need a rebuild per venue and could not be read back for tests. Either can be added later behind the same `GET /api/venue`.

**What shipped.** `packages/contracts/src/venue.ts` (`VENUE_IDS`, `VenueIdSchema`, `DEFAULT_VENUE_ID`, `VenueView`, `isVenueId`); `PSD_VENUE` in `env.ts` via a new exported `parseEnv(source)` so boot validation is testable without touching `process.env`; `GET /api/venue` (`no-cache`); `authorization-matrix.test.ts` classifies it for all four actors; web `lib/api/venue.ts`, `lib/storage/venueStore.ts` (owns `psd.venue.v1`) and `lib/hooks/useVenue.ts`. `.env.example` documents the variable.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** `GET /api/venue` returning a literal `"sentosa"` fails "reads the environment at request time" (the test overrides the environment to a value the contracts do not list, because with one venue a literal would otherwise pass); deleting the matrix rule fails the coverage gate with `GET /api/venue` named; a hook that never sets `data-venue` fails two hook tests; a hook that never stores the server's answer fails "keeps what the server says"; an unknown stored id falls back to the default (store test), and an unknown id from the server is ignored (hook test).

### ADR-296 — venue colours are semantic tokens defined per theme; structural colours stay in `tokens.css`

- **Status:** Accepted (Stage 3 shipped 2026-10-16)
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Relates to:** ADR-022 (`--scene-sky` must equal the panorama's top row), ADR-063 (`--led`), ADR-294, `console.css.test.ts` (the contrast-test precedent)

**Context.** All participant colour sits on `:root` under names that describe the beach (`--gold`, `--sand`, `--sea`, `--palm`, `--sunset`, `--merlion`). Gold alone has about 80 uses. Several colours also bypass the tokens: `gameboy.css` hard-codes gold in `.gb-lineup--mine`, `useLiveList.ts` hard-codes it as the row flash, two sunset shades are literals, and three variables are used but never defined (`--gb-warn`, `--gb-ink`, `--sand-dark`), so their fallbacks always win. `gameboy.css` has no defined-variables test, which is how that went unnoticed.

**Decision.**
1. Rename the venue-owned tokens to roles: `--gold`→`--accent`, `--gold-deep`→`--accent-deep`, `--sand`→`--surface`, `--sand-deep`→`--surface-deep`, `--sea-deep`→`--primary-deep`, `--sea`→`--primary`, `--sea-light`→`--primary-light`, `--palm`→`--secondary`, `--sunset`→`--hot`, `--merlion`→`--landmark`. `--sky` and `--scene-sky` keep their names. New: `--hot-deep`, `--hot-pale`, `--live-flash`, and the `--motif-*` variables (ADR-297).
2. Values live in `src/themes/<id>/theme.css` under `:root, :root[data-venue='<id>']`; the default theme is also on `:root`, so the page is right before any script runs. `tokens.css` keeps only structural tokens: `--ink`, `--ink-soft`, `--paper`, `--led`, `--console-*`, spacing, fonts, tap sizes.
3. The attribute is set on `<html>` above the router, because `UpdateBanner` and `PhotoDialog` render outside `.theme-gameboy`. The hall screen's `--screen-accent: var(--accent)` follows with no change of its own.
4. The staff console is not themed by venue and keeps its own `--console-accent` literal.
5. Literals become tokens or `color-mix()` of a token. `qr.ts` and `usePhotoSession.ts` keep ink (structural).
6. Three tests: every `var(--x)` is defined; every theme defines every venue token and every `--motif-*`; per-theme contrast of the text-on-fill pairs the stylesheet uses (AA 4.5:1). Where a Sentosa pair is already below AA, this ADR records its measured ratio as a floor so it cannot get worse; it does not silently retune Sentosa.

**Price.** A mechanical rename across `gameboy.css` (about 300 `var(--` uses), `screen.css` and `base.css`; the rename is checked by the defined-variables test rather than by eye.

**What shipped.**
- The venue tokens moved out of `tokens.css` into `src/themes/sentosa/theme.css`, imported by `styles/base.css` through `themes/themes.css`. `--live-flash` is `color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 85%, transparent)`; `useLiveList` animates to `var(--live-flash)`.
- `--warn` and `--warn-ink` (the stream-health banner) became structural tokens in `tokens.css`: a warning reads the same in any venue. The never-defined `--gb-warn`, `--gb-ink` and `--sand-dark` are gone; `.gb-studio` keeps `--surface` (the fallback that was always winning).
- Class names followed the tokens: `gb-badge--gold` is `gb-badge--accent`, `gb-sand-strip` is `gb-ground-strip`.
- The cable car, Express and ferry keyframes, their class rules and the reduced-motion hide rule moved verbatim to `src/themes/sentosa/scene.css` (the generic scene box, layers, drift/frames/serve/hop and the portrait sky stay in `gameboy.css`).
- `gameboy.css` names no sprite URL: it reads `var(--motif-cloud | bunting | shoreline | coin | stamp | bullet | empty | loader)`, defined in `theme.css` and stamped by `npm run motifs`.

**Below-AA pairs, recorded rather than retuned.** Measured on 2026-10-16: white on `--hot` (danger button) 3.87:1, white on `--secondary` (ended chip) 3.51:1, `--warn-ink` on `--warn` 3.33:1. Each is pinned at its measured ratio in `themeCss.test.ts` as a floor. The danger button and the ended chip are large pixel-font labels; changing Sentosa's red or green to reach 4.5 would change the look the owner approved, so it is left for a decision of its own.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** A `var(--acent)` typo in `gameboy.css` fails "reads nothing undefined"; deleting `--landmark` from the theme fails both that test and "defines every venue token"; pointing `--motif-coin` into another directory fails "points every motif role into its own motifs directory"; setting `--accent: #223344` fails `--ink on --accent` at 1.21:1; declaring `--ink` in a theme fails "does not borrow a structural token's name".

**Equivalence check.** Every custom property in the old and new `gameboy.css`, `screen.css` and `base.css` was resolved to its final value and the rules compared: 287 selectors, no difference beyond the renames and moves above. That comparison caught one slip of mine (`.gb-studio` had picked up `--surface-deep` instead of `--surface`), fixed before commit.



### ADR-297 — motifs are named by role, and each venue draws the sprites in its own palette

- **Status:** Accepted (shipped 2026-10-16)
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Relates to:** ADR-014/067/068/070 (the pipeline, the stamp, the retired sprites, the four-tone ramps), ADR-294, `docs/design/motif-catalogue.md`

**Context.** The 192 sprites have their colours fixed in the SVG at generation, from `PALETTE` in `scripts/motif-art.mjs` (one 4,219-line file) and the ramps in `motif-palette.mjs`. A themed frontend with one set of SVGs would recolour everything but the sprites. Also, of the roughly 17 sprites actually placed in components or CSS, several are venue-specific: the merlion in the banner, the shell on the Social tab, the crab/shell/starfish strip, the sun, the sandcastle, and the wave, shell and starfish used from CSS.

**Decision.**
1. **Roles.** A venue maps `MotifRole` → one of its sprite names (`bannerMark`, `navSocial`, `groundStrip1..3`, `landingHero`, `teamsHero`, `teamsEmpty`; the final list is the set of `PixelMotif` call sites that name a venue sprite). Components render `<RoleMotif role>`; `PixelMotif` accepts only a `SharedMotifName`, so naming `merlion` in a page is a compile error.
2. **CSS roles.** The sprites `gameboy.css` places are exposed as `--motif-cloud`, `--motif-bunting`, `--motif-shoreline`, `--motif-coin`, `--motif-stamp`, `--motif-bullet`, `--motif-empty`, `--motif-loader`, defined in the theme's `theme.css`. `gameboy.css` contains no motif URL.
3. **Per-venue palette.** `scripts/motifs/core.mjs` is pure: `buildSprites({ palette, ramps, grids })`. Venue-independent ramps (ink, paper, skin tones, wood, steel, pink, orange, purple, turf, the PSD brand pair) stay in `base-palette.mjs`; the venue ramps (sand, sea, gold, sunset, palm, merlion) move to the theme's `palette.mjs`. The legacy single-character `PALETTE` and `LEGACY_MOTIFS` are deleted rather than moved: `LEGACY_MOTIFS` was already empty (every one of the 194 sprites is a two-character ramp grid), so nothing read the 22 legacy colours, and keeping them would have put dead Sentosa hexes in the corpus every future venue inherits. Shared grids live in `scripts/motifs/grids/<group>.mjs` split by the catalogue's groups (each under 800 lines); venue-only grids live in the theme's `motifs.mjs`.
4. **Output.** Every theme gets its own full set at `public/themes/<id>/motifs/`, its own stamp at `src/themes/<id>/art/motifVersion.ts` (ADR-067's hash of emitted bytes, unchanged in method), and its own `?v=` stamps inside its `theme.css`. The generator deletes stale SVGs only inside the directory it owns.
5. A venue's sprite names are not required to match another's. The registry test asserts that every role resolves to a file that exists, not that two themes share names.

**Not decided here.** Which new landmark sprites a second venue would draw. That is art, and belongs to that venue's own ADR.

**What shipped.**
- The 192 sprites split by where they are used: **156 shared** names (`SHARED_MOTIF_NAMES`) a page may name, **36 themed** names (`THEMED_MOTIF_NAMES`: the beach-and-sea group plus Sentosa's own landmarks and fauna) a page reaches only by role. The split is derived from the generator's own grids, not hand-typed.
- Nine roles (`MOTIF_ROLES`): `bannerMark`, `navSocial`, `groundStripLeft/Middle/Right`, `landingHero`, `teamsHero`, `teamsQuiet`, `myTeamHero`. Sentosa maps them to exactly what the pages named before, so nothing changed on screen.
- `PixelMotif` accepts only a shared name; `RoleMotif` resolves a role through the active theme; both render one `MotifImage` so the decorative contract (`aria-hidden`, empty alt) lives in one place. `motifUrl(theme, name)` builds the URL from the theme's directory and stamp.
- The Landing tagline and station phrase come from the theme (`copy.landingSubtitle`, `copy.landingStationsPlace`).

**Not changed.** The `?v=` stamp is still a hash of the emitted SVGs (ADR-067), now per theme. A sprite the nav shows (`badge`, `flag`, `trophy`, `volleyball`, `face`) stays shared: they are UI glyphs, not venue flavour.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** A role mapped to a sprite with no file fails both role tests in `themes.test.ts`; `<PixelMotif name="merlion">` fails `tsc`; and `secondVenue.test.ts` feeds the real pipeline a made-up venue (a different gold, one sprite of its own) and checks the shapes are the same, the colours differ, the stamp differs, a venue that redraws a shared sprite is refused, and a venue that forgets a ramp is told which one.


### ADR-298 — the four gaps a second venue exposed in the first (scene scripts, role typing, first paint, scene box)

- **Status:** Accepted (Phase A shipped 2026-10-16)
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-294 §3 (it said the scene scripts were parameterised by theme; they were not), ADR-297 §1 (roles were typed to one venue's sprite vocabulary), ADR-295 §4 (`data-venue` was applied after first paint, not before)
- **Relates to:** ADR-256 (the scene box at every width), ADR-265 (the portrait sky), `docs/design/venue-themes.md`

**Context.** ADR-294 to ADR-297 were written and tested against exactly one venue. Planning the second (CSC @ Tessensohn) showed that four of their claims were never true, and could not have been seen to be false with one venue: a test that iterates `THEMES` passes trivially when `THEMES` has one entry.

**The gaps, each found by reading the code, not inferred.**
1. **Scene scripts hard-coded Sentosa.** `generate-pixel.mjs` imported `themes/sentosa/scene/*` and wrote to `public/themes/sentosa/` and `src/themes/sentosa/`; `generate-real.mjs` had no `argv`. Only `motifs/generate.mjs` looped themes, so `npm run scene` could not build a second venue.
2. **Roles were typed to Sentosa's vocabulary.** `motifRoles: Record<MotifRole, ThemedMotifName>`, with `ThemedMotifName` a global list of 36 beach and Sentosa sprites, and `themes.test.ts` demanded every theme ship all 192 sprites. A venue whose banner mark is the shared `kueh` was a type error.
3. **`data-venue` landed after first paint.** `useVenue` applied it in a `useEffect`. With one venue nothing visible depends on it; with two, a returning phone would flash the default venue's colours.
4. **The scene box was one shape.** `.gb-scene { height: 56.25vw }` and the portrait-sky rule in `gameboy.css` assume a 16:9 strip pinned to the bottom.
5. **Nothing enforced a venue's reduced-motion hide rule.** The generic rule only stops animations; hiding what travels is each venue's own `scene.css`, and a venue that forgot would leave a car frozen mid-road with no test noticing.

**Decision.**
1. The scene generators take `--theme <id>` (default: every theme with a `scene` entry in its manifest) and read the venue's scene module, output directories and art-module path from `scripts/themes/<id>/manifest.mjs`. `generate-real` runs only for a venue that declares a `real` scene. Sentosa's output must be byte-identical (the 260-file hash check).
2. `motifRoles` is `Record<MotifRole, MotifName>`: a role may name any sprite, shared or themed. "Themed" stays as documentation of what is venue-flavoured and as the rule for what a *page* may name (`PixelMotif` still takes only shared names). The completeness test becomes "every sprite the venue's roles, CSS roles and the shared names use has a file for that venue".
3. `main.tsx` applies the stored venue to `<html>` and the `theme-color` meta once, before `createRoot(...).render`. `useVenue` still confirms from the server.
4. A venue declares its scene geometry in its own `scene.css` with `--scene-fit` (`strip` | `plate`) and `--scene-aspect`; `gameboy.css` reads them. `strip` is today's behaviour exactly. `plate` is a full-height box of the given aspect ratio, centred, with `--scene-edge` filling either side, and no portrait-sky gradient.
5. A test over every `themes/*/scene.css`: any `@keyframes` that translates by more than its own size must have its class named in a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block with `display: none`.

**Price.** `gameboy.css` changes (the scene box and portrait sky become variable-driven), so the resolved-value equivalence check from ADR-296 is rerun for Sentosa. Each fix has a Sentosa-unchanged proof and one test that fails without it.

**What shipped.**
1. `scripts/scene/pixel-scene.mjs` (build, hash, serialise; no Sentosa in it), `scripts/scene/layout.mjs` (`layoutFor(W, H)`: the anchor/frame/strip helpers, no longer closed over one plate's size), `scripts/themes/sentosa/scene/compose.mjs` (Sentosa's layer composition, moved verbatim, exporting `SCENE`), and `generate-pixel.mjs` as a thin CLI that loops every theme whose manifest declares `scene: { compose }` (or `--theme <id>`). `generate-real.mjs` is deliberately Sentosa-only and now says so and refuses any other `--theme`: it processes one venue's photographs and pretending it was pluggable would promise a build nobody can run.
2. `motifRoles` is `Record<MotifRole, MotifName>`. `themes.test.ts` now requires a file for every sprite a venue's roles and the shared set use, not for all 192.
3. `themes/applyVenue.ts` (`applyVenueToDocument`, `applyStoredVenue`) is shared by `main.tsx`, which calls it before `createRoot(...).render`, and by `useVenue`.
4. `.gb-scene` height is `calc(100vw / var(--scene-aspect, 1.7777778))` and `.gb-scene[data-fit='plate']` is a full-height, centred, never-cropped box. `--scene-aspect` and `--scene-edge` are venue tokens in `cssContract.ts`. The portrait-sky gradient applies only when no `[data-fit='plate']` scene is present. Sentosa is `strip` by default and declares its aspect in `theme.css`.
5. `themes/sceneMotion.test.ts` reads every `themes/*/scene.css`, finds keyframes whose transforms carry an element 20% / 20vw / 100px or more (or by a custom property), and requires the class that runs each one to be hidden under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

**Equivalence.** Sentosa's 30 scene PNGs and `pixelArt.ts` are byte-identical to `HEAD` after the generator rewrite (`SCENE_VERSION` `58892259`). Every custom property in the old and new `gameboy.css` + `scene.css` was resolved and compared: of 222 selectors, 5 differ and all are the intended geometry change (`.gb-scene` height written as `calc(100vw / 1.7777778)`, which is within 0.00002 px of `56.25vw` at every width from 320 to 2560; the new `plate` rules; the portrait-sky selector gaining `:not(:has(.gb-scene[data-fit='plate']))`). Browser pins, written and passing BEFORE the CSS change: at 390x844 and 1280x800 the Sentosa scene is `position: fixed`, left 0, full width, `width * 9/16` tall and flush with the bottom, and the portrait sky is still a fixed `linear-gradient` on a phone.

**Bite checks, watched to fail.** (1) `main.tsx` not calling `applyStoredVenue()` fails the e2e that observes `<html data-venue>` at the moment `#root` first gains a child (a MutationObserver installed before any page script; my first attempt at that test passed under sabotage, so it was rewritten to observe rather than infer). (2) Dropping `.gb-scene__ferry` from Sentosa's reduced-motion hide rule, and deleting the whole block, each fail `sceneMotion.test.ts`. (3) A pure-function unit test pins the detector: a 103% translate and a `var()` translate are travelling, a sprite flip and a 14% hop are not. (4) `generate-real.mjs --theme tessensohn` throws. My first version of the reduced-motion test also had a bug of its own, counting `.gb-scene--real` (an ancestor) as an animated element; the test caught Sentosa failing on a rule that was correct, and was fixed with a pinned case.


### ADR-299 — CSC @ Tessensohn is the second venue: a cool palette, a banner that can be a blue bar, and the Civil Service Club's own layered illustration as its backdrop

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-298 §5 (the reduced-motion test required everything that travels to be hidden; an entrance that ends at rest is now stopped instead)
- **Relates to:** ADR-294 to ADR-298, `docs/design/venue-themes.md`, `docs/design/tessensohn-scene-credits.md`

**Context.** The owner supplied an aerial photograph of Civil Service Club @ Tessensohn and a mockup of the landing screen wearing it, and asked for it as a second venue. The first attempt drew the backdrop in code as a pixel plate. The owner rejected it ("really does not resemble what I am after"), proposed instead the illustration on the club's own About page (`https://www.csc.sg/About-CSC-Membership`), and stated that **CSC has agreed we can reuse their SVGs**. That permission is the owner's statement; this repository cannot verify it, and the credits file says so rather than calling it a licence.

**What the CSC banner is.** A stack of about 70 absolutely positioned `<img>` layers, nearly all SVG, positioned in percentages of the banner's width inside a relative wrapper. Characters are cut into parts (the dog is body + tail, a bike is wheels + pedals + legs, a swimmer is arms + legs + head), and each part is animated on its own by CSS alone: no JavaScript drives it. The phone version is a separate 445 x 671 portrait scene (68 files, about 1 MB), which is the one that fits this app. Their art is a flat front elevation, not isometric; the owner accepted that ("we use CSC flat shape, it is fine").

**Decision.**
1. **The backdrop is CSC's phone scene**, ported: its files in `public/themes/tessensohn/scene/`, its 70 layers as typed data (`sceneLayers.ts`), and its CSS rules and keyframes in `scene.css`, every class prefixed `csc-` so their generic names (`.bg`, `.tree1`, `.pot`) cannot collide with ours. The owner then asked for two things the phone scene lacks: **the court with its two players** (CSC only ships them in the desktop banner; their rules are ported and the group is placed in the phone scene by us) and **the clubhouse sprite on the left** (CSC's `mobilebuilding.png`, drawn as CSC draws it).
2. **The scene is a `data-fit="plate"` box** of CSC's own 445 / 671 shape (ADR-298), so a wide screen pillarboxes and a tall phone leaves a strip of the venue's sky colour above it. The placeholder image CSC uses only to give the box a height is replaced by that aspect ratio.
3. **Entrances play once per page load, not once per route.** CSC's car drives in and parks, the building rises, and the bike rides away. All of those are one-shot (`forwards`). This app remounts the scene on every page, so they would replay on every tap. The first mount plays them; later mounts show the end state (car parked, building standing, bike gone). The car is CSC's implementation, as the owner asked.
4. **Reduced motion shows the end state and stops everything**, rather than hiding the scene: `animation: none` on every layer, the bike hidden (it has ridden away), the car parked. This also corrects ADR-298's test, which hid anything that travels; an entrance that ends at rest is not frozen mid-air, so for those the test requires `animation: none` instead of `display: none`.
5. **Static assets carry a content stamp.** `webStatic` serves `/themes/<id>/scene/` as immutable for a year, so every URL carries `?v=<hash of the files>` (ADR-067), written to `art/sceneVersion.ts` by `scripts/themes/tessensohn/stamp-scene.mjs` (`npm run scene:stamp`). The venue's manifest declares no `scene`, so `generate-pixel.mjs` skips it: nothing is drawn, the files are committed as CSC serves them. `sceneVersion.test.ts` recomputes the hash from the files on disk, so a replaced file with a stale stamp fails the build.
6. **Motif roles use shared sprites** (ADR-298): the banner mark is `kueh`, as in the mockup, so no Sentosa landmark appears at Tessensohn.
7. **Registration is three lines:** `'tessensohn'` in `VENUE_IDS`, one entry in `THEMES`, one `@import` pair in `themes.css`.

**Superseded within this ADR.** The code-drawn plate, its sprites and its car-drives-off-and-turns animation (the owner chose CSC's car instead). It is kept out of the repository; nothing in the tree draws it.

**Not decided here, by design.** The landing redesign in the mockup (venue plate, host credit, welcome card, button wording): it would redesign the landing page for every venue, which is not a theme.

**Two compositions (amended 2026-10-16, owner reports).** CSC draws two banners, so the scene does too. On a portrait screen it is CSC's phone banner (445 x 671, `data-layout="phone"`, `data-fit="plate"`). On a landscape screen (`min-aspect-ratio: 1/1`, read with `matchMedia` through `useSyncExternalStore`, so it follows a rotation) it is CSC's desktop banner (3259 x 1204, `data-layout="wide"`), a full-width strip pinned to the bottom exactly as Sentosa's is. Showing the phone plate on a desktop had put the art in a narrow centred column with flat colour either side, which the owner flagged as unlike Sentosa. The wide list is 51 layers and needs 48 more of CSC's files (130 in all, 1.9 MB); the same `csc-` prefix, one-shot entrances and stamp apply, and its rules are scoped `[data-layout='wide']` so the two sets cannot touch each other. Reduced motion stops everything in both and hides the travellers (the two cyclists, clouds, falling leaves, smoke, the ball).

**The phone court, and no pool.** CSC's phone banner has no court; the desktop one does. The first placement (left 3% / top 57% / width 46%) covered the barbecue and the clubhouse's lower floor, and the second (bottom left, width 35%) made two foreground players about a quarter of the height of the people behind them. The owner asked for the pool and swimmers to go and the court to take their place. In the phone scene the pool, pool shine, swimmer, child, float, beach ball and ring are therefore not drawn, and the court sits where the pool was (left 24%, top 78%, width 74%) with the two players drawn 1.6 times CSC's size, so a foreground player is roughly as tall as the barbecue figures further back. The wide scene keeps CSC's own pool and its own court, unchanged.

**The first visit.** `venueStartup.applyVenueBeforeFirstRender` (awaited before the first render) puts the right venue on `<html>` before anything paints: the stored venue at once, else the server's answer within 1500 ms. Without it a brand-new phone at Tessensohn painted Sentosa first and fetched its art before switching.

**Verified.** Unit: `TessensohnScene.test.tsx` (structure, every image under `/themes/tessensohn/scene/` with the stamp, court after the second ground, entrances `play` then `rest` then `play` after a reload), `sceneVersion.test.ts` (hash from disk, every layer has a file, every file is used, no script/handler/external reference in any SVG), `sceneMotion.test.ts` (entrances must be stopped under reduced motion, travellers hidden), `venueStartup.test.ts`. Browser, on its own stack (`PSD_VENUE=tessensohn`, `npm run test:e2e:tessensohn`, desktop + Pixel 7): 34 of 34 passed (28 of 28 on two consecutive runs before the wide layout was added), covering the computed palette and banner, no `/themes/sentosa/` request, every image decoded, the plate's aspect at five viewports, the running animations by name, the car's start and end transform, the once-per-load entrances across a route change and a reload, reduced motion (zero running animations, car parked, cyclist gone), and `?backdrop=real` fetching nothing. Not run: WebKit/Safari, and any real device.

**Bite checks (each watched to fail, then restored).**
- A stale `SCENE_VERSION` (`00000000`): `carries the content hash of the files on disk` fails.
- The intro forced to `play` on every mount: `plays the entrances on the first scene ... and holds them at rest after` fails.
- The car's entrance un-gated from `[data-intro='play']`: `sceneMotion.test.ts` fails naming `.csc-car (animates csc-carXmobile)`.
- (earlier, ADR-299 first-visit fix) removing the wait in `venueStartup` fails `on a first visit, waits for the server`.

**Known limits.** The permission to use CSC's art is the owner's statement only; no written licence is in the repository. The art is a flat front elevation, so the isometric feel of the aerial photograph is not reproduced. The car arrives and parks once per page load (CSC's behaviour); it does not drive off and turn, which was the earlier code-drawn idea.

### ADR-300 — Tessensohn drops Sentosa's gold accent, and a tab stays lit on every route it owns

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-299's palette note (gold kept from the mockup) and the `theme.css` / `palette.mjs` comments that recorded it
- **Relates to:** ADR-103 (`/teams` redirects to `/team`), ADR-296 (venue tokens), ADR-299

**Context.** The owner reported two things in the Tessensohn theme's bottom tab bar: the Teams tab showed no active highlight (the other tabs did), and the highlight was Sentosa yellow. Both had plain causes. ADR-103 sends a participant who already has a team from `/teams` straight to `/team`; React Router lights a `NavLink` only under its own `to`, so on `/team` the Teams tab was never current — for exactly the participants who have a team, which is most of them. (Social had the same shape of bug unreported: its Photos segment is `/social/photos`, outside its `/social/chat` link.) And ADR-299 had copied Sentosa's accent verbatim — `--accent: #ffc72c`, `--accent-deep: #e0a800` — so every accent surface in the venue (the lit tab, primary buttons, badges, focus outlines, segmented control, sliders, the live flash) rendered Sentosa gold. The owner directed the highlight to be a dark blue in the venue's palette and the other gold leftovers to follow.

**Decision.**
1. **A tab is lit on every prefix it owns.** `NAV_ITEMS` gains `activeOn` aliases (Teams: `/team`; Social: `/social`); the shell adds `is-current` when the location matches an alias, and `styles/gameboy.css` paints `a.is-current` exactly like the router's `a[aria-current='page']`, icon bob and reduced-motion stop included. The router still owns `aria-current` under each tab's own `to`; the alias routes carry the visual state only, because `NavLink` computes `aria-current` itself and overrides anything passed to it.
2. **Tessensohn's accent is its own blue family.** `--accent` becomes `#6fa8d6` (the palette's `--primary-light`) and `--accent-deep` `#2372bc` (`--primary`). Dark ink on the light blue still clears the AA floor `themeCss.test.ts` holds every venue to; a deep-blue accent fill would not, which is why the accent stops at the light blue and the depth token carries the mid blue.
3. **The lit tab itself is the deep blue.** A venue-scoped rule in `themes/tessensohn/theme.css` paints the current tab `--primary-deep` under `--paper` — the dark-blue highlight the owner asked for, with a pairing the contrast tests already hold to AA (it is the banner's own pairing). Sentosa's tab is unchanged (gold under ink).
4. **What did not change.** The drawn sprites keep their gold ramp (`scripts/themes/tessensohn/palette.mjs`): that gold is artwork — trophies, coins, badges — not chrome, and blueing it is an art decision, not a leftover fix. The console theme's gold (`--console-accent`) is venue-independent and also untouched.

**Verified.** Unit: `GameboyShell.test.tsx` (Teams lit by the router on `/teams`, by the alias on `/team`, Social lit on `/social/photos`, no bleed onto Board) and `themeCss.test.ts` (the accent pair pinned to the venue blues and held apart from Sentosa's, paper-on-primary-deep at AA; all existing contrast floors pass with the new accent). The Tessensohn e2e palette expectation now reads the light-blue button (`rgb(111, 168, 214)`). Playwright was not run in the sandbox (no browser); the e2e change is an expectation update only, to be confirmed on the owner's stack with `npm run test:e2e:tessensohn`.

### ADR-301 — The Kallang is the third venue: one photographic plate, imported minimal

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Relates to:** ADR-294 to ADR-300, `docs/design/venue-themes.md`

**Context.** The owner supplied a second, external implementation of a Kallang backdrop: a standalone animated scene of the Sports Hub waterfront (313 extracted sprites in three time-of-day grades, boats and kayaks stitched at measured anchors, a canvas animation engine, Python extraction tooling, and the AI-generated source plates it all came from — 218 MB in `tmp/Kallang`). The direction was explicit: import it modularly into this codebase keeping the bare minimum — no source images, no pipeline tooling, only the publicly served image data necessary to serve the backdrop — and then remove the import from the repository's history the same way the generic-composite photo sources were removed.

**Decision.**
1. **The venue is `kallang`** in `VENUE_IDS`; the `Record<VenueId, VenueTheme>` registry forced the theme into existence at compile time, as designed (ADR-294).
2. **Served data: exactly one file.** `public/themes/kallang/scene/backdrop-day.jpg` — the external project's clean daylight plate (National Stadium + Indoor Stadium across the basin, no people), recompressed from 2752 x 1536 / 3.0 MB to 1920 x 1072 / 475 KB. It carries the ADR-067 content stamp (`scripts/themes/kallang/stamp-scene.mjs`, cloned from Tessensohn's; `sceneVersion.test.ts` recomputes it and also pins that the shipped set is exactly the one file the scene draws).
3. **Not imported:** the sprite sets (313 × 3 grades), the dawn/dusk sky-and-scene layer pairs, the populated reference plate, the canvas engine (`src/scene`, `src/objects`, `src/lib` of the external app), the Python pipeline (`tools/`), its docs and QA. A backdrop here is decoration behind the panels (ADR-014); the plate alone carries the place, and the strip box every venue shares (`.gb-scene`, ADR-256) already fits its 1.79 aspect. If the venue later wants motion, it will be CSS over layers like the other venues', adopted on its own merits — not this engine by default.
4. **Scene component** `KallangScene`: one stamped `<img>` in the shared strip, `aria-hidden`, no classic/fine/real dispatch (the styles declare `['classic', 'fine']` and `?backdrop=` is ignored, Tessensohn's call in ADR-299). Being a photograph it keeps image smoothing on, the `gb-scene--real` reasoning (ADR-193).
5. **Palette and motifs** follow the venue pattern: river blue / stadium red / promenade stone / park green / dome silver (`scripts/themes/kallang/palette.mjs`), tokens in `src/themes/kallang/theme.css` held to the shared contrast floors, motif roles filled with shared sprites recoloured by `npm run motifs` (175 SVGs, `GRIDS = {}` — no venue-only sprites in v1).
6. **History:** the implementation landed as one commit whose tree excludes `tmp/Kallang/` entirely; the import commit was squashed out and the branch force-pushed, so the external app exists in this repository only as this ADR's description. (The owner's `tmp/DPA_…jpg` reference photo commit predates the import and is untouched.)

**Verified.** Unit: `KallangScene.test.tsx` (strip box, venue class, the one stamped plate, empty alt), `sceneVersion.test.ts` (stamp recomputed from disk, shipped set is exactly the plate), plus the auto-discovering suites — `themes.test.ts` (registry, stamps, files behind every role), `themeCss.test.ts` (token contract + every contrast pair for the new palette), `sceneMotion.test.ts`, `secondVenue.test.ts`. Typecheck across contracts/tournament/api/web. Not run: Playwright (no browser in the sandbox) — the venue needs its browser pass on the owner's stack (`PSD_VENUE=kallang`), and whether the plate reads well behind live panels at phone sizes is a visual judgement no unit test makes.

### ADR-302 — the Kallang scene is populated: the external scene's seeding, translated to CSS layers

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-301 §3 (the sprite sets not imported — now a curated subset is) and §4 (nothing to animate)
- **Relates to:** ADR-298 (reduced motion), ADR-301

**Context.** ADR-301 imported only the plate, on the owner's bare-minimum instruction. The owner then reported the obvious: the scene loaded but nothing moved — the life of the external project is its population. The owner reinstated `tmp/Kallang` as reference and directed that the animated elements be seeded and populated as the source does. Studying the source (`src/scene/scene.ts`, `src/objects/*`): a deterministic seeded RNG (`createRng(seed)`) builds entities in painter's layers — clouds at fixed picks with random speeds/starts; props at measured spots; people on two promenade lanes (feet-lines as polylines) with random kits/speeds/strides, joggers, boardwalk patrols, fixed cheerer and idler spots; players and balls in two fenced courts; eight boats (3 dragon boats, 5 kayaks) at three water lanes with measured waterlines, widths and speeds; and 34 water effects rejection-sampled into a mapped open-water polygon. Motion is per-object canvas code: 4-phase gait cycles, paddles stitched to rowers at measured anchor fractions and swung through a stroke cycle, wakes trailing hulls.

**Decision.**
1. **The population is imported; the engine is not.** 13 sprite files (~590 KB after resizing to strip scale) join the plate in `public/themes/kallang/scene/`: 3 clouds, 2 dragon boats, 1 kayak, 3 promenade runners, 2 cheerers, a ripple (×2 placements) and a splash. The other ~300 sprites, the dawn/dusk grades, court players, props and the populated-reference plate stay behind, as do all 8 boats → 3 and 34 water effects → 2: at strip scale the marginal sprites are invisible, and each file is served weight.
2. **Seeding translates, it does not re-invent.** `sceneLayers.ts` is the population as data — the source's lanes as strip percentages (promenade feet 76.7%/78.3%, boat waterlines 94.0%/93.1%/95.7%), crossing durations computed from its speeds, and its deterministic starts as negative animation delays, so the scene is populated on first paint and loops with no JavaScript state. Layer order is the source's painter order.
3. **Motion is CSS, per venue convention** (Tessensohn precedent): crossings on two `translateX` keyframes, a `steps(2)` gait bob (the 4-phase pose cycle is invisible at this scale), a cheerer hop, a ripple pulse. Leftward walkers flip via the `scale` property so the bob transform cannot override it. The paddle stitching — the source's most intricate mechanism — is consciously not reproduced: at strip scale a dragon boat reads as hull + crew + wake, and the trailing splash is imported instead.
4. **Reduced motion (ADR-298):** every traveller is `display: none` under `prefers-reduced-motion`, small motions stop, ripples vanish; the plate's baked waterfront remains. `sceneMotion.test.ts` enforces this from the keyframes, and passes.

**Verified.** Unit: `KallangScene.test.tsx` (plate then every layer in order, all stamped, travellers seeded with durations + negative delays), `sceneVersion.test.ts` (shipped set is exactly plate + population), `sceneMotion.test.ts`, `themes.test.ts`, `themeCss.test.ts`. Not run: Playwright (no browser in the sandbox). Whether the population reads as alive rather than busy behind live panels — densities were taken from the source, but the strip is smaller than its stage — is the owner's visual call on the dev stack.

### ADR-303 — the Kallang scene completed: full-height stage with portrait focus, full population, stitched oars

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-302 §1 (the curated subset — restored to the source's counts), §3 (no paddle stitching — now stitched)
- **Relates to:** ADR-256, ADR-298, ADR-301, ADR-302

**Context.** The owner reviewed ADR-302's scene and found four things wrong. (1) The backdrop rendered as a shallow strip — the shared `.gb-scene` box is a bottom strip by design (ADR-256), while the source renders its world full-height. (2) The responsive portrait behaviour was missing: the source crops horizontally around the National Stadium's opening on narrow screens (`computeSceneView`, focus x 750 of 2752; its addendum 0011). (3) There were far fewer boats and people than the source seeds (8 boats → 3, ~26 people → 7). (4) There was no real water animation and no oar animation — the paddle stitching ADR-302 had judged invisible and skipped is, in motion, the thing that makes the boats read as rowing. The owner suspended the history-squashing of the reference import until this is right, so `tmp/Kallang` remains in the tree as reference for now.

**Decision.**
1. **The scene owns a stage.** Kallang's `.gb-scene` is the full screen; `.kallang-stage` inside it carries the 2752 x 1536 world at its own aspect — bottom-anchored full-width on wide screens, and on screens narrower than the world, full-height with the stadium opening centred (`left: 50%` + `translateX(-27.25%)` under a `max-aspect-ratio` query), the source's camera translated to CSS. All layers are stage percentages, so the crop moves the world as one.
2. **The population is at the source's counts:** 4 clouds; 3 tents + canopy and the start/finish arch + podium as static props; 5 promenade walkers/joggers across both lanes, a boardwalk patrol, 4 cheerers, 2 idlers; 4 court shuttles + 2 bouncing balls in the two fenced courts; all 8 boats on their three lanes at the source's waterlines and speeds; the near dragon boat's wake; 4 water effects. Crossings animate `left` (stage percentages), because a transform's percentages belong to the element, not the stage.
3. **Oars are stitched as the source stitches them.** Each boat layer carries its paddle sprites at the `anchors.json` stations (9 per dragon boat; kayak seats by kind K1/K2/K3), swung by CSS keyframes built from the source's stroke tables (dragon 1.15 s, 4°→−28°; kayak double paddle 1.05 s, ±34° rock), pivot offsets folded into the keyframe translations. The files: 38 sprites, ~1.6 MB after resizing to stage scale.
4. **Reduced motion** is handled explicitly (the `left` crossings are invisible to ADR-298's keyframe detector, so the rule names every traveller, patrol, ball, paddle and water effect itself): travellers hidden, small motions stopped, statics and standing figures remain.

**Verified.** Unit: `KallangScene.test.tsx` (stage present, plate and all layers stamped, travellers seeded, 9 dragon paddles at the first station's exact anchor percentages, 3 paddles on the K3 kayak), `sceneVersion.test.ts` (shipped set = plate + population + paddles), the whole `src/themes` suite including `sceneMotion.test.ts`. Not run: Playwright (no browser in the sandbox) — density, focus crop and rowing all need the owner's eyes on the dev stack (`PSD_VENUE=kallang`), which is also why the reference import stays in history unsquashed until the owner calls it right.

### ADR-304 — the Kallang population is complete, with the source's gait: seeded assignments replayed, sprites stacked as frames

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-303 §2 (counts "where the strip can carry them" — now all of them) and ADR-302 §1
- **Relates to:** ADR-298, ADR-301, ADR-303

**Context.** The owner reviewed ADR-303 and still found noticeably fewer people than the reference, and the walking figures had lost their sprite animation — ADR-302/303 carried each person as one frozen pose with a bob. The direction: copy all the elements over from the reference implementation. The reference (`buildScene`, seed 20261017) seeds deterministically: a seeded RNG assigns kits, speeds, start positions, stride periods and phases in a fixed draw order, and walkers cycle a four-phase gait (contact → passing → contact → passing) chosen from per-kit pose sprites, with a phase-locked bob.

**Decision.**
1. **The seeding was replayed, not re-guessed.** The source's RNG and draw order were ported offline and run with its seed; the resulting assignments are baked into `sceneLayers.ts` as data (and the generated placement rules in `scene.css`). Same 8 clouds at the same picks/speeds/starts; 10 lane walkers with their actual kits (back lane runs orange/purple/yellow, not a representative sample), speeds and strides; 3 joggers; 2 boardwalk patrols; 9 cheerers and 5 idlers in their seeded kits at the source's spots; the courts' 10 shuttles, 4 standing players and 2 balls; all 34 water effects at the exact points the source's rejection sampler (seed ^ 0x9e3779b9, mapped open water, 108 px separation) placed them.
2. **Gait is stacked sprite frames.** Each walker/jogger/patrol/court shuttle renders its kit's four gait poses as stacked images, each visible for its quarter of the stride (mirrored poses use the art's own left-facing sprite, flipped by the `scale` property as the source's flip flag dictates), bobbing at half-stride. Cheerers run the source's two-frame celebration cycle. This is a CSS frame-window, not the canvas: no per-frame JavaScript.
3. **Everything else at entity parity:** 14 props including the swaying feathers, banner, balloon arch, trophy table, flag and the two bunting runs; wakes behind all 8 boats; a stroke-timed splash at the dragon boats' waterline. Total served art: plate + 88 sprite files, ~3.4 MB. The engine, sheets and grades remain unimported (ADR-301 §3 stands).

**Verified.** Unit: full `src/themes` suite — `KallangScene.test.tsx` now also pins the four-frame gait stack with quarter-stride delays and a mirrored frame, paddle anchoring unchanged; `sceneVersion.test.ts` shipped set = plate + every sprite, frame and paddle file. Direction audit: crossing directions re-checked against the seeded speed signs after one moonwalking lane was caught in review of the data (front-lane walkers 2 and 4 travel left). Not run: Playwright (no browser in the sandbox) — the owner judges density and gait on the dev stack; `tmp/Kallang` remains in history unsquashed until then, per the owner's suspension.

### ADR-305 — faithful water and gait: height-true figures, lane-layered ripples, wakes and splashes inside the boat

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-304 §2 (frame presentation), ADR-303 §2 (wake placement)
- **Relates to:** ADR-298, ADR-304

**Context.** The owner reviewed ADR-304 and found three mechanism-level unfaithfulnesses. (1) People had inconsistent sizing: layers were sized by width, so each gait frame — all drawn by the source at one height with per-frame widths — rendered at a different height, and different people used different width guesses. (2) The water was wrong: ambient effects sat in one painter's band instead of behind their boat lanes; the wake was a separate layer with a margin fudge instead of being drawn from the hull; and the "splash" was a constant pulse instead of appearing only when a blade bites. (3) People blinked: frames were top-anchored in a box sized by the first frame, so feet jumped between phases, and the frame windows played in reverse order.

**Decision** (each is the source's own mechanism, `objects/waterFx.ts`, `objects/dragonBoat.ts`, `objects/kayak.ts`, `objects/character.ts`):
1. **Figures are sized by height, feet planted.** A person's layer is the source's pixel height as a stage percentage; every frame is full-height, bottom-anchored and centre-pivoted (`drawPose`'s pivot 0.5/1), so phases change width, never height or feet. Static and patrolling figures place by centre, as the source draws them.
2. **Gait frames play in the source's order** — frame *i* owns quarter *i* of the stride (the complementary-quarter delay), not the reverse cycle the first cut produced.
3. **Ripples behave as `createRipple`:** opacity 0.95 fading quadratically to 0 while scaling 0.75 → 1.25, linear, centred on the seeded point; and they are layered by `layerForWaterEffect` — each effect sits just behind the boat lane in front of it, so hulls occlude them as hulls do in the source.
4. **The wake lives inside the boat's layer** (`drawWake`): squashed to half height at the waterline, trailing the stern (0.55 hull-widths for dragon boats, 0.48 for kayaks), alpha 0.55/0.5, width pulsing with the stroke (0.66/0.5 of hull width ± the source's sine). The hull itself bobs with the stroke (±1.6% of its height, phase-locked).
5. **Splashes happen on the catch.** Dragon boats splash only in the first 14% of each stroke cycle, at three station positions along the paddle row; kayaks splash twice per rocking cycle where a blade is buried (the |angle| ≥ 18° dips). No more constant foam.

**Verified.** Unit: full `src/themes` suite, with new pins for the in-layer wake and the three catch splashes; seeded-direction and frame-order regressions named in their tests. Not run: Playwright (no browser in the sandbox) — sizing consistency and water behaviour are motion judgements for the owner's eyes on the dev stack; `tmp/Kallang` remains unsquashed until the owner calls the scene right.

### ADR-306 — the Kallang animation is the reference engine, ported to canvas

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-17
- **Supersedes:** ADR-305; ADR-304 §2–§3; ADR-303 §2–§3; ADR-302 §1–§3; ADR-301 §3 (the canvas engine not imported)
- **Relates to:** ADR-014, ADR-298, ADR-301, ADR-303

**Context.** The owner reviewed ADR-305 and found the long boats carrying three bright, prominent splashes over the rowers. That was not a tuning miss: ADR-305 translated the source's stroke mechanism into CSS and, in translation, synchronised three oversized splash images at 19% of hull width, at a fixed opacity, below the hull and after the paddles in paint order. The reference instead draws one splash for each of its nine paddle stations, only while that station's lagged phase is in the catch (`stationPhase <= 0.14`), at the computed blade tip on the waterline, sized between 0.18 and 0.30 hull-heights and fading from alpha 0.95 to 0.3 as the catch weakens. The owner therefore directed that the animation code from the original be faithfully replicated rather than approximated again.

**Decision.**
1. **The reference animation engine is ported, not reinterpreted.** `apps/web/src/themes/kallang/engine/` carries its seeded RNG; cycle/wrap/stroke/blade-tip/polyline mathematics; anchored sprite drawing; sprite store; anchor data; character gait, cheerer and idler behaviour; clouds; dragon boats; kayaks; ambient water effects; props; court balls; mapped open-water placement; and the complete `buildScene` composition. Formulas, constants, stroke keyframes, phase lags, seeded draw order, painter layers, boat specifications and water-effect placement are retained. Where this repository's function-design rules prohibit the reference's long positional parameter lists, arguments are grouped into an options object; the calculations are unchanged.
2. **`KallangScene` is now one canvas, not a stack of CSS layers.** It renders the full 2752 × 1536 world into `.kallang-stage`; ADR-303's stage sizing and narrow-screen stadium-focus crop remain in CSS. The component loads the stamped plate and sprites, builds the scene at the reference default seed `20261017`, and advances the same deterministic clock pattern as the reference entrypoint (elapsed seconds, capped at 0.1 seconds per frame). It draws the plate while sprites load and leaves that plate composed if sprite loading fails.
3. **Boat water uses the source geometry and paint order.** Each dragon boat draws its wake, hull and lagged paddles, then one catch splash per biting station at the blade tip (`waterlineY + 0.04 × hullHeight`, pivot 0.65). Each kayak draws a dip only for a blade buried at `|angle| >= 18°`. No CSS wake, splash, paddle, gait or crossing approximation remains in `scene.css`.
4. **The complete sprite vocabulary is served.** Four previously missing plain-kit idler gestures (`char-{red,blue,green,yellow}-reach-right.png`) join the scene directory, resized to the served character-frame height. `spriteManifest.ts` enumerates the plate plus all 91 sprites the engine can reference; `sceneVersion.test.ts` pins that shipped set exactly. The scene content stamp is now `5408c0fe`.
5. **Reduced motion remains a composed still, not a frozen traveller.** Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, the component draws one populated frame at the reference project's QA-still moment (`t=17s`) and does not start the animation clock.

**Verified.** Unit: full `src/themes` suite passes (187 tests), including ported RNG/gait/stroke/water-map tests; canvas-lifecycle tests for loading, animation, reduced-motion stills and load failures; a recording-context regression proving nine dragon splashes at t=0 with waterline placement, source size and fading alpha, zero splashes at stroke phase 0.5, and kayak dips only when a blade is buried; exact shipped-file and content-stamp tests. The full web suite passes (1,837 tests) with its coverage thresholds met. Typecheck, ESLint for the Kallang tree, and the repository standards gate pass. As additional visual verification in this sandbox, the ported engine was rendered headlessly with `@napi-rs/canvas` against the served plate and sprites at t=2 and t=6.5 seconds; the near dragon boat showed small waterline splashes at its paddles rather than the three large overlays. Playwright was not run (no browser in the sandbox); live motion remains for the owner's dev-stack review, and `tmp/Kallang` remains unsquashed under the owner's existing suspension.

### ADR-307 — reset the practice day, keep the setup: a guarded danger zone on Operations

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-18
- **Relates to:** ADR-004 (sessions), ADR-027 (confirmations), ADR-117 (append-only ledgers), ADR-118 (the operations surface), ADR-140 (screen keys)

**Context.** Facilitators rehearse on the real system before the event: participants sign up, teams form, socials fill, tournaments run. On the morning of the real event that practice day has to go — but the setup the facilitators built (staff accounts, clusters, activities, courts, point settings, agenda, screen keys) must not go with it, or the rehearsal's whole value is lost. Until now there was no surface for this at all: the codebase's only deletes are soft, and the ledgers are append-only by design (ADR-117).

**Decision.**
1. **A danger zone at the foot of Operations (S61).** A dedicated red panel (`console-panel--danger-zone`: thick danger border, red ground in both console themes, danger-coloured heading) states plainly what will be deleted and what will be kept, with one huge danger button: "Reset users, teams, socials, tournaments and matches". It is not a settings form and does not look like one.
2. **Two proofs, both the server's.** The button first asks `POST /api/admin/system/reset/challenge` for a server-minted confirmation — the word `DELETE` in capitals followed by a random 10-character alphanumeric string (`lib/resetChallenge.ts`, `node:crypto`), bound to the acting superadmin, single-use, five minutes to live. The operator types that confirmation back exactly, plus their own superadmin passcode, which the reset route re-checks against the acting superadmin's account (a signed-in console left unattended must not be enough to wipe an event). Every reset attempt consumes the challenge, right or wrong, so neither the 4-digit passcode nor the confirmation can be ground through by repetition: each guess costs a fresh, visibly different code.
3. **The reset deletes activity, preserves setup** (`db/entities/systemReset.ts`, one transaction, foreign-key order). Deleted: participants; teams and memberships; all socials (chat, team chat, announcements, gallery photos with their votes, reports and byte blobs); all tournaments and matches with their stages, groups, slots, scheduler, events, awards and roster snapshots; and the practice records that cannot outlive their owners — fringe and swag rounds, scans and claims, score adjustments, award batches, and the void audit that referenced them. Every session ends except the acting superadmin's own, so the console stays signed in to report the outcome. Preserved untouched: superadmin and facilitator accounts, clusters, participant titles, fringe activities, swag stations, tournament courts, point config, agenda items, screen keys, and the operations switches in `service_state`. Scoreboard, chat, gallery, announcement, tournament, live-match and membership caches are invalidated so no memo answers for the practice day afterwards.
4. **It reports counts, not vibes.** The response (`SystemResetView`) carries the number of participants, teams, chat and team-chat messages, announcements, photos, tournaments, matches, fringe and swag rounds deleted and sessions ended, and the panel reads them back to the operator next to "your setup is untouched".

**Consequences.** This is the codebase's one wholesale hard delete, taken as a deliberate exception to the soft-delete rule: the rows removed are a rehearsal's, and an audit trail of a practice day has no one left to audit for. The append-only ledgers (ADR-117) are cleared only as part of this act, never row by row. The standards checker's `no-hard-delete` rule names `systemReset.ts` as its sole carve-out, citing this ADR, so the exception stays a findable decision rather than a spreading pattern. A reset mid-event would be catastrophic and is priced accordingly: superadmin session, own passcode re-entry, and an exact typed challenge that expires in five minutes and survives exactly one attempt.

**Verified.** API (`apps/api/src/tests/system-reset.test.ts`, real database): non-superadmins refused at both endpoints; no-challenge, mistyped, lowercase and wrong-passcode attempts each refused with the right contract message and delete nothing; a spent challenge cannot be retried even with the correct text; the happy path deletes participants/teams/socials/tournaments/matches/rounds/scans, ends every session but the acting superadmin's (a stale participant token then gets 401), preserves facilitator/superadmin accounts and the seeded fringe activity, and the readied system accepts a fresh signup. Web (`apps/web/src/acceptance/system-reset.test.tsx`): the panel is red-classed, fetches no challenge until the button is pressed, shows the server's string, enables submit only with both proofs, posts exactly `{passcode, confirmation}`, reports the returned counts, backs away cleanly, and retires the form after a refusal. Existing Operations suites (operations-switch, screen-keys) still pass.

### ADR-308 — the plain-kit runner's second contact is not mirrored art

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-18
- **Amends:** ADR-306 (the ported gait table's one wrong facing assumption)
- **Relates to:** ADR-306

**Context.** The owner watched the basketball court's yellow shuttle runner and saw him turn right-left-right-left as he ran. The cause was one metadata flag in the ported `gaitFrames`: for the plain kits (red/blue/green/yellow), the third gait frame, `run-left`, was marked `mirror: true` on the reference's assumption that the art natively faces left, so `drawGait` flipped it to face the direction of travel. Inspecting the served sprites shows the plain kits' `run-left` faces **right** like every other pose in those sheets — "left" names the contact foot, not the facing (and all generated art faces right by the project's standing rule). The runner therefore faced backwards for the third quarter of every stride, with the lean also reversed on that frame; at a 0.35s stride on a shuttle that also turns at each end, the flicker read as constant turning. The rich kits (orange/purple) are unaffected: their `run-side-left` genuinely faces left, and its `mirror: true` stands.

**Decision.** `gaitFrames` marks the plain-kit `run-left` frame `mirror: false`. This is a deliberate, documented departure from the reference engine (whose own sprite set has the same right-facing `run-left`, so the reference carries the same flicker). No assets change; the two pixel-distinct contact strides are preserved, and a plain-kit runner is flipped only as a whole, when travelling left.
