**Verified.** `engine.test.ts`: the metadata pin now expects `mirror: false` for plain kits and still `true` for the rich kits' `run-side-left`; a new recording-context regression draws a yellow walker at all four gait-frame centres in both directions and requires `flipX` to be constant (all false rightward, all true leftward) — the flipped third frame is exactly what it forbids. The Kallang suite passes (42 tests), and a frame strip of the four yellow gait poses reads as one coherent rightward stride. Playwright was not run (no browser in the sandbox); live motion remains for the owner's dev-stack review.

### ADR-309 — the Kallang crop centres the stadium only where centring still covers

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-19
- **Amends:** ADR-303 (stage geometry), as carried by ADR-306
- **Relates to:** ADR-303, ADR-306

**Context.** The owner resized a desktop browser from full width toward narrow and saw, in the early part of the resize, a band of plain blue (the `--scene-sky` ground) down the left of the screen with the backdrop plate pushed right. The stage CSS centred the stadium opening (`left: 50%; transform: translateX(-27.25%)`) at every aspect below the world's 2752/1536, but the reference's `computeSceneView` — whose geometry the CSS crop claims to mirror — clamps: `x = min(world − width, max(0, focus − width/2))`. The CSS kept the centring and dropped the clamp. Measured against the stage formulas, the centred left edge sat on-screen for every aspect between 2752/1536 and ≈125/128: a blue gap of 22.7% of screen width just inside the breakpoint, shrinking to nothing at ≈0.98 — and the crop shown in that band was not the source's crop either, since the source pins world-left to screen-left until centring is geometrically possible.

**Decision.** The stadium-centring media query applies only below `max-aspect-ratio: 125/128` — exactly 2·750/1536, the aspect at which the centred stage's left edge passes through 0, so the handover is continuous and the plate never jumps. Between the world's aspect and 125/128 the stage stays at `left: 0`, full-height and wider than the viewport: world-left flush to screen-left, which is precisely the clamped view the reference computes. Nothing else changes: wide screens still see the full world bottom-anchored, and below 125/128 the stadium-centred crop the owner reviewed is untouched.

**Verified.** The stage formulas were recomputed across aspects 2.2 → 0.4: the left edge is at or off screen-left and the right edge covered at every aspect, with the left edge passing through 0 exactly at 125/128. `KallangScene.test.tsx` now reads `scene.css` from disk and pins the breakpoint numerically against the engine's own constants (2·`STADIUM_OPENING_X`/`WORLD_HEIGHT`) and forbids the old `max-aspect-ratio: 2752/1536` centring, so the CSS and `computeSceneView` cannot drift apart again silently. Kallang + scene-motion suites pass (53 tests), as do typecheck, Kallang ESLint and the standards gate. Playwright was not run (no browser in the sandbox); the resize itself remains for the owner's eyes on the dev stack.

### ADR-310 — the stage pipeline: every stage its own format, source and duration

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-20
- **Relates to:** ADR-272 (the scheduler overlay), ADR-274 (the scheduler adapter), ADR-278 (format semantics)

**Context.** The day the owner described — nine teams, group matches at 15 minutes across three courts, then semi-finals and a final at 20, group points worth less than knockout points — is not expressible today: a tournament picks ONE of ten whole-tournament formats and ONE match length (`tournament_scheduler.match_minutes`), and the two example days (groups feed a knockout; pools pay less than brackets) have to be approximated into whichever canned format comes closest. One gap was in the core: `stage_place` on a grouped stage ranked only the group winners, so "the three winners and the best runner-up" could not be seated at all.

**Decision.**
1. **A free-form stage builder is the engine; templates are only a default presentation** (`scheduler/pipeline.ts`). A tournament may be activated with a `PipelineSpec` — an ordered list of stages — instead of a `formatId`. Each stage carries a scheduler stage format (`pool`, `bracket`, `open`), an entrant source (`initial` seeding, or `advancers` — the top N from an earlier stage), point rates, and its own `matchMinutes` (null inherits the tournament's). The whole-tournament formats are untouched and remain selectable; their per-stage pieces were decomposed into `scheduler/formats/stages.ts` so pipeline stages and canned formats build from the same fixtures (`snakeDeal`, `groupFixtures`, `buildKnockout`). A desk that deletes every default stage and writes its own has changed nothing about the machinery.
2. **Advancers are ranked place-major** (`advancersRanked` in core `standings.ts`): all of a stage's group winners ranked among themselves, then all its runners-up, then thirds — points, difference, scored, entry order inside each class (the one ranking rule, P-13). `stage_place` seats on a grouped stage read this order, which fixes the best-runner-up seat; where a stage advances only its winners, the reading is unchanged. A runner-up can never jump a winner on points alone.
3. **Pairings are the table's, not the desk's.** Advancer seats enter brackets in advancer order, so classic cross-seeding pairs 1v4 and 2v3 in a four-advancer knockout. This narrows the desk's editable-seats precedent on this surface deliberately: the desk controls structure (below), the table controls who advances.
4. **Durations live on matches.** A stage's `matchMinutes` is stamped onto its matches' `planned_minutes` at materialisation; the planner has always timed each match individually. A contingency that changes the tournament's match length retimes only the stages that *inherited* it (no match carrying a different length) — a 20-minute knockout keeps its 20 when the 15s become 18s, in preview and in application alike.
5. **Composed upfront, re-plannable in the small.** The whole pipeline is materialised at activation, as formats are today, so the day's plan (and its feasibility readout) is complete before play starts. Re-cutting an unstarted stage's *format* between stages is deliberately a later increment; this increment's between-stage levers are durations, pins and terminate-and-rebuild. Pools therefore validate as initial-only: membership cannot be snake-dealt before it is known. The scheduler row records `format = 'pipeline'` (the CHECK widened inline and by the ADR-173 drop-then-add pair); the spec itself is not persisted in this increment, and the stage-builder surface is the next one.

**Verified.** Engine (`packages/tournament/src/tests/pipeline.test.ts`, test-first): the 9-team template (snake-dealt groups A/B/C, nine 15-minute pool matches, semis seated stage_place 1v4/2v3, final off the semi winners, sequences ordered stage by stage); from-scratch single-bracket, single-pool and open pipelines; third-place `loser_of` seats; per-stage rates on draft stages; `validatePipeline` refusals (empty, duplicate codes, advancers from a later stage, pool from advancers, counts, durations, one-team groups); the advancer ladder on a played-out fixture, including the scored rung separating level runners-up and nobody seated before the stage finishes; the planner timing a 15-minute pool and a 20-minute semi on one clock. API (`apps/api/src/tests/tournament-pipeline.test.ts`, real database): activation writes `format = 'pipeline'` with per-stage `planned_minutes` (15/20 against a 12 neither stage chose); the full nine-team day plays its groups, auto-advances, and seats semis 1v4/2v3 with the designed best runner-up (seed 5, separated on score difference); knockouts close the tournament; activation refusals (later-stage advancers; format and pipeline together); a contingency retiming inherits-only (12→18 leaves the 20s standing). Existing format, planner, core and tournament API suites pass (engine 105/105; scheduler-adjacent API 70/70). The stage-builder UI is the next increment; nothing here is reachable from a surface yet.

### ADR-311 — the stage builder: the pipeline reaches the desk and the rehearsal

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-20
- **Relates to:** ADR-310 (the stage pipeline), ADR-279 (the tournament console), ADR-274 (the simulator)

**Context.** ADR-310 built the stage pipeline in the engine and the API and deliberately stopped at the surface: a desk could only activate one via the raw API contract, the Simulator could only rehearse the ten canned formats, and the Day panel would have printed the storage word `pipeline` as its heading. The owner's day (groups at 15, knockouts at 20, inside 90 minutes) is exactly the shape that needs the builder in front of a person, with the fit reading beside it before Start is pressed.

**Decision.**
1. **The Start form builds two ways** (`SetupPanel`, `useTournamentSetup`). A Build select chooses one whole-tournament format (unchanged) or stage-by-stage. Pipeline mode preloads the engine's own `defaultPipelineSpec` as editable stage drafts — the template stays a default presentation, deletable to an empty list and writable from scratch. The shared `StagePipelineEditor` edits an ordered stage list: code and name, format (pool / bracket / open), match minutes (blank inherits the tournament's), group size/count and per-group advancers for pools, source (entered teams in seed order, or the top N finishers of an earlier stage chosen from the stages above it) and third-place for brackets, and per-stage point rates (all three or none). Stages can be added, removed and reordered. A dealt stage (pool, open) is always dealt from the entered teams, so switching a stage's format to pool resets its source rather than offering a state the engine refuses.
2. **Refusals are the engine's, in advance** (`pipelineProblem`): field-level checks (codes, names, whole numbers, rates in threes) in the form's words, then `validatePipeline` itself over the spec the list describes, so the desk hears "KO: advancers must come from an earlier stage." before the server would say it. Start posts `{ pipeline }` with no `formatId` (the contract's either/or), and the web's `ActivateBody` now carries the engine's `PipelineSpec` type.
3. **The Simulator rehearses pipelines** (engine `simulate` accepts a `pipeline` in place of a format, planning matches at their stage's length; the Simulator subtab carries the same editor). The 90-minute question is answerable on screen before the day exists: the template at 9 teams on 3 courts from 10:00 reads "12 matches, last one ends 11:37 — 7 min past the hard stop" against an 11:30 deadline.
4. **The Day panel names it**: the scheduler heading reads "Stage pipeline, active" (`SchedulerFormatId = TournamentFormatId | 'pipeline'` in contracts; the admin view casts to it). Everything downstream of activation was already structure-driven and needed no change.

**Verified.** Engine (107/107): `simulate` plans the template at its per-stage durations and reads the fit (finish 697 from a 600 start, 7 past a 690 stop), and refuses an unbuildable pipeline in the validator's words. Web (`tournament-pages.test.tsx`): the builder starts the preloaded template (two stages, 15 and 20 minutes, no `formatId` in the request) and the live day's heading reads "Stage pipeline, active"; deleting the feeder stage refuses Start with the engine's "earlier stage" wording; a from-scratch single pool stage with edited minutes posts exactly that spec; the Simulator rehearses the template to an 11:37 finish against an 11:30 stop. Existing Control, courts, simulator and hook suites pass unchanged; the builder's field readings and list edits are pinned directly in `useTournamentSetup.test.ts`.

### ADR-312 — the demo fringe stations take the revised line-up, one completion tier each

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-176 (the passport bonus), ADR-237 (the demo-seed refresh), ADR-261/ADR-262 (repeat strikes at one station)

**Context.** The demo's five fringe stations still carried the line-up and the name-specific award tiers of the earlier programme: a podium at one station, a winning-team tier at another, and graded tiers at two more. The revised programme names five different stations, and the old tiers describe the old activities, so keeping them would have priced the new stations with somebody else's results.

**Decision.** The five seeded stations are, in order, Indoor Bocce Challenge, Netball Shooting Challenge, Hula Hoop Hero, Jump Rope Challenge and Giant Ball Slalom. Every station carries one generic tier — `Completed`, 30 points — marked in the seed as demo colour, not a published price. Round counts and participant windows are unchanged, so the passport still turns on four distinct stations and the Netball Shooting Challenge encore still stacks ADR-261's repeat strikes. `apps/api/src/db/seed-demo.sql` was regenerated through the sanctioned replay (`./refresh-demo-seed.sh --skip-record`), never hand-edited, so the 216 historical scans carry the new names and the `Completed` / 30 snapshot. The event-deck assessment keeps its original station names as historical source material.

**Verified.** The refresh replayed the recorded 120-participant dump through the real API and re-exported the demo database (120 participants verified by the refresh itself); its log seeds the five new stations with 9 / 51 / 42 / 54 / 60 scans, all snapshotted `Completed` at 30 points. A grep over the seed script and the exported SQL finds none of the replaced station or tier names.

### ADR-313 — a draft can save its Start configuration; the demo arrives as that draft

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-203 (the demo before the first whistle), ADR-279 (the tournament console), ADR-310/ADR-311 (the stage pipeline and its builder), ADR-286 (the demo's courts)

**Context.** ADR-203 kept the demo before the first whistle by starting no tournament at all: teams formed, courts existed, and a walkthrough still had to choose the format live before Start could mean anything. That protected the one irreversible click, but it also meant the demo could not show the tournament this event actually intends to run — nine teams in groups then knockouts inside 1 hour 40 — without the walkthrough operator inventing it on the spot. The console had nowhere to keep such an answer either: a draft persisted only its name, kind, rates and entrants, while the format, pipeline and timing existed only in the Start form's local state and in the scheduler row that activation writes.

**Decision.**
1. **A draft carries its Start configuration** (`tournament.draft_setup`, a nullable JSONB column; `TournamentDraftSetup` in contracts). It holds one format *or* a stage pipeline — never both — plus its options, the fallback match minutes, changeover and rest minutes, and a deadline kept as a local `HH:MM` time of day (the date belongs to the day Start is pressed, exactly as the Start form's own deadline field reads it). `POST /api/admin/tournament` accepts it as `setup`; the server validates it against the entrant count before writing anything — canned formats through `findFormat(...).validate`, pipelines through `validatePipeline` — and refuses in the validator's own words. Activation is untouched: `POST /activate` remains the only writer of stages, matches and the scheduler row, so a saved setup schedules nothing and Start is still the click that finalises it. The column is added additively (`ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` beside the in-file definition), so `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is not bumped: a nullable column is exactly what the bootstrap's self-repair heals.
2. **The console opens a saved draft with the answer in the fields.** The Control read returns `draftSetup`; `useTournamentSetup` initialises from the desk's tournament and hydrates once per draft id, so a saved pipeline arrives with Build already set to stage-by-stage and its stages in the editor — and a later poll never overwrites what the operator is typing. Creating a draft from the form saves its current Start answer with it when that answer describes a playable day; an answer the field cannot play yet is not allowed to stop the draft itself being made. Start then posts the (possibly edited) form exactly as before.
3. **The demo is seeded as that draft, through the UI's own API.** `scripts/seed-demo.mjs` creates `Captain’s ball` via `POST /api/admin/tournament` — the route the console's client calls — with the nine teams in seed order, flat 30/20/10, and the saved 1-hour-40 pipeline: `GRP` pool, three groups of three at 15 minutes, one through per group, then `KO` bracket, the top four cross-seeded at 20 minutes, changeover 3, rest 0, the tournament's own 12 minutes only a fallback neither stage inherits. That shape plans to about 97 minutes on three courts, inside the 100-minute window. It stays a draft: no scheduler, no stages, no matches. A re-run's 409 is the draft already there. `demo-export-cli.ts` now classifies `tournament` and `tournament_entrant` in foreign-key order; every later tournament table stays unlisted, so a started demo tournament would still fail the export's coverage check rather than be silently dropped. This narrows ADR-203 rather than superseding it: the day is still before the first whistle — it now arrives with the whistle's plan already written down.

**Verified.** API (`tournament-draft-setup.test.ts`, real database): a participant is refused 403; a saved pipeline whose knockout feeds from a stage that is not earlier is refused 400 with the engine's "earlier stage" wording and writes no row; the nine-team 1-hour-40 pipeline saves onto a draft that reads back `status: 'draft'` with `scheduler: null`, no stages and no matches, and the persisted `draft_setup` holds both stages at 15/20. Web: `useTournamentSetup.test.ts` round-trips the saved pipeline from view to form text and back unchanged; `tournament-pages.test.tsx` opens the saved draft with Build already on pipeline and Start posts the saved pipeline unchanged (no `formatId`). The demo seed was regenerated through `./refresh-demo-seed.sh --skip-record` (120 participants verified by the refresh itself): `seed-demo.sql` holds one `draft` tournament with the pipeline as `draft_setup`, nine entrants in seed order, three courts, and no scheduler, stage or match rows.

### ADR-314 — the demo seed carries today's sign-ups: 135 named participants, twelve Kallang teams, seven complete

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-040 (the recorded demo crowd), ADR-203 (the demo before the first whistle), ADR-270/ADR-313 (tournament rates and saved draft setup), ADR-279 (the tournament console and Simulator), ADR-286 (the demo's courts)
- **Supersedes in part:** ADR-313 §3 — the demo tournament no longer arrives with a saved nine-team pipeline. ADR-313's draft-setup capability itself is unchanged; only the seeded demo's entrant and format choice changes.

**Context.** The demo seed still described an earlier, tidier day: 120 recorded participants spread almost evenly across clusters, nine teams of six, and (after ADR-313) a saved 1-hour-40 pipeline for exactly those nine. Today's real sign-ups are messier and more useful: 135 sign-ups across the clusters, twelve teams rostered from Participant 001-094 in sign-up order, only seven of those teams complete, and a field that may still land anywhere from seven to twelve teams by the day. The event has also moved to Kallang, so the old beach-named teams no longer belong.

**Decision.**
1. **The crowd is 135 named participants, all on PIN 1000.** `scripts/seed-demo.mjs` replays the 120 recorded onboardings, then signs up fifteen supplemental named participants from `scripts/demo-supplemental-participants.json` (drawn avatars; they were never recorded, so they have no photo sprite). Every seeded participant — recorded or supplemental — signs up and signs in with PIN `1000`. Sign-up order is load-bearing: Participant 001-094 are the rostered players below, and the order carries the cluster distribution.
2. **Cluster names ride on the catalogue, and the catalogue grows by two.** The event's names map onto existing codes — Comms & Engagement → `Comms`, Cumulus/ACE → `Cumulus`, HRPS/HRMS → `HRPS`, SPR/IR → `SPR` — and `CentEx` and `HI` join `CLUSTER_SEED_CODES`, so an empty database now seeds eighteen clusters. The "16 clusters" counts and copy that pinned the old catalogue follow it to 18.
3. **Twelve Kallang-named teams carry the team table's rosters, in sign-up order:** Kallang Roar (10), Kallang Rush (9), Kallang Splash (1), Kallang Current (10), Kallang Wave (10), Kallang (10), Basin Breakers (8), Kallang Rally (6), Merdeka Crossing (3), Kallang Thunder (9), Stadium Lights (8) and Kallang Surge (10) — 94 rostered sign-ups. A roster of nine or more is the working definition of a complete team; on that reading exactly seven teams are complete (01, 02, 04, 05, 06, 10, 12), which is the owner's count.
4. **Where the two sign-up tables disagree, the seed says so instead of hiding it.** The cluster table's "also in tournament" column totals 91, while the team table rosters 94; PSC Sect alone shows one total sign-up and none in the tournament, yet fields the three-person Team 09. Both cannot be encoded at once. The team table wins for who is on a team (and their cluster), so PSC Sect is seeded with three; the cluster table wins for the 135 total and the non-roster fill, taken in cluster-table order until the 41 non-roster places run out. The seeded result is therefore exact for every cluster except the irreconcilable seam: PSC Sect 3 (table: 1), ServiceSG 39 (table: 40) and SPR 0 (table: 1). If the source tables are corrected, `CLUSTER_SIGNUPS` and `TEAM_PLAN` in the seed script are the two places to change.
5. **The tournament draft enters the seven complete teams and saves no format.** `Captain's ball` is created through `POST /api/admin/tournament` at flat 30/20/10 with the seven complete teams and no `setup`, so `draft_setup` is NULL and there are still no scheduler, stage or match rows. Seeding one count's pipeline would pretend the field is settled; instead the console's Simulator is the planning surface — the seed's twelve teams and three courts are its raw material, and the operator varies Teams from 7 to 12 there, picks the shape that fits the clock, and only then saves a Start format on the draft. Start remains the walkthrough's own irreversible click.

**Verified.** `./refresh-demo-seed.sh --skip-record` replayed the crowd through the real API and re-exported the demo database; the refresh itself now verifies 135 participants (120 recorded + 15 supplemental). Its seed log reports 135 participants ready, twelve teams with 94 rostered sign-ups and seven complete at 9+, a `Captain's ball` draft with seven complete teams entered and no format saved, the five ADR-312 stations' 9 / 51 / 42 / 54 / 60 scans, and the photo wall, announcements and swag counter as before. Reading the exported `seed-demo.sql` directly: 135 unique participants, every PIN `1000`; team memberships of 10 / 9 / 1 / 10 / 10 / 10 / 8 / 6 / 3 / 9 / 8 / 10 across the twelve Kallang teams; one `draft` tournament with `draft_setup` NULL, seven entrants (the complete teams, in order), three courts, and no scheduler, stage or match rows. Cluster counts in the SQL match the cluster table exactly except the documented seam (PSC Sect 3, ServiceSG 39, SPR 0). Targeted suites for the catalogue change pass: API auth (19/19), the bootstrap "seeds the 18 clusters" case, admin-directory F49, final-standings, web `useAuthForms` (9/9) and the leaderboard page case. `./verify.sh` passes typecheck, standards, the web build, tournament tests (107/107) and web tests (173 files / 1865 tests); its lint stage fails only on the seventeen pre-existing errors inside the retained `tmp/Kallang` reference tree, and its API stage aborts in this sandbox with tinypool `ERR_IPC_CHANNEL_CLOSED` after its first files pass — both recorded here rather than hidden, and both unrelated to this change.

### ADR-315 — the image carries both boot scripts, and a failed script names itself

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-249 (the app provisions via `db-provision.sh`), ADR-264 (`DB_INIT_RESET=stale` resets via `db-reset.sh`), ADR-175 (the Dockerfile twins), ADR-313/ADR-314 (the seeded demo day)

**Context.** A container deployment crash-looped on boot. The database was stamped schema version 0 against this build's 3, so `DB_INIT_RESET=stale` did its job and shelled out to `db-reset.sh` — and bash answered `bash: /app/db-reset.sh: No such file or directory`, exit 127, which failed DB_INIT and restarted the cycle. The image copied `db-provision.sh` and `_dev-common.sh` into `/app` but never `db-reset.sh`: the reset path (ADR-264) arrived after the image's COPY line (ADR-249) and nobody added the second script. A developer's checkout always has both files, so nothing local could see it. The failure was then misreported: the shared script runner's refusal read `db-provision.sh exited 127` whichever script had run, sending the reader to the wrong file.

**Decision.**
1. **Both Dockerfiles copy `db-provision.sh db-reset.sh _dev-common.sh`** — the identical line in each, as the twin rule (ADR-175) requires. `db-reset.sh` needs nothing else the image lacks: it sources `_dev-common.sh`, runs `setup-cli.ts` through the pruned `node_modules/.bin/tsx`, and reads `apps/api/src` — the same mechanism `db-provision.sh` already proves in the image on every `DB_INIT=demo` boot.
2. **The runner names the script that failed.** `runProvisionScript`'s refusal now uses the basename of the script it spawned, so a missing or failing `db-reset.sh` says so. The existing diagnostic test pins the new wording.
3. **A standards rule stands where the image would.** `checkDockerBootScripts` (rule 20) extracts every `*.sh` the API can spawn from `apps/api/src/db/dbInit.ts` and fails unless both Dockerfiles carry it in a COPY instruction — matching the COPY line specifically, not a passing mention in a comment. Proven both ways: it reports the pre-fix Dockerfiles and passes with the fix.

**Verified.** API: `connection-diagnostics.test.ts` and `db-init.test.ts` pass together (77/77, single worker), including the reset-before-provision ordering cases. Standards passes at 20 rules and fails (exit 1, both files named) when the COPY change is reverted in a scratch copy. No Docker daemon exists in this sandbox, so the image itself was not rebuilt here; the in-image proof is the standards rule plus the fact that `db-reset.sh`'s whole dependency set already ships for `db-provision.sh`. On the next deployment the expected log is the reset line followed by `setup-cli --reset` output, then DB_INIT rebuilding at schema version 3 — no exit 127.

### ADR-316 — the build context was the second missing half: `.dockerignore` excluded `db-reset.sh`

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-315 (the Dockerfile COPY and the runner's message), ADR-249 / ADR-264 (the two boot scripts), ADR-175 (the Dockerfile twins)
- **Completes:** ADR-315, whose Dockerfile fix was necessary but not sufficient.

**Context.** After ADR-315 the deployment still crash-looped with `/app/db-reset.sh: No such file or directory`. The log itself proved the code half had landed — the refusal now correctly read `db-reset.sh exited 127` instead of blaming `db-provision.sh` — while the file remained absent. The cause sat one layer earlier: `.dockerignore` ignores `/*.sh` wholesale and un-ignores only `!/db-provision.sh` and `!/_dev-common.sh`, an exception list written for ADR-249's single script. `db-reset.sh` therefore never entered the build context at all, and no COPY instruction, however correct, can copy a file the context does not carry.

**Decision.**
1. **`.dockerignore` un-ignores `!/db-reset.sh`** beside its two siblings, with the comment naming both boot scripts and the failure mode.
2. **The ADR-315 standards rule now checks the context as well as the COPY.** For every boot script `dbInit.ts` can spawn, rule 20 requires both a COPY instruction in each Dockerfile *and* — while the wholesale `/*.sh` ignore stands — a `!/name` exception in `.dockerignore`. Proven as before: deleting the exception in a scratch copy makes the rule fail naming `.dockerignore`; restoring it passes.

**Verified.** `node scripts/check-standards.mjs` passes at 20 rules with both halves in place, and fails (exit 1) when either half is reverted in a scratch copy — the COPY revert names both Dockerfiles, the exception revert names `.dockerignore`. A deployment built from this commit should show all three scripts at `/app/*.sh`; the boot then runs the reset (`setup-cli --reset`) and DB_INIT rebuilds at schema version 3. If a platform build cache serves the previous context, a no-cache rebuild is the remedy to reach for before doubting the files.

### ADR-317 — the ADR-265 phone type scale finally applies: its media block moves after the rules it overrides

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-265 (the phone type scale), ADR-046 (the nav label stays 8px), ADR-256 / ADR-298 (the venue scene boxes), ADR-301..309 (Kallang)
- **Corrects:** ADR-265's claim that the pixel-type steps ship; only its reading-face step did.

**Context.** The owner reported that on the Kallang deployment the banner and the middle UI look scaled down on a phone, "as if the phone is a tiny desktop browser", while the bottom bar is fine. ADR-265 had fixed exactly that for Sentosa. The first suspicion was a Kallang regression (its full-screen plate scene replaced the shared strip). It is not: measured in Chromium (Pixel 7, 412 px) and WebKit (iPhone 14, 390 px) against a `PSD_VENUE=kallang` stack, with the venue also forced to `sentosa`, **both venues compute identical sizes** — shell 22 px, but banner `h1` **15 px**, banner `p` 9 px, panel `h2` 11 px, `.gb-button` 11 px. ADR-265 specifies 16 / 10 / 12 / 12. Viewport meta, `visualViewport.scale` (1), horizontal overflow (none), `text-size-adjust` and the `100dvh` shell are all correct.

**Cause.** In `styles/gameboy.css` the `@media (max-width: 600px)` block sat at line 322, *before* the base rules it overrides (`.gb-banner h1` 438, `.gb-banner p` 456, `.gb-panel h2` 479, `h3` 487, `.gb-label` 500, `.gb-button` 556). A media query adds no specificity, so the later base rule always won. Only `.theme-gameboy { font-size: 22px }` took effect, because its base rule is earlier. The order was the same in ADR-265's own commit (`6a61a95`), so the pixel-type steps have never applied on any venue. The bottom nav looked right because ADR-265 deliberately leaves it at 8 px. Kallang makes it visible because its photographic plate shows directly behind the small type, where Sentosa's panels sit over flat sky. `gameboy.css.test.ts` could not catch it: it asserts the declarations exist inside the media block, not that they win.

**Decision.**
1. The phone block moves to just after `.gb-button` and its state/variant rules, **before** `.gb-button--small`. That is after every rule it overrides, and `.gb-button--small` (9 px, same specificity) keeps winning for small buttons, which is what they rendered at all along. No value changes: 22 / 16 / 10 / 12 / 10 / 10 / 12 exactly as ADR-265 wrote them.
2. A comment on the block says it must follow the rules it overrides.
3. Two pins: `gameboy.css.test.ts` asserts, for each selector in the block, that the block comes after that selector's base rule; and `e2e/participant/phone-type-scale.spec.ts` asserts the *computed* `font-size` at 412 px (scaled) and 1280 px (desktop sizes unchanged, nav 8 px at both).

**Verification.** Watched red first, for the right reason: the six new order pins failed (`expected 10879 to be greater than 13568`, the media block preceding `.gb-banner h1`) and the browser spec failed with banner title `Expected: "16px"  Received: "15px"`. After the move: `gameboy.css.test.ts` 15/15; `phone-type-scale.spec.ts` passes on desktop-chrome, mobile-chrome and mobile-safari against a `PSD_VENUE=kallang` stack; computed sizes at 412 px on both Kallang and Sentosa are now shell 22 / `h1` 16 / banner `p` 10 / `h2` 12 / button 12; `npm run typecheck`, `check-standards` (20 rules, 0 violations) and the web unit suite (1872) are green. **Not run:** the full `npm run verify` stops at `eslint .`, which fails only inside `tmp/Kallang/` (the reference import kept in the tree) with `max-params` errors in files this change does not touch; the API test suite and the rest of the Playwright suites were not run. The handset check is still owed: the banner and panels should now read one notch larger. If that is still not enough, a bigger phone scale is its own decision.

### ADR-318 — the spoken number on My QR is always above the fold: the code shrinks to the height that is left

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-266 (the QR badge's three essentials), ADR-098 (the shell's frame never scrolls, `.gb-main` does), ADR-088 / ADR-103 (the spoken scan number), ADR-317 (the phone type scale)
- **Refines:** ADR-266. It sized the code by **width** alone and assumed the nickname, code and number would still fit the height. They do not on a short phone.

**Context.** The owner wants the My QR tab (`/home`) to keep its UI as large as possible, but the 4-digit number a participant says to the facilitator must be visible without scrolling by default. Measured against a `PSD_VENUE=kallang` stack (bottom of the number pill vs bottom of the visible `.gb-main`): Pixel 7 (412x839) fits with 125 px to spare; Galaxy S9+ (320x658) is cut by 10 px; iPhone 15 (393x659) by 41 px; iPhone SE (320x568) by 101 px. The cause is ADR-266's `.gb-qr { width: min(320px, 76vw) }`: the code is as tall as it is wide, so on any phone shorter than about 800 px the card is taller than the space left under the banner and above the nav, and the number is the first thing to fall off.

**Decision.** The code gives up height; nothing else does. The banner, nickname row and number pill keep their sizes.
1. **The three essentials share one box.** `QrHomePage` wraps the nickname row, the code and the fallback hint (which holds the number pill) in `.gb-qr-essentials`; the points, the "My points" link and the ground strip stay after it and still fall below the fold, as ADR-266 intended. The 16 px spacer div becomes the box's `gap`.
2. **CSS sizes it, not JS.** `.gb-main:has(.gb-qr-essentials)` becomes a size container (`container-type: size`; `.gb-main` already has a definite height from the fixed-height shell, so containment changes no layout), and `.gb-qr-essentials` is capped at `100cqh` of it less the panel's own border and padding. The code lives in `.gb-qr-slot`, the one flexible child, and is the largest square that fits the width cap `min(320px, 76vw)` and the height the slot is left. ADR-266's rule stands: no `useFitScale`, no measuring in script, no transform-shrink of the card.
3. **A floor.** The code never goes below 120 px. Only on a screen too short even for that (a phone held in landscape) does the number fall below the fold; a code that small could not be scanned, which is worse than scrolling to a number.
4. **Where it already fits, nothing changes.** On a tall phone the slot is taller than the cap, so the code stays at its ADR-266 size.
5. **Browsers without `cqh` or `:has`** ignore the new declarations and keep ADR-266's layout.

**Verification.** Watched red first, for the right reason: the browser spec failed with `Galaxy S9+: number is inside the visible area  Expected: <= 590.5  Received: 600.46875` (and 101 px over on iPhone SE), and the stylesheet pin failed on the missing `:has` container. Two build mistakes were also caught by the spec before they shipped: a fixed-width code stopped being square once its height was clamped (`the code stays square  Received: 98.95`), and a percentage-height image inside a flex item overflowed its slot and drew over the number line, so the code is now absolutely positioned inside `.gb-qr-slot`, which carries the shrink (`flex: 0 1 min(320px, 76vw)`), and the spec gained a check that the number's line sits below the code. After the fix, at the four probed screens the number's bottom edge vs the visible bottom of `.gb-main` is Pixel 7 644/771, iPhone 15 567/591, Galaxy S9+ 566/590, iPhone SE 476/500; the code is 313 / 235 / 211 / 120 px (the Pixel 7 code is the unchanged ADR-266 size). `qr-badge-fold.spec.ts` and `phone-type-scale.spec.ts` pass on desktop-chrome, mobile-chrome and mobile-safari against a `PSD_VENUE=kallang` stack; `gameboy.css.test.ts` 16/16. **Cost:** on an iPhone SE-height screen the code is 120 px, half its former size, which is the price of keeping the number in view; the ADR-266 handset check (does it scan at counter distance) is owed again on a short phone. **Not run:** full `npm run verify` (eslint fails only inside `tmp/Kallang/`), the API suite and the other Playwright suites.

### ADR-319 — every editable field on the superadmin tournament surfaces carries an (i) help tooltip

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-279 (the Tournament tab), ADR-288 (courts), ADR-289 (placement), ADR-310 / ADR-311 (stage pipelines), AGENTS-frontend.md §2–§5 (hooks decide; copy lives in `@psd/contracts`), AGENTS-testing.md §1.1 (what has to be seen is asserted in a browser)

**Context.** The owner asked that each field on the superadmin tournament surfaces explain what its value does when the admin hovers or presses on it, and that the explanation goes away when focus leaves. The 52 editable fields (Setup, the stage builder, Courts, Placement, the desk-act dialog, the day-contingency panel and the Simulator) had no help at all: no `title=`, no `aria-describedby`, only a hint in brackets inside some labels and a few unlinked `console-meta` notes. The console had no tooltip of any kind; `AvatarPeek` is the only popover in the app and is a participant (`gb-*`) component the standards forbid on admin pages, so only its pattern is reusable. No popover library is installed.

**Decision.**
1. **The trigger is a small (i) button beside each label** (the owner's choice over making the whole field the trigger). Scope is the editable fields on the tournament surfaces only; read-only table column headers, PointConfig and the rest of the superadmin console are not touched. The mechanism is built to be adopted elsewhere.
2. **Three ways to open, one way to close.** Hovering the icon, focusing it (keyboard or click) and pressing it each open the tooltip. It is removed when the pointer leaves *and* focus has left *and* any press has been released: a press is released by a press anywhere outside the icon or by Escape, because Safari does not focus a button on click, so blur alone cannot be relied on. A press does not toggle (the hover-then-click double-toggle `AvatarPeek` documents).
3. **Markup.** `ConsoleField` renders the label and the icon as siblings and the control after them; the label no longer wraps the input, so the icon is never inside a `<label>` (a button in a label would also fire the label). It injects `id` and `aria-describedby` into its single child, so a field cannot forget either. The tooltip is `role="tooltip"`, always in the DOM and toggled with `hidden`, so `aria-describedby` resolves while it is closed. Checkboxes use `CheckField`; a group of checkboxes (the team picker, the courts in play) shares one tooltip on its legend or heading.
4. **The copy is data in `@psd/contracts`** (`fieldHelp.ts`, keyed by a typed topic), so the copy-ownership standard covers it and a field cannot inline its own. Each sentence was written from what the consuming hook or contract enforces (ranges from `tournament.ts`, blank-means-default from `useTournamentSetup`, the Ironman rest rule from `formats/basic.ts`), not from the label.
5. **Placement is clamped to the viewport** by the hook (a measured shift on open), because a field in the second column of a row on a 390 px screen would otherwise push a 320 px tooltip off the right edge.
6. **Nothing else about the pages changes**: every `data-testid` stands, labels are unchanged.

**Found while researching, reported not changed:** the dialog's Reason field always reads "(required)" yet closing a stage as its table stands, or a day that ended on time, takes none (`useTournamentActs.ts`); `fds.md` §2.5 says courts 1–5 where the code and the label allow 1–20; the stage builder's number fields lack `inputMode="numeric"`; `.console-hint` is used but has no rule.

**Verification.** Written test-first and watched fail for the right reason: the three new unit files failed to import (`useFieldHelp`, `ConsoleField`, `fieldHelp` did not exist) and seven completeness tests failed with `has no aria-describedby` before any page was converted. After the conversion: 217 tests across `components/console`, `useFieldHelp` and `routes-superadmin` pass, among them a generic walk that asks every input, select and textarea on the new-tournament form, the Start form (each build and several formats), a stage fed by an earlier stage, the courts form, the contingency panel, the move form, the correct / award / stop-scheduler dialogs and the Simulator in both builds for a tooltip that resolves and has text; `fieldHelp.copy.test.ts` pins that every topic is rendered and every requested topic exists. The browser spec `e2e/superadmin/tournament-field-help.spec.ts` (7 tests, desktop 1280 and phone 390) passes on desktop-chrome, mobile-chrome and mobile-safari, 42 of 42, ten full runs in a row. It reads the tooltip's copy against the contract, that it is inside the viewport, that it goes when the pointer leaves, when focus moves on, on a press elsewhere and on Escape, and that only one is open at a time. Three defects were found by the browser, not the unit tests: the tooltip ran off the right edge on Chrome's mobile emulation because a tooltip that overflows makes `window.innerWidth` grow to fit it, so the clamp measures `documentElement.clientWidth`; the Courts form moves under a resting pointer while the console loads, so the spec waits for the load before it hovers; and an unrelated `flag-parameter` standards rule caught two boolean parameters in the new hook. **Not run:** the full `npm run verify` (eslint stops inside `tmp/Kallang/`), the API suite, the other Playwright suites, and the Start form and desk-act dialogs in a browser (they need a tournament created, which writes to the shared stack; they are covered in jsdom). The handset check is owed: the 22 px icon with its 44 px hit area, and whether the 15 px tooltip reads well in sunlight.

### ADR-320 — stage handovers reconcile: per-stage internal table points, qualifiers first and shortfall fills after; the dumb-court mode assessed and planned; team-award test coverage assessed

- **Status:** Accepted (the dumb-court mode is planned, not built — see `docs/design/dumb-tournament-mode-plan.md`)
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-273 §4 (one ranking rule), ADR-276 (the points bridge), ADR-293 (one open tournament per kind), ADR-310/ADR-311 (the stage pipeline and its builder), ADR-313 (saved draft setups), ADR-319 (field help)

**Context.** Three questions arrived together. (1) A stage's output did not always match the next stage's appetite: three groups sending one winner each produce three teams, but a semi-final wants four — and the machinery that actually filled the fourth seat (`advancersRanked`, place-major: winners first, then the best runners-up) was invisible at setup time, unprotected at close time (the scheduler's tie-on-the-cut safeguard inspected only each group's own `advanceCount` line, never the cross-group "best runner-up" cut), unverifiable in the pipeline validator (nothing compared a feeder's field against a downstream intake), and ranked on table points (3/1/0) that were fixed in code while the day's *paid* rates were per-stage. (2) The owner asked for a parallel "dumb" tournament mode: courts run like fringe stations, court masters awarding configured tiers straight to teams, no QR, no winners or losers. (3) The owner asked whether the test suites actually exercise point awards to teams, given team points spread across the (mixed-cluster) individuals on the team.

**Decision — the handover reconciles, and ranking gets its own definable numbers.**

1. **Per-stage internal table points.** A stage now carries `tablePoints` (win/draw/loss) beside its paid `rates`, end to end: engine `Stage.tablePoints` → scheduler `DraftStage`/`StageOptions`/`FormatOptions` → contracts (`formatOptionsSchema`, hence pipeline stage options and draft setups) → `tournament_stage.table_*_points` columns (nullable, all-three-or-none, added additively like `draft_setup`) → the stage builder's three new fields. Null ranks on the default **3/1/0** (`DEFAULT_TABLE_POINTS`). Every ranking that decides anything — group tables, cross-group place rankings, stage tables, `advancersRanked`, Swiss pairing — runs on the stage's own table points, ties still broken on score difference, then scored, then entry order. Table points **rank; they are never paid.** What a result pays remains the stage's `rates`, a deliberately separate number, and the copy in the builder says so ("ranking only — nobody is paid these" / "these ARE paid").
2. **Qualifiers first, shortfall fills after, never overlapping.** The handover rule is stated once, in `stageAdvancers`: the next stage's intake (the highest `stage_place` read from the feeder, else the feeder's own qualifying count) is filled in advancer order — per-group qualifiers first (place-major), then the best non-qualifiers on the feeder's internal table — and every seat is labelled `qualifier` or `fill`. The canonical day now reads exactly as the owner described it: 3 groups × 1 = 3 winners, a 4-team knockout takes the best runner-up as a labelled fill. The engine already seated this way; it now *says* so — the desk's stage panel shows the internal table points and the through-list with fills marked (`AdminStageView.tablePoints` / `.advancers`, `DayPanel.advancerLine`).
3. **The validator reconciles before Start.** `validatePipeline` tracks each stage's field (entered teams, or the intake it was fed) and refuses an intake beyond the field the feeder ranks — *"FIN: KO only has 4 teams to send on, so it cannot feed 6"* — while an intake between the qualifiers and the field is a plan, not an error: shortfall fills are how the shape is satisfied. The refusal reaches the desk in the builder through `pipelineProblem`, unchanged.
4. **The close safeguard covers the reconciled cut.** `completeStage`'s tie check now also inspects the cut at the downstream intake on the advancer table: a tie for the last fill seat (two runners-up level on points, difference and scored) is the desk's to call, exactly like a tie on a group's own cut — the system actor is refused `tie_on_cut`, the desk may close, and the fill it seats is the one the table named. Frozen seats still never move afterwards.

**Assessed — the dumb-court mode (planned, not built).** The assessment and the phased plan live in `docs/design/dumb-tournament-mode-plan.md`. The short version: the expensive machinery already exists — a manual team award spread by the points bridge, the swag counter's armed-tier facilitator pattern, and ADR-293's one-open-per-kind slot for a parallel tournament. The recommended build adds a `'dumb_courts'` kind whose activation writes entrants and no structure, a tournament-level tier list snapshotted onto each award, one facilitator route with a client-UUID idempotency key and a ten-second void, and a swag-counter-shaped court page. The engine learns nothing. Open questions for the owner (tier vocabulary, whether roster-as-it-stands is the day's intent, the void window) are recorded in the plan.

**Assessed — do the suites exercise team point awards? Yes, in three layers.** (a) The engine suite pays results at tournament and stage rates to seated *entrants* (`core-lifecycle.test.ts`). (b) The API's points-bridge suite (`tournament-points-bridge.test.ts`, real database, read back off the board) plays a real match and asserts per-person totals: the kick-off roster is paid **in full, each** (a win pays every member 30 — spread means *replicated*, never divided), a mid-match joiner is not paid, a correction re-pays the same people, a void stops and unvoid starts payment, and a desk award pays the team as it stands (joiner included). (c) The desk suite (`tournament-desk.test.ts`) posts and voids a manual team award through the routes and checks the ledger. Because the bridge pays people, a mixed-cluster team's award credits each member's own cluster through the ordinary per-person leaderboard aggregation — that path is the same code the bridge suite reads its cluster-board total through. One honest gap, unchanged by this ADR: no suite assembles a deliberately mixed-cluster team and asserts the *per-cluster split* line by line; the per-person assertions plus the summed board make it a near-certainty rather than a demonstrated one, and it is the first test to add when the dumb-court mode lands, since that mode pays teams constantly.

**Verified.** Engine (114 tests, `npm run test:tournament`): a stage ranking on its own table points (draws outvaluing a win) reorders group and stage tables while paid rates stay put; the default stays 3/1/0; the pipeline carries table points per stage apart from rates; the validator accepts intakes of 4, 6 and 9 from a 3-qualifier pool and refuses a 6 fed by a 4; `stageAdvancers` labels the fourth seat of the canonical day a fill; a tie for that fill refuses the system actor and seats under the desk. API (real database, `--maxWorkers=1`): `tournament-pipeline.test.ts` persists `table_*_points` apart from the paid columns, reads them back through `loadState`, and refuses the over-fed chain at activation in the validator's words; `tournament-views.test.ts` reads the desk's table points and advancer list from `adminStageViews`. Web: the stage draft round-trips table points (spec → fields → spec, and into a saved draft setup), refuses a partial set in the form's own words, and `advancerLine` names the points ranking-only and marks the fill. Typecheck is green; the full `./verify.sh` outcome is stated in the commit message, including the layers this sandbox cannot finish.

### ADR-321 — dumb tournament mode built: courts as award stations, no line-ups, Results is the award ledger

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-293 (one open tournament per kind), ADR-276 (the points bridge), ADR-092/110/116 (armed tiers), ADR-320 (the plan this executes, and the mixed-cluster test it owed)

**Context.** ADR-320 assessed and planned the dumb mode. The owner then specified its participant-facing behaviour, which governs where it differs from a parallel-mode reading: **when the tournament operates in dumb mode there are no match line-ups, and under Results you only see entries like "Team XXX is awarded XXX points!"** This ADR records the build.

**Decision.**

1. **A kind, end to end.** `tournamentKinds` and the engine's `TournamentKind` gain `'dumb_courts'`; the `tournament.kind` CHECK widens additively (the same drop-and-recreate pattern as the scheduler format list), and `tournament.dumb_tiers jsonb` holds the tier list (1–4 label+points tiers, the contracts `awardTiersSchema` shape, snapshotted at draft creation). One open tournament per kind stands (ADR-293): the desk console is modal and resolves the open tournament of either kind, captain's ball preferred when both are open.
2. **Start builds nothing.** `activateDumb` flips the draft live in one update: no stages, no matches, no scheduler row. The desk refuses a format/pipeline Start for a dumb draft and vice versa. Courts, entrants and tiers are the whole tournament.
3. **The core learns exactly one thing.** In `awards.ts`, a facilitator may grant and void manual awards **only when `tournament.kind === 'dumb_courts'`** — awarding at the court is the game there; captain's ball keeps the desk-only rule. Bounds, reasons and the append-and-void ledger are unchanged, and dumb awards ride the ordinary points bridge (`runCommand` + `freezeRosters`), so the cluster leaderboard cannot tell them from desk awards. A tier's label and points are taken from the tournament's configured list at award time (never from the client), the label rides the award reason, and the one dumb-specific table — `tournament_dumb_award` (award, court, tier label, client UUID) — exists so a double-tap **replays** instead of double-paying and each court can show its own log. The court master who awarded may take it back inside the scan undo window (ten seconds, `SCAN_UNDO_WINDOW_SECONDS`); after that it is the desk's ordinary manual-award void, reason and all.
4. **The court page is a station, not a console.** `/staff/dumb-court/:courtId` (the station picker routes courts there while a dumb tournament is live): arm a tier, tap a team, confirm the exact Results sentence, done. No QR, no line-up, no start, no score. Awards are online-only — an award the server has not acknowledged has not happened, and the court master is standing in front of the team. The facilitator court **Line-ups** subtab and the schedule read are untouched and simply empty, because there are no matches.
5. **Participants see awards, not fixtures.** While a dumb tournament is live (or is the day that was), `GET /matches/feed` answers `mode: 'dumb'` with award entries only, and Results renders one line per award — **"Team XXX is awarded XXX points!"** — tier and time underneath, voided awards struck through and marked as not counting. `GET /lineups` answers `mode: 'dumb'` with no items, and the Line-ups tab says so: *"No match line-ups today — the courts are awarding points as games are played. See Results for the awards!"*
6. **Roster as it stands.** A dumb award pays the team as it stands at the moment of the award (the bridge's manual-award rule), each member in full. The mixed-cluster gap ADR-320 named is now closed by `apps/api/src/tests/tournament-dumb.test.ts`: a deliberately mixed-cluster team (captain in one cluster, member in another) is awarded a tier, and the per-cluster split is asserted line by line off the cluster board — 10 and 10, replicated, never divided.

**Not in this build.** Per-court tier lists (tiers are the tournament's), per-day award caps, offline award queueing, and any hall-screen treatment of dumb mode (the bracket read is unchanged). Tier lists are fixed at draft creation; changing them means a new draft — each award already carries its label, so history never rewrites.


### ADR-322 — field help on every staff surface

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-319 (field help on the tournament tab), AGENTS-frontend.md §5 (contracts owns copy)

**Context.** ADR-319 put an `(i)` beside every field on the superadmin tournament tab, with the
sentence living in `packages/contracts/src/fieldHelp.ts` and the control's `aria-describedby`
pointing at the tooltip whether it is open or not. The rest of the staff surfaces — the
superadmin's other tabs and every facilitator page — still presented bare fields, so a new
facilitator met a passcode box or a tier input with nothing saying what it does.

**Decision.** The ADR-319 pattern extends to all of it, unchanged in mechanism: `ConsoleField`
(or `CheckField` for checkboxes) for label-and-control pairs; where several controls form one
group with no single label — a tier-arming grid, a scan number, a roster — one `useFieldHelp()`
beside the group heading with `aria-describedby` on the group's controls. New topics land in the
same contracts file (sign-in, stations, courts, clusters, activities, agenda, people, points,
screens, swag, system reset), so the copy still has one owner and no page hardcodes a sentence.

Three classes of field needed care. Controls inside list rows (a swag limit, a screen's scene
tick) get the group's tooltip rather than one per row — the sentence is about the column, not
the row. Read-only surfaces with nothing editable (the dashboard, the audit log) get no tooltip
at all; an `(i)` that explains a display would be noise. And the same generic walk ADR-319
wrote for the tournament tab now runs over the other consoles (`test-utils/fieldHelpWalk.ts`):
any staff field rendered without a resolvable, non-empty tooltip fails the suite, so the next
field added anywhere ships explained or not at all.

**Verified.** The widened copy guard (`fieldHelp.copy.test.ts`, now scanning all three staff
route trees) keeps every topic used and every used topic defined; the generic walk passes over
the point-config, activity, facilitator, superadmin, cluster, participant-directory, swag and
agenda forms, the court team pickers, and the PIN reset and staff sign-in fields; the dumb
court's tier and team groups carry their sentences. Full-gate results are stated in the commit
message.

### ADR-323 — the production image is one process on port 3000: no supervisord, no tunnel

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-043 (one container, supervisord + cloudflared — still true of the demo `Dockerfile`), ADR-118 (the Restart button), ADR-175 (demo and production images), ADR-315/316 (boot scripts in the image)

**Context.** `Dockerfile-prd` was the demo image with one line changed, which meant production carried supervisord and a Cloudflare tunnel it did not want: a platform in front of the container (Northflank, ECS, k8s) already owns ingress, TLS and restarts, and a second process manager inside hides the app's exit code from the one that matters. The owner asked for a production image with no supervisord that exposes port 3000. The Cloudflare tunnel is out of scope of this review and is left as it was in the demo image.

**Decision.**

1. `Dockerfile-prd` runs **one** Node process under `tini` (PID 1, which forwards SIGTERM and reaps the bash children of `db-provision.sh`/`db-reset.sh`), as the unprivileged `node` user, with `PORT=3000` and `EXPOSE 3000`. `CMD` is `node --import tsx apps/api/src/index.ts` — no tsx CLI wrapper standing between tini and the app's signal handler. No supervisord, no cloudflared download, no `docker/` directory.
2. **The Restart button stays enabled** (owner decision): the image sets `PROCESS_SUPERVISED=true`, so the console's restart exits 0 (ADR-118). The restart policy is therefore part of the image's contract and is written at the top of the file and in `DEPLOYMENT.md`: `always`/`unless-stopped`, never `on-failure`. A plain `docker run --restart` does not act on an unhealthy HEALTHCHECK; only an orchestrator does.
3. `Dockerfile` (demo) is untouched: supervisord, cloudflared, 8787, `PSD_SEED=demo`.
4. **ADR-175's "differ by exactly one line" rule is replaced** by what is actually true: the two files are one app built two ways. `check-standards.mjs` `docker-twins` now requires the builder stage and every `COPY --from=builder` to be identical (the production image carries the bits that were tested), `ENV PSD_SEED=` to be `demo`/`default` respectively, and `Dockerfile-prd` to contain `EXPOSE 3000`, `PORT=3000`, `PROCESS_SUPERVISED=true` and tini, and to mention neither `supervisor` nor `cloudflared`. `checkDockerBootScripts` is unchanged.
5. Knock-on: `docker-compose.yml` maps `3000:3000` and sets `PORT=3000` for either image; the SHIP-HATS prompts default to port 3000 and `-p 3000:3000`; `DEPLOYMENT.md`, `docs/design/ship-hats-pipeline.md` and the pipeline comments describe the two images accurately.

**Not covered.** No Docker daemon is available in this sandbox, so the image was **not built or run**: the `FROM`, `tini`, `USER node` / `/data` ownership and `node --import tsx` start layers are reviewed, not exercised. Two things to confirm on the first real build: PGlite can write `/data` as `node`, and `node --import tsx` resolves workspace imports as `tsx apps/api/src/index.ts` did. The readiness endpoint and graceful shutdown that make the HEALTHCHECK and SIGTERM meaningful arrive in ADR-324; until then the HEALTHCHECK probes `/api/health` (liveness only) and the app has no SIGTERM handler, so `docker stop` ends in SIGKILL after the grace period.

**Verified (bite checks watched to fail).** `npm run standards` with each of: `supervisor` added to the `apk add` line; the builder `FROM` changed to `node:20-alpine`; `EXPOSE 8787`; `PSD_SEED=demo` in `Dockerfile-prd` — each reports a `docker-twins` violation; the restored file passes (20 rules, 0 violations).

### ADR-324 — one fault, one request: nothing a single connection, stream or tick does may end the process

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-21
- **Relates to:** ADR-118 (the Restart button), ADR-122 (stream reconnect), ADR-128 (status stream stays open), ADR-228 (error reports carry no bound values), ADR-251 (boot diagnostics), ADR-323 (production image, tini, restart policy)

**Context.** A one-day event runs hundreds of phones on long-lived event streams, so a process exit disconnects all of them at once and loses every in-memory state (presence, rate limits, caches, the up-soon map). An audit of what could cause one found these, each reproduced or traced to a line rather than assumed:

| Id | Condition | Before |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | `pg` emits `'error'` on the pool for an idle connection the server dropped (restart, failover, NAT idle cut) | no listener, so an uncaught exception |
| C2 | the same on a **checked-out** client — every `db.transaction`, because pg-pool detaches its own listener at checkout | same |
| C3 | `void deliver(frame)` in the status stream awaits a membership read | a database error is an unhandled rejection; Node 22 exits |
| C4 | `void send(message)` in the team-chat stream awaits the same read | same |
| W2 | `tickSchedule` had no overlap guard | every minute added another waiter on a stalled database |
| W3 | PGlite's WebAssembly runtime aborts (2 GB heap, full volume) | process stays up, every query fails, `/api/health` says OK, nothing restarts it |
| W5 | Swiss `pairWithoutRematch` backtracks exhaustively | **measured 44 s** of synchronous work for 20 teams with one unpairable team, inside a transaction |
| B1/B2 | `server` `'error'` (EADDRINUSE) and `child.stdin` `'error'` (EPIPE) | uncaught exceptions during boot, with no boot report |
| S1 | no SIGTERM handling; the Restart button called `process.exit(0)` | every stop was a kill with the embedded database mid-write |
| M1 | `decodeURIComponent` throws on `GET /%` | an empty 500, no log |

**Decision.** A fault fails the request or socket that met it, never the process. The one exception is a state the process cannot recover in-process (W3), which exits deliberately so the platform replaces it.

1. `db/poolGuards.ts` gives the pool a listener and gives every client one at birth (`pool.on('connect')`), with the connection string redacted (C1, C2). The failed query still rejects to its caller.
2. `lib/detached.ts` `runDetached(promise, onError)` is the named idiom for a promise nobody awaits. The status stream drops the one frame; the team-chat and chat streams close the one socket, and the client reconnects from its cursor (ADR-122). A `check-standards` rule (`detached-promise`) forbids a bare `void call()` in `routes-*/**/stream.ts` (C3, C4).
3. `lib/processGuards.ts`: an unhandled rejection is logged through the scrubbing reporter, **counted**, and the process keeps serving; an uncaught exception is logged and runs a graceful shutdown with exit code 1, because the state it interrupted is unknown.
4. `lib/shutdown.ts` + `processLifecycle.ts`: SIGTERM/SIGINT, the Restart button and a fatal database error all run one ordered shutdown — stop accepting, end the streams, flush presence, close the database — with an 8 s deadline under Docker's 10 s, closers that may throw or hang, and idempotence. `index.ts` registers it; the Restart button now goes through it (still exit 0, ADR-118).
5. `lib/fatalDatabase.ts`: a `RuntimeError` (the WebAssembly abort) anywhere in an error's cause chain, or PGlite reporting itself closed, is reported from `app.onError` to the process owner, which shuts down with exit 1 where something will restart it (W3). `createApp`'s error handler became `handleError` to stay under the function-length cap.
6. `index.ts` listens for the server's `'error'` (B1); `db/dbInit.ts` listens on the script's stdin (B2); `webStatic.ts` answers 400 to a malformed escape (M1); `tickSchedule` skips a tick while one is running (W2).
7. `swiss.ts` bounds the search at `PAIRING_STEP_BUDGET` = 20 000 pairings; exhausting it is treated as "no rematch-free pairing", where the caller already falls back to a rematch (W5).

**Reviewed and left alone.** `routes-chat/stream.ts:89` and `team-chat/stream.ts:102,106` could not reject (Hono's `stream.write` swallows write errors and `writeSSE` only throws on CR/LF in an id); they were moved to `runDetached` anyway so the rule has no exceptions. Every `setInterval` body already caught its own errors.

**Not covered here.** The readiness endpoint (so a wedged database is *noticed*) is ADR-324 part 2; pool timeouts, body limits, throttling and the remaining exhaustion fixes are part 3. Until part 2, W3 relies on the first failing request reaching `app.onError`. The shutdown order is unit-tested with injected targets; it has **not** been exercised against a real SIGTERM, because the sandbox could not start the server.

**Verified (sabotages watched to fail).** Pool/client listeners removed (3 tests fail); `runDetached` neutralised (2 fail); tick guard removed (1 fails after a 60 s timeout); both stream fixes reverted (the status and team-chat regression tests fail — and two of my own test bugs were found on the way: `createTeam` returns an id, and the published message id must sort after the cursor); shutdown deadline race removed (fails); idempotence removed (fails); `child.stdin` listener removed (`write EPIPE` surfaces); `noteDatabaseError` call removed (fails); step budget raised to unbounded (the 44 s hang returns). `npm run standards`: a bare `void call()` added to each of the three stream files is reported three times each.

**ADR-324, part 2 — the readiness endpoint.**

`GET /api/health` is unchanged: liveness, `{ok:true}`, no database, so a database blip cannot get a healthy process restarted by a liveness probe, and everything that depends on it (Playwright's `webServer`, the service-worker spec, `web-static.test.ts`) keeps working. It said OK while the pool was starved, the database was gone, or the event loop had been blocked, which is why a second endpoint exists.

`GET /api/health/ready` (`lib/health.ts`, route in `app.ts`) walks the path a real request takes and reports each stage on its own:

| Check | Proves | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `listener` | the server is accepting, and is not draining for shutdown | `server.listening` is false or the shutdown has begun (registered by `index.ts`, the only file that sees either) |
| `app` | the request path through the compress, db-injection and session middleware ran, and the loop is not stalled | p99 event-loop delay over the last window exceeds `HEALTH_MAX_LOOP_DELAY_MS` (1 000) |
| `db` | a pool connection can be checked out and a **`READ ONLY` transaction** can read a seeded table (`superadmin_account`, written on every boot) | error, no answer within `HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS` (2 000), or the table is not there |

The transaction is deliberate: it is the checkout-and-transaction path that dropped connections and exhausted pools fail on, so `pool.query` alone would pass while a real write could not. Reading a real table is deliberate too: a connection that opens to the wrong database, or as a role that cannot read, would otherwise pass.

Because the route is public and unauthenticated it must not be a way to hammer the database: concurrent callers share one in-flight probe and the answer is reused for one second, so the database is touched at most once a second however often the orchestrator, the Docker `HEALTHCHECK` and a person with `curl` ask. The route sits ahead of the session lookup, so a request with no cookie makes no database read of its own. `Cache-Control: no-store`. Anonymous callers get check names and `ok`/`fail` (200, or 503) and nothing that describes the topology; a superadmin also gets latency, loop delay, the unhandled-rejection count (`lib/processGuards.ts`) and the error text.

`Dockerfile-prd`'s `HEALTHCHECK`, the `docker-twins` rule, the SHIP-HATS `READINESS_PATH` default and the pipeline doc now use it. The caveat from ADR-323 stands: plain `docker run --restart` does not act on an unhealthy container; an orchestrator does.

**Verified (sabotages watched to fail).** Deadline race removed: the hung-database test fails (it would wait the full 8 s test budget). Memo removed: "at most once a second" fails. Single-flight and memo both removed: the concurrency test fails too. The database check turned into a no-op: the "schema is not there" test fails (this one was added after the first no-op run **passed all 11 tests**, which showed the suite could not tell a real probe from a fake one).

**Found by running the suite in parallel, not by reading the code.** The first version of the `app` check enabled the event-loop histogram when `lib/health.ts` was imported. Under parallel test files, PGlite's boot (a WebAssembly Postgres, which blocks the loop for over a second) landed inside that window, and a healthy app answered 503 on about one run in five. The same would have happened in production: a boot-time stall failing a probe a minute later. The histogram is now started and cleared by `registerHealthSources`, which `index.ts` calls once the database is open and the port is bound, and every read restarts the window. The test that pins this blocks the real loop for 1.6 s and asserts the check fails, then passes a second later; with the measurement replaced by a constant 0 it fails. After the fix, eight consecutive parallel runs had no failure.

**ADR-324, part 3 — nothing a stranger or a stall can make the app buffer, hold, or wait on without bound.**

An audit of resource exhaustion (the Cloudflare tunnel excluded at the owner's direction) found the following, each traced to a line:

| Id | Condition | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | JSON bodies | no limit except the photo upload; `c.req.json()` buffers all of it, including on the unauthenticated sign-in route | `lib/bodyLimit.ts`: `JSON_BODY_MAX_BYTES` = 2 × the largest legitimate body (an avatar sprite, `AVATAR_SPRITE_MAX_LENGTH`) + 8 KiB, mounted ahead of the session lookup on `/api/*`; the photo route keeps its own. Counts bytes as they arrive, so a chunked body with no `Content-Length` is refused too. 413 with the standard JSON envelope. |
| R1b | request delivery | Node defaults: 300 s per request, 60 s for headers | `serverLimits.ts`: 60 s / 15 s, `keepAliveTimeout` 65 s (above a typical proxy's 60 s idle timeout, so the proxy never reuses a socket this process closed) |
| R2 | sign-in guessing | no limit; every credential is four digits | `lib/signInThrottle.ts`: failed attempts only, keyed on the account (staff 5, participant 10, one more per 30 s), checked BEFORE the lookup so a correct guess made while blocked cannot succeed. **Not keyed on address**: behind the platform's proxy every phone shares one, so an address limit would lock the whole event out after a few typos. Accepted cost, stated in the module: someone can keep the superadmin account blocked with one wrong guess every 30 s; sessions already signed in are unaffected and the block never outlasts the attack. |
| R3 | social-pause read | one uncached query on every chat, team-chat and gallery request (photo bytes included) | memoised through the tag system for 1 s and **voided by both writers of the row**, so a pause still lands on the next request. The first version put the void in the wrong writer and two tests caught it. |
| R5/W4 | concurrent uploads | unbounded; a 12 MB original measured 1.1 s blocked and a 1.1 GB peak under PGlite | `lib/uploadGate.ts`: 1 slot under PGlite, 4 under Postgres, taken BEFORE the body is read (a refused upload costs no memory); 503 |
| R6 | gallery size and quota | no ceiling (worst case ≈ 38 GB); the quota counted visible photos only, was checked many awaits before the insert, and so could be dodged by hiding photos or by uploading in parallel | `GALLERY_MAX_TOTAL_BYTES` (default 8 GB) answered with 507, the reading cached 30 s and incremented as this process stores; the quota count is now inside the insert's transaction behind a per-uploader advisory lock and **counts hidden photos** |
| R7 | cache | 5 000 entries and no byte budget; chat pages are keyed by a caller-supplied cursor | `maxSize` 96 MiB with a size calculation; sprite bodies 32 MiB |
| R8 | `GET /api/avatars` | an unknown id read every avatar photo (up to 50 kB each), every time | a bounded set of ids a full scan could not find, cleared whenever ANY photo is saved (avatar update **and** signup) |
| R9 | event streams | no ceiling | `lib/streamLimits.ts`: 4 per session (three kinds plus one so a reconnect can overlap its dead predecessor) and `SSE_MAX_STREAMS` (2 000) overall; 429, and the client's reconnect backoff is the retry. Released in each stream's existing `finally`. |
| W1 | pool | `pg`'s defaults are "wait forever" in four places | `db/poolOptions.ts`: `DATABASE_POOL_MAX`, connect timeout, `statement_timeout` + client `query_timeout`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, TCP keepalive; 0 means none for the two server-side ones. Provisioning's `runSql` now uses its own connection with no deadline, because the schema file and the 11 MB demo seed are single statements the pool's timeout must not cut. |
| R10 | boot values the database refuses | `SUPERADMIN_INITIAL_PASSCODE=12345` passed `env.ts` and died in the seed on every boot | validated against `PIN_PATTERN` and the username length in `env.ts`, never echoed |

**Found by testing, not reading.** (1) The readiness test and the stream tests each passed on the first run and then turned out to be unable to fail; each was fixed to bite (see part 2 and the stream regression). (2) The pause-switch void was first placed in the wrong one of two writers. (3) `GET /api/avatars` could return a face a signup saved after its id was remembered as missing, which is the case the negative cache is cleared for. (4) The first server-limits test passed against a handler that answered without reading the body, which proves nothing about a trickling client.

**Not done, and why.**
- **R4** (tournament commands serialise on one row; `reconcile` issues one UPDATE per placement): no change. It needs measurement against a real Postgres under concurrent facilitators, which this sandbox cannot do; the pool timeouts above bound the damage in the meantime.
- **`DatabaseHandle.stats()` and the readiness `disk` check** (T3.2, T3.8): not built. The readiness body carries no pool numbers, and nothing watches free space on `/data`; the gallery ceiling is the mitigation until it does.
- **The pool limits and the real `pg` error paths are unit-tested, not integration-tested**: no Postgres server is reachable here, so `postgres-driver.test.ts` stays skipped. `npm run test:api` against `docker compose -f docker-compose.db.yml up -d` should be run before this ships.

**Verified (sabotages watched to fail).** Body limit unmounted (two 413 tests fail) and the gallery exemption removed (the upload test fails); each throttle line removed or made case-sensitive; limiter eviction made to drop spent keys; upload ceiling, slot gate, hidden-photo count and advisory lock each removed; each stream's `release()` removed and chat's reservation removed; pause memo and the pause writer's void removed; main-cache and sprite-cache byte budgets removed; signup clear, update clear and the negative cache removed; pool `max` and `keepAlive` removed. Server timeouts are checked against a control with no limits applied.

### ADR-325 — any stage can take the qualifiers of an earlier one; every stage shows its ingress and egress

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-22
- **Supersedes:** ADR-310 decision 5 ("pools therefore validate as initial-only"), and the ADR-311 clause that a pool or open stage "resets its source rather than offering a state the engine refuses"
- **Relates to:** ADR-273 (seats are forecasts until frozen), ADR-276 (the points bridge pays the people in a seat), ADR-310/311 (the stage pipeline and its builder), ADR-320 (qualifiers first, shortfall fills after)

**Context.** In the stage-by-stage builder, "Teams come from" appeared only on a knockout. Choosing a pool for stage 2 hid the control and forced its source back to the entered teams, because the engine refused a pool fed by an earlier stage: its groups were snake-dealt from the entered teams when the pipeline was built, and nobody has qualified at that point. The owner chose real support over a disabled option, and asked for every stage to show read-only what it takes in and sends on.

**Decision.**

1. **Deal seats, not teams.** A bracket already plays future teams through `stage_place` seats and the planner waits on them. A pool fed by advancers is dealt the same way: `buildPoolStage` snake-deals `advancerSeats(feeder, count)` into groups and builds the round robin over seats (`seatFixtures`), with empty `entrantIds`. The scheduler, the planner's dependency wait, seat freezing and the tie-on-cut gate are unchanged.
2. **Fill on close.** `completeStage` freezes the seats (as before), then `fillFedGroups` sets each empty group's members from the people now in its seats, in place order; a group that already has members is left alone. An override on a seat is widened to its place (`placeOverridden`), so every fixture that reads "#1 overall" names the same person.
3. **A fed open stage plays only its roster.** `Stage` gains `intake` (the feeder and how many) and `roster` (frozen on close, from `stageAdvancers` with overrides applied). `stageAdHocMatch` refuses a team outside the roster (`not_in_stage`, 400) and any match before the feeder closes (`stage_not_fed`, 409). A stage with no intake, and any kind other than open, accepts any two teams as before. `downstreamIntake` now also honours a declared `intake`, because an open stage has no fixtures from which to infer it.
4. **Codes unique across a structure.** The adapter mints ids keyed by group and match code, and every pool names its groups A, B, C and numbers its fixtures A1, A2. Two pool stages used to give two matches one id on activation (`tournament_match_pkey`). The first stage keeps its codes; a later stage's collisions are prefixed ("P2-A", "P2-A1"), with every `winner_of`/`loser_of` reference renamed with them. This was found by the real-database test, not by the engine suite.
5. **Persistence.** `tournament_stage.intake_stage_id` / `intake_count` (paired by CHECK, additive like ADR-320's columns) and a new append-only `tournament_stage_entrant (stage_id, entrant_id, place)`; group members and rosters are inserted once, when they first appear. `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` 3 → 4.
